name: Default Probabilities Credit Spreads and Funding Costs
source: Gregory, J. (2015). The xVA Challenge, 3rd Edition

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between a real-world default probability and a risk-neutral default probability?
questions.answer_short: Real-world default probability is estimated from historical default data, while risk-neutral default probability is derived from market prices (like CDS spreads) and includes a risk premium that investors demand for taking credit risk.
questions.answer_long: Real-world default probabilities come from historical default statistics and credit ratings, representing the actual observed frequency of defaults. Risk-neutral default probabilities are extracted from market instruments like credit default swaps and bonds, and are systematically higher because they embed a risk premium. This premium reflects that investors are risk-averse and demand compensation beyond expected losses. Empirical studies show risk-neutral probabilities can be 2-17 times higher than real-world equivalents, with the ratio being larger for higher quality credits.
questions.why_it_matters: Using the wrong type of default probability fundamentally changes CVA from an actuarial reserve to a market price. Basel III and IFRS 13 require risk-neutral probabilities, making this distinction critical for regulatory compliance, accounting standards, and proper CVA hedging strategies.
common_traps: Assuming real-world probabilities are appropriate for CVA because they represent 'actual' default risk
Not recognizing that risk-neutral probabilities are required even for illiquid counterparties where no CDS trades
Believing the risk premium component is constant across ratings and maturities
questions.real_world_example: A single-A rated counterparty might have a 1-year real-world default probability of 0.13% (13 bps) based on historical data, but the market-implied risk-neutral probability from its CDS spread could be 1.28% (128 bps) - nearly 10 times higher. Using the wrong one would dramatically understate CVA.

questions.question: Why have banks moved from using real-world to risk-neutral default probabilities for CVA, even for illiquid counterparties where no direct market data exists?
questions.answer_short: Regulatory requirements (Basel III) and accounting standards (IFRS 13) mandate the use of market-observable inputs and risk-neutral measures, treating CVA as a market price requiring hedging rather than an actuarial reserve.
questions.answer_long: The shift was driven by three forces: Basel III capital rules explicitly reference credit spreads in CVA formulas, IFRS 13 requires exit pricing using market-observable inputs wherever possible, and the growth of CDS markets made CVA hedging more common. By 2014, the vast majority of major banks used risk-neutral probabilities to align CVA calculation with market pricing and hedging practice. This created consistency between trading book valuations and CVA, even though it introduces challenges for illiquid credits requiring proxy mapping. The ECB's CVA challenger model explicitly requires benchmark parameters from CDS curves.
questions.why_it_matters: This industry-wide shift means CVA is now much larger and more volatile than under historical methods, requiring sophisticated hedging programs and credit spread mapping systems. It also means CVA cannot be reduced simply by arguing a counterparty is unlikely to default based on historical statistics.
common_traps: Attempting to use blended real-world and risk-neutral approaches to reduce CVA volatility - regulators reject this
Arguing that illiquid counterparties should use historical probabilities since they cannot be hedged
Not recognizing that this requirement applies even to loan portfolios and other traditionally illiquid credits on trading books
questions.real_world_example: A regional bank with 500 SME counterparties, none with traded CDS, must still use risk-neutral probabilities derived from proxy curves based on rating, sector, and region. An Ernst & Young 2012 survey showed 13 of 19 banks already used market data, with convergence accelerating after IFRS 13 implementation.

questions.subtopic: Extracting Default Probabilities from Credit Spreads
questions.question: Given a credit spread of 400 bps and an assumed LGD of 60%, what is the approximate 1-year risk-neutral default probability using the simple formula?
questions.answer_short: The 1-year default probability is approximately 7.12% using PD ≈ (s × Δt) / LGD = (0.04 × 1) / 0.60 = 0.0667 or 6.67%, though the more precise calculation gives 7.12%.
questions.answer_long: Using the approximation formula PD(t-1, t) ≈ (st × Δt) / LGD, we get (400 bps × 1 year) / 60% = 0.04 / 0.60 ≈ 6.67%. However, this is a simplified approximation. The more accurate calculation accounting for survival probability and discounting gives 7.12%. The simple formula works reasonably well for flat credit curves but becomes less accurate when curves are steeply sloped, as it doesn't account for the shape of the curve prior to the period in question. The formula gives unconditional default probabilities, not conditional on survival to the start of the period.
questions.why_it_matters: This calculation is fundamental to CVA computation - you perform it for every time step in your exposure simulation. Getting it wrong systematically mis-prices credit risk. The approximation is used millions of times in Monte Carlo simulations, so understanding its limitations prevents systematic bias.
common_traps: Forgetting to divide by LGD, which dramatically understates default probability
Using conditional rather than unconditional probabilities in CVA calculations
Applying the simple formula to steeply sloped credit curves where it's most inaccurate
Not recognizing this gives a different answer than bootstrapping from CDS spreads
questions.real_world_example: A CVA desk calculates quarterly default probabilities for a 5-year swap portfolio. With a 300 bps credit spread and 60% LGD, each quarter has roughly (0.03 × 0.25) / 0.60 = 1.25% default probability. Over 20 quarters, this compounds to a significantly different cumulative probability than simple multiplication would suggest.

questions.question: Two counterparties both have 5-year credit spreads of 300 bps, but one has a flat curve and the other has an upward-sloping curve. How do their 1-year default probabilities differ and why does this matter for CVA?
questions.answer_short: The flat curve gives a 1-year PD around 4.88%, while the upward-sloping curve gives a significantly lower 1-year PD (perhaps 2-3%), because the lower short-term spread implies less near-term default risk despite identical 5-year levels.
questions.answer_long: With both curves at 300 bps for 5 years but different shapes, the upward-sloping curve must have lower spreads in year 1 (perhaps 150 bps), giving a much lower near-term default probability. The flat curve distributes default probability evenly over time, while the upward-sloping curve concentrates it in later years. This dramatically affects CVA because exposure profiles also evolve over time - for an amortizing swap with high near-term exposure, the flat curve produces much higher CVA. The cumulative 5-year default probability is the same (around 22%), but the timing of defaults differs substantially. This shows why knowing only the 5-year spread is insufficient.
questions.why_it_matters: CVA is not just exposure times credit spread - it's the time-weighted integration of exposure and default probability. Curve shape can change CVA by 30-50% even with identical 5-year spreads. This is why proper interpolation and term structure modeling is critical, especially for portfolios with varying exposure profiles over time.
common_traps: Using only a single tenor (e.g., 5-year) spread and assuming flat default probability
Linearly interpolating default probabilities rather than credit spreads (introduces arbitrage)
Not recognizing that inverted curves (common in distressed credits) dramatically increase near-term CVA
Extrapolating beyond observable tenors without considering default probability constraints
questions.real_world_example: During the European sovereign crisis, Greek CDS showed an inverted curve with 1-year at 2500 bps but 5-year at 1800 bps, implying 80%+ cumulative default probability within 1 year but lower annual rates thereafter. A dealer with near-term exposure faced far higher CVA than the 5-year spread alone would suggest.

questions.subtopic: Loss Given Default and Recovery Rates
questions.question: What is the difference between 'settled recovery' and 'actual recovery' on OTC derivatives, and why does this matter for CVA valuation versus CVA hedging?
questions.answer_short: Settled recovery is the market price soon after default (e.g., CDS auction around 8% for Lehman), while actual recovery is what you eventually receive after the bankruptcy process (30-40% for some Lehman derivatives). CVA hedging uses settled recovery, but actual P&L depends on the final amount.
questions.answer_long: Settled recovery can be realized immediately by selling the claim in the CDS auction or secondary market shortly after default, establishing a market-clearing price. Actual recovery on derivatives takes months or years to determine because derivative claims are bespoke, subject to complex netting and collateral calculations, and must work through bankruptcy proceedings. For Lehman, the CDS auction settled at 8.625%, but some derivative creditors eventually recovered 30-40%. This creates a timing and valuation mismatch: CVA models and CDS hedges reference settled recovery (priced into CDS spreads), but your actual economic loss depends on actual recovery, which is uncertain at valuation time. The difference can be 20-30 percentage points of the notional claim.
questions.why_it_matters: If you hedge CVA with CDS and your counterparty defaults, you receive settled recovery on the CDS immediately but must wait years for actual derivative recovery. This creates significant P&L uncertainty and potential losses if actual recovery is lower. It also means CVA calculations using market-implied 60% LGD may not reflect the true economic risk of your specific derivative portfolio.
common_traps: Assuming CDS hedges perfectly offset derivative credit losses - they only hedge settled recovery
Using actual recovery experience to adjust CVA below market levels (auditors reject this)
Not recognizing that derivative seniority can differ from bond seniority in some structures
Believing recovery is certain at 60% or 40% rather than highly variable (Table 12.3 shows 0.1% to 99.9%)
questions.real_world_example: After Lehman's default, a bank holding $100M in derivative receivables could sell its claim for approximately $8.6M (settled recovery). However, the bank eventually received $35M over several years (actual recovery). If they had bought $100M of Lehman CDS as a hedge, they netted $91.4M from the CDS but gave up the claim, missing the additional $26.4M recovery differential.

questions.question: A bank has 1,000 SME counterparties with no traded CDS or bonds. What are the trade-offs between mapping all of them to a broad single-A index versus creating granular proxy curves by sector and region?
questions.answer_short: Broad index mapping provides liquidity and hedging but fails to distinguish credit differences, potentially mispricing CVA by averaging over disparate risks. Granular mapping better reflects individual risk but creates more curves with fewer data points, introducing idiosyncratic noise and making hedging harder.
questions.answer_long: Using a single index (e.g., iTraxx Non-Financials) for all counterparties provides maximum liquidity for hedging, clear capital relief under Basel III, and stable curves with deep market data. However, it ignores material differences - a German manufacturer differs from an Italian retailer. This systematic mispricing can accumulate across 1,000 names. Granular mapping (e.g., single-A, European, industrial sector) creates 50+ curves, each calibrated to only 1-5 CDS names, introducing volatility from idiosyncratic movements in those few names. The CVA desk faces a choice: accept systematic mispricing with better hedging, or improve accuracy but face basis risk and potentially no capital relief for sector-specific hedges. Most banks use 2-3 tiers of granularity (rating, region, broad sector) as a compromise, accepting that illiquid credits require subjective judgment.
questions.why_it_matters: Credit curve mapping is often the largest source of CVA model uncertainty, dwarfing exposure modeling assumptions. For a bank with €50B in derivatives exposure to SMEs, choosing mapping granularity can change total CVA by €200-500M and determine whether hedging is even feasible. Regulators increasingly scrutinize these choices.
common_traps: Creating overly granular curves that are dominated by 1-2 reference names, importing their idiosyncratic volatility
Using very broad curves that ignore obvious credit quality differences (e.g., treating BB and A the same)
Focusing only on capital relief rather than economic hedging effectiveness
Not documenting the mapping methodology clearly enough to survive regulatory review
Changing mapping frequently, creating artificial CVA P&L volatility
questions.real_world_example: A European bank mapped all single-A Italian corporates to the broad iTraxx Main index (125 names, mostly non-Italian). When Italian sovereign spreads widened in 2011, the bank's CVA understated the risk because iTraxx Main only moved modestly. Switching to an Italian corporate proxy caused a €150M CVA write-down, even though no actual defaults occurred. The trade-off is real-time economic accuracy versus hedgeable, stable metrics.

questions.question: What is the difference between a single-name CDS and a CDS index, and which is more liquid for CVA hedging purposes?
questions.answer_short: A single-name CDS references one specific entity (e.g., BMW) and provides exact default protection but is less liquid. A CDS index (e.g., iTraxx Main with 125 names) is a portfolio of single-name CDS, is much more liquid, but only provides spread hedging without specific default protection.
questions.answer_long: Single-name CDS contracts reference a single borrower and pay out if that specific entity defaults, providing both spread risk hedging and default protection. However, outside the top 500 global credits, single-name CDS liquidity is poor with wide bid-ask spreads. CDS indices like iTraxx Europe (125 investment-grade European credits) or CDX North America trade much more actively with tight spreads and deep markets. Indices provide excellent spread hedging - if the market's view of credit risk changes, the index moves. But indices don't provide default protection for a specific counterparty: if your Italian bank counterparty defaults, the iTraxx Financials index only falls by 1/25th (4%) of one entity's impact. For CVA purposes, most banks use indices for spread hedging and accept the basis risk on actual defaults.
questions.why_it_matters: Understanding this distinction is critical for CVA hedging strategy. Indices provide 80-90% of the spread hedging benefit at 10x better liquidity and execution cost. However, concentration risk (many similar counterparties) creates unhedged jump-to-default risk. This is why Basel III gives capital relief for index hedges but requires concentration add-ons.
common_traps: Believing index hedges provide default protection - they only reduce spread risk
Using illiquid single-name CDS for hedging due to 'better match' despite poor execution and capital inefficiency
Not recognizing that index composition changes every 6 months as constituents default or are replaced
Assuming all names in an index have equal weight in determining the index spread
questions.real_world_example: A bank has €2B exposure to 20 single-A European corporates. Buying 20 single-name CDS costs 25-50 bps in bid-ask spread and faces poor liquidity. Buying €2B of iTraxx Main (125 names including similar credits) costs 2-3 bps in spread, trades in seconds, and provides 85% of the spread hedging benefit. However, if one specific counterparty defaults, the iTraxx hedge barely moves while CVA jumps.

questions.question: When would you use an LGD different from the standard 60% assumption for senior unsecured derivatives, and what are the risks of doing so?
questions.answer_short: You might use lower LGD for structurally senior derivatives (e.g., in securitizations), derivatives with credit enhancements beyond modeled collateral, or based on workout experience. However, regulators and auditors require strong evidence and may reject assumptions that reduce CVA below market-implied levels.
questions.answer_long: Standard CDS contracts assume 60% LGD for senior unsecured claims (40% recovery), which is the starting point for derivative CVA. Three situations justify deviations: (1) Structural seniority - derivatives in special purpose vehicles may be super-senior to other debt, justifying 30-40% LGD. (2) Credit enhancements like guarantees or set-off rights that aren't captured in the exposure model, potentially reducing LGD by 10-20 points. (3) Historical experience showing better recovery on derivative portfolios than bonds, though this is dangerous without strong evidence. The key risk is that auditors view CVA as an exit price concept: if you can't sell the position at your assumed LGD, it's wrong. Using 50% LGD instead of 60% reduces CVA by 17%, which is material. Market-implied LGD from CDS should be the default unless you have concrete structural reasons to deviate.
questions.why_it_matters: LGD is the second-largest driver of CVA after credit spread and exposure. Getting it wrong by 10 percentage points can change CVA by 15-25%. More importantly, incorrect LGD assumptions create false confidence in credit risk management and can mask inadequate exposure limits. If your recovery assumptions are aggressive and wrong, losses in an actual default will exceed reserves.
common_traps: Using Lehman's eventual 35% actual recovery to justify lower LGD across all counterparties - it's not generalizable
Double-counting collateral by using low LGD and also modeling collateral in exposure
Applying subordinated LGD (70-80%) to senior derivative claims or vice versa
Not documenting the basis for LGD assumptions rigorously enough for audit review
Forgetting that LGD and credit spread are coupled - changing one without the other creates arbitrage
questions.real_world_example: A bank trades derivatives with a securitization SPV where the derivatives are explicitly senior to the notes, backed by specific collateral pools. They use 40% LGD (60% recovery) instead of 60% LGD, reducing CVA by 33%. However, when challenged by auditors, they must document the legal seniority, demonstrate the collateral is sufficient even in stress, and show this would be the exit price assumption another market participant would use. Weak documentation resulted in several banks being forced to increase CVA reserves by €50-100M.

questions.question: A UK regional bank counterparty has a liquid 5-year CDS at 200 bps but no other tenors trade. Your exposure extends to 15 years. What are three approaches to construct the full credit curve and what are the trade-offs?
questions.answer_short: Option 1: Use 5Y CDS and assume flat (simple but wrong). Option 2: Bootstrap the single 5Y point and interpolate/extrapolate using a model (more accurate but model-dependent). Option 3: Combine the 5Y CDS with a UK bank index curve shape (hybrid approach balancing accuracy and observability).
questions.answer_long: Approach 1 (flat) uses 200 bps for all tenors - simplest but economically wrong since credit curves are almost never flat, mispricing long-dated exposure potentially by 30-50%. Approach 2 uses the 5Y point as an anchor and applies a term structure model (e.g., Nelson-Siegel, hazard rate interpolation) to generate 1Y through 30Y points. This is more accurate but introduces model risk - the 10-15Y extrapolation is particularly uncertain. Approach 3 takes the 5Y CDS as ground truth and borrows the curve shape from iTraxx Financials index, scaling to match the 5Y. This gives 'market-implied' term structure while anchoring to the specific name. Most practitioners use Approach 3 for liquid single names, accepting that it imports some generic volatility but provides the best balance. The key is consistency - use the same method for all similar names to avoid relative value distortions.
questions.why_it_matters: With a 15-year swap portfolio, getting the term structure wrong by using flat spreads can mis-price CVA by €5-10M on a €1B notional exposure. The compounding effect of default probabilities over long horizons is enormous - a 200 bps flat curve gives 24% cumulative default probability at 15Y, but an upward-sloping curve starting at 200 bps at 5Y might give 35-40%.
common_traps: Using flat credit curves beyond the observable tenor - creates systematic mispricing
Extrapolating linearly rather than ensuring default probabilities remain bounded (cannot exceed 100%)
Not stress-testing the extrapolation approach with different curve shapes
Forgetting that the 5Y CDS spread itself has bid-ask spread (5-10 bps), creating uncertainty in the anchor point
Mixing different methodologies across counterparties, creating false relative value signals
questions.real_world_example: In 2012, major European banks had liquid 5Y CDS but illiquid 10Y+ points. A dealer with 10-year cross-currency swaps to Société Générale used the 5Y CDS at 250 bps and scaled the iTraxx Financials curve shape (5Y: 250 bps, 10Y: 280 bps in the index). This gave SocGen 10Y at 280 bps, producing €30M higher CVA than flat extrapolation. When SocGen's 10Y CDS later became liquid at 290 bps, the error was only 10 bps versus 40 bps under flat assumption.

questions.question: What is the fundamental trade-off between granularity and data availability when constructing generic credit curves, and how do you decide the right level of granularity?
questions.answer_short: More granular classification (e.g., rating + sector + region) better differentiates counterparties but provides fewer data points per curve, increasing noise from idiosyncratic movements. The right level ensures at least 5-10 observable credits per curve while still capturing material risk differences.
questions.answer_long: Generic curves aggregate market data across similar credits. A broad classification like 'Single-A' might have 200+ observable CDS, providing very stable curves but treating all A-rated credits identically (ignoring that utilities differ from tech companies, or that US differs from Italy). Narrow classification like 'Single-A, European, Utilities' might have only 2-3 CDS, creating curves dominated by idiosyncratic volatility of those specific names - when one credit widens for company-specific reasons, the entire curve moves incorrectly. The optimal granularity balances these: use rating (7 buckets) × region (5-7 buckets) × broad sector (3-5 buckets) only where each combination has 5+ reference credits. This typically yields 30-50 curves for a global bank. Below 5 reference credits, combine adjacent buckets. For example, collapse CCC/CC/C into one 'High Yield' category, or combine Eastern Europe with Western Europe for some sectors.
questions.why_it_matters: Getting granularity wrong creates either systematic mispricing (too broad) or false CVA volatility (too granular). A bank that used overly granular curves with 1-2 reference names per bucket experienced 15% CVA volatility from idiosyncratic credit movements unrelated to their actual counterparties. Conversely, a bank using only broad rating buckets underpriced CVA to emerging market counterparties by 30% versus Western peers.
common_traps: Mechanically implementing rating × region × sector without checking data availability in each bucket
Creating curves for every theoretical combination even when some have zero observable credits
Not having a clear rule for collapsing adjacent buckets when data is insufficient
Ignoring that granularity should differ by region (more granular for US/Europe, broader for Asia)
Failing to review and update the classification scheme as CDS market liquidity changes
questions.real_world_example: A global bank initially created 147 curves (7 ratings × 7 regions × 3 sectors) but found 68 had fewer than 3 reference CDS. After consolidation, they used 42 curves: single curves for AAA/AA/CCC across all regions due to scarcity, 3 regional curves each for A/BBB (Europe, Americas, Asia), and 2 broad sector curves for BB/B (financial vs non-financial). This gave stable, well-calibrated curves. Later, as Asian CDS markets deepened, they split Asian curves into separate China/Japan/Rest-of-Asia buckets.

questions.question: What are the advantages and disadvantages of using third-party credit curves (like Markit sector curves) versus building your own curves in-house?
questions.answer_short: Third-party curves are independent (satisfying auditors), cheaper to implement, and methodologically transparent. However, they're inflexible in classification, can create volatility you cannot control, may not align with your hedging approach, and could differ from peers, creating relative value issues.
questions.answer_long: Third-party providers like Markit build curves using documented, consistent methodologies across many names and tenors, updated daily. This gives independence that auditors value and avoids the cost of building infrastructure. The downside is lack of control: if Markit changes their methodology or weighting scheme, your CVA moves without any economic change in your portfolio. The classification may not match your counterparty base - for example, Markit uses their sector taxonomy which might differ from yours. More critically, if your hedging strategy uses CDS indices but Markit curves use bond data, you have a structural basis. For capital purposes, you may not get Basel III credit for hedges if they don't align with your curve methodology. Many large banks use third-party curves as a secondary validation but build primary curves in-house for control. Smaller banks may use third-party exclusively to avoid infrastructure costs.
questions.why_it_matters: The choice affects not just CVA levels but also volatility, hedge effectiveness, and capital treatment. A bank using Markit curves while hedging with iTraxx may find hedges poorly correlated because Markit weighs bond data heavily. This can reduce hedge effectiveness by 20-30%, making the overall CVA program more expensive and less stable. For regulatory reporting, you must demonstrate your curves are consistent with your hedging and capital models.
common_traps: Using third-party curves without understanding their construction methodology and how it differs from yours
Assuming third-party curves are automatically 'auditor-approved' without proper documentation
Not testing whether hedge effectiveness degrades due to mismatch between curves and instruments
Failing to have a backup plan if the vendor changes methodology or discontinues curves
Mixing third-party curves for some counterparties and internal curves for others without a clear policy
questions.real_world_example: A mid-sized bank used Markit sector curves for CVA and hedged with iTraxx indices. Markit heavily weighted illiquid bonds while iTraxx is pure CDS. During the 2015-16 energy sector stress, illiquid energy bonds widened 200 bps while CDS widened 120 bps. The bank's CVA increased €40M while iTraxx hedges only offset €25M, creating €15M loss. Investigation showed 40% of the Markit curve weight came from bonds with bid-ask spreads over 100 bps. They switched to building CDS-only curves internally.

questions.question: Why might using CDS spreads to derive default probabilities for CVA create a basis risk, even if you hedge with the same CDS contract?
questions.answer_short: CDS credit events (failure to pay, bankruptcy, restructuring) may not perfectly match derivative default triggers, CDS typically delivers bonds not derivatives creating LGD basis, and the timing of CDS settlement differs from derivative workout, creating recovery and reinvestment risk.
questions.answer_long: Three fundamental mismatches exist: (1) Credit event definitions - failure to make a derivative payment may not constitute 'failure to pay' under ISDA CDS definitions if it doesn't meet materiality thresholds or if it's cured within grace periods. Some CVA exposures trigger on cross-default, but not all CDS include this. (2) Deliverable obligation - CDS settles by delivering bonds or loans, with recovery determined by the auction price of those instruments. Your derivative claim may have different seniority or structural features, leading to different actual recovery (Section 12.2.5 showed 8.6% CDS vs 35% derivative for Lehman). (3) Timing - CDS auctions settle within weeks while derivative claims in bankruptcy take years, creating reinvestment risk on the proceeds and uncertainty on final recovery. These bases are usually small (2-5% of exposure) but can be material for large positions or in unusual bankruptcy scenarios.
questions.why_it_matters: This basis means CDS hedges are not perfect, even when you can trade the exact counterparty name. In Lehman's default, the CDS-derivative recovery basis was 25-30 percentage points, representing €billions in unexpected losses for dealers who thought they were perfectly hedged. Understanding these technical details prevents overconfidence in hedging programs and ensures proper reserve allocation for residual basis risk.
common_traps: Assuming CDS on the counterparty is a 'perfect hedge' that eliminates all CVA risk
Not recognizing that modified restructuring and other clauses change credit event scope
Forgetting that the CDS notional should match the exposure at default, not current exposure
Ignoring that CDS settles in the deliverable currency (usually USD or EUR) while derivative claims may be in other currencies
Overlooking that upfront CDS premiums change the hedge ratio versus running spread CDS
questions.real_world_example: A dealer had $500M exposure to a European corporate and bought $500M CDS protection. The corporate underwent a 'soft' restructuring (maturity extension without missed payments) that triggered the CDS (modified restructuring clause) but did not trigger the ISDA derivative Master Agreement default provisions. The dealer received $200M on the CDS (60% LGD on $500M notional) but still had $500M exposure to the counterparty, which later deteriorated further. The 'hedge' created a $200M unintended profit but left the original risk in place, plus now the counterparty was aware of the protection purchase, souring the relationship.

questions.question: What is a hazard rate in credit risk modeling, and how does it relate to the term structure of default probabilities?
questions.answer_short: A hazard rate is the instantaneous rate of default at time t, conditional on survival to that point. It's the fundamental building block for default probabilities: PD(0,T) = 1 - exp(-∫h(t)dt), allowing flexible term structures while ensuring mathematical consistency.
questions.answer_long: The hazard rate h(t) represents the instantaneous conditional default probability at time t. Unlike default probabilities, hazard rates can be positive for all times without being constrained to sum to less than 1, making them mathematically cleaner for modeling. The relationship is: cumulative survival probability Q(T) = exp(-∫₀ᵀ h(t)dt), and default probability PD(0,T) = 1 - Q(T). Marginal default probability in interval (t,t+Δt) is approximately h(t)×Δt. For CVA, we extract hazard rates from CDS spreads (s ≈ h × LGD for flat curves) and use them to generate consistent default probabilities across all tenors. Constant hazard rate implies exponentially declining survival (similar to radioactive decay), while time-varying hazard rates allow realistic term structures like increasing default risk over time or humped curves for distressed credits.
questions.why_it_matters: Hazard rates ensure your default probabilities are arbitrage-free - you can't have situations where marginal default probabilities sum to more than 100%. They also enable consistent interpolation between observed tenors. If you linearly interpolate default probabilities instead of hazard rates, you can create negative implied forward default probabilities (arbitrage). All rigorous CVA systems work with hazard rates internally, even if they display default probabilities to users.
common_traps: Interpolating default probabilities linearly rather than hazard rates - creates arbitrage
Confusing conditional and unconditional default probabilities when working with hazard rates
Assuming constant hazard rate when the credit curve is steeply sloped
Forgetting that hazard rate = credit spread / LGD only holds for flat curves and continuous compounding
Not ensuring that cumulative default probability approaches 100% as time approaches infinity
questions.real_world_example: A credit curve shows 1Y CDS at 200 bps and 2Y CDS at 300 bps (LGD 60%). If you linearly interpolate default probabilities, you get PD(0,1Y) = 3.28% and PD(0,2Y) = 9.41%, implying PD(1Y,2Y) = 6.13%. But using hazard rates: h(0,1Y) = 200/60 = 3.33%, h(1Y,2Y) = 400/60 = 6.67% (to match 300 bps average), giving PD(0,1Y) = 3.28%, PD(0,2Y) = 9.66%, and forward PD(1Y,2Y) = 6.59%. The difference is 0.46%, which seems small but on a $10B portfolio creates $46M CVA difference.

questions.question: A bank uses iTraxx Main index to hedge CVA on 100 single-A European corporates, providing good spread hedging but no capital relief under current Basel III rules. The bank could alternatively use proxy single-name CDS on similar companies, which gives capital relief but costs 40 bps more in bid-ask and has poor liquidity. How should they decide which approach to use?
questions.answer_short: Compare total economic cost: iTraxx gives 20-30% lower hedging cost but higher capital charge, while single-name gives capital relief but expensive execution. Most banks use indices for the majority and single-name only for largest exposures where capital relief exceeds the hedging cost premium.
questions.answer_long: The decision requires quantifying multiple factors: (1) Hedging effectiveness - iTraxx provides 80-85% of spread beta with 5 bps bid-ask, while single-name CDS averages 40 bps bid-ask. (2) Capital impact - index hedges receive only partial relief (the correlation multiplier reduces capital by 50-60%), while eligible single-name hedges give full offset. (3) Operational complexity - managing 100 single-name positions versus one index. For a typical $5B exposure with 200 bps CVA, the analysis shows: iTraxx hedge costs $10M upfront (bid-ask), saves $8M annually in P&L volatility, but leaves $400M RWA ($32M capital at 8%). Single-name costs $40M upfront, saves $12M annually, and reduces RWA to $150M ($12M capital). Break-even is around 3-4 years. However, BCBS 2015 proposals suggest single-name proxies will get capital relief, changing the calculus. The practical solution most banks use: index hedges for 70-80% of exposure (managing aggregate spread risk) plus single-name hedges for the 10-20 largest exposures where notional justifies the cost.
questions.why_it_matters: This trade-off determines whether CVA is capital-intensive or P&L-intensive. Banks that chose not to hedge (keeping CVA as P&L volatility) in 2011-2012 saw €billions in losses during the European sovereign crisis. Banks that hedged with single-names paid €hundreds of millions in unnecessary transaction costs. The optimal strategy is dynamic: bias toward indices when spreads are stable and volatility is low, shift to single-names when CVA volatility creates excessive P&L hits or when capital becomes constrained.
common_traps: Choosing hedges based only on capital relief without considering economic hedging effectiveness
Not quantifying the total cost of ownership (bid-ask, funding, capital, operational) for each approach
Assuming regulatory treatment is static - rules change and proposals like BCBS 2015 alter the economics
Hedging everything or hedging nothing rather than optimizing on a counterparty-by-counterparty basis
Not considering that index hedges are easier to exit if counterparty exposure rolls off
questions.real_world_example: During 2011 European crisis, Bank A hedged €20B corporate CVA exposure entirely with iTraxx Main, paying €15M annually but holding €1.2B RWA (€95M capital). Bank B used single-name CDS on 200 names, paying €120M upfront plus €40M annually, but RWA of only €400M (€32M capital). Over 5 years, Bank A's total cost was €15M×5 + €95M×5 = €550M in capital charges plus hedging costs. Bank B's total was €120M + €40M×5 + €32M×5 = €480M. Bank B's approach was better, but only because they held positions for 5+ years. Most dealers saw positions roll off in 2-3 years, making Bank A's approach cheaper.

questions.subtopic: Risk Premium Component of Credit Spreads
questions.question: If risk-neutral default probabilities are consistently 2-10 times higher than real-world probabilities (Table 12.1), what does this imply about the expected return from selling credit protection, and how does this affect CVA as a P&L reserve versus a market price?
questions.answer_short: Selling credit protection at risk-neutral levels provides positive expected return equal to the risk premium (the difference between risk-neutral and real-world PD). CVA as a market price reserves at risk-neutral levels, creating an 'embedded profit' that releases over time if defaults follow real-world rates, but this is compensation for bearing risk.
questions.answer_long: The risk premium is the excess return investors demand for bearing credit risk beyond expected losses. If risk-neutral PD is 128 bps but real-world PD is only 13 bps (10× ratio for single-A in Table 12.1), the risk premium is 115 bps per year. Selling protection at 128 bps earns this premium if only 13 bps is realized in losses. This is why corporate bonds historically outperform Treasuries by more than their default losses (Altman 1989). For CVA, using risk-neutral PD means reserving at 128 bps when expected losses are only 13 bps - the bank holds an extra 115 bps reserve. If defaults follow historical rates, this reserve is too high and releases to earnings over time as positions mature without default. However, this is not 'wrong' - it's the price needed to transfer the risk to another party. The reserve compensates for taking on credit risk that could have been hedged. This is why CVA is now seen as market pricing rather than actuarial reserve - it represents exit value, not expected loss.
questions.why_it_matters: This distinction is central to CVA debates: CFOs ask why they must reserve 10× expected losses, arguing it reduces lending capacity. The answer is that CVA represents the cost to exit the position today, not the expected future loss. Without this reserve, institutions understate the economic cost of their derivatives business, misallocate capital, and undercharge for credit risk. The 2008 crisis revealed that banks using real-world PD had CVA reserves 5-10× too low, causing massive unexpected losses when counterparties defaulted.
common_traps: Viewing the risk premium as 'excess reserve' that should be released immediately to earnings
Arguing that since real-world losses will be lower, risk-neutral CVA is too conservative
Not recognizing that the risk premium varies over time and across credit quality (smaller for worse credits)
Believing you can arbitrage the difference by selling protection and buying real-world insurance (no such insurance exists)
Forgetting that the risk premium is compensation for bearing wrong-way risk, concentration risk, and uncertainty
questions.real_world_example: In 2006-2007, a bank's corporate derivatives portfolio had €500M CVA using real-world PD (average 20 bps) but would have been €2.5B using risk-neutral PD (average 100 bps for the mix of counterparties). The CFO argued the higher number was 'too conservative' since historical losses were low. In 2008-2009, actual defaults triggered €2.2B in losses (multiple investment grade names defaulted, plus severe markdowns on surviving exposures). The risk-neutral CVA would have covered this, while the real-world reserve left €1.7B uncovered. The 'excess' reserve wasn't excess - it was the cost of the risk being taken.

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between a real-world default probability and a risk-neutral default probability?
questions.answer_short: Real-world default probability is estimated from historical default data (via credit ratings), while risk-neutral default probability is derived from market prices like CDS spreads and includes a risk premium investors demand.
questions.answer_long: Real-world default probabilities are based on actual historical default frequencies, typically estimated from rating agency data. Risk-neutral default probabilities are extracted from market instruments like bonds or CDS and are systematically higher because they include a risk premium—the extra compensation investors require for bearing default risk. Empirical studies show risk-neutral probabilities can be 2-17 times higher than real-world probabilities, especially for investment-grade credits.
questions.why_it_matters: This distinction is critical for XVA practitioners because using real-world PDs would dramatically undervalue CVA. Modern accounting standards (IFRS 13) and regulatory capital rules (Basel III) mandate risk-neutral PDs for fair value calculations, fundamentally changing CVA from an actuarial reserve to a market price.
common_traps: Thinking the difference is just a technicality rather than a fundamental pricing philosophy change
Using historical default rates for CVA because they seem more 'realistic'
Not recognizing that risk-neutral PDs imply the existence of hedging instruments that may not actually exist for illiquid credits
questions.real_world_example: When Lehman Brothers had a 5-year CDS spread of 300 bps in early 2008, the risk-neutral default probability was around 22% (assuming 60% LGD), while the historical 5-year default rate for A-rated financials was only about 2%. The CDS market was pricing in both default risk and a substantial risk premium.

questions.question: Why did the banking industry shift from real-world to risk-neutral default probabilities for CVA calculation, and what are the practical challenges this creates for illiquid credits?
questions.answer_short: The shift was driven by IFRS 13 accounting requirements and Basel III capital rules requiring market-observable inputs. The challenge is that most counterparties lack liquid CDS or bonds, forcing banks to use proxy mapping methods.
questions.answer_long: Banks moved to risk-neutral PDs because IFRS 13 requires exit price valuations using market-observable inputs wherever possible, and Basel III explicitly references CDS spreads in CVA capital formulas. However, this creates a paradox: risk-neutral PDs imply hedging instruments exist, but most counterparties (especially SMEs, regional corporates) have no liquid CDS market. Banks must use subjective proxy mapping methods to assign credit spreads, leading to higher CVA volatility without corresponding hedging ability. This is particularly problematic outside US/European markets where CDS markets are even less liquid.
questions.why_it_matters: This fundamental shift increased CVA values by 2-5 times for many portfolios and created significant P&L volatility that cannot be fully hedged. XVA desks must now manage large CVA exposures to illiquid credits using proxy hedges (like indices) that provide imperfect protection, introducing basis risk and potential capital inefficiency.
common_traps: Assuming liquid CDS markets exist for most counterparties (they don't—only a few hundred names globally)
Using a blend of real-world and risk-neutral PDs to 'compromise', which auditors and regulators typically reject
Not considering that proxy methods can introduce idiosyncratic volatility from the proxy credit itself
questions.real_world_example: A European bank with 3,000 corporate counterparties might have liquid single-name CDS for only 50-100 of them. The remaining 2,900 must be mapped using proxies (parent companies, sector indices, or rating-based curves), creating significant subjectivity in CVA calculation and making hedge effectiveness difficult to demonstrate.

questions.question: Given a credit spread of 400 bps and an LGD of 60%, what is the approximate annual default probability using the simplified hazard rate formula?
questions.answer_short: Using PD ≈ (s × Δt) / LGD: PD = (0.04 × 1) / 0.60 = 6.67% annual default probability.
questions.answer_long: The simplified formula PD(t, t+Δt) ≈ (s × Δt) / LGD gives us (400 bps × 1 year) / 60% = 0.04 / 0.60 = 0.0667 or 6.67%. This is an unconditional default probability for the one-year period. The formula assumes a flat credit spread and constant hazard rate, which makes it less accurate for steep credit curves. For a 400 bps spread, this translates to roughly one expected default in every 15 similar credits per year (ignoring the survival probability adjustment).
questions.why_it_matters: This quick approximation is essential for on-the-fly CVA estimates and risk limit calculations. While more sophisticated bootstrapping methods exist, this formula provides intuitive understanding of the relationship between spreads, recovery assumptions, and default probability—a mental model every XVA practitioner needs.
common_traps: Forgetting to convert basis points to decimal (400 bps = 0.04, not 400)
Using this formula for multi-year periods without adjusting for survival probability
Applying it to steeply sloped credit curves where the approximation breaks down
questions.real_world_example: A junior trader sees a counterparty's 5-year CDS at 500 bps and quickly estimates the 5-year cumulative default probability as roughly (0.05 × 5) / 0.60 = 41.7%. While crude, this gives an immediate sense of the credit risk without needing complex bootstrapping tools.

questions.question: Two counterparties both have 5-year CDS spreads of 300 bps. One has an upward-sloping credit curve (1Y: 150 bps, 5Y: 300 bps), the other has a flat curve. How do their annual default probabilities differ over time, and why does this matter for CVA?
questions.answer_short: The upward-sloping curve has lower near-term default probabilities (about 2.4% in year 1) but higher long-term probabilities (about 6.1% in year 5), while the flat curve has constant probabilities (about 4.9% annually).
questions.answer_long: Despite identical 5-year cumulative default probabilities, the term structure dramatically affects the timing of expected defaults. The upward-sloping curve implies the market sees deteriorating credit quality over time (or increasing uncertainty), concentrating default risk in later years. The flat curve spreads risk evenly. For CVA, this matters because exposure profiles interact with default timing—a front-loaded exposure benefits from an upward-sloping credit curve (lower near-term defaults), while a back-loaded exposure is hurt. This also affects hedge ratios: a 5-year CDS hedge provides different protection depending on when defaults are expected.
questions.why_it_matters: CVA is the integral of exposure × default probability × LGD over time. The interaction between exposure profile and credit curve shape can change CVA by 20-40% even with identical 5-year spreads. Sophisticated XVA desks model full term structures and may use tenor-specific hedges (e.g., 2-year + 5-year CDS combination) rather than single-tenor hedges.
common_traps: Only looking at a single tenor (typically 5-year) and assuming flat default probabilities
Extrapolating beyond observable tenors without considering curve shape constraints
Ignoring that inverted curves (short spreads higher than long spreads) often signal near-term distress
questions.real_world_example: In 2008, many financials had inverted credit curves (1Y: 500 bps, 5Y: 350 bps), indicating severe near-term stress but market belief in government support preventing long-term default. A CVA desk with a 5-year swap exposure would see very different risk profiles depending on whether they used the 1-year spread (implying ~8% annual PD) or interpolated across the curve.

questions.subtopic: Loss Given Default and Recovery Rates
questions.question: What is the difference between 'settled recovery' and 'actual recovery' in the context of OTC derivatives, and why is this distinction important?
questions.answer_short: Settled recovery is the market value achievable shortly after default (e.g., via CDS auction), while actual recovery is what you eventually receive through the bankruptcy process, which may take years.
questions.answer_long: Settled recovery represents the price at which you could sell your claim immediately following a credit event, typically determined by CDS auction or secondary market trading (usually within weeks). Actual recovery is what you ultimately receive after the bankruptcy administrators wind up the estate, which can take years. For derivatives, this gap can be significant because OTC positions are complex to value (due to netting and collateral), cannot be easily traded, and often rank pari passu with senior unsecured debt but may benefit from additional setoff rights. In Lehman's case, settled recovery was ~9% while some actual derivative recoveries reached 30-40%.
questions.why_it_matters: This distinction affects CVA calculation and hedge effectiveness. If you calculate CVA using standard 60% LGD but can achieve 40% LGD through workout processes, you're overcharging clients. Conversely, if you hedge with CDS (settled at ~9% for Lehman) but your actual CVA loss is based on 30% recovery, you have basis risk. Understanding this helps in pricing, capital calculation, and explaining P&L attribution after defaults.
common_traps: Assuming CDS recovery rates (e.g., 40% for senior unsecured) perfectly match derivative recovery
Not recognizing that recovery timing differences create funding costs (you may wait years for actual recovery)
Using overly optimistic recovery assumptions based on historical workouts without auditor/regulator acceptance
questions.real_world_example: After Lehman's bankruptcy, banks with derivative portfolios initially marked CVA losses using the CDS auction recovery of ~8.6%. However, as actual recoveries came in at 30-35% over subsequent years, they had to reverse significant CVA reserves, creating P&L volatility spanning multiple accounting periods and making hedge effectiveness reporting extremely complex.

questions.question: When mapping an illiquid BBB-rated European corporate counterparty, should you use iTraxx Europe Main or iTraxx Europe Crossover index? What are the trade-offs?
questions.answer_short: iTraxx Main includes only investment-grade (BBB and better) names, so it's a better fundamental match. Crossover includes sub-investment grade names and would overstate credit risk. Use Main with a spread adjustment if the counterparty is BBB-minus.
questions.answer_long: iTraxx Europe Main comprises 125 investment-grade credits (mostly A/BBB rated) and is the appropriate choice for BBB counterparties. iTraxx Crossover contains 40 sub-investment grade names with much wider spreads (typically 2-3x Main), making it inappropriate for an investment-grade mapping. However, if the counterparty is BBB-minus (close to sub-investment grade), you might apply a small spread add-on to Main to reflect the higher risk within the BBB bucket. Main also offers better liquidity for hedging. The trade-off is that Main is less granular—it doesn't distinguish between BBB+ and BBB- risk—so you may need additional overlays based on internal ratings.
questions.why_it_matters: Choosing the wrong index can misstate CVA by 100-200% (Crossover trades 200-300 bps wider than Main typically). This affects client pricing, hedge ratios, and capital calculations. Regulators expect mapping to be conservative but not excessively so—using Crossover for all BBB names would be viewed as unjustifiably punitive and might harm client relationships while attracting regulatory scrutiny for excessive conservatism.
common_traps: Mapping all BBB names to Crossover 'to be conservative', massively overstating CVA
Not adjusting for the credit quality distribution within the chosen index (Main is mostly A-rated, not BBB)
Forgetting that index composition changes every six months (new series), requiring mapping methodology updates
questions.real_world_example: In 2020, iTraxx Main traded around 60 bps while Crossover was at 350 bps. A bank mapping 500 BBB-rated corporates to Crossover instead of Main would overstate CVA by roughly 300 bps / 60 bps ≈ 5x, potentially pricing themselves out of new business and overstating capital requirements by hundreds of millions.

questions.question: A derivatives desk is calculating CVA for a portfolio with a securitization SPV where the derivative ranks structurally senior to the SPV's debt. The standard market LGD is 60%. Should they use this value, and if not, what should they consider?
questions.answer_short: No, they should use a lower LGD (higher recovery) because structural seniority means the derivative claim gets paid before debt holders, improving recovery expectations. Typical adjustments might reduce LGD to 40-50%.
questions.answer_long: Standard CDS contracts assume senior unsecured debt recovery (60% LGD for corporate indices), but derivatives in securitization structures often have structural seniority through features like subordination of other liabilities or first-loss protections. This means in default, the derivative counterparty gets paid before other creditors, improving expected recovery. However, using lower LGD must be supported by legal documentation (confirming seniority), similar precedents, and typically requires auditor approval. Banks might also consider whether the improved recovery is already priced into their margin (it should be, to avoid double-counting the benefit).
questions.why_it_matters: LGD directly scales CVA: using 60% vs. 40% LGD changes CVA by 50% (40/60 = 0.67x). For large securitization portfolios, this can mean tens of millions in CVA differences. However, unsupported LGD assumptions that later prove wrong create audit issues, regulatory scrutiny, and potential CVA reserve additions. The key is balancing realistic economic recovery with defensible, conservative assumptions.
common_traps: Using favorable LGD assumptions without legal documentation proving structural seniority
Double-counting recovery benefits if they're already reflected in collateral modeling or exposure calculations
Applying non-standard LGD without considering how CDS hedges (which settle at standard recovery) create basis risk
questions.real_world_example: Many banks had derivative exposures to AIG's securitization vehicles (Maiden Lane) that were structurally senior. They used LGD assumptions of 30-40% rather than the standard 60%, reducing CVA charges. When AIG was bailed out and no default occurred, this assumption was never tested, but it had been crucial for pricing decisions and capital calculations at the time.

questions.question: Compare the three credit curve mapping approaches (direct observables, single-name proxies, generic proxies) in terms of capital relief under Basel III. Why does this create a tension with hedging effectiveness?
questions.answer_short: Direct observables provide full capital relief, generic proxies (indices) provide partial relief, but single-name proxies currently provide none despite often being better hedges than indices.
questions.answer_long: Basel III CVA capital rules give full capital relief only for hedges of the exact counterparty. Index hedges receive partial relief based on a formula involving index composition. Single-name proxy hedges (e.g., using parent company CDS to hedge subsidiary exposure) receive zero capital relief under current rules, even though they may provide excellent spread and partial default protection. This creates a perverse incentive: banks might prefer an index hedge (worse economic hedge, some capital relief) over a proxy single-name hedge (better economic hedge, no capital relief). BCBS (2015) proposed changing this to allow capital relief for approved proxies, recognizing the problem.
questions.why_it_matters: Capital is expensive (10-15% ROE targets), so capital relief can make the difference between hedging and leaving positions unhedged. The current rules force banks into suboptimal hedging strategies where capital considerations trump economic risk management. Understanding this tension is crucial for XVA desk decision-making—sometimes the 'worse' hedge is chosen because it reduces capital more effectively.
common_traps: Choosing hedges based purely on spread correlation without considering capital implications
Assuming all CDS hedges provide capital relief (single-name proxies don't under current rules)
Not documenting why proxy single-names are appropriate hedges, making future capital relief impossible if rules change
questions.real_world_example: A bank has exposure to a subsidiary of a large corporate. The parent company CDS (liquid, 90% correlation) provides better default protection than the sector index (60% correlation), but the bank hedges with the index because it provides 30% capital relief while the parent CDS provides none. This costs them in hedge ineffectiveness but saves millions in capital charges.

questions.question: You are building generic credit curves for 'A-rated European Financials'. You have 15 single-name CDS quotes available. What are the main methodological challenges, and how might you address them?
questions.answer_short: Key challenges: outliers (distressed names), tenor gaps (most liquidity at 5-year), weighting schemes (equal-weight vs. market-cap), and time-series stability (avoiding jumps when names enter/exit). Address via outlier filters, interpolation methods, and liquidity-based weighting.
questions.answer_long: With 15 names you have reasonable data but face several issues: (1) Outliers—one distressed name can skew the average by 50+ bps; use median instead of mean or apply outlier filters (e.g., exclude spreads >3 standard deviations). (2) Tenor structure—most CDS trade at 5Y, fewer at 1Y, 3Y, 7Y, 10Y; you must interpolate and extrapolate, possibly using typical curve shapes for financials as constraints. (3) Weighting—should you equal-weight (gives small banks too much influence) or market-cap weight (but then it's not really 'generic')? (4) Stability—when a name defaults or gets downgraded and exits your bucket, the curve can jump 20-30 bps; smooth this via transition rules. (5) Granularity trade-off—splitting into 'Northern European' vs. 'Southern European' improves accuracy but reduces sample size per bucket.
questions.why_it_matters: These generic curves determine CVA for thousands of counterparties representing billions in exposure. Poor methodology creates excessive volatility (hurting P&L stability), regulatory challenges ('explain this 30% CVA increase'), and potential client disputes ('why did our CVA charge double when nothing changed?'). Robust, stable methodology is essential infrastructure for an XVA desk.
common_traps: Using simple averages without outlier treatment, allowing one distressed name to corrupt the entire curve
Not documenting methodology clearly, making it impossible to explain MTM changes to auditors or clients
Over-fitting to current market conditions, creating curves that behave unstably in stress scenarios
Making the curves too granular (e.g., 'A-rated French banks') with only 2-3 data points, introducing noise
questions.real_world_example: During the 2011 European sovereign crisis, Italian and Spanish banks widened dramatically while Northern European banks were stable. A bank using a single 'European Financials' curve saw their generic curve widen by 100+ bps due to a few peripheral names, forcing them to split into 'Core Europe' and 'Peripheral Europe' curves to avoid overstating CVA for German corporate counterparties.

questions.question: What are the advantages and disadvantages of using third-party credit curve providers (like Markit sector curves) versus building curves in-house for CVA calculation?
questions.answer_short: Third-party curves offer independence (good for audits), lower cost, and standardization but lack customization, create dependence on external methodology, and may not align with the bank's specific hedging strategy or capital requirements.
questions.answer_long: Advantages: (1) Auditability—external vendor provides independence that auditors value; (2) Lower cost—avoid building/maintaining internal infrastructure; (3) Industry standard—easier to benchmark against peers; (4) Expertise—vendors specialize in credit data. Disadvantages: (1) Lack of control—can't adjust methodology when market conditions change; (2) Misalignment—curves may not match your actual hedges, creating basis risk; (3) Capital inefficiency—vendor curves might not align with Basel III capital models; (4) Vendor lock-in—changing providers is costly; (5) Black box—limited transparency into calculation methodology. Mid-sized banks often use vendor curves for 'vanilla' exposures and custom curves for strategic counterparties.
questions.why_it_matters: This is a strategic build-vs-buy decision affecting hundreds of millions in CVA valuation and tens of millions in operational costs. The wrong choice can lead to regulatory challenges (if methodology doesn't align with capital calculations), excessive P&L volatility (from curves you can't control), or client relationship damage (if vendor curves seem unreasonable for specific counterparties).
common_traps: Assuming third-party curves are 'better' because they're external, without validating methodology appropriateness
Not having fallback procedures if the vendor feed fails during critical period-end calculations
Using vendor curves for CVA but different curves for capital calculations, creating unexplainable gaps
questions.real_world_example: A regional bank used Markit sector curves to save costs but found that during the COVID-19 crisis, the vendor's 'Energy' curve widened to 800 bps based on US shale companies, while their actual European utility counterparties were much more stable. They had to implement overlays manually, undermining the original cost-saving rationale and creating audit questions about the 'adjustments'.

questions.question: A counterparty has CDS spreads of 200 bps (1Y), 250 bps (2Y), and 300 bps (3Y) with 60% LGD. Calculate the conditional default probability for year 2 (i.e., probability of defaulting in year 2 given survival through year 1) using proper bootstrapping.
questions.answer_short: First, calculate 1Y survival (96.70%). Then bootstrap 2Y cumulative PD considering the 1Y survival. The conditional PD for year 2 is approximately 4.17%.
questions.answer_long: Step 1: Year 1 PD ≈ (0.02 × 1) / 0.60 = 3.33%, so survival = 96.67%. Step 2: The 2-year CDS at 250 bps must be consistent with PDs in both years. Using proper bootstrapping (not the simple formula), we solve for PD2 such that the present value of expected losses equals the present value of premium payments. This gives cumulative 2Y PD ≈ 8.06%. Step 3: The marginal PD for year 2 = 8.06% - 3.33% = 4.73%. Step 4: Conditional PD = marginal PD / survival to year 1 = 4.73% / 96.67% = 4.89%. This is higher than the simple approximation (250 bps / 60% = 4.17%) because it properly accounts for survival probability and discounting.
questions.why_it_matters: Proper bootstrapping is essential for accurate CVA calculation, especially when exposure profiles have lumpy cashflows or peak exposures at specific tenors. Using the simplified formula can understate default probabilities by 15-20% for steeply sloped curves, leading to material CVA undervaluation. Sophisticated XVA systems implement full bootstrapping with discount factors and survival probabilities.
common_traps: Using the simple formula PD = s·Δt / LGD for sequential periods without adjusting for survival probability
Not discounting cashflows when bootstrapping, which matters for longer-dated exposures
Assuming independence between periods (marginal PD ≠ conditional PD × survival probability)
questions.real_world_example: A bank calculated CVA on a 10-year interest rate swap using simple approximations for each annual PD. When they switched to proper bootstrapping, CVA increased by 12% because the method correctly captured the decreasing survival probability over time, which meant later-year default probabilities should be higher conditional on survival.

questions.question: You map a Greek corporate counterparty to the Greek sovereign CDS plus a 100 bps spread adjustment. What wrong-way risk issue does this create, and how might it understate CVA?
questions.answer_short: The corporate's credit quality is highly correlated with the sovereign. When the sovereign weakens (spreads widen), both the exposure (if you have wrong-way trades like selling EUR/GRD protection) and the default probability increase simultaneously, creating second-order effects the simple mapping misses.
questions.answer_long: Standard CVA assumes exposure and default probability are independent. Mapping a Greek corporate to Greek sovereign CDS creates strong correlation: if Greece faces crisis, (1) the sovereign spread widens (increasing PD), (2) Greek corporates become more distressed (spread should widen more than the +100 bps adjustment), and (3) if your exposure is wrong-way (e.g., Greek equity derivatives, selling CDS protection on Greek names), the exposure increases when PD increases. The simple mapping captures (1) but understates (2) because the spread adjustment is static, and completely misses (3), which requires joint simulation of exposure and credit quality. This can understate CVA by 30-50% for significant wrong-way exposures.
questions.why_it_matters: Wrong-way risk is one of the largest sources of CVA loss in crises. The Greek/Cypriot sovereign crises, Lehman's correlation with financial markets, and energy company exposures to oil prices are all examples where standard mapping approaches dramatically understated risk. Regulators increasingly expect banks to identify and model material wrong-way risk, especially for sovereigns and concentrated sector exposures.
common_traps: Using a sovereign proxy for corporates in that country without recognizing the embedded correlation
Thinking a spread adjustment (e.g., +100 bps) captures the additional risk, when it needs to be dynamic
Not stress-testing CVA under scenarios where both exposure and credit quality deteriorate together
Mapping financials to sovereign CDS in countries where banks hold large sovereign bond portfolios (classic wrong-way)
questions.real_world_example: During the 2010-2012 Eurozone crisis, banks that mapped Greek, Portuguese, and Irish corporates to sovereign curves plus static spreads found their CVA losses were 40-60% higher than models predicted. The corporates' spreads widened much more than sovereigns (contrary to the static spread assumption), and banks with exposures to these names often had wrong-way exposures (e.g., cross-currency swaps, equity derivatives) that increased in value as the countries deteriorated.

questions.question: Why is assuming a constant 60% LGD for all investment-grade corporates problematic, and what factors drive recovery rate variation?
questions.answer_short: Recovery rates vary significantly (10-90% range historically) based on seniority, sector, economic conditions, and security type. Using constant 60% LGD ignores subordination, collateral, and cyclical effects (recoveries drop in recessions).
questions.answer_long: Historical data shows enormous recovery variation: secured debt recovers 60-80%, senior unsecured 40-50%, subordinated 20-30%. Sector matters: financials and utilities often have higher recoveries (40-50% LGD) than retailers or energy (70-80% LGD) due to asset tangibility. Economic cycles are critical—recoveries in the 2008 crisis averaged 25-30% vs. 40-45% in normal times due to fire-sale dynamics and correlation of defaults. The 60% LGD assumption is a market convention for CDS pricing but doesn't reflect actual loss experience. For accurate CVA, especially for large exposures, using stochastic or scenario-based LGD provides more realistic risk assessment.
questions.why_it_matters: LGD directly scales CVA—a change from 60% to 40% reduces CVA by 33%. For large counterparty exposures (e.g., $500M+ notional), this is millions of dollars. More importantly, LGD correlates with default probability (both worsen in crises), creating second-order effects. Sophisticated banks use stochastic LGD in stressed CVA calculations and scenario analysis, though day-to-day CVA typically uses deterministic values for operational simplicity.
common_traps: Using the same LGD for all corporates regardless of capital structure or collateral
Not adjusting LGD for credit cycle—using 60% in boom times when crisis recoveries might be 30-40%
Applying bond/CDS recovery assumptions to derivatives without considering structural differences
questions.real_world_example: Lehman's senior CDS settled at 8.6% recovery (91.4% LGD) versus the standard 60% LGD assumption—a 50% difference. Banks using standard LGD had understated CVA by 35% (60%/91.4% ≈ 0.66). Conversely, some Lehman derivative counterparties eventually recovered 30-35% through the bankruptcy process, showing the settled vs. actual recovery gap discussed earlier.

questions.question: When constructing a funding curve for FVA calculation, why can't you simply use your own bank's CDS curve? What adjustments are needed?
questions.answer_short: Your CDS curve reflects unsecured senior debt costs, but funding comes from multiple sources (deposits, secured funding, senior/subordinated debt). The funding curve must be a blended rate reflecting your actual funding mix and costs, typically inside your CDS curve.
questions.answer_long: A bank's CDS curve represents the market's view of senior unsecured default risk and trades at a spread to the risk-free rate (e.g., OIS). However, actual funding comes from diverse sources: (1) Deposits—cheapest, often below risk-free rates due to deposit insurance; (2) Secured funding (repo)—cheaper than unsecured due to collateral; (3) Senior unsecured debt—roughly at CDS levels; (4) Subordinated debt—more expensive. The funding curve for FVA should reflect the marginal cost of funding an incremental derivative position, which depends on the bank's funding strategy. Most banks use a curve inside their CDS (e.g., CDS - 20-50 bps) reflecting that derivatives funding doesn't tap the most expensive sources. The curve also needs tenor structure—short-term funding is often cheaper than long-term.
questions.why_it_matters: Using the wrong funding curve directly impacts FVA magnitude, which can be 30-50% of CVA for uncollateralized exposures. If you use your CDS curve (too wide), you'll overcharge clients and be uncompetitive. If you use risk-free (too tight), you'll understate FVA and hurt profitability. This is a strategic pricing decision with P&L impact of millions for large derivatives books and directly affects ROE calculations.
common_traps: Using senior CDS curve directly without considering actual funding mix (overstates FVA by 20-30%)
Not updating funding curves to reflect changes in bank funding strategy or market conditions
Assuming funding costs are symmetric (funding long exposure costs the same as funding short exposure), when deposit funding is asymmetric
Ignoring tenor effects—assuming flat spread to risk-free when actually term funding spreads vary significantly
questions.real_world_example: In 2012-2014, many European banks had senior CDS at 150-200 bps but were funding at ECB facilities at risk-free + 25 bps and had large deposit bases at risk-free - 50 bps. Using their CDS curve would have overstated FVA by 100-150 bps, pricing them out of new business. They constructed blended funding curves at roughly risk-free + 40-60 bps based on their marginal funding costs, resulting in competitive but realistic FVA charges.

questions.question: When calculating KVA (capital valuation adjustment), banks must determine the required return on capital. How does this differ from the firm's overall cost of equity, and why is this distinction important?
questions.answer_short: KVA typically uses hurdle rates (12-18% ROE) that are higher than the firm's WACC or cost of equity (8-12%) because they reflect target returns for risky trading activities, management's strategic priorities, and capital allocation decisions, not just investor requirements.
questions.answer_long: The cost for KVA has three possible interpretations: (1) Cost of equity—what shareholders require (perhaps 10-12% based on CAPM); (2) Hurdle rate—what management demands for capital allocation to trading businesses (often 15-18%); (3) Incremental funding cost—what it costs to raise additional equity (includes issuance costs, dilution). Most banks use the hurdle rate approach because it reflects strategic decisions: trading desks must clear a higher bar than the firm's overall cost of capital to justify the risk and operational complexity. This makes KVA more subjective than other xVA terms—changing the hurdle rate from 12% to 18% increases KVA by 50%. Different business lines may also use different rates (exotic derivatives might need 20% ROE while vanilla swaps need 12%).
questions.why_it_matters: KVA is becoming material for capital-intensive trades (uncleared derivatives, long-dated exposures), often reaching 10-30% of the CVA charge. The hurdle rate directly determines deal economics and competitive positioning. Setting it too high prices you out of business; too low underestimates true capital costs and destroys shareholder value. This is a C-suite decision with strategic implications for which businesses the bank wants to be in.
common_traps: Using WACC (includes debt at 2-3%) when derivatives capital is pure equity—need equity cost only
Not adjusting for the riskiness of different businesses (applying same 15% to all derivatives)
Forgetting that capital costs include trapped capital inefficiency (Basel capital > economic capital)
Using historical cost of equity when forward-looking hurdle rates differ based on strategic priorities
questions.real_world_example: Bank A uses 12% ROE for KVA, Bank B uses 18%. For a $1B derivatives portfolio requiring $200M capital over 10 years, this creates a $12M vs. $18M annual KVA charge—a 50% difference. Bank B loses competitive tenders but maintains better ROE discipline, while Bank A wins more business but potentially takes on unprofitable capital-intensive trades. Both can be 'right' depending on strategic priorities.

questions.question: What is the key difference between a real-world default probability and a risk-neutral default probability?
questions.answer_short: Real-world default probability is estimated from historical default data, while risk-neutral default probability is derived from market prices (like CDS or bond spreads) and includes a risk premium that investors demand for taking credit risk.
questions.answer_long: Real-world default probabilities come from historical default statistics, typically organized by credit rating. Risk-neutral default probabilities are extracted from market instruments like credit default swaps or corporate bonds. The risk-neutral probability is systematically higher because it includes a risk premium - investors demand extra compensation beyond expected losses when accepting credit risk. Studies show risk-neutral probabilities can be 2-16 times higher than real-world rates, especially for high-quality credits.
questions.why_it_matters: This distinction is fundamental to CVA calculation. Using real-world probabilities would significantly underestimate CVA and fail to match market pricing. Modern accounting standards (IFRS 13) and regulatory capital rules (Basel III) explicitly require risk-neutral probabilities for CVA, making this a non-negotiable aspect of professional XVA practice.
common_traps: Assuming the difference is small or negligible - it can be 10x or more for investment grade credits
Using historical default rates for liquid credits when CDS prices are available
Forgetting that risk-neutral probabilities reflect market pricing, not actuarial expectations
questions.real_world_example: A bank trading desk uses historical A-rated default probability of 13 bps for CVA calculation. However, the A-rated CDS index trades at 128 bps, implying a risk-neutral probability nearly 10 times higher. Using the historical rate would massively undervalue CVA and create P&L surprises when hedging with market instruments.

questions.subtopic: Credit Spread to Default Probability Formula
questions.question: Using the approximation formula PD(t,t+1) ≈ s × Δt / LGD, calculate the one-year default probability for a counterparty with a 300 bps credit spread and 60% LGD.
questions.answer_short: PD = 300 bps × 1 year / 60% = 5.0%. The annual default probability is approximately 5%.
questions.answer_long: Using the formula, we convert the credit spread to a default probability by dividing by the loss given default: PD = (300 basis points / 10,000) × 1 year / 0.60 = 0.03 / 0.60 = 0.05 or 5%. This approximation assumes the spread is constant and doesn't account for the precise credit curve shape before time t. While simple, this formula is widely used in practice for initial CVA estimates and gives reasonable accuracy for relatively flat credit curves.
questions.why_it_matters: This is the workhorse formula for converting observable market credit spreads into the default probabilities needed for CVA calculations. Every CVA desk uses variants of this conversion thousands of times daily. Understanding when this approximation breaks down (steep credit curves, very short time periods) is essential for avoiding calculation errors.
common_traps: Forgetting to convert basis points to decimal (300 bps = 0.03, not 3.0)
Using the wrong LGD - derivatives typically rank as senior unsecured (60% LGD), not subordinated
Applying this to very short periods where the approximation becomes inaccurate
questions.real_world_example: A CVA desk needs to price a 5-year swap with a corporate counterparty whose 5-year CDS trades at 450 bps. They quickly estimate the annual default probability as 450/10000/0.60 = 7.5% per year to get an initial CVA estimate before running the full Monte Carlo simulation with bootstrapped hazard rates.

questions.subtopic: Loss Given Default (LGD) and Recovery Rates
questions.question: What is Loss Given Default (LGD) and what is the typical market convention for senior unsecured derivatives?
questions.answer_short: LGD is the percentage amount lost when a counterparty defaults (LGD = 1 - Recovery Rate). For senior unsecured derivatives, market convention typically uses 60% LGD (40% recovery).
questions.answer_long: Loss Given Default represents the fraction of exposure that will not be recovered following a counterparty default. It equals one minus the recovery rate. OTC derivatives typically rank pari passu with senior unsecured debt, and CDS market convention uses 60% LGD (40% recovery) for corporate credits.
