However, actual recoveries vary significantly by sector, seniority, and economic conditions. The Lehman bankruptcy showed how actual derivative recoveries (30-40% eventually) can differ substantially from settled CDS recoveries (9%).
questions.why_it_matters: LGD is essential for converting credit spreads to default probabilities and calculating expected credit losses. While seemingly important, LGD has less impact on CVA than credit spreads due to a cancellation effect - the same LGD assumption used to extract default probabilities from spreads partially cancels when computing expected loss. Understanding this helps prioritize where to focus modeling effort.
common_traps: Confusing LGD with recovery rate (they sum to 100%, not the same thing)
Using subordinated debt recovery rates (lower) when derivatives rank senior
Assuming settled recovery (from CDS auction) equals actual derivative recovery after bankruptcy workout
questions.real_world_example: Following Lehman's bankruptcy in 2008, the CDS auction settled at 8.6% recovery (91.4% LGD). However, derivative counterparties who went through the actual bankruptcy process received 30-40% over several years - a material difference driven by the time value of money and the complexity of valuing derivative claims in bankruptcy.

questions.question: Why do three credit curves with the same 5-year spread (300 bps) but different shapes (flat, upward-sloping, inverted) produce very different annual default probabilities?
questions.answer_short: The curve shape determines when defaults are expected to occur. An upward-sloping curve implies lower near-term default risk (spreads widen later), while an inverted curve implies higher near-term risk, even though all have the same 5-year cumulative probability.
questions.answer_long: Credit curve shape contains critical information about the timing of default risk. A 300 bps 5-year spread with an upward-sloping curve might imply 2% 1-year default probability but 9% in year 5, concentrating risk later. An inverted curve reverses this, putting 8% default probability in year 1 but only 2% in year 5. The 5-year cumulative probability (22.12%) is identical for all three because all pass through 300 bps at 5 years, but the distribution through time differs dramatically. For CVA, this matters because exposure profiles interact with these time-dependent default probabilities.
questions.why_it_matters: CVA is highly sensitive to the timing match between exposure peaks and default probability. A wrong assumption about curve shape can lead to material CVA mispricing. When extrapolating beyond liquid points (e.g., 5-year CDS to 10-year exposure), curve shape assumptions become crucial. The choice between flat extrapolation, parallel shift, or fitted curve can change CVA by 20-30%.
common_traps: Using only the 5-year CDS spread and assuming flat default probability for all periods
Ignoring that credit curve inversion typically signals near-term stress (higher immediate default risk)
Extrapolating beyond liquid tenors without considering market conditions - distressed credits steepen, improving credits flatten
questions.real_world_example: In March 2023, Credit Suisse 1-year CDS traded at 800 bps while 5-year was at 400 bps (inverted), signaling immediate default concerns. A CVA desk with long-dated exposure couldn't simply use the 5-year spread - the inverted curve meant near-term default probability was far higher, requiring curve bootstrapping to properly capture the 1-year risk at ~13% vs 5-year cumulative at 25%.

questions.question: Why have accounting standards (IFRS 13) and Basel III capital rules forced banks to use risk-neutral default probabilities even for illiquid counterparties where no market data exists?
questions.answer_short: IFRS 13 requires market-observable inputs and 'exit price' valuation. Basel III CVA capital explicitly uses CDS spreads. Both frameworks prioritize market consistency over historical statistics, forcing risk-neutral approaches even when market data must be proxied or mapped.
questions.answer_long: IFRS 13 accounting mandates that fair value reflect exit price - what you could trade the position for today - and requires use of market-observable inputs wherever possible. Since CVA is meant to reflect the cost of counterparty risk that would be priced into a transaction exit, risk-neutral probabilities (derived from CDS/bond markets) are required. Basel III CVA capital rules explicitly reference credit spreads in formulas and require CDS or proxy mapping. This creates a practical problem: banks have thousands of illiquid counterparties with no traded CDS or bonds, yet must map them to risk-neutral probabilities through rating/region/sector proxies rather than using their own historical default data.
questions.why_it_matters: This regulatory and accounting requirement fundamentally changed CVA practice. It forces banks to: (1) build extensive credit curve mapping infrastructure for illiquid names, (2) accept much higher CVA volatility (risk-neutral moves more than historical), (3) hedge using instruments that may not perfectly match the counterparty (basis risk), and (4) justify mapping methodologies to auditors and regulators. Understanding why this requirement exists helps navigate the tensions between theoretical purity and practical challenges.
common_traps: Thinking you can use internal historical PD models for small/illiquid counterparties to reduce CVA volatility - auditors and regulators will reject this
Using blended (mix of historical and risk-neutral) approaches without strong justification - increasingly hard to defend
Forgetting that 'exit price' concept means: what would a third party charge to assume this risk today, not what you expect to lose historically
questions.real_world_example: A regional bank has 200 small corporate counterparties, none with traded CDS. Their internal models suggest 0.5% annual default probability based on 20 years of history. However, BBB corporate CDS indices trade at 150 bps (implying 2.5% probability with 60% LGD). Basel III and IFRS 13 force them to map to the index-implied 2.5%, creating 5x higher CVA and capital charges despite their own experience showing lower losses.

questions.question: A bank must map credit curves for an unlisted single-A rated pharmaceutical company in Brazil. What are the key tradeoffs between using: (1) Brazilian sovereign CDS plus spread, (2) single-name proxy of similar pharma company in US, or (3) generic BBB corporate index?
questions.answer_short: Sovereign CDS + spread gives regional match but wrong sector and wrong-way risk. US pharma proxy gives sector match but wrong region and no default correlation. BBB index (if downgrade likely) gives liquidity and hedge but loses company-specific information. Each has different implications for accuracy, hedging ability, and capital relief.
questions.answer_long: Each approach has distinct tradeoffs: (1) Brazilian sovereign CDS plus credit spread captures regional risk but creates wrong-way risk (sovereign and corporate default together) and misses pharma sector dynamics. It's liquid and hedgeable. (2) US pharma single-name proxy captures sector credit dynamics but misses Brazil-specific risk (FX, political, economic) and provides spread hedge only, no capital relief under current Basel III. (3) BBB generic corporate index (if company is near downgrade) provides maximum liquidity, hedging, and partial capital relief, but loses all company-specific and regional information, just bucketing by rating. The choice depends on: exposure size (large = justify specific proxy), hedge portfolio (what can you actually trade), capital optimization (relief matters), and risk opinion (which risk factors dominate).
questions.why_it_matters: Credit curve mapping is not a pure mathematical exercise but a risk management decision with direct P&L, capital, and hedge effectiveness implications. Poor mapping creates basis risk - your CVA moves don't match your hedge moves. The 'right' answer depends on your risk view, hedge portfolio constraints, and capital optimization goals. This is why banks have credit curve mapping committees to make these judgment calls.
common_traps: Optimizing purely for capital relief (e.g., always use indices) while creating large unhedgeable basis risk
Using sovereign CDS for corporate counterparties without recognizing this creates wrong-way risk correlation
Choosing the most 'accurate' single-name proxy that has no liquidity and can't actually be traded for hedging
questions.real_world_example: A European bank has €50M exposure to a Brazilian single-A pharma company. They initially map to US pharma peer CDS (200 bps) as 'best fundamental match.' When Brazil sovereign spreads blow out from 150 to 400 bps during a crisis, their counterparty risk clearly increased, but their CVA barely moves because it's mapped to US name. They realize they need a blended approach: 70% Brazil sovereign + 50 bps pharma premium to capture regional risk, even though pure sector match seemed better.

questions.question: What are the main types of CDS instruments available for credit curve mapping, and which are most liquid?
questions.answer_short: Main types are single-name CDS (individual companies/sovereigns) and CDS indices (portfolios like iTraxx Europe, CDX North America). Indices are generally more liquid than single-names, especially at 5-year and 10-year tenors.
questions.answer_long: The CDS market offers several instrument types for mapping. Single-name CDS reference individual entities (corporates, financials, sovereigns) and provide the most specific credit information but can be illiquid except for large names. CDS indices pool together multiple entities - for example, iTraxx Europe Main (125 investment grade corporates), iTraxx Financials (financial institutions), CDX High Yield (100 high yield US names). Indices trade more frequently with tighter bid-offer spreads. The most liquid tenors are 5-year and 10-year, with 3-year and 7-year also available. Sub-indices exist by sector (TMT, energy, industrials) and geography (SovX Western Europe, Asia Pacific), though liquidity decreases with granularity.
questions.why_it_matters: Understanding the CDS instrument landscape is essential for building a credit curve mapping framework. Indices provide the backbone for generic curves (rating/region/sector buckets) while single-names allow specific mapping when available. Liquidity differences directly impact hedging costs - indices have tight spreads and deep markets, single-names can be wide and thin. For CVA hedging and capital relief, you must work within the constraints of what actually trades.
common_traps: Assuming all CDS trade frequently - many single-names rarely trade after issuance
Using illiquid sector sub-indices instead of main index, creating unhedgeable positions
Forgetting that CDS liquidity is concentrated at 5Y and 10Y; other tenors may be stale or interpolated quotes
questions.real_world_example: A CVA desk needs to hedge exposure to 30 different single-A European corporates. Individual single-name CDS for most names trade only a few times per month with 20-30 bps bid-offer spread. Instead, they use 80% hedge notional in iTraxx Europe Main (5Y trades continuously, 1 bp bid-offer) plus 20% single-name for the three largest exposures with liquid CDS, balancing cost, liquidity, and accuracy.

questions.question: Using the decision tree approach, how should a bank map credit curves for: (a) Apple Inc, (b) a small unlisted German manufacturing company rated A-, and (c) a regional Australian bank?
questions.answer_short: (a) Direct CDS observable for Apple; (b) No direct observable or single-name proxy, map to generic A-rated European industrials index; (c) Australian bank may have direct CDS, otherwise map to iTraxx Asia financials or use large Australian bank as single-name proxy.
questions.answer_long: Applying the decision tree: (a) Apple has very liquid single-name CDS trading at multiple tenors - use direct observable CDS spreads, provides hedge and full capital relief. (b) Small German manufacturer has no traded CDS or bonds, no obvious single-name proxy. Map to generic curve: A-rated + European region + industrials sector, likely using iTraxx Europe non-financials as base, possibly adjusted for rating if only BBB names in index. No default hedge, only spread hedge, partial capital relief via index. (c) Australian regional bank: check if direct CDS exists (many Australian banks do trade). If not, options are: use large Australian bank (NAB, ANZ) as single-name proxy with small spread adjustment, or map to iTraxx Asia financial sub-index. Choice depends on whether spread correlation to large Aussie bank or broader Asian financial index is better, and hedge portfolio constraints.
questions.why_it_matters: The decision tree approach ensures systematic and consistent credit curve assignment across thousands of counterparties. It prioritizes market observables (most accurate, hedgeable) but provides fallback to proxies and generic mapping when needed. Different banks implement variations of this tree, but the logic flow (direct → single-name proxy → generic) is standard. Documenting this process is essential for audit and regulatory review.
common_traps: Skipping straight to generic mapping without checking for reasonable single-name proxies
Using parent company CDS without checking if guarantee exists - may need spread adjustment
Over-engineering the decision tree with too many branches - complexity creates operational risk and inconsistency
questions.real_world_example: A bank maps 2,000 counterparties: 50 have direct liquid CDS (large corporates, banks, sovereigns), 200 use single-name proxies (subsidiaries of traded parents, small banks in same country as large banks), and 1,750 map to 25 generic curves (rating × region × sector). The generic bucket contains most names but often smaller individual exposures. The direct CDS bucket is small in count but represents 60% of total CVA due to large exposures.

questions.question: What is the key tradeoff between granular classification (e.g., single-A US utilities) versus broad classification (e.g., single-A corporates) when constructing generic credit curves?
questions.answer_short: Granular classification better distinguishes between different counterparty risks but has fewer data points per curve, creating potential idiosyncratic noise. Broad classification has more data for stable curves but loses important risk differentials between sectors and regions.
questions.answer_long: Generic curve construction faces a fundamental tradeoff. More granular classification (rating + region + sector, e.g., 'A-rated US utility companies') provides better economic differentiation - utilities have different default characteristics than technology companies. However, splitting into many buckets means each curve is calibrated to fewer CDS quotes, making curves vulnerable to idiosyncratic moves in individual names. If only 3 CDS quotes exist for 'A-rated US utilities,' one name widening 50 bps moves the entire curve materially. Broader classification (e.g., all A-rated corporates globally) has many more data points (potentially 50+ CDS), creating stable curves less sensitive to single-name noise, but fails to distinguish that European utilities trade 50 bps tighter than US technology names. The optimal granularity depends on data availability in each market and exposure concentration in different sectors.
questions.why_it_matters: This tradeoff directly impacts CVA volatility and accuracy. Too granular creates noisy CVA with jumps driven by idiosyncratic single-name moves in the calibration basket, even though your counterparty hasn't changed. Too broad creates stable CVA that doesn't move appropriately when sector-specific or regional risks emerge. Banks constantly adjust granularity as markets evolve - adding sector splits when more data becomes available, consolidating when markets become illiquid.
common_traps: Over-engineering with 7 ratings × 7 regions × 10 sectors = 490 curves when market liquidity only supports 20-30 distinct curves
Using global aggregation when exposure is concentrated regionally (e.g., Asian bank using global A-curve when 90% exposure in Asia)
Not monitoring calibration basket size - as CDS market liquidity declines, granular curves become based on 1-2 names only
questions.real_world_example: A European bank initially built curves for rating × region × sector (100+ curves). They found many curves had only 1-3 CDS inputs. When one Italian A-rated energy company widened 100 bps, the entire 'A-rated European energy' curve jumped, moving CVA for 50 unrelated counterparties. They consolidated to: Financials vs Non-financials × rating × Europe/US/Asia (42 curves), ensuring minimum 5 CDS per curve. Less precise but more stable.

questions.question: Why might the actual recovery on OTC derivatives following a bankruptcy differ significantly from the settled recovery determined in a CDS auction, and how should this affect CVA calculation?
questions.answer_short: CDS auctions settle within days based on tradeable bonds, giving quick 'settled recovery.' OTC derivatives go through bankruptcy process (years), creating 'actual recovery' that may be higher due to netting, collateral, setoff rights, and time value. However, CVA should still use settled recovery for exit price consistency.
questions.answer_long: The difference arises from timing and claim characteristics. CDS auctions settle quickly (within 30 days of credit event) by establishing a price for deliverable bonds, giving 'settled recovery' - what you could monetize immediately by selling bonds. OTC derivatives can't be sold individually due to netting and bespoke nature. They go through bankruptcy workout lasting years. 'Actual recovery' emerges later and may differ because: (1) netting/collateral may be more favorable than bond claims, (2) setoff rights against other obligations, (3) time value of money during workout, (4) negotiation leverage. Lehman shows this - 8.6% CDS auction vs 30-40% actual derivative recovery. However, for CVA accounting (exit price), use settled recovery - that's what an arm's length third party could achieve today. Actual recovery is your proprietary advantage, not market price.
questions.why_it_matters: This distinction matters for two separate purposes that are often confused. For accounting CVA (IFRS 13 exit price), use settled recovery derived from liquid CDS/bond markets - this is what someone would charge today to assume the risk. For internal economic capital and reserve management, you might use actual recovery based on your workout experience. Mixing these creates audit issues and potentially overstates CVA benefit from your workout expertise.
common_traps: Using Lehman's eventual 35% derivative recovery to justify lower LGD in CVA (should use market's 8-10% at time of default for exit price)
Assuming derivatives always recover better than bonds - this was true for Lehman but isn't universal
Not considering that higher actual recovery takes years to receive, so NPV adjustment may eliminate much of the benefit
questions.real_world_example: Following Lehman bankruptcy in 2008, CDS auction settled at 8.6% (91.4% LGD). A bank with $100M gross exposure, $60M net after netting, and $55M after collateral initially booked CVA loss using 91.4% LGD = $50.3M charge. Over 2009-2014, through bankruptcy process, they eventually recovered 35% = $19.2M, but present value in 2008 terms was only ~$12M due to time delay. The incremental $12M recovery vs initial $5M assumption was a windfall, but not something to rely on for CVA accounting.

questions.subtopic: CDS-Bond Basis and Credit Spread Definition
questions.question: What is the CDS-bond basis, and in what market situations would you prefer to use bond spreads versus CDS spreads for extracting risk-neutral default probabilities?
questions.answer_short: CDS-bond basis is the difference between CDS spread and bond-implied spread for the same reference entity. Prefer CDS when liquid (cleaner credit view, hedgeable). Use bonds when: CDS market is illiquid/closed, credit is not in CDS market, or significant distortions exist (CDS technical squeeze, bond liquidity premium).
questions.answer_long: The CDS-bond basis exists because CDS spread and asset-swap spread on bonds for the same entity can differ by 20-50+ bps. Reasons include: (1) CDS technical factors (collateral requirements, counterparty risk on CDS itself, funding), (2) bond-specific features (liquidity premium, repo specialness, tax treatment, cheapest-to-deliver option in CDS), (3) market segmentation (different investor bases). CDS is generally preferred for CVA because: it's a purer credit instrument (bonds have interest rate, liquidity components), it's two-way market (can buy/sell protection easily), it's what you'd hedge with. However, use bonds when: emerging markets where CDS doesn't exist or is extremely thin, during market stress when CDS market freezes but bond market functions, or for entities (small corporates, some sovereigns) never referenced by CDS. Bond spreads require deriving spread over benchmark (treasury, swap curve) and removing non-credit components.
questions.why_it_matters: Basis risk between CDS and bonds creates hedging challenges and marks differences between banks. If you mark CVA using bond spreads but hedge with CDS (or vice versa), the basis becomes unhedged P&L volatility. During 2008-2009 crisis, CDS-bond basis widened to 100+ bps for many names, creating significant CVA hedge ineffectiveness for banks using bond-derived curves but CDS hedges. Understanding when basis matters and how to extract comparable credit spreads from bonds is essential.
common_traps: Using bond yields without subtracting benchmark rate - this includes interest rate risk, not pure credit
Mixing CDS spreads and bond spreads in the same curve without basis adjustment
Not recognizing that bond spreads include liquidity premium (typically 20-40 bps) that isn't default risk
questions.real_world_example: In March 2023, Credit Suisse 5Y CDS traded at 800 bps while comparable maturity bonds implied 600 bps spreads (basis = 200 bps, CDS wider). The difference reflected CDS technical squeeze (everyone rushing to buy protection, limited dealer balance sheet) rather than fundamental default risk difference. A bank mapping counterparties to Credit Suisse parent had to choose: use CDS (what hedges cost), use bonds (arguably cleaner economic credit view), or blend. Most used CDS because that's exit price for risk transfer.

questions.question: When would you adjust the standard 60% LGD assumption for OTC derivatives, and what would be appropriate adjustments for: (a) derivatives with a securitization SPV, and (b) subordinated derivative claims?
questions.answer_short: (a) Securitization SPV derivatives often have structural seniority, use lower LGD like 30-40% (higher recovery). (b) Subordinated derivatives are rare but would use higher LGD like 75-85% (lower recovery), similar to subordinated debt.
questions.answer_long: Standard 60% LGD assumes derivatives rank pari passu with senior unsecured debt, which is typical. Adjust when: (a) Structural seniority: Some securitization SPVs grant derivatives 'super-senior' status, paying derivative counterparties before noteholders. This dramatically improves recovery; appropriate LGD might be 30-40% (60-70% recovery), similar to secured debt. Justify with legal opinion on seniority. (b) Subordination: Rare, but some structured transactions have subordinated derivative claims. Use LGD of 75-85% (15-25% recovery), similar to subordinated bonds. Historical recovery data shows sub debt recovers ~25% vs 40% for senior. (c) Enhanced credit support: CSAs with strong collateral may warrant modest LGD reduction (55% instead of 60%), though collateral should mainly be modeled in exposure, not LGD. Need strong justification for auditors - can't just use favorable LGD to reduce CVA without documented basis.
questions.why_it_matters: LGD adjustments can materially impact CVA, though less than credit spreads. A move from 60% to 40% LGD reduces risk-neutral PD by 33% (for same spread), significantly reducing CVA. However, auditors scrutinize LGD assumptions heavily because they're subjective and hard to verify. You need legal documentation of seniority, not just belief that recovery will be better. Inappropriately aggressive LGD is a common audit finding in CVA reviews.
common_traps: Using lower LGD based on 'good relationship with counterparty' - this isn't structural seniority
Adjusting LGD for collateral protection when collateral should be modeled in exposure simulation instead
Using Lehman's eventual 35% derivative recovery to justify 65% LGD universally - that's one data point, not market standard
questions.real_world_example: A bank has swap exposure to a CLO SPV. The SPV documents show derivatives have payment priority above all debt tranches (super-senior status) and overcollateralization tests protect derivative claims. Legal opinion confirms this structural seniority. Bank uses 35% LGD (65% recovery) instead of standard 60%, reducing CVA by 42% [(60-35)/60]. However, they document this with legal opinion, precedent transaction recoveries, and rating agency analysis to satisfy auditors.

questions.question: Explain why the simple approximation PD ≈ s×Δt/LGD breaks down for upward-sloping credit curves, and what more accurate bootstrapping method should be used instead.
questions.answer_short: The approximation ignores survival probability from prior periods and assumes flat hazard rate. For upward-sloping curves, it overestimates early default probabilities. Bootstrapping iteratively solves for hazard rate at each tenor, conditioning on survival to that point and matching CDS spreads exactly.
questions.answer_long: The approximation PD(t,t+Δt) ≈ s(t+Δt)×Δt/LGD implicitly assumes you can use the spread at time t+Δt to determine default probability in period t to t+Δt. This ignores that the t+Δt spread reflects all possible default times up to t+Δt, weighted by survival probabilities. For accurate calculation, bootstrap hazard rates: (1) Start with shortest maturity CDS spread (e.g., 1Y). Solve for hazard rate λ₁ such that CDS premium leg equals protection leg, using S(t)=exp(-λt). (2) Move to next maturity (2Y). Use previously calibrated λ₁ for first year, solve for λ₂ in second year to match 2Y CDS spread. (3) Iterate for all maturities. This produces piecewise-constant (or interpolated) hazard rate term structure. Default probability PD(t,t+Δt) = S(t) × [1-exp(-λ×Δt)] properly accounts for survival to time t. The approximation formula works reasonably for flat or gently sloping curves but can be off 20-30% for steep curves.
questions.why_it_matters: Precise hazard rate calibration matters most for: (1) steep credit curves (distressed or improving credits), (2) long-dated exposures where small errors compound, (3) regulatory capital calculations that scrutinize methodology. All professional CVA systems use bootstrapping, not approximations. Understanding the math lets you diagnose when simplified methods are acceptable (quick estimates, flat curves) versus when full bootstrap is required (official CVA, steep curves, long dates).
common_traps: Using the simple approximation for distressed credits with inverted curves (1Y > 5Y) - error can be 50%+
Forgetting that hazard rate λ relates to default probability as PD(t,t+Δt) = S(t)×[1-exp(-λΔt)], not simply λΔt
Not handling the premium leg accrual in CDS valuation when bootstrapping - CDS pays accrued premium on default
questions.real_world_example: A bank has 10-year swap exposure to a counterparty. Credit curve is steeply upward sloping: 1Y=100 bps, 5Y=300 bps, 10Y=500 bps. Using simple approximation gives 10Y cumulative PD of ~66% [1-exp(-0.05×10/0.6)]. Proper bootstrapping, accounting for survival through early years where spreads are much lower, gives cumulative PD of 55%. This 20% difference translates to ~20% difference in CVA, material for a large exposure.

questions.question: Under Basel III CVA capital rules, why do index CDS hedges receive partial capital relief while single-name proxy CDS hedges receive none (under current rules), and how does this affect mapping methodology choices?
questions.answer_short: Basel III CVA capital formula explicitly recognizes index hedges (weighted by proportion of index rating/sector matching counterparty), assuming indices are liquid and provide spreading/spread risk hedge. Single-name proxies, even if economically similar, don't provide default protection on actual counterparty, so no capital relief. This incentivizes mapping to indices even when less accurate.
questions.answer_long: The Basel III standardized CVA capital charge (Section 8.7.3) allows capital reduction for index CDS hedges through explicit formula terms that account for index notional and basis. Regulators view indices as liquid, tradeable hedges that reduce spread risk, even though they don't provide default protection on specific counterparty. Index hedge reduces capital by approximately √(1-correlation) factor. However, single-name CDS proxies (e.g., using parent company CDS when trading with subsidiary, or using similar-sector company) receive zero capital relief under current rules because they don't reference the actual counterparty legal entity - no default protection. BCBS (2015) proposed to change this, recognizing single-name proxies with 'appropriate basis adjustment,' but not yet implemented. This creates perverse incentive: map counterparties to generic curves hedged with indices (capital relief, but less accurate spread dynamics) versus single-name proxies (more accurate, hedges spread, but no capital relief). Banks balance capital efficiency against hedge effectiveness.
questions.why_it_matters: This regulatory constraint directly shapes credit mapping frameworks at all banks. Capital-constrained banks tilt toward index-based generic mapping to maximize capital relief, accepting lower accuracy. Banks with excess capital or using internal models can optimize for economic hedge effectiveness over regulatory capital. The upcoming regulatory change to recognize single-name proxies will materially change optimal mapping strategies. Understanding these regulatory incentives explains why bank mapping frameworks differ and why seemingly less accurate indices are sometimes preferred.
common_traps: Optimizing purely for capital relief by mapping everything to indices, then finding huge CVA-hedge basis blowout when specific counterparty spreads diverge from index
Not recognizing that index hedge capital relief depends on correlation assumption - regulators may challenge this
Assuming single-name proxy for subsidiary automatically gets same capital treatment as direct hedge (it doesn't under current rules)
questions.real_world_example: A bank has €200M exposure to subsidiaries of various A-rated European banks, each subsidiary with no traded CDS. Option 1: Map each to parent bank single-name CDS (very accurate spread dynamics), buy parent CDS protection. Hedge is effective but gets zero capital relief - capital charge stays €200M × 10% = €20M. Option 2: Map all to iTraxx Financials Senior index, hedge with index. Less accurate (misses idiosyncratic parent moves) but gets 60% capital relief (assuming 75% correlation) - capital charge drops to €8M. Bank chooses blended approach: 50% parent CDS (hedge effectiveness), 50% index (capital relief).

questions.question: What are the advantages and disadvantages of using third-party generic credit curves (e.g., Markit sector curves) versus building your own internal curves?
questions.answer_short: Third-party curves: advantages are independence (auditor-friendly), consistent methodology, lower cost. Disadvantages are rigidity (can't adjust for your risk view), you don't control volatility, and classification may not match your needs. Internal curves allow customization but require infrastructure and auditor justification.
questions.answer_long: Third-party vendor curves (e.g., Markit sector curves) offer: (1) Independence - auditors prefer external pricing sources, removes conflict of interest; (2) Consistent methodology - vendor applies same approach across all curves, no cherry-picking; (3) Lower cost - no need to build curve calibration infrastructure; (4) Market standard - easier to explain to clients, auditors, regulators. However, disadvantages include: (1) Rigidity - you can't adjust curves for your specific risk view or proprietary information about counterparty; (2) Volatility beyond your control - curve jumps when vendor changes methodology or calibration basket; (3) Classification may not match exposure - vendor uses their rating/sector taxonomy, not yours; (4) Lack of transparency - vendor may not disclose which CDS are in calibration basket or exactly how interpolation/extrapolation works. Internal curves allow full control and customization (adjust for exposure concentration, risk views, hedge portfolio) but require significant infrastructure (curve calibration models, data feeds, governance) and must be justified to auditors (why is your curve 'better' than market standard?).
questions.why_it_matters: The choice between third-party and internal curves is strategic. Small/mid-size banks often use third-party curves due to cost and resources - building robust curve calibration infrastructure requires 5-10 quant developers. Large banks use internal curves because: exposure size justifies investment, need customization for complex hedge portfolios, and want control over CVA volatility. Many banks use hybrid: third-party curves as 'challenger' model for validation, internal curves for official marks, with governance process when differences exceed threshold.
common_traps: Using third-party curves without understanding their methodology - you're accountable for marks even if you outsource calculation
Building overly complex internal curves that can't be explained to auditors - simplicity has value
Not having challenger model (internal vs external curves) to identify when your curves diverge from market consensus
questions.real_world_example: A mid-size European bank initially built internal generic curves (30 rating/sector combinations). Audit review found insufficient documentation of calibration basket choices and interpolation methodology. Curve construction took 2 days/month of quant time, delaying month-end close. They switched to Markit sector curves for all generic buckets, reducing operational burden and satisfying auditors. However, they lost ability to adjust for their view that Nordic financials were stronger than Markit's Europe Financials curve, accepting some accuracy loss for operational efficiency.

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between real-world and risk-neutral default probabilities, and why does this difference exist?
questions.answer_short: Risk-neutral default probabilities are systematically higher than real-world probabilities because they include a risk premium that investors demand for accepting default risk.
questions.answer_long: Real-world default probabilities are estimated from historical default data, while risk-neutral probabilities are derived from market prices (bonds, CDS). Risk-neutral probabilities are higher because risk-averse investors demand a premium above expected default losses when accepting credit risk. Empirically, corporate bonds outperform risk-free benchmarks after accounting for actual defaults, proving investors receive compensation beyond just expected losses. This risk premium varies by rating quality, being proportionally larger for higher-rated credits.
questions.why_it_matters: Using the wrong type of default probability completely changes CVA interpretation—from an actuarial reserve (real-world) to a market price (risk-neutral). This impacts fair value accounting, hedge effectiveness, and capital requirements. Modern practice has converged on risk-neutral for CVA, but this creates challenges for illiquid credits where no market prices exist.
common_traps: Assuming real-world probabilities can be used for CVA because they seem more 'realistic'—regulators and auditors reject this
Thinking the difference between real-world and risk-neutral is small—it can be 5-17x for high-quality credits
Using historical default rates for pricing or hedging when counterparties expect market-implied levels
questions.real_world_example: A Aa-rated bank has a historical 1-year default probability of 6 bps but a risk-neutral probability of 78 bps (13x higher). Using real-world PD would drastically undervalue CVA compared to what the market charges for CDS protection, creating immediate P&L issues and regulatory capital shortfalls under Basel III.

questions.question: Using the simple approximation, what is the one-year unconditional default probability for a counterparty with a 300 bps credit spread and 60% LGD?
questions.answer_short: The default probability is approximately 4.88%, calculated as PD ≈ s/(1-LGD) = 300 bps / 0.60 = 500 bps × 0.60 ≈ 0.0488.
questions.answer_long: Using the formula PD(t-1, t) ≈ s_t × Δt / (1 - LGD), with s = 300 bps (0.03), Δt = 1 year, and LGD = 60% (0.60), we get PD ≈ 0.03 / 0.40 = 0.075 for the hazard rate, which translates to approximately 4.88% for the actual probability. This approximation works reasonably well for flat or gently sloping credit curves but breaks down when curves are steep or inverted, because it ignores the shape of the curve prior to time t.
questions.why_it_matters: This simple formula is widely used in CVA systems for quick calculations and stress testing. Understanding when it's accurate versus when you need more sophisticated bootstrapping methods is critical for model validation. The approximation quality directly impacts CVA accuracy, especially for long-dated exposures.
common_traps: Forgetting that the probability is unconditional (not survival-adjusted)—must account for prior survival separately
Using this formula on steeply sloped curves where it significantly overestimates or underestimates PD
Mixing up LGD and recovery rate (RR = 1 - LGD) in the denominator
questions.real_world_example: A CVA desk calculates exposure to a BBB corporate with 400 bps 5Y spread. Using the approximation gives 6.67% annual PD at year 5. But the curve is steeply upward-sloping (150 bps at 1Y). Proper bootstrapping shows the 5Y forward PD is actually 8.2%, creating a 23% CVA underestimation with the simple formula.

questions.question: Why does the shape of a credit curve matter for CVA calculation, even when two curves have identical 5-year spreads?
questions.answer_short: Different curve shapes (flat, upward-sloping, inverted) produce vastly different forward default probabilities at each tenor, even with the same 5-year point, dramatically affecting the timing and magnitude of expected credit losses.
questions.answer_long: The term structure determines when defaults are most likely. An upward-sloping curve implies lower near-term default risk but higher long-term risk, while an inverted curve suggests elevated near-term stress. For CVA, this matters because exposure profiles interact with default timing—early defaults on long-dated trades have different impacts than late defaults. The same 5-year cumulative default probability can translate to 2% annual PD in year 1 for an inverted curve versus 8% for an upward-sloping curve, completely changing CVA contributions by time bucket.
questions.why_it_matters: CVA desks must calibrate the entire term structure, not just key tenors. Incorrect curve interpolation or extrapolation can create 20-40% CVA errors on portfolios with significant long-dated exposure. This is especially critical when exposure peaks don't align with liquid CDS tenors (e.g., peak at 7 years when only 5Y and 10Y CDS trade).
common_traps: Assuming a flat curve when only one tenor is observable—creates systematic pricing errors
Linear interpolation between widely-spaced tenors (e.g., 5Y and 10Y)—misses convexity in credit spreads
Extrapolating beyond 10 years without considering fundamental credit deterioration or mean reversion
questions.real_world_example: A bank has €500M exposure peaking at year 7 to an A-rated corporate. The 5Y CDS is 150 bps, 10Y is 250 bps. Simple linear interpolation gives 200 bps at 7Y. But actual 7Y bonds trade at 180 bps due to curve shape. The 20 bps difference on a 7-year forward PD creates a €2M CVA difference on this single counterparty.

questions.question: What is Loss Given Default (LGD) and how does it relate to recovery rate in the context of OTC derivatives?
questions.answer_short: LGD is the percentage amount lost when a counterparty defaults, equal to (1 - recovery rate). For derivatives ranking pari passu with senior unsecured debt, standard market LGD is typically 60% (40% recovery).
questions.answer_long: Loss Given Default (LGD) measures the economic loss from a credit event as a percentage of exposure. It equals one minus the recovery rate. For OTC derivatives, the claim typically ranks pari passu with senior unsecured bonds, giving a standard 60% LGD assumption in line with CDS market conventions. However, actual LGD varies by seniority, sector, economic conditions, and workout process timing. LGD is crucial for converting credit spreads into default probabilities and for calculating CVA, though there's a cancellation effect that makes precise LGD estimation less critical than credit spread accuracy.
questions.why_it_matters: LGD is required to extract risk-neutral default probabilities from credit spreads and to calculate expected credit losses in CVA. While CVA is relatively insensitive to LGD assumptions due to offsetting effects, capital calculations and risk limits may depend more directly on LGD. Understanding the difference between settled recovery (e.g., CDS auction) and actual derivative recovery (bankruptcy process) is critical for P&L forecasting.
common_traps: Using bond LGDs for subordinated or secured debt when derivatives rank senior unsecured
Assuming LGD is constant across scenarios—it correlates with default probability in stress
Confusing settled recovery (9% for Lehman CDS auction) with actual recovery received years later (30-40%)
questions.real_world_example: After Lehman's default, the CDS auction settled at 8.6% recovery (91.4% LGD). Derivatives counterparties initially wrote down positions assuming this LGD. However, the actual recovery received through the bankruptcy process over several years was 30-40%, creating significant positive CVA adjustments. This 20-30% difference highlights the importance of distinguishing settled vs. actual LGD.

questions.question: Why is credit curve mapping for illiquid counterparties one of the most challenging aspects of CVA calculation, and what trade-offs must banks consider?
questions.answer_short: Most counterparties lack liquid CDS or bonds, requiring subjective proxy mapping based on rating/region/sector. Banks must balance accuracy, hedgeability, and capital relief when choosing between single-name proxies, generic curves, or indices.
questions.answer_long: Large banks have thousands of counterparties (corporates, SMEs, regional entities) with no observable credit spreads. Regulators require risk-neutral default probabilities, but without market prices this requires proxy mapping. The trade-offs are severe: (1) single-name proxies may be accurate but unhhedgeable and provide no capital relief; (2) generic rating/sector curves allow hedging via indices and partial capital relief but are less accurate; (3) more granular mappings are precise but suffer from insufficient data points and idiosyncratic volatility. The choice affects CVA size, P&L volatility, hedge effectiveness, and regulatory capital.
questions.why_it_matters: For a typical bank, 70-80% of counterparties may be illiquid credits collectively representing 30-50% of CVA exposure. Poor mapping creates mispricing, ineffective hedges, and capital inefficiency. The mapping methodology must be consistent with the CVA capital model (standardized vs. advanced), and auditors scrutinize it heavily. Changes to mapping can create millions in P&L volatility.
common_traps: Over-granular classification with insufficient data points—creates artificial volatility from single-name idiosyncratic moves
Using illiquid bond prices that appear 'direct' but are stale or unreliable versus liquid index proxies
Ignoring that proxy single-name CDS provide no capital relief under current Basel III (though BCBS 2015 proposes changes)
questions.real_world_example: A European bank has €50M exposure to a single-A Italian utility with no CDS. Options: (1) map to a Spanish utility with CDS (good credit proxy, no capital relief); (2) map to iTraxx Non-Financials A-rated curve (liquid, hedgeable, partial capital relief but less accurate); (3) use an Italian government bond spread adjusted for corporate risk (accurate region, but illiquid and unhhedgeable). The choice impacts CVA by 15-25% and hedge P&L by €500k annually.

questions.question: What are the main types of CDS instruments used for credit curve mapping, and what is the difference between single-name CDS and CDS indices?
questions.answer_short: Single-name CDS reference individual entities (corporates, banks, sovereigns) and provide default protection. CDS indices (e.g., iTraxx, CDX) are portfolios of single-name CDS, offering spread hedges but not individual default protection. Indices are more liquid.
questions.answer_long: Single-name CDS are bilateral contracts providing credit protection on a specific reference entity, settling upon credit events (failure to pay, restructuring, bankruptcy). They offer both spread and default hedges but can be illiquid. CDS indices are standardized portfolios of typically 100-125 liquid single-name CDS, categorized by rating (investment grade, crossover, high yield), sector (financials, non-financials), or region (Europe, North America, Asia). Indices are more liquid and trade at standard tenors (3Y, 5Y, 7Y, 10Y), but provide only spread hedges since they dilute idiosyncratic default risk across many names.
questions.why_it_matters: Understanding CDS instrument types is fundamental for CVA hedging strategy and capital relief. Single-name CDS provide precise hedges for liquid credits but limited capital relief for proxies. Indices enable efficient spread hedging for portfolios of illiquid credits and partial capital relief, but introduce basis risk. The choice directly impacts CVA P&L volatility, hedge costs, and regulatory capital requirements.
common_traps: Assuming CDS indices provide default protection for individual counterparties—they only hedge spread risk
Expecting capital relief from single-name proxy CDS under current Basel III rules—generally not allowed
Overlooking technical differences: CDS may not trigger on derivative payment failures, only on bond/loan events
questions.real_world_example: A bank has CVA exposure to 50 BBB-rated European corporates with no individual CDS. Hedging with iTraxx Europe Main (125 IG names) provides liquid spread protection and reduces CVA capital by ~50%. But when one counterparty defaults, the index barely moves (1/125 impact), creating a €5M loss that the hedge doesn't cover. The bank still considers this preferable to unhedged exposure.

questions.question: When might a bank use an LGD different from the standard 60% assumption, and what evidence would auditors require to support this?
questions.answer_short: Banks may use lower LGDs for structurally senior derivatives (e.g., in securitizations), credit-enhanced trades, or based on superior workout experience. Auditors require documented seniority analysis, legal opinions, or statistical evidence from realized recoveries.
questions.answer_long: Deviations from standard 60% LGD are justified when: (1) structural seniority differs—derivatives in SPVs may rank super-senior; (2) explicit credit support exists beyond standard collateral; (3) historical workout experience demonstrates systematically higher recoveries with statistical significance. For the Lehman case, some banks argued for lower LGDs based on higher actual recoveries (30-40%) versus CDS auction (8.6%), but this required extensive documentation. Auditors scrutinize LGD assumptions because even small changes (55% vs. 60%) can create 10-15% CVA swings. Evidence must be contemporaneous, not cherry-picked from favorable outcomes.
questions.why_it_matters: LGD assumptions directly impact CVA size and capital requirements. While CVA has some LGD insensitivity due to offsetting effects, capital models may not. Using aggressive (low) LGDs reduces CVA charges but creates audit risk and potential regulatory pushback. Understanding when deviations are defensible is critical for optimizing CVA charges without compromising control quality.
common_traps: Assuming better recoveries on derivatives without legal analysis of bankruptcy priority—rankings may be identical to bonds
Using Lehman's high actual recovery (30-40%) as standard without accounting for its unique circumstances and long workout period
Applying collateral benefits through reduced LGD instead of modeling explicitly in exposure—double-counts the benefit
questions.real_world_example: A bank trades derivatives with a CLO structure where derivatives rank senior to the notes. Legal analysis confirms structural seniority, supporting a 30% LGD (vs. 60% standard). This reduces CVA by 40% on a €200M exposure, saving €8M. However, auditors require annual legal opinions and stress testing to ensure the structural seniority holds under various default scenarios, adding €100k annual compliance costs.

questions.question: Walk through the decision process for mapping credit spreads for a mid-sized Asian corporate with no CDS but where the parent company has a liquid 5Y CDS trading.
questions.answer_short: Use the parent company CDS as a single-name proxy, potentially with a spread adjustment if the subsidiary is perceived as weaker. This provides a spread hedge but no default hedge or capital relief under current Basel III rules.
questions.answer_long: Following the standard decision tree: (1) No direct CDS exists for the subsidiary. (2) No liquid bonds trade for the subsidiary. (3) Parent company has liquid 5Y CDS—this becomes the single-name proxy. Assessment needed: does the parent guarantee the subsidiary or is credit risk substantially similar? If no explicit guarantee, add a spread adjustment (e.g., +25-50 bps) to reflect incremental risk. The parent CDS can hedge spread moves but won't settle if only the subsidiary defaults (no default hedge). For tenors beyond 5Y, interpolate to 10Y CDS if available, or blend with generic sector curves. Capital relief will generally not be available under current Basel III for proxy CDS, though this may change.
questions.why_it_matters: Parent-subsidiary relationships are extremely common in derivative counterparty portfolios (e.g., regional subsidiaries of global banks, local entities of multinational corporates). Correctly assessing the credit linkage, calibrating spread adjustments, and understanding hedge/capital implications is essential for accurate CVA. Over-reliance on parent spreads without adjustments can underprice subsidiary risk by 20-40%.
common_traps: Assuming perfect credit correlation between parent and subsidiary without analyzing legal separation and guarantees
Using parent CDS directly when subsidiary operates in a different country/sector with different risks
Expecting full capital relief from parent CDS hedges—generally not allowed for proxies
questions.real_world_example: A bank trades with the Singapore subsidiary of a Japanese conglomerate. The Japanese parent has 5Y CDS at 80 bps. Legal review shows no explicit guarantee, and the subsidiary has concentrated exposure to regional real estate. The bank maps to parent CDS + 30 bps adjustment (110 bps total). When regional real estate stress hits, the subsidiary's implied spread widens to 180 bps while parent stays at 85 bps, creating a €3M CVA loss that the hedge doesn't capture.

questions.question: What is the fundamental trade-off between granularity and stability when constructing generic credit curves, and how should a bank optimize this balance?
questions.answer_short: More granular curves (e.g., rating + sector + region) are more accurate but require more data points and are vulnerable to idiosyncratic volatility. Less granular curves (e.g., rating only) are more stable but less discriminating. Optimize by testing data sufficiency and P&L volatility.
questions.answer_long: Granular curves better distinguish counterparty-specific risks (e.g., Single-A US utilities vs. Single-A European telecoms trade at different spreads). However, granularity requires sufficient observable credits per bucket—sparse data means one credit's idiosyncratic moves contaminate the entire curve. For example, 'Single-A Asian Healthcare' may have only 2-3 observable CDS, making the curve unstable. Optimization requires: (1) statistical testing for sufficient data points per bucket (typically 10+ names minimum); (2) backtesting P&L volatility from curve updates; (3) analyzing hedge effectiveness for each granularity level; (4) consistency with capital model classification. Banks often use 3-4 granularity levels: rating + sector for liquid markets, rating + region for emerging markets.
questions.why_it_matters: Curve construction methodology drives CVA accuracy, P&L volatility, and hedge effectiveness for the majority of a bank's counterparty portfolio. Poor granularity choices create either significant mispricing (too coarse) or excessive volatility (too fine). Changes to the curve framework can create €10-50M P&L swings in large banks. Regulators scrutinize the statistical rigor and consistency with capital models.
common_traps: Creating 100+ curve buckets without checking data sufficiency—most buckets end up with 1-2 names and unstable spreads
Using different granularity for CVA pricing vs. capital calculation—creates inconsistency and regulatory issues
Over-fitting to current market structure—curves break when one or two observable credits default or become illiquid
questions.real_world_example: A bank initially constructs curves with rating + sector + region (7×10×7 = 490 buckets). Analysis shows 380 buckets have <3 observable credits. After a single-A European auto manufacturer defaults, all single-A European auto counterparties' CVA spikes 40% due to the granular curve, even though most are financially sound. The bank consolidates to rating + broad sector (50 buckets), reducing idiosyncratic volatility by 60% while maintaining 85% of pricing accuracy.

questions.question: What are the main advantages and disadvantages of using third-party generic credit curves (e.g., Markit sector curves) versus building proprietary curves in-house?
questions.answer_short: Third-party curves are cheaper, independent (audit-friendly), and consistent across users, but are rigid in classification and introduce uncontrollable volatility. Proprietary curves are flexible and optimized for the bank's portfolio but require significant infrastructure and are subject to scrutiny.
questions.answer_long: Third-party advantages: (1) lower cost—no need for dedicated quant team and systems; (2) independent—auditors view as objective; (3) industry-standard—facilitate comparison and pricing with counterparties. Disadvantages: (1) rigid classification—may not match bank's risk view or portfolio composition; (2) uncontrollable volatility—curve updates create P&L swings beyond bank control; (3) limited transparency—methodology may be black-box; (4) generic—not optimized for bank-specific hedge strategy or capital model. Proprietary curves offer full customization but require significant investment in data, analytics, and governance. Choice depends on bank size, portfolio complexity, and CVA materiality.
questions.why_it_matters: This decision impacts CVA infrastructure costs (€500k-€5M annually), P&L volatility, hedge effectiveness, and audit costs. Smaller banks often use third-party curves due to cost constraints, while large banks with complex portfolios and active CVA hedging require proprietary solutions. Understanding the trade-offs is critical for cost-benefit analysis and explaining CVA volatility to senior management.
common_traps: Assuming third-party curves are 'model-free'—they embed significant modeling assumptions and require validation
Using third-party curves without understanding the underlying methodology—creates unexplainable P&L volatility
Building proprietary curves without adequate governance and control framework—creates operational risk and audit issues
questions.real_world_example: A mid-sized European bank uses Markit sector curves, saving €2M annually versus building proprietary curves. However, when Markit changes its averaging methodology for financials, the bank experiences a €15M overnight CVA charge with no change in actual credit risk. Management demands explanation, but the bank has limited transparency into Markit's methodology. The bank subsequently builds a validation framework to anticipate such changes, adding back €500k annual costs.

questions.question: A bank has a 20-year exposure to a counterparty but only observes liquid CDS at 5Y and 10Y tenors. What are the risks of different extrapolation approaches beyond 10 years, and how might this impact CVA?
questions.answer_short: Linear extrapolation likely overstates long-term spreads (unrealistic perpetual widening). Flat extrapolation understates long-term deterioration. Both can create 30-50% CVA errors on long-dated trades. Better: use structural models, bond data, or prudent assumptions with sensitivity analysis.
questions.answer_long: Extrapolation beyond observable tenors is highly subjective and model-dependent. Options include: (1) Linear continuation—assumes constant spread steepening rate, implying unrealistic perpetual deterioration and likely overstating long-term default probability; (2) Flat extrapolation—assumes 10Y spread holds to all maturities, ignoring realistic long-term credit deterioration and understating risk; (3) Mean reversion—assumes spreads revert to some long-term average, requiring calibration; (4) Structural credit models—use fundamentals (leverage, volatility) to project long-term PDs. For a 20Y exposure with 5Y at 150 bps and 10Y at 250 bps, linear extrapolation gives 20Y at 450 bps, while flat gives 250 bps—the cumulative PD difference is 25-35%, creating massive CVA differences. Best practice: use multiple approaches, calibrate to any available long-dated bonds, apply prudent floors/caps, and show sensitivity to senior management.
questions.why_it_matters: Long-dated derivatives (e.g., inflation swaps, long-dated interest rate swaps, project finance derivatives) can have 20-40 year tenors. Extrapolation methodology can swing CVA by 40-60% for these trades, impacting pricing competitiveness and P&L. Regulators increasingly scrutinize long-dated curve extrapolation as a source of model risk. Poor extrapolation can create persistent CVA overcharging (losing business) or undercharging (risk accumulation).
common_traps: Linear extrapolation without bounds—can produce absurd spreads like 1,000+ bps at 30 years for IG credits
Flat extrapolation beyond 10Y—ignores that credit quality deteriorates over very long horizons for most corporates
Using equity-based structural models for banks and financials—doesn't capture regulatory intervention and bailout dynamics
questions.real_world_example: A bank prices a 25-year inflation swap with a AA-rated sovereign counterparty. The 10Y CDS is 80 bps. Using flat extrapolation (80 bps to 25Y) gives €5M CVA. Linear extrapolation from 5Y (60 bps) and 10Y (80 bps) projects 20Y at 120 bps and 25Y at 140 bps, giving €9M CVA—an 80% difference. Review of the sovereign's 30Y bond (trading at 95 bps spread) suggests flat extrapolation is more appropriate, but the bank uses 100 bps (splitting the difference) with ±€2M sensitivity disclosed.

questions.question: A bank has 30 BBB-rated European non-financial counterparties with no individual CDS. Should they map to iTraxx Europe Main or iTraxx Europe Crossover, and what are the implications for CVA and hedging?
questions.answer_short: Map to iTraxx Europe Main (125 IG names including many BBBs), not Crossover (sub-IG). Main provides appropriate spread level and liquid hedging. Crossover would overstate credit risk and create basis risk in hedges.
questions.answer_long: iTraxx Europe Main includes 125 investment-grade European credits (typically 40-50 BBB-rated) and is the standard for IG credit exposure. iTraxx Crossover includes 40 sub-investment-grade names with much wider spreads (typically 3-5x Main). For BBB counterparties, Main is appropriate because: (1) rating match—most Main constituents are A/BBB; (2) spread levels align—Main at ~80 bps vs. Crossover at ~300 bps; (3) hedge effectiveness—Main hedges provide tighter basis to actual BBB spreads. Using Crossover would overstate CVA by 2-3x and create negative carry on hedges (paying away 220 bps spread difference). Within Main, consider sector sub-indices if most counterparties are concentrated (e.g., all industrials), but Main overall is sufficiently liquid for efficient hedging.
questions.why_it_matters: Index selection directly impacts CVA size (up to 3x difference), hedge costs (200+ bps annual drag), and capital relief efficiency. Mapping BBB credits to Crossover is a common error in less sophisticated banks, creating systematic overpricing and business loss. Correct index mapping is essential for competitive pricing and efficient hedge portfolio management. Regulators also scrutinize index selection for appropriateness and consistency.
common_traps: Mapping all non-IG and stressed BBB credits to Crossover without considering individual circumstances—overstates risk
Using index spreads directly without basis adjustment for lower liquidity of individual counterparties
Ignoring sector composition of indices—e.g., Main is 30% financials, so mapping non-financial corporates requires adjustment
questions.real_world_example: A bank prices derivatives with 25 BBB-rated European industrial corporates. Initially, risk management maps to Crossover (280 bps 5Y), generating €18M CVA. Business complains they're uncompetitive versus peers. Analysis shows peers use Main (85 bps) with a +15 bps adjustment for liquidity, giving 100 bps total. Switching to this approach reduces CVA to €6M, enabling the bank to win €2B notional of new business at competitive pricing while maintaining appropriate credit charges.

questions.question: What is the difference between settled recovery and actual recovery for OTC derivatives, and why does this matter for CVA accounting and capital?
questions.answer_short: Settled recovery is achieved quickly (days/weeks) via CDS auction or bond trading. Actual recovery on derivatives comes through bankruptcy process (months/years) and is often higher. This creates timing differences in CVA adjustments and potentially different recovery assumptions for accounting vs. economic reality.
questions.answer_long: Settled recovery occurs immediately after a credit event through mechanisms like CDS auctions—creditors can monetize claims quickly by delivering bonds or participating in the auction. For derivatives, actual recovery requires: (1) agreement on net claim value across all netting sets; (2) resolution of collateral disputes; (3) bankruptcy court proceedings; (4) final distribution. This can take years. Lehman illustrated this: CDS auction settled at 8.6% recovery within weeks, but derivative counterparties received 30-40% over several years through the bankruptcy estate. For CVA accounting, IFRS 13 requires using market-observable recovery (CDS auction level initially), but actual recoveries may be higher, creating later positive CVA adjustments. For capital, regulators may require conservative (low) recovery assumptions regardless of later actual experience.
questions.why_it_matters: Recovery timing impacts CVA P&L recognition, hedge effectiveness, and capital forecasting. Using CDS auction recovery for initial CVA adjustment aligns with market hedges but may be economically conservative. Banks must decide whether to adjust CVA as bankruptcy proceeds (creating multi-year P&L impacts) or maintain conservative assumptions until final settlement. This also affects whether to sell derivative claims to distressed investors at settled recovery or hold for actual recovery.
common_traps: Assuming CVA recovery matches CDS hedge payout—derivatives often recover more but later, creating basis
Immediately adjusting CVA upward when bankruptcy recovery estimates improve—may not be consistent with exit price
Using historically high actual recoveries (e.g., Lehman 30-40%) as standard assumptions without accounting for specific circumstances
questions.real_world_example: When a European bank defaults in 2023, CDS auction settles at 12% recovery. A dealer bank has €80M net exposure and takes a €70.4M CVA charge (88% LGD). Over 3 years, bankruptcy process recovers 35%, providing additional €18.4M. The bank must decide: (1) hold claims and recognize €18.4M positive CVA adjustment over 3 years; or (2) sell claims at 20% recovery to a distressed fund for immediate €6.4M gain. Selling provides liquidity and certainty but leaves €12M on the table.

questions.question: How does the capital relief available from different hedge types (single-name CDS, proxy CDS, indices) impact a bank's overall credit curve mapping strategy, and what is changing under BCBS 2015 proposals?
questions.answer_short: Current Basel III gives full capital relief for direct single-name CDS, none for proxy single-name CDS, and partial (index-based formula) for indices. This biases banks toward index hedging even when single-name proxies are more accurate. BCBS 2015 proposes to allow proxy single-name CDS relief, which would encourage more precise hedging and mapping.
questions.answer_long: Under current CVA capital rules, only hedges that exactly match the counterparty (direct single-name CDS) or use approved indices get capital relief. Proxy single-name CDS—even when they're excellent credit substitutes (e.g., parent company, sister entity, same-sector peer)—get zero capital relief. This creates perverse incentives: banks map to indices (getting partial capital relief via the index formula in BCBS 2011) even when single-name proxies are more accurate and provide better spread hedges. The index formula typically gives 30-60% capital relief depending on the number of index constituents. BCBS 2015 proposes allowing capital relief for proxy single-name CDS (subject to supervisory approval), which would align hedging incentives with economic risk management. This would encourage banks to use more precise single-name proxies for mapping when available, improving CVA accuracy and hedge effectiveness.
questions.why_it_matters: Capital relief drives hedge strategy more than pure risk management for most banks—RWA optimization is critical for ROE. Current rules create systematic bias toward less accurate index hedges simply for capital treatment. This suboptimal hedging increases basis risk and reduces CVA quality. The BCBS 2015 proposals would be a significant improvement, potentially reducing CVA capital by 15-25% for banks with good proxy hedging programs while improving risk sensitivity. Banks need to prepare systems to identify, document, and justify proxy relationships for regulatory approval.
common_traps: Optimizing CVA hedges purely for capital relief without considering basis risk and P&L volatility—can create larger losses
Assuming BCBS 2015 proxy CDS relief will be automatic—will likely require formal supervisory approval with strict criteria
Using capital-relieved index hedges as justification for index-based mapping when better single-name data exists—creates audit issues
questions.real_world_example: A bank has €500M CVA exposure to the subsidiary of a large US corporate. Parent CDS trades at 120 bps (5Y), providing an excellent spread hedge with 0.95 correlation. CDX IG index is at 70 bps, with only 0.60 correlation to the subsidiary. Under current rules, parent CDS hedge gets zero capital relief (€40M RWA remains), while CDX hedge gets 40% relief (€24M RWA reduction). The bank reluctantly uses CDX, accepting higher basis risk for capital efficiency. When the subsidiary's sector faces stress, spreads widen to 250 bps while CDX moves to 85 bps—the parent CDS would have captured 80% of the move versus 20% for CDX, creating a €15M hedge loss that better mapping could have avoided.

questions.question: How do funding curves differ from credit curves in terms of construction and purpose, and why is FVA calculation more controversial than CVA?
questions.answer_short: Credit curves reflect market-implied default risk for CVA calculation. Funding curves reflect a bank's own borrowing costs for FVA calculation. FVA is controversial because funding costs are entity-specific, not market-observable, and there's debate over whether they represent exit price or bank-specific economics.
questions.answer_long: Credit curves use market observables (CDS, bonds) to derive risk-neutral default probabilities, representing tradeable risk that can be hedged. Funding curves represent a bank's cost of raising unsecured funding across different tenors, typically based on: (1) the bank's own CDS/bond spreads; (2) actual issuance costs; (3) internal funds transfer pricing. FVA is controversial because: (1) funding costs are entity-specific (AA bank vs. A bank have different costs); (2) they're not directly observable for all tenors; (3) accounting debate exists on whether funding costs represent exit price or just internal economics; (4) there's no natural hedge for funding spreads unlike CVA. FVA calculation requires subjective choices on funding tenor, inclusion of liquidity premiums, and whether to use own CDS or actual issuance costs.
questions.why_it_matters: FVA has become one of the largest xVA components for many banks, often exceeding CVA. Understanding the distinction from CVA is critical because FVA methodology is less standardized, more subjective, and faces ongoing accounting scrutiny. Different banks calculate FVA differently, creating competitive distortions. The funding curve construction methodology can swing FVA by 30-50%, directly impacting derivative pricing and profitability.
common_traps: Using the same curve for credit risk (CVA) and funding risk (FVA)—they represent different economics and different counterparties
Assuming FVA is universally accepted for accounting—debate continues, with IFRS not explicitly requiring it
Using a single funding curve for all transactions—should vary by funding tenor, collateral type, and potentially desk strategy
questions.real_world_example: A European bank's own 5Y CDS trades at 150 bps, but it can issue 5Y senior unsecured bonds at 120 bps (tight to CDS) and has depositor funding at 80 bps. For FVA, should it use 150 bps (CDS), 120 bps (issuance), or 80 bps (deposits)? Each choice creates 20-50 bps difference in funding curve, translating to €10-25M FVA on a €10B derivatives portfolio. The bank uses a blended approach (100 bps) based on actual marginal funding costs, but faces auditor questions about whether this represents true exit price.

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between a real-world default probability and a risk-neutral default probability?
questions.answer_short: Real-world default probability is estimated from historical default data, while risk-neutral default probability is derived from market prices (bonds, CDS) and includes a risk premium that investors demand for accepting credit risk.
questions.answer_long: A real-world default probability represents the actual expected frequency of default based on historical experience, typically mapped to credit ratings. A risk-neutral default probability is implied from market instruments like CDS spreads or bond yields, and systematically exceeds real-world probabilities because risk-averse investors demand compensation beyond expected losses. This risk premium accounts for uncertainty, liquidity concerns, and investor preferences. The difference is significant—for investment-grade credits, risk-neutral probabilities can be 5-16 times higher than real-world equivalents.
questions.why_it_matters: This distinction is crucial for CVA calculation—using real-world probabilities would drastically underestimate counterparty risk cost compared to market-implied pricing. Since Basel III and IFRS 13 require risk-neutral approaches, understanding this difference affects pricing, hedging, capital, and P&L volatility.
common_traps: Assuming real-world and risk-neutral probabilities are interchangeable—they differ by a factor of 2-17x depending on rating
Believing the risk premium only reflects default risk—it also captures liquidity, systematic risk, and market sentiment
Using historical default rates for market-traded derivatives without adjusting for the embedded risk premium
questions.real_world_example: A BBB-rated corporate has a 0.47% annual real-world default probability from historical data, but its 5-year CDS trades at 238 bps, implying a 2.38% annual risk-neutral probability (5x higher). A CVA desk using historical rates would underprice credit risk by 80% versus market-based valuation.

questions.question: Why have banks moved from using real-world to risk-neutral default probabilities for CVA calculation, even for illiquid counterparties?
questions.answer_short: Basel III capital rules and IFRS 13 accounting standards require market-observable inputs wherever possible, mandating risk-neutral (CDS-based) probabilities to ensure CVA represents exit price and aligns with regulatory capital calculations.
questions.answer_long: The shift to risk-neutral probabilities was driven by three forces: (1) IFRS 13 requires exit price valuation using market-observable inputs, (2) Basel III CVA capital charge explicitly references credit spreads rather than historical defaults, and (3) the development of CDS markets made credit risk tradeable. By 2012-2014, most major banks converged on risk-neutral methods even though many counterparties lack liquid CDS quotes. Regulators and auditors generally reject blended or historical approaches, requiring proxy spreads based on rating, region, and sector for illiquid names. This creates challenges around subjectivity in mapping and inability to hedge mapped credits.
questions.why_it_matters: This regulatory requirement fundamentally changed CVA from an actuarial reserve to a market-based valuation. It increased CVA volatility 2-10x, created demand for CVA hedging (even where unavailable), and made credit curve mapping a critical infrastructure for banks with thousands of illiquid counterparties.
common_traps: Attempting to use blended historical/risk-neutral approaches—regulators and auditors generally reject this
Assuming all counterparties have liquid CDS—most corporate/SME clients require proxy mapping
Treating risk-neutral probabilities as predictions of actual default—they're hedging prices, not forecasts
questions.real_world_example: A European bank has 3,000 corporate counterparties but only 150 have liquid CDS quotes. ECB's CVA challenger model requires all CVA to be benchmarked against CDS index curves with market-standard 60% LGD, forcing the bank to develop systematic mapping for 95% of its names despite no direct hedging ability.

questions.subtopic: Hazard rate approximation for default probability
questions.question: What is the standard approximation formula for converting a credit spread to an unconditional default probability for a single period, and what assumption does it make?
questions.answer_short: The approximation is PD(t_{i-1}, t_i) ≈ s_t × Δt / LGD, where s_t is the credit spread, Δt is the time period, and LGD is loss given default. It assumes a flat hazard rate over the period.
questions.answer_long: The standard approximation PD(t_{i-1}, t_i) ≈ s_t × Δt / LGD converts an observed credit spread into an unconditional default probability for a specific time period. This formula assumes that the hazard rate (instantaneous default intensity) is constant over the interval, which is reasonable for short periods but becomes less accurate when the credit curve is steeply sloped. The formula doesn't account for the shape of the credit curve prior to time t_{i-1}, so for more accurate calculations (especially for sloped curves), a bootstrapping procedure that builds cumulative survival probabilities forward in time should be used instead.
questions.why_it_matters: This formula is the workhorse for converting market CDS spreads into the marginal default probabilities needed for CVA calculations. Errors in this conversion directly affect CVA pricing—a 10% error in default probability translates roughly to a 10% error in CVA for that time bucket.
common_traps: Using this formula for long time periods—accuracy degrades with Δt, especially for non-flat curves
Forgetting to divide by LGD—this is essential since spreads reflect both probability and severity
Applying it to cumulative probabilities instead of marginal period-by-period defaults
questions.real_world_example: A 5-year BBB corporate CDS trades at 238 bps with 60% LGD. The annual default probability is approximately 238 bps × 1 year / 60% = 3.97%. For quarterly CVA calculation, you'd use 238 bps × 0.25 / 60% = 0.99% per quarter. The full bootstrapping approach might give 0.96% due to survival probability effects.

questions.question: How does the shape of a credit curve (flat, upward-sloping, inverted) affect the distribution of default probability over time, even when the 5-year cumulative default probability is identical?
questions.answer_short: An upward-sloping curve concentrates default probability in later years, while an inverted curve concentrates it in earlier years. A flat curve distributes default probability evenly. The 5-year cumulative can be identical across all three shapes.
questions.answer_long: Credit curve shape dramatically affects the time distribution of default risk through the bootstrapping process. Consider three curves all with 300 bps 5-year spread and 60% LGD (22.12% cumulative 5Y default probability): (1) Flat curve shows roughly constant annual default probabilities around 5%, (2) Upward-sloping curve (e.g., 100→500 bps) shows increasing annual probabilities from ~2% to ~8%, implying stressed future conditions, (3) Inverted curve (500→100 bps) shows decreasing probabilities from ~8% to ~2%, implying near-term stress. The shape beyond observable tenors (e.g., extrapolating to 10Y) becomes highly sensitive to assumptions about curve continuation.
questions.why_it_matters: For CVA, the timing of default matters enormously because exposure profiles vary over time. A long-dated swap may have peak exposure at year 5—if an inverted curve puts most default probability in year 1, CVA will be much lower than if an upward curve puts it at year 5. Incorrect curve shape can cause 30-50% CVA errors.
common_traps: Using only a single credit spread point and assuming flat hazard rates—this ignores valuable term structure information
Interpolating credit spreads linearly and assuming this gives correct default probabilities—PD requires bootstrapping
