Extrapolating beyond observed tenors without considering what curve shape implies about credit deterioration
questions.real_world_example: A bank has 10-year interest rate swaps with a corporate whose 5Y CDS is 300 bps. If they assume a flat curve, they use ~5% annual PD throughout. But if the actual curve is inverted (1Y=500bps, 5Y=300bps), year 1 PD should be ~8% and year 5 only ~3%. If exposure peaks at year 5 due to forward rate volatility, the flat assumption overstates CVA by 40%.

questions.subtopic: Loss given default and recovery rates
questions.question: What is the relationship between Loss Given Default (LGD) and recovery rate, and what is the standard market convention for senior unsecured debt?
questions.answer_short: LGD = 1 - Recovery Rate. Standard market convention for senior unsecured debt is 60% LGD (40% recovery rate), which is the assumption embedded in most CDS contracts like iTraxx Europe and CDX NA.
questions.answer_long: Loss Given Default represents the percentage loss experienced when a counterparty defaults, while recovery rate is the percentage recovered. The relationship is simply LGD = 1 - R. Market convention for OTC derivatives, which typically rank pari passu with senior unsecured debt, is 60% LGD (40% recovery). This matches standard CDS contracts. However, actual recovery rates vary widely by sector, seniority, and economic conditions—as shown by 2008 recoveries ranging from 0.1% (Glitnir subordinated) to 99.9% (Fannie Mae subordinated due to delivery squeeze). The CDS-settled recovery and actual derivative workout recovery can differ substantially, as Lehman showed with ~9% CDS auction versus 30-40% eventual derivative recoveries due to the lengthy bankruptcy process.
questions.why_it_matters: LGD directly scales default probability impact on CVA. However, there's a partial cancellation effect in CVA calculation (covered in Chapter 14) that reduces LGD sensitivity. Still, using 60% versus 40% LGD changes the implied default probability from a spread by 50%, which then affects CVA proportionally for unhedged positions.
common_traps: Confusing LGD with probability of default—they're separate components of credit risk
Using CDS-auction recovery rates for derivatives without considering the actual workout timeline difference
Applying subordinated debt recovery assumptions to senior derivative claims or vice versa
questions.real_world_example: A bank calculates CVA on Lehman derivatives using the 8.6% CDS auction recovery (91.4% LGD). However, through the bankruptcy process over several years, they ultimately recover 35% (65% LGD). The actual credit loss was 30% lower than the market-implied CVA suggested, though mark-to-market losses occurred immediately at the auction recovery level.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'settled recovery' and 'actual recovery' for OTC derivatives, and why does this matter for CVA versus credit loss provisioning?
questions.answer_short: Settled recovery is the market value achieved quickly after default (e.g., via CDS auction), while actual recovery is received after the full bankruptcy process (potentially years later). Settled recovery determines CVA mark-to-market losses; actual recovery determines final economic losses.
questions.answer_long: Settled recovery represents the value that could be achieved shortly after a credit event by participating in the CDS auction or selling bonds in the secondary market—this typically occurs within days or weeks. Actual recovery for bilateral OTC derivatives is the amount ultimately received after the bankruptcy process completes, which may take many years due to the complexity of netting calculations, collateral disputes, and priority negotiations. For CVA accounting purposes, the settled recovery (market price) creates immediate mark-to-market losses. However, the actual recovery determines the true economic loss. The Lehman case exemplifies this: 9% CDS auction recovery caused immediate CVA write-downs, but actual derivative recoveries of 30-40% meant ultimate losses were much smaller—though the P&L impact was spread over many years.
questions.why_it_matters: This distinction affects CVA volatility, hedging strategy, and capital planning. Banks must recognize mark-to-market losses based on settled recovery immediately, creating potential liquidity stress. However, actual recoveries may be better, especially if the bank can offset derivative claims against other assets or use legal set-off rights. This timing mismatch creates accounting volatility even when economic losses are moderate.
common_traps: Assuming CDS auction recovery represents the final economic outcome for derivatives—it's just the market price
Not reserving for the possibility that actual recovery differs from settled recovery due to netting complexities
Using actual recovery experience to set CVA when accounting requires market-observable (settled) recovery
questions.real_world_example: When Lehman defaulted, a dealer bank held $500M notional of interest rate swaps with positive mark-to-market of $50M. The CDS auction settled at 8.625%, implying a $45.7M loss. The bank's CVA desk immediately recognized this loss. However, after 4 years of bankruptcy proceedings and netting calculations, the bank ultimately recovered $32.5M (65% recovery), making the actual loss only $17.5M—but this was recognized gradually over time.

questions.question: Why is credit curve mapping particularly challenging for banks compared to end-users, and what are the key trade-offs in choosing a mapping methodology?
questions.answer_short: Banks have thousands of counterparties (many illiquid SMEs/corporates without CDS), while end-users trade with few banks that have liquid CDS. The key trade-off is between mapping accuracy versus hedgeability and capital relief.
questions.answer_long: Banks face a fundamentally different challenge than end-users: they may have thousands of derivative counterparties, most of whom are relatively small entities (corporates, SMEs, regional governments) without liquid CDS quotes, bond prices, or even external ratings. End-users typically trade with 5-20 dealer banks, all of which have liquid single-name CDS. For illiquid names, banks must choose between: (1) single-name proxies that may be good credit representations but don't provide capital relief under current Basel III rules, (2) liquid CDS indices that provide hedgeability and capital relief but may be poor fundamental matches, or (3) illiquid instruments like secondary bond prices that match the credit but can't be hedged. Regional challenges compound this—Asian banks have far less credit market data than European/US banks.
questions.why_it_matters: Poor credit curve mapping creates multiple risks: mispriced CVA (potentially 30-100% errors), unhedgeable CVA volatility, regulatory capital penalties, and audit challenges. For a large bank with $1-2 trillion notional and 5,000 counterparties, systematic mapping errors of 50 bps translate to hundreds of millions in CVA mispricing. The choice also affects whether CVA hedges attract capital relief.
common_traps: Optimizing for capital relief over accuracy—using index hedges that don't match the actual credit risk
Creating too-granular classifications with insufficient data points—this introduces idiosyncratic noise
Not distinguishing between liquidity for pricing versus liquidity for hedging—they're different requirements
questions.real_world_example: A European bank has exposure to 200 single-A rated German mid-cap corporates (Mittelstand). Only 5 have CDS quotes. They could map all 200 to iTraxx Europe Main (liquid, hedgeable, capital relief) but this is BBB average. Or map to iTraxx Non-Financial (better, but still diverse). Or use the 5 liquid names to create a German single-A corporate curve (most accurate, but based on limited data and not hedgeable).

questions.question: What are the main CDS indices used for credit curve mapping in Europe, and how do they differ by credit quality and entity type?
questions.answer_short: Main European indices are iTraxx Europe (125 investment-grade names), iTraxx Non-Financials (100 BBB+ corporates), iTraxx Crossover (40 sub-investment grade), iTraxx Financials (senior/sub), and iTraxx SovX (sovereigns by region). They segment by rating and sector.
questions.answer_long: The European CDS index family provides several mapping tools: (1) iTraxx Europe Main contains 125 of the most liquid investment-grade credits across all sectors, (2) iTraxx Non-Financials focuses on 100 corporate credits rated BBB or better, (3) iTraxx Crossover covers 40 sub-investment grade credits with wider spreads, (4) iTraxx High Volatility contains the 30 widest spread names from the main index, (5) iTraxx Financials separates into senior and subordinated debt of financial institutions, and (6) iTraxx SovX covers sovereign credits by region (Western Europe, CEEMEA, Asia Pacific, etc.). These indices trade at 3Y, 5Y, 7Y, and 10Y maturities, with 5Y being most liquid. The US equivalent is CDX North America with similar structure.
questions.why_it_matters: These indices form the foundation of generic credit curve mapping. They're the most liquid credit instruments (often more liquid than single-name CDS), provide spreadable hedging instruments, and offer partial capital relief under Basel III. Understanding their composition ensures appropriate mapping—for example, using iTraxx Main (average BBB rating) for single-A corporates would systematically overprice CVA.
common_traps: Using iTraxx Europe Main for all corporates—it includes financials and has BBB average rating
Assuming index liquidity equals constituent liquidity—index may trade while single-names don't
Forgetting that indices rebalance semi-annually—historical spreads may not reflect consistent credits
questions.real_world_example: A CVA desk needs to map a portfolio of 50 unrated German industrial companies. Their internal ratings average single-A. They choose iTraxx Europe Non-Financials (average A/BBB) as the base curve, then add a 30bp premium based on their assessment that unrated Mittelstand companies are slightly riskier than large-cap rated industrials. This index hedge will attract capital relief under Basel III standardized approach.

questions.subtopic: Standard LGD assumptions in credit curves
questions.question: When would it be appropriate to use an LGD different from the standard 60% assumption when mapping credit curves for CVA calculation?
questions.answer_short: When there is structural seniority (e.g., derivatives with SPVs ranking super-senior), credit enhancements beyond standard collateral, or documented recovery experience that auditors will accept. Generally, deviations from 60% require strong justification.
questions.answer_long: The standard 60% LGD assumption (40% recovery) embedded in CDS contracts is appropriate for pari passu senior unsecured claims, which describes most OTC derivatives. However, deviations may be justified in specific cases: (1) Structural seniority—derivatives with securitization SPVs may rank super-senior to other claims, justifying lower LGD (e.g., 30-40%), (2) Credit enhancements—guarantees or collateral beyond variation margin might improve recovery (though margin should be modeled in exposure, not LGD), (3) Documented recovery experience—some banks have consistently achieved better recoveries due to effective workout processes, though auditors require strong evidence. It's generally not acceptable to use lower LGD simply because Lehman derivatives recovered more than the CDS auction suggested, without systematic evidence. Recovery locks/swaps don't trade, so market-implied LGD is unavailable except for distressed names.
questions.why_it_matters: LGD directly affects the conversion from credit spread to default probability. Using 40% LGD instead of 60% increases implied default probability by 50% (since PD ≈ spread/LGD), which proportionally increases CVA for unhedged positions. However, the CVA cancellation effect (Chapter 14) moderates this impact. Auditor acceptance is critical—unjustified LGD assumptions create audit adjustments.
common_traps: Using favorable LGD assumptions based on single instances like Lehman without systematic evidence
Double-counting collateral by both modeling it in exposure simulation and using lower LGD
Applying subordinated debt LGD (e.g., 75%) to derivatives that rank pari passu with senior debt
questions.real_world_example: A bank has derivatives embedded in a CLO structure where the derivative explicitly ranks senior to the AAA notes, effectively making it super-senior. Legal analysis confirms this would result in ~20% LGD versus 60% standard. The bank uses 20% LGD for CVA after obtaining auditor approval with legal documentation. This reduces the implied default probability from the CLO's spread by 67%, lowering CVA by the same proportion.

questions.question: Walk through the decision process for mapping the credit curve of a mid-sized unrated Brazilian steel manufacturer, considering liquidity, hedgeability, and capital relief. What are the trade-offs at each step?
questions.answer_short: Check for: (1) liquid single-name CDS (unlikely) → (2) liquid benchmark like bonds (maybe illiquid) → (3) single-name proxy like parent or sector peer (possible but no capital relief) → (4) generic proxy via rating/region/sector. Likely outcome: map to EM corporate index with basis adjustment.
questions.answer_long: Following the decision tree: (1) Liquid CDS check—unlikely for mid-sized Brazilian corporate, move to next step, (2) Bond benchmark—may exist but illiquid secondary market, would need to derive spread with basis adjustment to CDS-equivalent, (3) Single-name proxy—could use a larger Brazilian steel company (e.g., Gerdau) if their CDS trades, or the Brazilian sovereign CDS plus corporate spread premium; this gives a spread hedge but no default hedge and currently no capital relief under Basel III standardized approach, (4) Generic proxy—map to CDX Emerging Markets index (14 credits) or create a Brazilian corporate curve from available EM credits, then adjust for sector (industrials are typically tighter than EM sovereign). The practical choice is likely (3) or (4): use Brazilian sovereign CDS + 150bp corporate premium as single-name proxy, or map to CDX EM with basis adjustment. The trade-off: single-name proxy is more accurate but no capital relief; generic index proxy is less accurate but provides hedgeability and partial capital relief. Most banks would use the generic approach and monitor basis risk.
questions.why_it_matters: This decision directly impacts CVA pricing accuracy, P&L volatility, hedging effectiveness, and regulatory capital. For a $500M notional portfolio, a 50bp mapping error translates to roughly $1-2M CVA mispricing. The hedgeability choice affects whether CVA volatility can be managed, and the capital relief choice affects whether the hedge reduces RWA or just P&L volatility.
common_traps: Choosing the most liquid instrument without checking fundamental credit match—liquidity ≠ accuracy
Using parent company CDS without confirming there's no explicit guarantee (creates basis risk)
Mapping to Brazilian sovereign without adding appropriate corporate spread premium
Not documenting the decision process and assumptions—auditors will challenge undocumented choices
questions.real_world_example: A European bank has $300M derivative exposure to a mid-sized Brazilian manufacturer. No single-name CDS exists. They initially map to Brazilian sovereign CDS (trading ~250bps) but auditors challenge this as too tight for corporate risk. They add a 100bp premium based on historical corporate-sovereign spreads in Brazil during stressed periods, arriving at 350bps. They hedge 50% with CDX EM index (trading ~320bps) which provides capital relief. The 30bp basis risk is accepted as the cost of getting regulatory capital benefit.

questions.question: What is the fundamental trade-off between granularity and data availability when constructing generic credit curves, and how should this balance be struck?
questions.answer_short: More granular classification (e.g., single-A US utilities) better distinguishes counterparties but provides fewer data points, risking idiosyncratic volatility. Broader classification (e.g., single-A) has more data but less differentiation. Optimal granularity requires sufficient liquid quotes (typically 3-5 minimum) per bucket.
questions.answer_long: Generic curve construction faces a fundamental tension: granular categorization (e.g., rating + region + sector) creates curves that better distinguish between different counterparty types, but each category has fewer observable data points for calibration. With sparse data, individual credits' idiosyncratic movements create unrealistic volatility in the generic curve that affects many counterparties. Conversely, broad categorization (e.g., only by rating) provides many data points for robust calibration but fails to distinguish, say, between US tech companies and European utilities. Best practice suggests each category should have at least 3-5 liquid observable points; otherwise, the granularity should be reduced. Even the standard regulator-suggested categorization of 7 ratings × 7 regions × 3 sectors = 147 combinations cannot be fully populated with liquid CDS data globally, requiring interpolation or extrapolation across some dimensions.
questions.why_it_matters: Curve construction methodology affects CVA for hundreds or thousands of counterparties simultaneously. Too granular with sparse data creates CVA volatility from individual credit noise. Too broad causes systematic mispricing across sectors or regions. For a bank with 2,000 counterparties mapped to generic curves, the methodology determines whether CVA volatility is 20% or 200% annually in P&L terms.
common_traps: Creating highly granular classifications that sound sophisticated but have 0-1 data points per bucket
Not monitoring how many counterparties map to each generic curve—some may be used for 500 names, others for 2
Using outdated classification schemes that don't reflect current market structure or liquidity
questions.real_world_example: A bank creates separate generic curves for 'Single-A European Telecommunications' based on 2 observable CDS (Deutsche Telekom, Telefonica). One name has idiosyncratic widening of 100bps due to M&A announcement. This causes the generic curve to widen 50bps, affecting CVA for 30 telecom counterparties, most of which have no M&A activity. The CVA desk takes a €5M P&L hit from noise. They redesign to use 'Single-A European Corporates' with 15 observable points, which dampens individual name noise.

questions.question: What are the advantages and disadvantages of using third-party generic credit curves (like Markit sector curves) versus building proprietary curves in-house?
questions.answer_short: Third-party curves offer independence (auditor-friendly) and lower cost, but are rigid in classification and behavior is outside user control. In-house curves allow customization and control but require infrastructure investment and may face auditor scrutiny.
questions.answer_long: Third-party providers like Markit offer sector curves across ratings and industries based on systematic averaging of liquid single-name CDS spreads with defined interpolation and extrapolation rules. Advantages: (1) independence valued by auditors, (2) lower cost than building infrastructure, (3) transparent methodology, (4) consistent with external valuations. Disadvantages: (1) rigid classification may not match bank's exposure profile (e.g., a regional bank needs local granularity not provided), (2) MTM volatility is determined by provider's methodology not the bank's risk management needs, (3) no ability to incorporate bank-specific information or adjust for known issues, (4) dependency on external provider. In-house curves offer customization to actual exposure concentrations, control over volatility through methodological choices, and ability to integrate with internal ratings. However, they require significant technology/data investment and face auditor questions about objectivity and independence.
questions.why_it_matters: The choice affects operational cost (third-party is simpler), CVA volatility (methodology determines behavior), audit outcomes (third-party simplifies defense), and business flexibility (in-house allows customization). For smaller banks, third-party solutions may be the only practical option. For large banks with concentrated exposures, customized in-house curves may be essential for accurate CVA.
common_traps: Assuming third-party curves are 'right' because they're external—they're just a consistent methodology
Building in-house curves that are so customized they can't be defended to auditors as market-based
Not stress-testing whether third-party curve classifications match your actual counterparty distribution
questions.real_world_example: A mid-sized European bank uses Markit sector curves for 80% of counterparties (standardized, auditor-accepted). However, they have concentrated exposure to German Sparkassen (regional savings banks) which don't fit Markit's financial institution categories well. They build a custom 'German Sparkassen' curve from 5 local bank CDS quotes plus Landesbank spreads, and document the methodology for auditors. This hybrid approach balances cost, accuracy, and auditability.

questions.question: What are the risks of extrapolating credit spreads beyond the last liquid tenor (e.g., from 10Y to 20Y), and what assumptions could a practitioner make? How would you validate the choice?
questions.answer_short: Extrapolation risks include assuming unrealistic credit deterioration or improvement beyond observed data. Common approaches: flat extrapolation (constant spread), flat hazard rate (increasing spread), or mean reversion. Validation requires stress-testing CVA sensitivity and comparing to similar long-dated credits if available.
questions.answer_long: Extrapolating beyond the last liquid tenor (typically 10Y for CDS) is necessary for long-dated derivatives but highly uncertain. Options include: (1) Flat spread—assumes constant credit spread beyond 10Y, implying hazard rate declines over time (since cumulative survival probability decreases), often seen as optimistic, (2) Flat hazard rate—implies credit spread increases to maintain constant instantaneous default intensity, more conservative, (3) Mean reversion—spreads gradually revert to long-term average, requires assumptions about reversion speed and level, (4) Forward rate analogy—extrapolate spread curve similar to interest rate forward curves, problematic since credit isn't arbitrage-free like rates. The choice materially affects long-dated CVA: for a 20Y swap with exposure peaking at 15Y, flat spread versus flat hazard rate can differ by 30-50% in CVA. Validation approaches: (1) test sensitivity of total CVA to extrapolation method—if 10Y+ exposures are small, it doesn't matter much, (2) compare to any available long-dated instruments (even if illiquid), (3) use regulatory stress scenarios to bound the range, (4) peer benchmarking if available.
questions.why_it_matters: Long-dated derivatives (especially inflation swaps, long-dated cross-currency swaps, and pension hedges) can have significant exposure beyond 10 years. Extrapolation assumptions directly determine CVA for these trades. A bank with $50B notional in 15-30Y swaps could have CVA differences of $50-100M based purely on extrapolation methodology. This also affects XVA pricing and competitiveness in long-dated markets.
common_traps: Using flat spread extrapolation without realizing it implies decreasing default probability per year—often unrealistic
Applying interpolation methods (like cubic splines) to extrapolation—this often produces nonsensical shapes
Not stress-testing CVA sensitivity to extrapolation assumptions before setting policy
Extrapolating inverted curves flatly—if 10Y spread is below 5Y, flat extrapolation implies long-term improvement that may be unrealistic
questions.real_world_example: A pension fund trades a 30Y inflation swap with a dealer bank. The counterparty is BBB-rated with liquid CDS to 10Y (450bps). The bank must extrapolate to 30Y. Option A: flat spread at 450bps gives cumulative 30Y default probability of 56%. Option B: flat hazard rate (7.5% annual) gives 30Y spread of 550bps and cumulative probability of 81%. Option C: mean reversion to long-term BBB average of 300bps gives 30Y probability of 51%. The CVA differs by €3M across methods on €100M notional. The bank chooses flat hazard rate (conservative, defendable) and discloses the sensitivity in their methodology documentation.

questions.subtopic: CDS-bond basis and choice of reference instrument
questions.question: When both CDS spreads and bond yields are available for a counterparty, which should be used for CVA calculation and why? What drives the CDS-bond basis?
questions.answer_short: CDS spreads should generally be preferred because they represent clean default risk, are more liquid, and match hedging instruments. Bonds include factors like funding costs, repo specialness, and liquidity premia that aren't pure credit risk. The CDS-bond basis arises from these technical factors.
questions.answer_long: When both instruments exist, CDS is generally preferred for CVA because: (1) it's a cleaner credit instrument—the premium directly represents credit risk without embedded funding costs, (2) it's typically more liquid, providing better price discovery, (3) it matches the hedging instrument banks actually use (buying CDS protection), (4) it aligns with regulatory requirements (Basel III references CDS explicitly), (5) accounting standards prefer market-based observable instruments, and CDS is the credit derivative market. Bond yields reflect credit spread but also include: (i) issuer's funding costs, (ii) repo specialness (some bonds are expensive to borrow, depressing yields), (iii) liquidity/bid-ask spreads, (iv) supply/demand technicals, (v) coupon effects. The CDS-bond basis is the difference between CDS premium and asset-swap spread (bond yield vs. swap curve). This basis has been persistently positive (CDS wider than bonds) since the financial crisis, ranging from 10-100+ bps, driven by collateralized bond financing being cheaper than unsecured CDS margin requirements, bank deleveraging reducing CDS dealer capacity, and CVA desk demand for CDS protection. Despite this basis, CDS remains the standard for CVA.
questions.why_it_matters: Instrument choice affects CVA level, hedging effectiveness, and regulatory capital. Using bonds when available CDS trades 50bps wider would understate CVA by 10-20% for some credits. More importantly, if you price CVA off bonds but hedge with CDS, you lock in a loss equal to the basis. The CDS-bond basis also creates arbitrage opportunities for relative value traders but represents real risk for CVA desks.
common_traps: Using bond yields because they're 'tighter' and give lower CVA—this creates hedge basis risk
Not adjusting bond yields for funding/repo effects when deriving credit spreads (asset swap spread is better than raw yield)
Assuming CDS-bond basis represents model error or mispricing—it's often driven by rational economic factors
Using illiquid bond prices without checking if the quote is actually tradeable or indicative
questions.real_world_example: A bank calculates CVA on a portfolio with a large European utility. The 5Y bond trades at 180bps ASW spread (asset swap spread), while 5Y CDS trades at 230bps—a 50bp basis. Using the bond spread would reduce CVA by ~$2M on a $200M exposure portfolio. However, the bank hedges with CDS at 230bps. If they price at 180bps but hedge at 230bps, they lock in a 50bp loss on the hedge. They use 230bps CDS for CVA, resulting in higher CVA charge but aligned hedge economics.

questions.subtopic: Single-name proxy methodology and capital relief
questions.question: Why do single-name proxy CDS hedges (e.g., using a parent company CDS to hedge subsidiary risk) currently not attract capital relief under Basel III standardized CVA charge, and what are the implications for hedge strategy?
questions.answer_short: Basel III standardized approach only recognizes hedges with the exact reference entity or approved indices. Single-name proxies don't match either category. This forces banks to choose between accurate hedging (no capital relief) or capital relief (less accurate index hedges), creating inefficiency.
questions.answer_long: Under the Basel III standardized CVA capital charge (Section 8.7.3), only two hedge types attract capital relief: (1) single-name CDS referencing the exact counterparty in the CVA calculation, and (2) approved credit indices (e.g., iTraxx, CDX). Single-name proxies—such as using a parent company CDS when the subsidiary is the counterparty, or using a similar peer company's CDS—provide spread hedging and potentially good fundamental correlation, but don't meet the regulatory recognition criteria. The rationale is that proxy hedges don't eliminate jump-to-default risk (basis risk remains if subsidiary defaults but parent doesn't) and correlation isn't perfect. However, BCBS (2015) has proposed allowing proxy single-name CDS to attract capital relief in recognition of their hedging value. Current implications: (1) banks face a choice between economically optimal hedges (proxies) with no capital benefit, versus capital-efficient hedges (indices) that may be poor fundamental matches, (2) this creates situations where hedging increases capital (hedge cost + no RWA reduction), reducing willingness to hedge CVA volatility, (3) banks may warehouse proxy-hedged CVA risk rather than getting capital relief, increasing systemic risk.
questions.why_it_matters: This regulatory treatment creates significant operational tension: CVA desks want to minimize economic risk through best-available hedges, but capital teams want to minimize RWA through recognized hedges. For large portfolios, the capital impact can exceed the P&L impact—a $100M CVA position might require $8M in capital under standardized approach; if a proxy hedge reduces CVA volatility by 80% but gets zero capital relief, the capital cost outweighs the volatility benefit.
common_traps: Hedging with single-name proxies assuming capital relief will be available—it won't under current rules
Using parent company CDS without checking if there's an explicit guarantee (which might make it the actual counterparty)
Not quantifying the capital cost of hedge strategies before implementation—hedging could increase total cost
Assuming all index hedges automatically qualify—only specific approved indices attract capital relief
questions.real_world_example: A bank has $500M CVA exposure to a wholly-owned subsidiary of a major corporate. The subsidiary has no CDS, but the parent trades at 200bps (5Y). The bank could: (1) Hedge with parent CDS—reduces spread risk by ~90%, but zero capital relief; CVA RWA remains $40M, requiring $4M capital; hedge costs $1M annually. (2) Hedge with iTraxx Non-Financials at 180bps—basis risk of 20bps remains, plus default correlation is weaker, but gets 50% capital relief; CVA RWA drops to $20M, requiring $2M capital. Despite worse economic hedge, option 2 saves $2M in capital cost, making it preferable from a total cost perspective.

questions.question: A bank has CVA exposure to 100 single-A European corporates with no liquid CDS. They can hedge with: (A) iTraxx Non-Financials index (BBB average), or (B) 10 single-name CDS proxies of similar companies. Compare these strategies considering P&L volatility, capital relief, and hedge effectiveness. What would you recommend?
questions.answer_short: Strategy A provides capital relief but significant basis risk (single-A vs BBB). Strategy B provides better hedge but no capital relief. Recommendation: use blended approach—hedge 60% with index (capital relief) and 40% with proxies (volatility reduction), optimizing total cost including P&L volatility and capital charges.
questions.answer_long: Full analysis: Strategy A (Index Hedge): iTraxx Non-Financials is BBB-rated average versus single-A portfolio, creating ~30-50bp systematic basis. Correlation in spread moves ~70%, so 30% residual volatility remains. However, gets ~60% capital relief under standardized approach, reducing RWA from say $100M to $40M (saving ~$6M in required capital). Strategy B (Proxy Hedges): 10 similar single-name CDS correlate better (~85%) with the 100 counterparties, creating only ~15% residual volatility—much better P&L hedge. But zero capital relief under current rules, keeping RWA at $100M. If annual CVA volatility is $20M, Strategy A leaves $6M P&L volatility but saves $6M capital cost. Strategy B leaves $3M P&L volatility but saves zero capital. Optimal solution: Blended approach hedges systematic spread risk with index (60% weight) to get capital relief, and hedges residual idiosyncratic risk with single-name proxies (40% weight) to reduce P&L volatility. This achieves ~35% capital relief (~$3.5M saving) while reducing P&L volatility to ~$4M (from $20M unhedged). The blend optimizes total economic cost = P&L volatility cost + capital cost - capital relief. Weights should be optimized based on relative costs.
questions.why_it_matters: This trade-off is fundamental to CVA desk strategy and affects billions in hedge notional across the industry. Optimal hedging isn't just about minimizing P&L volatility—it requires balancing volatility reduction, capital relief, and hedge costs. Banks that ignore capital relief may over-hedge with expensive proxies; banks that focus only on capital relief may accept excessive P&L volatility. The optimal blend depends on: (1) cost of capital, (2) cost of P&L volatility (management tolerance, impact on bonus pools), (3) relative hedge costs, (4) regulatory environment.
common_traps: Optimizing purely for P&L hedging without considering capital impact—total cost may increase
Optimizing purely for capital relief without considering residual P&L volatility—may create unacceptable earnings volatility
Not rebalancing the hedge blend as market conditions change (e.g., if single-name proxies become more expensive)
Using equal weighting between strategies without quantifying optimal allocation based on marginal costs
questions.real_world_example: A European bank has €2B CVA exposure to single-A EU corporates, creating €15M CVA volatility (1% vol). Unhedged CVA RWA is €160M (€16M capital at 10% ratio). Option 1: Full iTraxx hedge costs €4M annually, reduces volatility to €5M, provides €10M capital relief (net benefit = €11M volatility reduction + €10M capital relief - €4M cost = €17M). Option 2: Full proxy hedge costs €8M annually, reduces volatility to €2M, zero capital relief (net benefit = €13M volatility reduction - €8M cost = €5M). Option 3: 70% iTraxx + 30% proxies costs €5.2M, reduces volatility to €3.5M, capital relief €7M (net benefit = €11.5M volatility reduction + €7M capital relief - €5.2M cost = €13.3M). The blended approach is optimal.

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between a real-world default probability and a risk-neutral default probability?
questions.answer_short: Real-world PD is estimated from historical default data, while risk-neutral PD is derived from market prices (like CDS or bonds) and includes a risk premium demanded by investors.
questions.answer_long: A real-world default probability represents the actual expected likelihood of default based on historical data for similar credits. A risk-neutral default probability is extracted from market instruments like CDS spreads or bond yields and is systematically higher because it includes a risk premium - compensation that risk-averse investors demand for bearing default risk. Empirical studies show risk-neutral PDs are typically 2-17 times higher than real-world PDs, especially for high-quality credits.
questions.why_it_matters: This distinction is crucial for CVA calculation. Using real-world PDs underestimates market CVA values and creates inconsistencies with hedging strategies. Modern practice requires risk-neutral PDs for fair value accounting and regulatory capital, making this a foundational concept for any XVA practitioner.
common_traps: Assuming the two probabilities are interchangeable or similar in magnitude
Using historical default rates when market-implied values are required for accounting or regulatory purposes
Not understanding that the difference is larger for better-quality credits (can be 10-15x for AA/AAA)
questions.real_world_example: A bank calculates CVA on a portfolio with an A-rated corporate. The real-world 1-year PD might be 0.13%, but the risk-neutral PD from CDS spreads is 1.28% - nearly 10 times higher. Using the wrong measure would massively undervalue CVA and create P&L surprises when hedging.

questions.question: How do you calculate the annual default probability from a credit spread using the simple approximation formula?
questions.answer_short: PD ≈ (spread × Δt) / LGD, where spread is in decimal form, Δt is the time period (typically 1 year), and LGD is loss given default (e.g., 0.60 for 60%).
questions.answer_long: The simple formula PD(t, t+Δt) ≈ s(t) × Δt / LGD converts a credit spread into an unconditional default probability for the period. For example, with a 300bp (3%) spread and 60% LGD, the 1-year PD = 0.03 × 1 / 0.60 = 5%. This approximation assumes constant hazard rate and neglects discounting effects, making it less accurate for steep credit curves or very short periods.
questions.why_it_matters: This is the most common calculation CVA desks perform daily. Every credit spread observation needs converting to default probability for exposure weighting. Even though more sophisticated bootstrapping methods exist, this approximation is used extensively for speed and simplicity in production systems.
common_traps: Forgetting to convert basis points to decimal (300bp = 0.03, not 300)
Using the wrong LGD assumption - market standard is often 60% but varies by instrument
Not recognizing this gives unconditional PD, which differs from conditional survival probability
questions.real_world_example: A CVA analyst needs to calculate quarterly default probabilities for 500 counterparties. Using this formula with interpolated CDS spreads at each quarter and standard 60% LGD allows rapid calculation. For a BBB credit with 5Y spread of 400bp, annual PD ≈ 6.7%.

questions.subtopic: Credit Curve Shape and Term Structure
questions.question: Why does the shape of a credit curve (flat, upward-sloping, or inverted) significantly affect calculated default probabilities even when the 5-year spread is identical?
questions.answer_short: The curve shape determines how default risk is distributed across time. An upward-sloping curve implies lower near-term default probability but higher long-term risk, while an inverted curve suggests imminent stress with higher near-term default probability.
questions.answer_long: Three credit curves with identical 5-year spreads of 300bp produce vastly different default probability profiles. An upward-sloping curve might show 2% 1Y PD rising to 8% 5Y PD (deteriorating credit quality over time). An inverted curve might show 8% 1Y PD falling to 2% 5Y PD (near-term distress expected to resolve). A flat curve shows constant ~5% annual PD. The cumulative 5Y default probability remains around 22% for all three, but the timing and quarterly distribution differs dramatically, affecting CVA calculations where exposure timing matters.
questions.why_it_matters: CVA is exposure-weighted by time-dependent default probability. For trades with peak exposure in early years (e.g., forward starting swaps), an inverted curve produces much higher CVA than an upward curve. Practitioners who ignore curve shape and use only spot spreads can misprice CVA by 30-50%.
common_traps: Using only a single tenor (like 5Y) spread and assuming flat hazard rates across all maturities
Not calibrating the full term structure when trades extend beyond the most liquid 5Y tenor
Extrapolating long-dated spreads linearly when market data suggests different dynamics
questions.real_world_example: A bank calculates CVA on a 10Y cross-currency swap with a European corporate. The 5Y CDS trades at 300bp (upward sloping curve). Naively assuming flat 300bp across all tenors overestimates near-term default risk and underestimates 7-10Y risk, potentially mispricing CVA by $500k on a $100M notional trade.

questions.subtopic: Loss Given Default and Recovery Rates
questions.question: What is Loss Given Default (LGD) and how does it relate to recovery rates in derivative transactions?
questions.answer_short: LGD is the percentage loss in the event of default, equal to (1 - recovery rate). For senior unsecured derivatives, market convention typically assumes 60% LGD (40% recovery), matching CDS contract standards.
questions.answer_long: Loss Given Default represents what percentage of exposure is actually lost when a counterparty defaults. It equals one minus the recovery rate - if you recover 40 cents on the dollar, LGD is 60%. For OTC derivatives ranking pari passu with senior unsecured debt, standard market assumption is 60% LGD. However, actual recovery can vary dramatically: the Lehman bankruptcy saw settled recoveries around 9% initially, with eventual recoveries reaching 30-40% for derivatives after a multi-year workout process.
questions.why_it_matters: LGD directly scales CVA calculations - assuming 40% vs 60% LGD changes CVA by 50%. While LGD choice matters less than credit spread due to cancellation effects in bilateral CVA, it's critical for unilateral CVA, DVA calculations, and determining capital requirements. Practitioners must justify LGD assumptions to auditors.
common_traps: Using CDS auction recovery rates for derivatives when actual workout recovery differs materially
Assuming structural seniority (like in securitizations) without adjusting LGD accordingly
Not distinguishing between 'settled recovery' (quick CDS auction price) and 'actual recovery' (multi-year bankruptcy process)
questions.real_world_example: After Lehman defaulted, CDS settled at ~9% recovery (91% LGD). Banks using this for CVA calculations took immediate losses. However, derivatives claims eventually recovered 30-40% through the bankruptcy process over several years, though this couldn't be monetized immediately. Traders who sold their claims early locked in the 9% recovery.

questions.subtopic: Regulatory and Accounting Move to Risk-Neutral
questions.question: Why have regulators and accounting standards pushed banks to use risk-neutral default probabilities rather than real-world probabilities for CVA, despite the challenges for illiquid credits?
questions.answer_short: IFRS 13 requires market-observable inputs for fair value (exit price), and Basel III CVA capital explicitly references CDS spreads. Risk-neutral PDs reflect what a market participant would pay to hedge credit risk, aligning with fair value principles.
questions.answer_long: The shift to risk-neutral PDs stems from fair value accounting principles requiring 'exit prices' - what you'd pay to transfer a position to another market participant. Since CDS markets allow hedging of credit risk at risk-neutral levels (with embedded risk premiums), this represents the market price of credit risk. Basel III reinforced this by explicitly requiring CDS spreads in CVA capital calculations and accepting proxy spreads based on rating/region/sector where direct quotes unavailable. Despite challenges with illiquid credits, auditors and regulators argue that banks already mark illiquid bonds and loans using similar spread mapping, making this a consistent approach.
questions.why_it_matters: This fundamentally changed CVA from an actuarial reserve to a mark-to-market value. Banks must now build sophisticated credit curve mapping frameworks for thousands of counterparties, most lacking liquid CDS. This drives CVA volatility higher, creates hedging challenges for illiquid names, and affects P&L significantly. Understanding this rationale is essential for defending CVA methodologies to auditors and regulators.
common_traps: Using blended historical/risk-neutral approaches without explicit regulatory approval
Applying different standards to 'liquid' vs 'illiquid' credits inconsistently
Not understanding that this requirement applies even when hedging is impossible or impractical
questions.real_world_example: A European bank has 3,000 corporate counterparties, but only 200 have liquid CDS quotes. They must map the remaining 2,800 to proxy curves using rating/sector/region, introducing basis risk. When iTraxx spreads widen 50bp, CVA on all mapped corporates moves even though individual credit quality hasn't changed, creating P&L volatility that can't be fully hedged.

questions.question: What are the key trade-offs a CVA desk faces when choosing between using an illiquid single-name bond spread versus a liquid CDS index for mapping an unrated corporate counterparty?
questions.answer_short: The bond spread is more counterparty-specific but illiquid and unhedgeable; the index is highly liquid and hedgeable but creates basis risk as it represents average sector credit quality rather than the specific counterparty.
questions.answer_long: This represents a fundamental tension in credit curve mapping. An illiquid bond spread observed in secondary markets is more representative of the actual counterparty's credit quality, but suffers from stale pricing, wide bid-offer spreads, and cannot be used for hedging (can't short corporate bonds easily). A liquid CDS index (like iTraxx Crossover) allows daily marking, tight spreads, easy hedging, and provides Basel III capital relief, but introduces basis risk - the index moves based on average constituent credits, not the specific counterparty. If the counterparty's credit deteriorates idiosyncratically while the index is stable, CVA won't capture this until default. The choice often depends on whether hedging/capital relief or accurate pricing is prioritized.
questions.why_it_matters: This decision affects thousands of counterparty mappings and drives CVA P&L volatility, hedging effectiveness, and capital consumption. Banks must document their hierarchy of choices and defend it to auditors. The wrong choice can lead to basis losses of millions when credit events occur on unhedged, incorrectly mapped exposures.
common_traps: Prioritizing hedgeability over representativeness, leading to basis risk accumulation
Using stale bond prices that don't reflect current market conditions
Not documenting a clear, consistent decision hierarchy across all counterparty mappings
Ignoring that Basel III doesn't give capital relief for single-name proxy CDS (though this may change)
questions.real_world_example: A bank maps a mid-sized European auto parts supplier with no CDS to iTraxx Autos index. The index tightens 30bp as the sector improves, reducing mapped CVA. However, the specific supplier faces bankruptcy due to loss of a major customer - an idiosyncratic event. The bank suffers a large CVA loss not captured by the index mapping and has no effective hedge in place.

questions.question: What are the three levels of credit spread mapping (direct observables, single-name proxies, generic proxies) and when should each be used?
questions.answer_short: Direct observables use the counterparty's own CDS/bonds when liquid; single-name proxies use similar credits (parent, peer) when no direct quote exists; generic proxies use index/rating curves when no suitable single-name exists. Choice depends on liquidity and similarity.
questions.answer_long: The three-tier hierarchy works as follows: (1) Direct observables: Use the counterparty's actual CDS or liquid bond spread - provides best price discovery and full hedging/capital relief, but only available for ~200-500 credits globally. (2) Single-name proxies: Use a similar entity's CDS (parent company, peer, sovereign) possibly with a spread adjustment - provides partial spread hedging but no default protection and currently no Basel III capital relief. Suitable when relationship is strong. (3) Generic proxies: Map to rating/sector/region curves built from indices or bond composites - provides spread hedging via indices and partial capital relief but significant basis risk. Used for the majority of counterparties lacking specific observables.
questions.why_it_matters: This hierarchy must be systematically applied across thousands of counterparties with clear escalation rules. It determines CVA accuracy, hedging effectiveness, capital consumption, and audit defensibility. Most banks end up with 60-80% of counterparties mapped to generic proxies, making that methodology critical.
common_traps: Using single-name proxies that are too distant (wrong sector/region), creating larger basis risk than a good generic proxy
Not adjusting proxy spreads when credit quality clearly differs from the reference
Failing to document why each counterparty is assigned to each tier
Using indices that are too broad (e.g., all corporates) when more granular data exists
questions.real_world_example: A bank has exposure to a subsidiary of a large automotive manufacturer. Direct observable: none (subsidiary has no CDS). Single-name proxy: parent company CDS exists at 250bp, but subsidiary is weaker, so add 50bp adjustment to get 300bp. Generic proxy: iTraxx Autos at 180bp is too tight given subsidiary's lower quality. The bank chooses the single-name proxy at 300bp despite no capital relief because it better represents credit risk.

questions.question: When constructing generic credit curves by rating/region/sector, what is the key trade-off between granularity and data availability?
questions.answer_short: More granular classification (e.g., A-rated US utilities) better distinguishes counterparties but has fewer data points, risking idiosyncratic volatility. Broader classification (e.g., all A-rated) has more data but less differentiation between different credit types.
questions.answer_long: Generic curve construction faces a fundamental trade-off: Granular mapping (rating × region × sector, e.g., 7×7×3 = 147 combinations) provides better risk differentiation - a European financial should price differently than an Asian industrial. However, many combinations have few or zero liquid CDS quotes, forcing extrapolation or merging categories. This risks a single credit's idiosyncratic spread moves creating unrealistic volatility across all mapped counterparties. Broader mapping (e.g., just by rating) has ample data for stable curves but treats very different credits identically. Best practice uses maximum granularity where sufficient liquid quotes exist (typically 5+ names per bucket) and merges adjacent categories when data is sparse.
questions.why_it_matters: This choice affects CVA accuracy and stability for the majority of a bank's counterparty portfolio. Too granular creates noisy, unstable CVA; too broad fails to differentiate genuinely different risks. Banks must document and defend their bucketing methodology to regulators and auditors, showing data sufficiency and stability analysis.
common_traps: Using overly granular buckets with 1-2 names, where idiosyncratic moves create false signals
Not adjusting bucketing over time as CDS market liquidity evolves
Applying the same granularity globally when regional CDS markets have very different liquidity (Asia vs. Europe)
Failing to test curve stability and basis risk from bucketing choices
questions.real_world_example: A bank creates an 'A-rated Asian industrials' curve with only 3 liquid CDS names. When one (representing 33% of the curve) widens 100bp on company-specific news, the entire curve widens 33bp, affecting CVA on 200 mapped counterparties despite their credit being unchanged. After review, they merge to 'A-rated Asian corporates' with 15 names for better stability.

questions.question: What is a funding curve and why is it needed for calculating FVA and MVA?
questions.answer_short: A funding curve represents the interest rate at which a bank can borrow or lend cash over different tenors. It's needed for FVA to value the cost of funding uncollateralized exposure and for MVA to value the cost of funding initial margin.
questions.answer_long: A funding curve is a term structure of funding spreads (above risk-free rates like OIS) at which a bank raises unsecured funding across different maturities. Unlike credit curves used for counterparty default, funding curves reflect the bank's own cost of borrowing to fund derivative positions. For FVA, this curve determines the present value of expected funding costs when posting collateral or facing uncollateralized exposure. For MVA, it values the cost of funding segregated initial margin that cannot be rehypothecated. The curve is typically constructed from the bank's own debt issuance levels or asset swap spreads on its bonds.
questions.why_it_matters: Funding curves are central to the FVA and MVA debates. Using the wrong funding curve (e.g., risk-free vs. bank's actual cost) can change derivative valuations by millions. Banks must decide whether to use a single corporate funding curve or multiple curves by collateral type, creating methodology debates with counterparties and auditors.
common_traps: Using risk-free (OIS) rates when actual funding costs are significantly higher
Assuming funding curves are symmetric for borrowing and lending when banks have asymmetric access
Not considering that funding costs vary by collateral type and segregation requirements
questions.real_world_example: A bank calculates MVA on a cleared portfolio requiring $50M initial margin. Using OIS as the funding curve gives MVA of ~$500k (assuming 1% NPV factor), but using the bank's actual 5Y senior unsecured funding cost at OIS+150bp gives MVA of ~$1.25M - a material difference in derivative pricing that affects competitiveness.

questions.question: Why can the 'settled recovery' from a CDS auction differ materially from the 'actual recovery' eventually received on derivatives, and what are the implications for CVA?
questions.answer_short: Settled recovery occurs quickly via CDS auction and reflects liquid bond prices; actual recovery from derivatives comes years later through bankruptcy workout. Derivatives can't be sold individually due to netting/bespoke nature, and set-off rights may improve recovery.
questions.answer_long: CDS contracts settle quickly (typically within weeks) through an auction process that establishes a market-clearing price for deliverable bonds. This 'settled recovery' allows bondholders and CDS holders to monetize their claims immediately. However, bilateral derivatives cannot be sold individually - they're netted at portfolio level, are bespoke/illiquid, and may have complex collateral arrangements. The claim must be agreed with bankruptcy administrators (taking months), then workout occurs over years. The 'actual recovery' can differ significantly due to: (1) ranking in capital structure becoming clearer, (2) set-off against other claims, (3) asset recovery improving over time. Lehman showed a 9% settled vs 30-40% actual recovery spread. For CVA, this creates timing uncertainty - should you mark to settled recovery for liquidity or wait years for actual recovery?
questions.why_it_matters: This distinction affects billions in default-related P&L. Banks that marked Lehman CVA to 9% recovery took immediate losses but ultimately recovered more. Those who anticipated higher recovery faced auditor challenges. It affects whether to sell claims early (locking in settled recovery) or hold through workout (hoping for actual recovery). This is an ongoing debate in CVA methodology.
common_traps: Assuming CDS auction recovery equals derivative recovery without considering structural differences
Not accounting for the multi-year delay in receiving actual recovery and associated funding costs
Ignoring potential set-off rights or other assets that could improve derivative recovery above settled levels
Using settled recovery for CVA but not provisioning for the liquidity gap until actual recovery
questions.real_world_example: Bank A had $500M exposure to Lehman derivatives. At 9% CDS auction recovery, they took $455M CVA loss. Bank B held claims through workout, eventually recovering 35%, reducing loss to $325M - a $130M difference. However, Bank B had to fund the receivable for 5+ years and faced auditor pressure annually to write down to settled recovery levels.

questions.question: Why is the simple formula PD ≈ s×Δt/LGD only an approximation, and when does it break down most severely?
questions.answer_short: The formula ignores discounting, assumes constant hazard rate, and doesn't account for prior curve shape. It breaks down most for steep/inverted curves, long time periods, or very high spreads where discounting matters.
questions.answer_long: The approximation PD(t,t+Δt) ≈ s(t)×Δt/LGD is derived assuming: (1) constant hazard rate λ = s/LGD, (2) no discounting effects, (3) continuous default intensity. Proper bootstrapping solves the equation: CDS spread = Σ[PV(premium leg)] - Σ[PV(default leg)] = 0, accounting for: discount factors, survival probabilities from prior periods, and accrued premium on default. The approximation fails when: curve is steep (prior period spreads affect current period PD via survival probability), spreads are high (>500bp) making discounting material, or Δt is large (annual vs quarterly). For a 1000bp spread, the approximation might give 16.7% annual PD but proper bootstrapping gives 14.2% due to discounting and survival probability adjustments.
questions.why_it_matters: For high-yield credits, distressed names, or steep curves (common in stress scenarios), the approximation error can be 20-30%. This directly affects CVA calculations and capital. Production CVA systems use proper bootstrapping, but traders often use the approximation for quick estimates - knowing when it's acceptable vs when full calculation is needed separates junior from senior practitioners.
common_traps: Using the approximation for high-yield credits (BB and below) where spreads exceed 300-400bp
Applying it to inverted or steep curves without recognizing the survival probability dependencies
Not understanding that quarterly PDs from the approximation don't sum correctly to annual PDs
Using it for long-dated extrapolations beyond 10Y where compounding errors accumulate
questions.real_world_example: A stressed European bank has 5Y CDS at 800bp. Simple approximation gives 5Y cumulative PD = 5×0.08/0.6 = 66.7%. Proper bootstrapping accounting for survival probabilities and discounting gives 52.3% - a 14.4pp difference. On a $100M exposure with 50% EE, this is a $7.2M CVA difference, material enough to affect capital and hedging decisions.

questions.question: What is the difference between single-name CDS and CDS indices, and what are the trade-offs for using each in credit curve mapping?
questions.answer_short: Single-name CDS references one entity, providing default protection and spread hedging for that specific credit. Indices reference a basket (e.g., 125 names in iTraxx Main), providing only spread hedging for sector average but with much better liquidity.
questions.answer_long: Single-name CDS is a bilateral contract referencing one specific entity - provides both default protection (pays out on credit events) and spread hedging. Available for ~500-1000 liquid credits globally, with typical bid-offer of 3-10bp. Allows precise hedging of a specific counterparty but limited liquidity and no capital relief for proxies under current Basel III. CDS indices (iTraxx Europe, CDX NA, etc.) reference 125 equally-weighted entities in a sector - provide only spread hedging (diversified default risk makes default payout unlikely) but highly liquid with 0.5-1bp bid-offer. Allow capital relief under Basel III standardized approach. Trade-off: single-name gives precision but limited liquidity; indices give liquidity and capital relief but basis risk from index composition not matching specific counterparty.
questions.why_it_matters: Most CVA hedging in practice uses index tranches and single-names together. Understanding when index basis risk is acceptable vs when single-name precision is essential affects hedge effectiveness. Large losses occur when banks over-rely on index hedges and face idiosyncratic defaults (basis events). This distinction drives hedging strategy and capital optimization.
common_traps: Using index hedges for concentrated single-name exposures, creating large basis risk on default
Not understanding that index constituents roll every 6 months, creating hedge discontinuities
Assuming index liquidity will persist in stress when it can evaporate
Ignoring that index spreads reflect average credit quality, masking deterioration in specific names
questions.real_world_example: A bank has $200M exposure to an Italian bank and hedges with iTraxx Financials Senior at 100bp (50 names). The specific bank's CDS widens from 150bp to 600bp on idiosyncratic stress while the index only moves from 100bp to 140bp (most constituents stable). The CVA increases $4M but hedge gains only $800k - a $3.2M basis loss from using an index instead of single-name hedge.

questions.question: What are the advantages and disadvantages of using third-party generic credit curves (like Markit sector curves) versus building proprietary curves in-house?
questions.answer_short: Third-party curves offer independence (audit-friendly) and lower cost but lack customization and control. In-house curves allow tailoring to specific portfolios and hedging but require more resources and may face audit scrutiny over subjectivity.
questions.answer_long: Third-party curves (e.g., Markit sector curves across rating/sector at 1Y/5Y/10Y tenors): Advantages - (1) Independent, auditor-friendly, (2) Lower cost than building infrastructure, (3) Consistent across industry, (4) Daily updates without internal effort. Disadvantages - (1) Fixed classification may not match bank's portfolio, (2) Methodology changes beyond bank's control, (3) Can introduce P&L volatility from provider methodology changes, (4) May not align with bank's hedging instruments. In-house curves: Advantages - (1) Customized granularity matching portfolio, (2) Aligned with actual hedges, (3) Full transparency and control, (4) Can blend multiple data sources. Disadvantages - (1) Requires significant build/maintenance resources, (2) Auditors may challenge subjectivity, (3) Higher operational risk from model errors.
questions.why_it_matters: This is a strategic choice affecting CVA infrastructure for years. Larger banks typically build in-house for control and alignment with trading strategies. Smaller banks or end-users often use third-party for cost and simplicity. Understanding the trade-offs helps in vendor selection, audit defense, and explaining CVA volatility sources to senior management.
common_traps: Blindly using third-party curves without understanding their construction methodology
Not testing alignment between third-party curves and actual hedging instruments
Building overly complex in-house curves that are hard to maintain and explain
Switching between providers frequently, creating P&L discontinuities
questions.real_world_example: A mid-sized European bank used Markit sector curves, which worked well until Markit changed their averaging methodology for BBB industrials, causing a 15bp shift in curves and €2M CVA MTM move overnight. The bank had to explain to auditors why CVA moved without any credit event or market move. They eventually moved to in-house curves with explicit control over methodology but at 3x the annual cost.

questions.question: How is the 'cost of capital' determined for KVA calculations, and why is it more subjective than credit spreads or funding costs?
questions.answer_short: Cost of capital represents the required return on shareholder equity allocated to support a trade's regulatory capital. It's subjective because it depends on internal hurdle rates, tax treatment, market equity valuations, and strategic priorities rather than observable market prices.
questions.answer_long: Cost of capital for KVA reflects the opportunity cost of tying up shareholder equity to meet regulatory capital requirements. Determination involves: (1) Bank's return on equity (ROE) target - typically 10-15% post-crisis, varying by bank strategy and market conditions, (2) Tax adjustments - since equity is not tax-deductible like debt, cost must be grossed up (divide by (1-tax rate)), (3) Market multiples - price-to-book ratios affect whether equity is expensive to raise, (4) Regulatory buffers - banks may target higher returns on constrained capital. Unlike credit spreads (observable from CDS) or funding costs (from debt issuance), cost of capital is a management decision driven by shareholder expectations, strategic goals, and competitive positioning. Different businesses within a bank may use different hurdle rates (e.g., 12% for flow trading, 18% for structured products).
questions.why_it_matters: KVA can be the largest xVA component for capital-intensive trades (long-dated, uncollateralized, high CVA volatility). Using 10% vs 15% cost of capital changes KVA by 50%, potentially making trades unprofitable. This is a key driver of pricing disagreements between banks and clients. Understanding how to defend and benchmark cost of capital assumptions is critical for KVA implementation.
common_traps: Using the bank's overall ROE target without adjusting for trade-specific capital consumption
Not grossing up for tax effects, understating true cost of capital
Ignoring that cost of capital should vary by capital type (RWA vs leverage vs stressed VaR)
Using historic cost of equity when current market conditions or bank strategy has changed materially
questions.real_world_example: Bank A uses 12% cost of capital (post-tax ROE target). Bank B uses 8% (arguing for lower hurdle given current low rates). On a 10Y uncollateralized swap requiring $10M CVA capital, annual capital charge is $1.2M vs $800k. Over 10 years, NPV difference is ~$3M in KVA - enough to change who wins the trade. Client plays banks against each other on cost of capital assumptions to get better pricing.

questions.question: What is the CDS-bond basis and what are the main drivers that cause CDS spreads and bond spreads for the same entity to diverge?
questions.answer_short: CDS-bond basis is the difference between CDS spread and asset swap spread on the same reference entity. Drivers include: deliverable bond optionality in CDS, funding advantages of bonds, counterparty risk in CDS, and supply/demand technicals in each market.
questions.answer_long: The CDS-bond basis = CDS spread - bond asset swap spread. In theory both should equal the credit spread, but in practice they diverge significantly due to: (1) Cheapest-to-deliver option in CDS - protection seller is short an option to receive the worst bond, adding value to CDS vs bonds, (2) Funding benefits - repo markets allow financing bonds at favorable rates; CDS requires posting variation margin without interest (pre-2020), making bonds more attractive and compressing bond spreads, (3) Counterparty risk in CDS - CDS is an unfunded derivative with counterparty risk; bonds are funded assets, (4) Technical factors - bond supply constraints (few bonds outstanding), regulatory capital treatment differences (bonds may be HQLA-eligible), and different investor bases. Basis was dramatically negative (CDS wider) during the crisis as CDS liquidity and counterparty concerns dominated, reaching -200bp for some financials.
questions.why_it_matters: When mapping credit curves, choosing CDS vs bonds as the reference affects CVA levels. Large basis means the two give materially different credit spreads for the same entity. Basis trading is a hedge fund strategy, but for CVA purposes it creates ambiguity about the 'true' credit spread. Banks must choose consistently and document the choice, especially where both markets exist for a counterparty.
common_traps: Assuming CDS and bond spreads are equivalent and using whichever is available without basis adjustment
Not understanding that the basis can flip sign depending on market conditions (normally positive, but negative in crisis)
Using cash bonds for curve construction without understanding embedded optionality differences vs CDS
Ignoring that basis can vary by bond maturity and seniority
questions.real_world_example: During 2011-2012 European crisis, Italian sovereign 5Y CDS traded at 500bp while 5Y BTP asset swap spread was 350bp - a +150bp basis (CDS wider). A bank mapping Italian corporates to sovereign curves would get very different credit spreads depending on using CDS vs bonds. Using CDS gives higher CVA, bonds give lower. With €500M exposure and 50% credit duration, this is a €3.75M CVA difference requiring a documented methodology choice.

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between real-world and risk-neutral default probabilities in credit risk measurement?
questions.answer_short: Real-world probabilities come from historical default data, while risk-neutral probabilities are derived from market prices (CDS, bonds) and include a risk premium that investors demand.
questions.answer_long: Real-world default probabilities are estimated from historical default frequencies for given credit ratings. Risk-neutral default probabilities are backed out from market instruments like CDS spreads or bond yields. Risk-neutral probabilities are systematically higher because they embed a risk premium - the extra compensation investors require beyond expected losses. For example, studies show risk-neutral probabilities can be 2-16 times higher than real-world equivalents, especially for better credits.
questions.why_it_matters: Using the correct probability type is critical for CVA: risk-neutral probabilities are required for fair value accounting (IFRS 13) and Basel III capital, making CVA a market price rather than an actuarial reserve. Using real-world probabilities would significantly understate CVA.
common_traps: Thinking the difference is just measurement error rather than a fundamental conceptual distinction
Believing risk-neutral is 'wrong' because defaults don't actually occur at those rates
Not recognizing that the risk premium component can be larger than the expected loss component
questions.real_world_example: A single-A corporate might have a 0.13% real-world 1-year default probability but a 1.28% risk-neutral probability from CDS markets - nearly 10x higher. This gap means CVA calculated with market data will be much larger and more volatile.

questions.subtopic: Extracting Default Probabilities from Credit Spreads
questions.question: Given a credit spread of 400 bps and an LGD of 60%, what is the approximate 1-year default probability using the simple formula?
questions.answer_short: Using PD ≈ spread × Δt / LGD: PD = 0.04 × 1 / 0.60 = 6.67%
questions.answer_long: The simple approximation formula is PD(t, t+Δt) ≈ s(t) × Δt / LGD, where s is the credit spread, Δt is the time period, and LGD is loss given default. For a 400 bps (4%) spread, 1-year period, and 60% LGD: PD = 0.04 × 1 / 0.60 = 0.0667 or 6.67%. This formula works reasonably well for relatively flat credit curves but becomes less accurate when curves are steeply sloped.
questions.why_it_matters: Converting credit spreads to default probabilities is the foundational step in CVA calculation. Getting this conversion wrong means your entire CVA number is built on a faulty foundation, affecting both P&L and capital requirements.
common_traps: Forgetting to divide by LGD (which makes PD artificially low)
Using this formula for longer periods without adjusting for curve shape
Applying the formula with spread in basis points instead of decimal form
questions.real_world_example: A CVA desk sees a counterparty's 5-year CDS widen from 300 to 400 bps. Using 60% LGD, the 5-year cumulative default probability jumps from roughly 22% to 28%, immediately increasing CVA by about 27% even if exposure hasn't changed.

questions.question: Why do two counterparties with identical 5-year credit spreads of 300 bps produce different CVA values if one has an upward-sloping curve and the other has an inverted curve?
questions.answer_short: The curve shape determines when defaults are most likely: upward-sloping curves have lower near-term default risk but higher long-term risk, while inverted curves show the opposite pattern.
questions.answer_long: Even with identical 5-year spreads, the term structure matters enormously. An upward-sloping curve (e.g., 100 bps at 1Y, 300 at 5Y) implies lower default probability in early years when exposure might be highest, reducing CVA. An inverted curve (e.g., 500 bps at 1Y, 300 at 5Y) concentrates default probability near-term. Since CVA is PV[exposure × PD × LGD], the timing of default probability relative to exposure profile is critical. The 10-year extrapolation differs wildly between curve shapes.
questions.why_it_matters: For long-dated portfolios (interest rate swaps, cross-currency swaps), the curve shape beyond the liquid 5-year point can drive 30-50% of total CVA. Assuming a flat curve when the market implies a shape is a material modeling error.
common_traps: Only looking at the 5-year CDS point and ignoring term structure
Using flat interpolation between sparse points (1Y, 5Y, 10Y)
Not recognizing that curve shape affects different portfolios very differently based on their exposure profiles
questions.real_world_example: A bank has 20-year receiver swaps with a corporate counterparty. The 5-year CDS is 300 bps. If they assume flat extrapolation to 20 years, they might calculate CVA of $5mm. But if the curve is actually inverted and 20-year should be 200 bps, the true CVA might be $3.5mm - a $1.5mm error.

questions.question: Why might the actual recovery on a derivative claim differ from the standard 40% (60% LGD) assumed in CDS contracts, and what are the two types of recovery values?
questions.answer_short: Settled recovery (from CDS auction, immediate) versus actual recovery (from bankruptcy process, years later). Derivatives take longer to settle than bonds, and recoveries can be enhanced by netting, collateral, and set-off rights.
questions.answer_long: CDS contracts settle quickly via auction (days/weeks after default) with a 'settled recovery'. Derivatives claims take much longer because they're bespoke, netted portfolios that must be valued through bankruptcy. This creates 'actual recovery' realized months or years later. For Lehman, CDS settled at 9% recovery but some derivative actual recoveries reached 30-40%. Derivative recoveries can be higher due to: (1) netting reducing claims, (2) collateral held, (3) set-off against other obligations. The timing delay creates funding costs if you can't monetize the claim early.
questions.why_it_matters: Using standard 60% LGD may overstate CVA if your actual recovery experience is better. However, auditors typically require market-standard LGD unless you have strong documentation of structural enhancements (like SPV seniority). The settled vs actual distinction also affects DVA timing.
common_traps: Assuming Lehman's high actual recoveries justify using lower LGD for all counterparties
Not recognizing the time value cost of waiting years for actual recovery
Ignoring that set-off rights are valuable but not priced into exit value CVA
questions.real_world_example: A bank holds $100mm gross exposure to a defaulted counterparty, netted to $30mm. They hold $5mm collateral. CDS auction settles at 10% recovery ($3mm on $30mm). They negotiate claim and sell it for 25% ($7.5mm) after 6 months. Final recovery comes 3 years later at 35% ($10.5mm). Which should CVA assume?

questions.question: Why have banks largely converged on using risk-neutral (market-implied) default probabilities for CVA calculation despite the challenges for illiquid counterparties?
questions.answer_short: IFRS 13 accounting requires market-observable inputs for fair value, and Basel III capital rules explicitly reference CDS spreads, forcing convergence to risk-neutral probabilities as the standard.
questions.answer_long: The shift happened due to three forces: (1) IFRS 13 requires using market-observable inputs and defines fair value as exit price - risk-neutral is the price at which you could transfer the risk; (2) Basel III CVA capital explicitly uses CDS spreads in formulas; (3) the growth of CVA hedging with CDS makes risk-neutral the natural pricing measure. By 2015, EBA noted most banks use market-implied data. This creates challenges for illiquid credits (most counterparties), requiring proxy mapping methods that introduce subjectivity.
questions.why_it_matters: This is a foundational methodology choice affecting every CVA calculation. Using risk-neutral makes CVA 2-10x larger and more volatile than real-world approaches, but aligns with accounting standards and regulatory capital. Understanding this shift explains why CVA became such a large P&L item post-crisis.
common_traps: Thinking smaller regional banks can still justify real-world probabilities
Not understanding that 'market-implied' doesn't mean you have an actual market for most counterparties
Missing that this creates a hedge-ability problem: CVA sized on risk-neutral but no hedge available
questions.real_world_example: A regional bank has 500 corporate counterparties. Only 20 have liquid CDS. Pre-2012, they used rating agency default rates (real-world). Post-IFRS 13, they must map all 500 to CDS proxies. Their CVA reserve tripled, but they can only hedge 20 names directly.

questions.question: What are the main types of CDS instruments used for credit curve mapping, and why are indices often preferred over single-name CDS?
questions.answer_short: Single-name CDS (specific companies), sector indices (iTraxx, CDX), and sovereign indices. Indices are more liquid, allow easier hedging, and provide capital relief, but are less precise for individual counterparties.
questions.answer_long: The CDS market has three main layers: (1) Single-name CDS on specific entities (hundreds of names, but liquidity declining); (2) Sector indices like iTraxx Europe (125 names), iTraxx Financials, CDX North America, differentiated by rating (main, crossover, high-yield); (3) Sovereign indices like iTraxx SovX by region. Indices trade in standard tenors (3Y, 5Y, 7Y, 10Y) with good liquidity. Banks often map illiquid counterparties to indices because they're liquid enough to hedge and provide partial capital relief, even though the fit is less precise than a single-name proxy.
questions.why_it_matters: Understanding the CDS market structure is essential for constructing practical credit curve mapping. The trade-off between precision (single-name) and practicality (index) drives methodology choices. For CVA desks managing thousands of counterparties, index-based mapping is often the only scalable approach.
common_traps: Thinking single-name CDS exists for most counterparties (it doesn't)
Assuming index hedges provide good default protection (they don't - only spread hedges)
Not recognizing that 5-year is typically the only truly liquid tenor even for single-names
questions.real_world_example: A bank has exposure to a mid-sized European consumer goods company. No single-name CDS exists. They map to iTraxx Europe Main (125 investment-grade names).
