This allows them to hedge spread risk with the index, get partial capital relief, but they're exposed to idiosyncratic default risk of the specific counterparty.

questions.question: When is it appropriate to use an LGD different from the standard market convention (60% for corporates), and what evidence do auditors typically require?
questions.answer_short: Use non-standard LGD only for structural seniority differences (e.g., SPV derivatives), credit enhancements with legal support, or well-documented recovery experience. Auditors require legal opinions or significant historical data.
questions.answer_long: Standard LGD assumptions are 60% for senior unsecured (iTraxx/CDX convention). Deviations require justification: (1) Structural seniority - derivatives with securitization SPVs may be super-senior, supporting lower LGD with legal documentation; (2) Credit enhancements - guarantees or collateral (but collateral should be modeled in exposure, not LGD); (3) Historical experience - if the bank has decades of data showing 45% LGD on their derivative book with statistical significance. Simply pointing to Lehman's eventual 30-40% recovery isn't sufficient without showing why your portfolio would systematically achieve this.
questions.why_it_matters: LGD is less critical than credit spreads for CVA due to cancellation effects (discussed in Ch. 14), but wrong assumptions still matter. Using 40% instead of 60% LGD reduces CVA by 33% - material enough that auditors scrutinize this choice carefully.
common_traps: Using favorable LGD based on one or two recovery experiences
Not documenting the legal basis for claiming super-seniority
Applying recovery enhancements (like netting) in LGD that should be in exposure calculation
questions.real_world_example: A bank trades derivatives with SPVs in securitizations where the derivative is documented as senior to the notes. Legal opinions confirm super-senior status. They use 30% LGD (70% recovery) for these specific counterparties, while using standard 60% LGD for all corporate and bank counterparties.

questions.question: Compare the three credit curve mapping approaches (direct observables, single-name proxies, generic proxies) in terms of hedging effectiveness and capital relief.
questions.answer_short: Direct observables: full hedge and capital relief. Single-name proxies: spread hedge but no default hedge or capital relief (currently). Generic proxies: spread hedge via indices with partial capital relief.
questions.answer_long: Direct observables (counterparty's own CDS): You can hedge both spread and jump-to-default risk, get full capital relief under Basel III standardized or advanced CVA charges. Single-name proxies (e.g., parent company CDS): You hedge spread movements but not idiosyncratic default, and under current rules get no capital relief (though BCBS 2015 proposes changing this). Generic proxies (indices): Hedge spread via indices, get partial capital relief (under standardized approach, indices count), but no default hedge and basis risk from index composition changes.
questions.why_it_matters: The mapping choice directly impacts capital efficiency. A bank using mostly generic proxies might calculate CVA of $100mm but need $50mm capital. Using more single-name proxies might have same CVA but $80mm capital (no relief). This drives commercial decisions about which counterparties to accept.
common_traps: Thinking a single-name proxy provides full capital relief (it doesn't under current rules)
Not quantifying the basis risk between generic index and specific counterparty
Optimizing for capital relief at expense of actual risk management
questions.real_world_example: Bank has $50mm CVA to an unrated regional utility company. Option 1: Map to BBB industrials index - can hedge with iTraxx, get 50% capital relief, but 30% basis volatility. Option 2: Map to national utility company with CDS - better spread tracking, can hedge, but zero capital relief. They choose Option 1 for capital efficiency.

questions.question: A bank needs to create a generic single-A European financials curve. They have 15 single-name CDS quotes at 5Y tenor ranging from 120-180 bps, but only 5 quotes at 10Y tenor (200-240 bps). What methodological challenges must they address?
questions.answer_short: They must weight/average the 5Y points (handling outliers), interpolate to other tenors with sparse data, extrapolate beyond 10Y, and balance granularity vs. idiosyncratic noise in a small sample.
questions.answer_long: Key challenges: (1) At 5Y: decide if simple average (145 bps) or weighted by liquidity/size; handle outliers (drop the 120 and 180?); (2) At 10Y: only 5 quotes creates stability problems - is average of 220 bps representative or driven by one name's idiosyncratic risk? (3) Interpolation: connect 5Y and 10Y - linear in spread space, or bootstrap default probabilities? (4) Extrapolation: need 15-20Y for long-dated swaps but no data - flat extrapolation, or fit to a curve model? (5) Update frequency: daily updates will show volatility from small sample. Too granular classification with insufficient data adds noise rather than information.
questions.why_it_matters: These methodological choices directly impact CVA stability and P&L volatility. A poorly constructed generic curve might swing 50 bps day-to-day from single-name noise, creating false CVA P&L. Auditors and regulators scrutinize these methods as they affect hundreds of counterparties mapped to each curve.
common_traps: Using arithmetic average without weighting by liquidity or removing outliers
Interpolating spreads linearly instead of bootstrapping properly in probability space
Creating too many granular buckets (rating × region × sector) with 1-2 names per bucket
questions.real_world_example: A bank built separate curves for 'A-rated European banks' vs 'A-rated European insurers'. Each had only 4-5 names. When one Italian bank widened 100 bps on idiosyncratic news, it moved the entire 'banks' curve by 20 bps, creating $15mm CVA loss on 200 unrelated counterparties. They collapsed it to one 'A-rated European financials' curve.

questions.question: What are the advantages and disadvantages of using third-party provider curves (like Markit sector curves) versus building your own credit curve mapping?
questions.answer_short: Advantages: cheaper, independent (auditors like this), consistent methodology. Disadvantages: rigid classification, no control over behavior/updates, may not align with your portfolio or hedging approach.
questions.answer_long: Third-party curves (Markit, Bloomberg, etc.) offer consistency and independence - auditors appreciate that you're not manipulating curves. They're cheaper than building full infrastructure. However, you lose control: the provider's rating/sector classification may not match yours; their weighting and outlier treatment is a black box; updates happen on their schedule and might create P&L volatility you can't explain. Most importantly, their curve construction may not align with your hedging instruments, creating basis risk between your CVA and your hedges.
questions.why_it_matters: For smaller banks without extensive CVA infrastructure, third-party curves can be a practical solution for illiquid names. But for larger banks managing active CVA hedging and reporting to regulators on methodology, control over curve construction is usually essential. The choice depends on scale and sophistication.
common_traps: Thinking third-party curves are 'more correct' because they're external
Not understanding what's in the black box (sector definitions, weighting schemes)
Using third-party curves that don't match your hedging universe, creating unexplainable hedge basis
questions.real_world_example: A mid-sized bank uses Markit sector curves for CVA on 1,000 corporate counterparties. Markit updates their 'BBB industrials' curve methodology, changing the composition rules. Overnight, the bank's CVA on 300 counterparties moves by $5mm with no market event. Auditors question the volatility; the bank can't explain it because they don't control the methodology.

questions.question: Why might using a subordinated CDS spread to value a senior derivative claim lead to significant CVA overstatement, and how can this be corrected?
questions.answer_short: Subordinated debt has lower recovery (higher LGD) and higher spread than senior. Using sub spread with senior LGD dramatically overstates default probability. Must adjust spread or LGD for seniority mismatch.
questions.answer_long: Subordinated debt typically trades 100-300 bps wider than senior debt for the same issuer due to lower recovery in default (sub might recover 20% vs. 40% for senior). If you extract PD from a 500 bps sub CDS using 60% LGD (senior assumption), you get PD = 500/0.6 = 8.3% annual. But if properly adjusted for sub's 80% LGD, PD = 500/0.8 = 6.25%. Using the wrong combination overstates PD by 33%. For derivatives (typically senior unsecured rank), you need: either (1) use senior CDS with senior LGD, or (2) adjust subordinated spread down to senior-equivalent before applying senior LGD.
questions.why_it_matters: Seniority mismatches are common in practice: a bank subsidiary might only have sub debt traded, while derivatives with parent rank senior. Financial institutions often have more liquid sub CDS (bank Tier 2). Using wrong seniority can overstate CVA by 30-50%, creating excess capital charges and P&L volatility.
common_traps: Grabbing the first available CDS spread without checking seniority
Thinking the seniority doesn't matter much if you're just using it as a proxy
Adjusting LGD without adjusting spread, or vice versa, creating double-counting
questions.real_world_example: A bank trades derivatives with European Bank X. The liquid CDS is on Bank X's Tier 2 subordinated debt (600 bps). Derivatives rank senior. Using 600 bps with 60% LGD gives PD of 10%/year. Bank X's senior CDS (less liquid) is 350 bps. This should be used, giving PD of 5.8%/year. The CVA difference on a $100mm exposure portfolio is roughly $4mm.

questions.question: If a credit curve is characterized by a constant hazard rate λ, derive the relationship between the hazard rate, the t-year credit spread s(t), and the LGD.
questions.answer_short: For constant hazard rate: s(t) ≈ λ × LGD, so λ ≈ s(t) / LGD. The survival probability to time t is Q(t) = exp(-λt), and the default probability over [0,t] is 1 - Q(t).
questions.answer_long: The hazard rate λ represents the instantaneous default intensity. For constant λ, the survival probability (no default by time t) is Q(t) = exp(-λt). A CDS spread approximates s(t) ≈ λ × LGD / (1 - 0.5 × λ × LGD × t), but for small λt, this simplifies to s(t) ≈ λ × LGD. Therefore, λ ≈ s(t)/LGD. For time-varying curves, λ(t) changes, and you bootstrap: start from short end, use s(t1) to get λ(0,t1), then use s(t2) to get λ(t1,t2), building up the piecewise constant hazard rate structure. The instantaneous default probability density is f(t) = λ(t) × Q(t).
questions.why_it_matters: Hazard rates are the fundamental building block for pricing credit derivatives and calculating CVA. Understanding the relationship between observable spreads and hazard rates allows proper calibration of credit models. For wrong-way risk or exotic structures, you need the full hazard rate term structure, not just simplified formulas.
common_traps: Confusing hazard rate (instantaneous) with default probability (cumulative)
Using constant hazard rate assumption when curve is clearly sloped
Not recognizing that hazard rates are always extracted under an LGD assumption
questions.real_world_example: A CVA model for long-dated (30-year) derivatives needs granular default probability term structure. The system bootstraps piecewise constant hazard rates from CDS at 1Y (λ1=2%), 5Y (λ5=3%), 10Y (λ10=3.5%), then extrapolates flat at 3.5% beyond 10Y. This allows computing conditional default probabilities for each simulation date.

questions.question: A bank has $200mm CVA from exposure to 50 single-A emerging market corporates (no direct CDS). They hedge 50% with iTraxx EM index and 50% with single-name proxies of similar EM corporates. How does Basel III standardized CVA capital treatment differ between these hedges?
questions.answer_short: iTraxx EM index hedge gets partial capital relief (recognized in standardized approach). Single-name proxy hedges get no capital relief under current rules. Total hedge is same notional but capital impact differs dramatically.
questions.answer_long: Under Basel III standardized CVA capital (Section 8.7): Index hedges are recognized - the bank gets to reduce capital based on index exposure (typically 50% relief for 50% notional). Single-name proxy hedges (even if excellent spread correlation) get zero capital relief under current framework because they don't reference the actual counterparty. So despite having $100mm of each hedge type providing similar economic protection, capital might be: unhedged $80mm, with index hedge $40mm, with single-name hedge still $80mm. BCBS 2015 proposals would change this to recognize single-name proxies, but not yet implemented. This creates a strong incentive to use index hedges for capital purposes even if single-names are better risk management.
questions.why_it_matters: Capital relief drives hedging strategy as much as risk management. A CVA desk might achieve 90% spread risk reduction but only 40% capital reduction due to hedge recognition rules. Understanding regulatory hedge recognition is essential for optimizing the cost of CVA (capital + hedging costs).
common_traps: Assuming all hedges get equal capital treatment if they're effective risk management
Not understanding that single-name proxies currently get no relief (this surprises many)
Confusing standardized approach (limited recognition) with advanced approach (model-based recognition)
questions.real_world_example: A bank's CVA desk proposes hedging $500mm EM CVA with single-name proxies on parent companies (excellent correlation). Capital team objects: this provides zero capital relief, requiring $200mm capital. They compromise: hedge $250mm with EM index (gets $100mm capital relief) and $250mm with single-names (no relief). Total capital need: $150mm instead of $200mm.

questions.question: Why is defining the appropriate funding spread for FVA calculation more subjective than defining credit spreads for CVA, and what are the key components?
questions.answer_short: Funding spreads depend on bank-specific funding strategy, tenor, secured vs unsecured, and collateral remuneration terms. Unlike credit spreads (market observable via CDS), funding spreads reflect internal treasury decisions and aren't directly market-quoted.
questions.answer_long: CVA uses counterparty credit spreads from CDS/bonds - relatively objective market data. FVA requires your own funding spread, which depends on: (1) Funding strategy - do you issue covered bonds, senior unsecured, Tier 2, or access interbank markets? (2) Tenor - funding curve term structure differs from credit curve; (3) Secured vs unsecured - can you repo out collateral received? (4) Collateral remuneration - what rate do you pay on CSA cash? (5) Regulatory treatment - LCR/NSFR affect funding optimization. There's no single market quote for 'your 5-year funding spread' - it's a weighted blend of actual issuance and treasury assumptions about marginal funding costs.
questions.why_it_matters: FVA can be 50-200% the size of CVA for uncollateralized derivatives. If your funding spread assumption is wrong by 20 bps, FVA on a $1bn exposure portfolio could be off by $20mm. Auditors and regulators scrutinize these assumptions heavily, and there's legitimate diversity of practice across banks.
common_traps: Using average historical funding cost instead of marginal cost for new trades
Not distinguishing between secured and unsecured funding for collateralized vs uncollateralized exposure
Assuming funding spread = CDS spread (it's related but not identical due to LGD and funding structure)
questions.real_world_example: Bank A (AA-rated) issues 5-year senior unsecured bonds at CDS + 30 bps (total 120 bps). Bank B (A-rated) uses covered bonds at 80 bps. For FVA on identical uncollateralized swap portfolios, Bank A uses 120 bps funding spread, Bank B uses 80 bps. Their FVA differs by 33% despite similar credit quality, due to funding strategy.

questions.question: How should a bank determine the hurdle rate (return on equity) to use in KVA calculations, and why does this vary significantly across institutions?
questions.answer_short: Hurdle rate = (expected ROE - risk-free rate) × (1 - tax rate). It varies based on bank's actual ROE targets, equity investors' required returns, business mix, and regulatory capital regime (standardized vs. internal models).
questions.answer_long: KVA compensates for the cost of holding regulatory capital against non-hedgeable risks (see Ch. 16). The hurdle rate reflects: (1) Shareholders' required return - typically 8-15% ROE depending on bank, region, and market conditions; (2) Risk-free rate - subtract this to get excess return required; (3) Tax rate - capital cost is after-tax; (4) Regulatory regime - internal models banks use lower capital, so lower absolute cost, but might use higher hurdle rate; (5) Business strategy - a bank targeting 15% ROE on capital markets uses higher hurdle than one targeting 10%. Formula: KVA = ∫ hurdle_rate × Capital(t) × DF(t) dt. A bank with 12% ROE target, 2% risk-free, 25% tax rate: hurdle = (0.12 - 0.02) × 0.75 = 7.5%.
questions.why_it_matters: KVA can be 20-50% of total XVA for capital-intensive trades (long-dated exotics, uncollateralized). The hurdle rate assumption directly scales KVA: using 8% vs 12% hurdle changes KVA by 50%. This affects pricing and trade acceptance. Unlike CVA/FVA, there's no market standard - it's a firm-specific business decision.
common_traps: Using the bank's overall ROE target instead of the marginal ROE for capital markets division
Forgetting the tax adjustment (using pre-tax instead of after-tax)
Not updating hurdle rate when market conditions or investor expectations change
questions.real_world_example: European Bank uses 10% hurdle rate (15% pre-tax ROE target, 33% tax). They price a 15-year uncollateralized swap requiring $50mm capital, generating $20mm KVA charge. US Bank uses 6% hurdle (10% ROE target, 40% tax), calculates only $12mm KVA on identical trade. European bank appears uncompetitive by $8mm despite same risk, purely due to hurdle rate choice.

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between real-world and risk-neutral default probabilities?
questions.answer_short: Real-world default probabilities are estimated from historical default data, while risk-neutral probabilities are derived from market prices (like CDS spreads) and include a risk premium that investors demand for taking credit risk.
questions.answer_long: Real-world default probabilities come from historical analysis of actual defaults by rating category. Risk-neutral default probabilities are extracted from market instruments like bonds or CDSs and are consistently higher due to an embedded risk premium. This premium compensates investors for accepting default risk beyond just the expected loss. Empirical studies show risk-neutral probabilities can be 2-17 times higher than real-world equivalents, with the ratio being largest for high-quality credits.
questions.why_it_matters: This distinction is critical because using real-world versus risk-neutral probabilities dramatically changes CVA calculations. Modern accounting (IFRS 13) and regulatory rules (Basel III) require risk-neutral probabilities for CVA, making this understanding essential for proper valuation and capital calculations.
common_traps: Thinking the difference is just measurement error rather than a fundamental economic premium
Using real-world probabilities for CVA when regulations require risk-neutral
Assuming the risk premium is constant across credit qualities (it's proportionally much larger for better credits)
questions.real_world_example: A single-A rated counterparty might have a 0.13% real-world one-year default probability from historical data, but the market-implied (risk-neutral) probability from their CDS spread could be 1.28% - nearly 10 times higher. This means your CVA charge will be substantially larger using market data.

questions.subtopic: Extracting Default Probabilities from Credit Spreads
questions.question: What is the simple formula to approximate the unconditional default probability between two dates from a credit spread?
questions.answer_short: PD(t₁, t₂) ≈ s × Δt / LGD, where s is the credit spread, Δt is the time interval, and LGD is the loss given default.
questions.answer_long: The standard approximation is PD(t₁, t₂) = s × Δt / LGD. For example, with a 300 bps credit spread, one-year period, and 60% LGD, the annual default probability is 0.03 × 1 / 0.60 = 5%. This is an approximation because it doesn't account for the full term structure of spreads before time t₁. The more upward or downward sloping the credit curve, the less accurate this simple formula becomes.
questions.why_it_matters: This is the practical calculation used thousands of times daily in CVA desks to convert observable CDS spreads into the default probabilities needed for pricing. Understanding both the formula and its limitations prevents material pricing errors on portfolios with non-flat credit curves.
common_traps: Forgetting to divide by LGD (assuming recovery is zero)
Using this formula when the credit curve is steeply sloped (gives poor approximation)
Confusing unconditional with conditional default probabilities
questions.real_world_example: A trader sees a counterparty's 5-year CDS at 450 bps. Using 60% LGD, they quickly estimate the 5-year cumulative default probability as roughly 450/60 = 7.5% per year average. For a flat curve, this gives about 32% cumulative default probability over 5 years, which they use for initial CVA pricing before running a full bootstrap.

questions.question: How does the shape of a credit curve (flat, upward-sloping, or inverted) affect the timing distribution of default probabilities even when the 5-year spread is identical?
questions.answer_short: The curve shape drastically changes when defaults are expected to occur. An upward-sloping curve implies lower near-term and higher long-term default risk, while an inverted curve suggests higher near-term default risk, even with identical 5-year spreads.
questions.answer_long: Three curves with the same 5-year spread of 300 bps will have identical 5-year cumulative default probabilities but very different annual probabilities. An upward-sloping curve might have 2% default probability in year 1 but 8% in year 5. An inverted curve could show 8% in year 1 and 2% in year 5. A flat curve would have roughly 5% in each year. This matters enormously for CVA because exposure profiles interact with these time-varying default probabilities - the timing of both exposure peaks and default likelihood determines CVA magnitude.
questions.why_it_matters: CVA calculations are highly sensitive to the timing of default risk relative to exposure peaks. A long-dated interest rate swap with high exposure in 10 years will have very different CVA depending on whether the credit curve is flat or upward-sloping. Ignoring term structure can lead to CVA errors of 30-50% or more.
common_traps: Assuming a flat credit curve when the market clearly shows term structure
Using only the 5-year CDS point and ignoring available 1Y, 3Y, 7Y, 10Y quotes
Not understanding that extrapolation beyond observed tenors is extremely sensitive to assumed curve shape
questions.real_world_example: A bank has a 15-year interest rate swap with a corporate counterparty. The counterparty's CDS curve is inverted (5Y at 400 bps, 1Y at 600 bps), suggesting near-term stress. The swap has low exposure now but high exposure in years 10-15. Using a flat 400 bps curve would overestimate CVA substantially because it ignores that default risk is front-loaded while exposure is back-loaded.

questions.subtopic: Loss Given Default and Recovery Rates
questions.question: What is the relationship between Loss Given Default (LGD) and recovery rate, and what typical value is used for senior unsecured claims?
questions.answer_short: LGD = 1 - Recovery Rate. For senior unsecured claims (which includes most OTC derivatives), the market convention is typically 60% LGD (40% recovery rate).
questions.answer_long: Loss Given Default is the percentage lost when a counterparty defaults, while recovery rate is what you get back. They sum to 100%. Standard CDS contracts for investment-grade corporates and financials assume 60% LGD / 40% recovery for senior unsecured debt, which is where OTC derivatives typically rank. However, actual recoveries vary widely - from near 0% (Lehman subordinated debt) to over 90% (Fannie Mae senior debt). The choice of LGD is important for extracting default probabilities from spreads but has less impact on final CVA due to a cancellation effect.
questions.why_it_matters: You need LGD to convert credit spreads to default probabilities and to calculate the actual loss in CVA formulas. While the choice matters less for CVA than you might think (due to offsetting effects in the calculation), using inconsistent or unrealistic LGD assumptions can still create errors and problems with hedge accounting.
common_traps: Confusing LGD and recovery rate (they are complements, not the same thing)
Using subordinated debt LGD when derivatives rank senior
Thinking you can use any LGD you want without basis risk to hedges (CDS contracts assume standard recovery rates)
questions.real_world_example: During Lehman's default, the senior CDS settled at around 8.6% recovery (91.4% LGD). However, some derivatives counterparties eventually recovered 30-40% through the bankruptcy process several years later. This difference between 'settled recovery' (CDS auction) and 'actual recovery' (final payout) creates timing and valuation challenges for CVA desks.

questions.question: Why have banks moved from using real-world to risk-neutral default probabilities for CVA despite the challenges this creates for illiquid counterparties?
questions.answer_short: Accounting standards (IFRS 13) require market-observable inputs and 'exit price' valuation, while Basel III explicitly requires CDS spreads for CVA capital. These regulatory and accounting mandates have forced convergence to risk-neutral probabilities despite illiquidity challenges.
questions.answer_long: The shift to risk-neutral probabilities is driven by three factors: (1) IFRS 13 requires 'exit price' fair value using market-observable inputs wherever possible, (2) Basel III CVA capital rules explicitly reference CDS spreads in formulas, and (3) the CVA hedging market developed using CDS instruments. While this creates significant challenges for illiquid credits (thousands of counterparties with no tradable CDS), regulators and auditors generally do not accept deviations. Banks must use proxy spreads based on rating, region, and sector for illiquid names, even though this increases volatility and creates unhedgeable risk.
questions.why_it_matters: This is a fundamental operational reality for CVA desks. You cannot simply use actuarial historical default rates anymore - auditors will challenge you. Understanding the regulatory and accounting drivers helps you design defensible credit curve mapping methodologies for the 80-90% of counterparties that have no liquid CDS.
common_traps: Trying to use blended real-world/risk-neutral approaches without strong justification (auditors typically reject this)
Not understanding that 'illiquid' doesn't excuse you from using risk-neutral probabilities
Underestimating the operational challenge - you need credit curves for thousands of names, most with no direct market observables
questions.real_world_example: A regional European bank has 3,000 corporate counterparties. Perhaps 50 have liquid CDSs. The bank cannot use historical default rates for the other 2,950 - they must map each to a credit curve using proxies based on rating/sector/region. This creates a complex credit curve library that must be maintained daily, even though most counterparties cannot be hedged directly.

questions.question: What are the main types of CDS instruments available for credit curve mapping, and which are most liquid?
questions.answer_short: The main types are single-name CDSs (specific company/sovereign) and CDS indices (portfolios of credits). Indices like iTraxx Europe, CDX North America, and their sub-indices are generally more liquid than single-name CDSs.
questions.answer_long: Single-name CDSs reference specific entities (corporates, banks, sovereigns) and provide the most precise mapping but are often illiquid except for the largest credits. CDS indices group many names together by category - for example, iTraxx Europe Main (125 investment-grade credits), iTraxx Crossover (sub-investment grade), CDX North America, and regional/sector variations. Indices trade more actively than most single-names and are available at 3Y, 5Y, 7Y, and 10Y tenors. They're used as generic proxies when no single-name CDS exists, providing spread hedging capability even without perfect default correlation.
questions.why_it_matters: Understanding the CDS market structure is essential for building a credit curve mapping framework. You need to know what instruments are available, which are liquid enough to use, and the trade-offs between precision (single-name) and liquidity/hedgeability (indices). Most of your counterparties will map to indices, not single-names.
common_traps: Assuming single-name CDSs are always available and liquid (they're not, even for medium-sized corporates)
Not understanding that indices provide spread hedging but limited default protection for specific names
Ignoring that even 'liquid' CDS markets have deteriorated significantly since 2008
questions.real_world_example: A CVA desk wants to map a medium-sized European industrial company with A rating. There's no liquid single-name CDS. They map to the iTraxx Europe Main index (investment grade) and potentially add a small spread adjustment. They can hedge their credit spread risk by trading the index, and this hedge provides partial capital relief under Basel III, even though it won't protect them if this specific company defaults.

questions.question: When might you use an LGD different from the standard 60% for senior unsecured claims, and what are the risks?
questions.answer_short: Lower LGDs might be justified for structurally senior derivative claims (like in securitizations), credits with strong collateral, or based on favorable workout experience. However, this creates basis risk to CDS hedges and requires strong justification to auditors.
questions.answer_long: Standard LGD is 60% for senior unsecured claims matching CDS contract assumptions. You might use lower LGD (better recovery) for: (1) derivatives with securitization SPVs where the derivative ranks super-senior, (2) transactions with additional credit enhancements beyond standard collateral, or (3) counterparty types where you have consistent historical evidence of better recoveries. However, using non-standard LGD creates basis risk if you hedge with standard CDS contracts (which assume 60% LGD). Auditors typically require strong evidence before accepting deviations from market standard assumptions.
questions.why_it_matters: LGD assumptions affect both the default probabilities you extract from spreads and the loss amount in CVA calculations. While there's some cancellation effect, using unrealistic LGD can create pricing errors and hedge basis risk. More importantly, you need to defend your LGD choices to auditors and understand when deviations from market standard are justified.
common_traps: Using better LGD than 60% based on one favorable recovery experience (sample size too small)
Not considering that non-standard LGD creates basis risk to any CDS hedges
Confusing 'settled recovery' (CDS auction, quick) with 'actual recovery' (bankruptcy workout, years later)
questions.real_world_example: A bank trades derivatives with a securitization SPV where the derivatives rank super-senior to all other claims. They use 30% LGD (70% recovery) based on structural seniority analysis. This lowers their CVA charge. However, if they hedge with a standard senior CDS on the SPV (60% LGD assumption), they have basis risk - the CDS will pay out more in default than their assumed loss, creating a hedge accounting problem.

questions.question: What is the typical decision hierarchy for mapping a counterparty's credit curve, and what are the trade-offs at each level?
questions.answer_short: The hierarchy is: (1) Direct observables (counterparty's own CDS/bonds), (2) Single-name proxies (parent company or similar credit), (3) Generic proxies (indices by rating/region/sector). Each step down sacrifices precision but gains liquidity and hedging ability.
questions.answer_long: Start with the counterparty's own liquid CDS if available - this gives precise default and spread hedging but is often illiquid and may only exist at 5Y tenor. If not available, use a single-name proxy like a parent company's CDS (possibly with a spread adjustment), which provides spread hedging but no default protection and currently gets no Basel III capital relief. Finally, map to a generic proxy like a credit index based on rating/region/sector - this is most liquid, allows hedging, provides partial capital relief, but has no specific default correlation. Most counterparties end up in category 3.
questions.why_it_matters: This hierarchy drives the operational reality of CVA desks - you'll spend enormous effort building and maintaining a credit curve mapping framework because most counterparties don't have direct observables. Understanding the trade-offs helps you make defensible choices and explains to senior management why CVA volatility might not be fully hedgeable.
common_traps: Stopping at single-name proxies without considering that they provide no Basel III capital relief (under current rules)
Using generic proxies that are too granular without sufficient market data
Not documenting the mapping logic in a way that auditors can validate
questions.real_world_example: A bank has exposure to a mid-sized Australian mining company with BBB rating. No liquid CDS exists. The parent company (also BBB) has a CDS but it's illiquid. The bank decides to map to the iTraxx Australia index and add 50 bps spread adjustment based on the sector and relative size. They can hedge spread risk with the index and get partial capital relief, accepting that there's no default correlation for this specific credit.

questions.question: What is the fundamental trade-off between granularity and stability when constructing generic credit curves, and how should you balance it?
questions.answer_short: More granular classification (e.g., A-rated US utilities) distinguishes counterparties better but has fewer data points per curve, creating idiosyncratic volatility. Broader classification (e.g., A-rated) is more stable but less discriminating. Balance by using granularity only where sufficient liquid data exists.
questions.answer_long: Generic curves require classifying counterparties by rating, region, and sector. A granular approach (e.g., 7 ratings × 7 regions × 3 sectors = 147 combinations) better differentiates counterparties but faces a data problem - many combinations will have few or no liquid CDS quotes. Using limited data makes curves unstable and incorporates idiosyncratic risk of specific credits that happens to trade. Broader classification (e.g., just by rating) provides more data points for stable curves but doesn't distinguish between very different credits. Best practice is to use granularity where data supports it (e.g., liquid combinations like 'A-rated Western Europe Financials') and broader proxies elsewhere, accepting that regulators push for rating/region/sector differentiation.
questions.why_it_matters: This trade-off affects CVA volatility and defensibility. Too granular and your CVA moves erratically based on idiosyncratic behavior of the few names in each bucket. Too broad and auditors/regulators question why you're not using available market segmentation. Getting this balance right is a key operational decision for CVA infrastructure.
common_traps: Building 147 curves because regulation mentions rating/region/sector without checking if you have data for all combinations
Using just one or two names to construct a 'generic' curve (idiosyncratic risk dominates)
Not reviewing and adjusting granularity as market liquidity changes over time
questions.real_world_example: A bank builds a 'BBB-rated Asian Industrials' curve using only 3 liquid CDS names. One name's spread widens 200 bps due to company-specific issues. The generic curve jumps, causing CVA MTM losses on 50 unrelated counterparties mapped to this curve. The bank realizes the classification is too granular for available liquidity and moves to 'BBB-rated Asia ex-Japan' combining industrials and other sectors.

questions.question: Explain the difference between 'settled recovery' and 'actual recovery' for OTC derivatives, and why this matters for CVA calculation and hedge accounting.
questions.answer_short: Settled recovery is the quick market price from the CDS auction (e.g., 9% for Lehman senior). Actual recovery is what you eventually receive through the bankruptcy process (potentially 30-40% for Lehman derivatives, years later). This timing and amount difference creates valuation and hedge accounting challenges.
questions.answer_long: When a counterparty defaults, CDS contracts settle quickly via an auction that establishes a 'settled recovery' price for bonds - this was around 8.6% for Lehman senior debt. This is what your CDS hedge pays out. However, OTC derivatives are bilateral, netted claims that cannot be traded and must work through bankruptcy, which takes years. The 'actual recovery' on derivatives can be substantially different - some Lehman derivatives counterparties eventually recovered 30-40%. This creates problems: (1) You assumed 60% LGD in CVA but might recover more, creating a P&L surprise years later, (2) Your CDS hedge paid out based on 8.6% recovery while you eventually get 35%, creating basis risk, (3) The timing difference means even if amounts match, the present value doesn't.
questions.why_it_matters: This is a critical real-world complication that theoretical CVA models ignore. When defaults actually happen, the recovery assumption you used in CVA pricing may prove wrong, and the timing of actual recovery (versus hedge payout) creates operational and accounting challenges. Understanding this helps you explain CVA model limitations and manage expectations during credit events.
common_traps: Assuming your CDS hedge recovery and actual derivative recovery will match (they often don't)
Not reserving for the possibility of recovery timing differences
Using non-standard LGD without considering you might have to accept whatever the market settles at for hedge accounting
questions.real_world_example: Bank has €10M exposure to Lehman, hedged with CDS. Lehman defaults. CDS auction settles at 8.6% recovery; bank receives €9.14M payout quickly. Bank's netted derivative claim is agreed at €10M after 18 months, but actual recovery payments trickle in over 5 years, eventually totaling €3.5M. The bank made €9.14M on the hedge but only lost €6.5M net on the exposure - a €2.64M basis that has to be explained to auditors across multiple accounting periods.

questions.question: What is the CDS-bond basis, and when would you prefer to use bond spreads versus CDS spreads for credit curve mapping despite the basis?
questions.answer_short: The CDS-bond basis is the difference between CDS spreads and bond-derived spreads for the same credit, which can be significant. You might prefer bonds when CDS is very illiquid, the bond market is deeper, or you can actually hedge by shorting bonds (rare).
questions.answer_long: For a given credit, the spread derived from bond prices (versus a treasury curve) often differs from the CDS spread - this is the CDS-bond basis. It arises from funding differences, repo market effects, deliverable option in CDS, and differing liquidity in each market. The basis can be 50-100+ bps during stress. Generally CDS is preferred because it's a clean credit spread (bonds mix credit and interest rate risk) and matches hedge instruments. However, bonds might be better when: (1) CDS is completely illiquid but secondary bond market exists, (2) You're in a region where CDS barely trades, (3) You can actually short bonds to hedge (though this is difficult/expensive), or (4) Regulatory/accounting requirements accept bond spreads. Any choice requires basis-adjusting to estimate the equivalent CDS spread for consistency.
questions.why_it_matters: You need to understand this basis because sometimes you'll be forced to use bonds (e.g., no CDS market in some Asian regions) and need to adjust to avoid inconsistency with CDS-based hedges. The basis also explains why your CVA might differ from a counterparty's even when pricing the same trades - you might be using different credit spread sources.
common_traps: Using bond spreads directly without adjusting for the CDS-bond basis when your hedges are CDS
Not understanding that bond spreads include non-credit components (liquidity, repo rates)
Thinking you can always short bonds to hedge (in practice bond shorting is expensive and difficult)
questions.real_world_example: During the 2008 crisis, some financial institution CDS spreads were 200-300 bps wider than bond-implied spreads due to funding stress and deliverable squeezes. A bank using bond spreads for CVA would have materially underpriced credit risk compared to the CDS market, creating losses if they tried to hedge with CDS. They needed to apply a basis adjustment to the bond spreads to estimate the equivalent CDS spread.

questions.question: How do Basel III capital relief rules for CVA hedges affect your choice of credit curve mapping methodology, and what tension does this create?
questions.answer_short: Basel III gives full capital relief for direct CDS hedges and partial relief for index hedges, but no relief for single-name proxies. This creates tension between economic hedging (proxy might be best) and capital efficiency (indices get relief even if less correlated).
questions.answer_long: Under current Basel III rules, you get full capital relief for hedging CVA with a CDS on the actual counterparty, partial relief for index hedges (with a correlation factor), and zero relief for single-name proxy CDS. This creates a problematic dynamic: economically, using a parent company's CDS as a proxy might provide excellent spread and default hedging, but you get no capital benefit. Using a broader index provides worse hedging but gets 50%+ capital relief. Banks are therefore incentivized to map counterparties to indices even when better single-name proxies exist, and to hedge with indices to minimize capital. This can lead to basis risk where the mapping and hedge don't economically match well, but the capital treatment forces this choice. BCBS (2015) has proposed giving capital relief to single-name proxies, which would reduce this tension.
questions.why_it_matters: This is a critical real-world constraint on CVA desk operations. Your 'optimal' mapping methodology from a pure pricing perspective might be terrible from a capital efficiency perspective. Understanding this tension helps explain why banks sometimes make mapping choices that seem to sacrifice precision for capital efficiency, and why regulatory changes to capital relief rules can force complete redesign of mapping frameworks.
common_traps: Designing a mapping framework based purely on credit correlation without considering capital relief implications
Not quantifying the capital cost of different mapping choices (might dwarf the CVA pricing difference)
Assuming the capital rules are static (regulatory proposals like BCBS 2015 can change the economics fundamentally)
questions.real_world_example: A bank has exposure to a European utility company whose parent trades CDS at 150 bps. The relevant iTraxx sector index is at 100 bps. Economically, the parent CDS is a much better hedge. But using the parent CDS for mapping means any hedge gets zero capital relief. Mapping to the index (even though it's 50 bps tighter and less correlated) allows 50% capital relief on index hedges. The capital cost of the first approach is so high that the bank maps to the index plus a 50 bps spread adjustment, accepting the basis risk.

questions.question: What are the advantages and disadvantages of using third-party generic curves (like Markit sector curves) versus building your own credit curve mapping framework?
questions.answer_short: Third-party curves are cheaper, independent (good for auditors), and maintained by specialists. However, they're rigid in classification, produce volatility outside your control, and may not align with your hedging strategy or capital optimization.
questions.answer_long: Third-party providers like Markit offer pre-built generic curves by sector, rating, and region using their methodologies for averaging, interpolation, and data selection. Advantages: (1) Lower cost than building infrastructure, (2) Independence appeals to auditors, (3) Professional maintenance and quality control, (4) Industry standard that facilitates comparison. Disadvantages: (1) Fixed classification may not match your counterparty segmentation needs, (2) You can't control methodology changes that create MTM volatility, (3) May not align with your specific hedging instruments or capital optimization strategy, (4) Less flexibility to incorporate your own credit views or internal ratings, (5) Doesn't adapt to your specific regional or sectoral concentrations. Larger banks typically build their own frameworks for control and optimization; smaller banks often use third-party curves to avoid infrastructure costs.
questions.why_it_matters: This is a fundamental build-vs-buy decision for CVA infrastructure. Your choice affects ongoing costs, P&L volatility, audit defensibility, and alignment with your hedging strategy. Understanding the trade-offs helps you make appropriate decisions based on your firm's size, sophistication, and counterparty profile.
common_traps: Using third-party curves without understanding their methodology (creates unexplained P&L moves)
Building your own framework without sufficient resources to maintain quality and independence
Not realizing third-party curves may change methodology, forcing you to accept their P&L impact
questions.real_world_example: A regional bank uses Markit sector curves for 90% of counterparties. Markit changes their methodology for averaging illiquid points, causing a 15% shift in BB-rated curves. The bank's CVA moves by €50M overnight due to a methodology change they didn't control and can't hedge. They have to explain to senior management and auditors that this is a 'day one' impact from a vendor methodology change, not a real market move or model error.

questions.subtopic: CDS Credit Events vs Derivative Defaults
questions.question: Why might a CDS contract not pay out even when you experience a default on an OTC derivative with the same counterparty, and how does this affect CVA hedging?
questions.answer_short: Standard CDS credit events are failure to pay (on bonds), restructuring, or bankruptcy. A failure to make a derivative payment may not trigger these events, especially failure to pay. This creates basis risk where you suffer a derivative default but your CDS hedge doesn't pay out.
questions.answer_long: ISDA standard CDS contracts define credit events as: (1) failure to pay on bonds/loans, (2) restructuring, or (3) bankruptcy. A counterparty could fail to make a derivative payment without triggering (1) if they're still current on bonds, and without (3) if they haven't filed bankruptcy - perhaps they're in pre-bankruptcy workout or dispute the derivative valuation. This creates 'jump-to-default' risk that's not hedged. Additionally, CDS requires delivery of a bond or loan, not a derivative, so even if the credit event triggers, the payout depends on bond recovery, not derivative recovery. Some CDS contracts include cross-default language to improve this, but they're more expensive. This means CDS hedges provide spread risk protection but imperfect default protection for derivatives.
questions.why_it_matters: This is a subtle but important limitation of using CDS to hedge CVA. In theory, you're hedged. In practice, there are scenarios where you experience a derivative default but your CDS hedge doesn't pay out, creating a loss. This affects how you should think about CVA hedge effectiveness and whether you're truly economically hedged versus just accounting-hedged.
common_traps: Assuming CDS hedges provide perfect default protection for derivatives (they don't in all scenarios)
Not understanding that failure to pay on a derivative may not be a CDS credit event
Ignoring that CDS settles based on bond recovery, not your specific derivative recovery
questions.real_world_example: A counterparty in financial distress stops posting collateral on out-of-the-money derivatives and disputes valuations, creating an effective default. They continue paying bond coupons to avoid triggering broader defaults. The bank's CDS hedge doesn't trigger because there's no 'failure to pay' credit event (bond payments are current) and no bankruptcy filing. The bank terminates the derivatives and takes a loss, but the CDS hedge is worthless. They had CVA spread risk hedged but not this jump-to-default scenario.

questions.subtopic: Regional Variations in Credit Curve Mapping
questions.question: How do credit curve mapping challenges differ between a global bank operating in Europe/US versus a regional bank in Asia, and what adaptations are needed?
questions.answer_short: European/US banks benefit from liquid CDS and bond markets, allowing granular rating/sector mapping. Asian banks face much more limited liquidity, forcing greater reliance on sovereign curves, broader proxies, and potentially greater acceptance of bond spreads over CDS.
questions.answer_long: European and US banks operate in regions with relatively deep CDS markets (single-name and indices), active secondary bond trading, and comprehensive rating coverage. They can implement granular mapping by rating/sector/region and have hedging options. Asian banks (especially Southeast Asia, excluding Japan) face: (1) Very limited single-name CDS markets, (2) Illiquid or non-existent credit indices for many sectors, (3) Many counterparties without external ratings, (4) Bond markets that may be more liquid than CDS in some cases. This forces adaptations: heavier reliance on sovereign CDS as proxies with spread adjustments, broader (less granular) generic curves due to limited data, potentially greater use of bond spreads (with basis adjustments), more subjective spread add-ons based on internal ratings, and acceptance that hedging is very limited. Regulators in these regions may be somewhat more flexible about methodology given market realities.
questions.why_it_matters: Credit curve mapping frameworks cannot be one-size-fits-all globally. Understanding regional market differences is critical for designing appropriate methodologies and setting realistic expectations for hedging and capital efficiency. Asian regional banks face fundamentally different challenges than European/US banks, requiring different solutions.
common_traps: Trying to apply European/US mapping frameworks in Asian markets without adaptation
Not recognizing that 'illiquid markets' justification has limits with auditors/regulators
Underestimating the operational challenge when you must map most counterparties using sovereign proxies plus judgmental spread adjustments
questions.real_world_example: A Hong Kong bank has exposure to Thai and Vietnamese corporates. No single-name CDS exist, no relevant credit indices, bond markets are illiquid. The bank maps these counterparties to Thai and Vietnamese sovereign CDS (which do trade) and adds 200-400 bps spread adjustments based on internal credit analysis and rating equivalents. They accept they cannot hedge these specific credits and that the mapping is highly judgmental, but it's the best available approach given market liquidity. Auditors accept this after reviewing the limited market alternatives.

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between real-world and risk-neutral default probabilities?
questions.answer_short: Real-world probabilities are estimated from historical default data, while risk-neutral probabilities are derived from market prices (bonds/CDS) and include a risk premium that investors demand for accepting credit risk.
questions.answer_long: Real-world default probabilities represent actual historical default frequencies observed for a given rating class over time. Risk-neutral default probabilities are higher because they are extracted from market prices of credit instruments like bonds or CDS, and they incorporate both the expected default loss AND a risk premium that compensates investors for bearing credit risk. Empirical studies show risk-neutral probabilities can be 2-17 times higher than real-world probabilities, especially for investment-grade credits.
questions.why_it_matters: Using the wrong type of probability fundamentally changes CVA calculation results. Modern accounting (IFRS 13) and Basel III capital rules require risk-neutral probabilities, making CVA a market price rather than an actuarial reserve. This shift significantly increases CVA values and volatility, especially for illiquid credits where hedging is difficult.
common_traps: Assuming real-world probabilities are 'correct' because they match actual defaults
Not recognizing that risk-neutral probabilities include a substantial non-default premium
Using historical data for CVA when regulations require market-implied probabilities
questions.real_world_example: A BBB-rated company might have a 0.47% one-year real-world default probability based on historical data, but its risk-neutral probability derived from a 238 bps CDS spread could be 2.38% (5 times higher). Using real-world PD would drastically undervalue CVA and misalign with hedging instruments.

questions.subtopic: Extracting Default Probabilities from Credit Spreads
questions.question: How do you calculate an approximate annual default probability from a credit spread using the simple formula approach?
questions.answer_short: The simple formula is: PD(t) ≈ s(t) × Δt / LGD, where s(t) is the credit spread, Δt is the time period, and LGD is loss given default.
questions.answer_long: The approximation PD(ti-1, ti) ≈ s(ti) × Δt / LGD converts a credit spread into an unconditional default probability for a time period. For example, with a 300 bps spread and 60% LGD, the one-year PD is approximately 300 bps / 60% = 5%. This formula assumes the spread is constant over the period and neglects the precise shape of the credit curve prior to the period, making it less accurate for steep curves. More sophisticated bootstrapping methods exist but this approximation is widely used for its simplicity.
questions.why_it_matters: Converting credit spreads to default probabilities is a daily operational requirement for CVA desks. The simple formula provides quick estimates for pricing, risk reports, and preliminary analysis. Understanding when this approximation breaks down (steep curves, long periods) prevents pricing errors that could accumulate across thousands of counterparties.
common_traps: Forgetting to divide by LGD, leading to default probabilities that are too low
Using this formula for long time periods where curve shape matters significantly
Not recognizing the probability is unconditional (not conditional on survival)
questions.real_world_example: A trading desk receives a 5-year CDS quote of 450 bps for a new corporate counterparty. Using 60% LGD, the approximate 5-year cumulative default probability is 450 bps × 5 / 60% = 37.5%. This quick calculation helps the desk decide if CVA charges on proposed trades are reasonable before running full analytics.

questions.question: Why does the shape of a credit curve (flat, upward-sloping, inverted) matter even if two curves have the same 5-year spread?
questions.answer_short: The curve shape determines when defaults are expected to occur. An upward-sloping curve implies lower near-term default risk but higher later, while an inverted curve suggests imminent stress with lower tail risk.
questions.answer_long: Three credit curves with identical 5-year spreads of 300 bps will have the same 5-year cumulative default probability (e.g., 22.12%), but vastly different annual default probabilities. An upward-sloping curve might have 2% PD in year 1 but 8% in year 5, while an inverted curve could show 8% in year 1 and 2% in year 5. This matters enormously for CVA because exposure profiles interact with the timing of default. A frontloaded exposure with an inverted curve creates much higher CVA than with an upward-sloping curve. Extrapolation beyond observable tenors is particularly sensitive to assumed curve shape.
questions.why_it_matters: CVA and DVA calculations multiply exposure by default probability at each time point. Getting the term structure wrong misallocates risk across time. For a pay-fixed interest rate swap (exposure increases over time), assuming a flat curve when the real curve is inverted could underestimate CVA by 30-50%. This affects pricing, hedging, and capital allocation.
common_traps: Using only the 5-year CDS spread and assuming a flat curve for all maturities
Not considering that curve shape reflects market expectations about credit deterioration timing
Extrapolating beyond 10 years without recognizing high uncertainty
questions.real_world_example: A European bank has 7-year cross-currency swaps with an emerging market sovereign. The sovereign's curve is inverted (1Y: 500 bps, 5Y: 300 bps) due to near-term political risk. Using a flat 300 bps assumption would significantly underestimate CVA because the high early default probability coincides with peak FX exposure from notional exchanges.

questions.subtopic: Loss Given Default and Recovery Rates
questions.question: What is Loss Given Default (LGD) and how does it relate to recovery rate?
questions.answer_short: LGD is the percentage amount lost when a counterparty defaults. It equals one minus the recovery rate. For senior unsecured claims, market convention typically uses 60% LGD (40% recovery).
questions.answer_long: Loss Given Default measures what percentage of exposure is actually lost in default after the bankruptcy process. It's calculated as LGD = 1 - Recovery Rate. For derivatives that rank pari passu with senior unsecured debt, the standard assumption is 60% LGD (40% recovery), matching CDS conventions. However, actual recoveries vary widely by seniority, sector, and economic conditions. Historical data shows financial institution recoveries ranging from 0.1% (Glitnir subordinated) to 99.9% (Fannie Mae subordinated due to a delivery squeeze).
questions.why_it_matters: LGD directly scales CVA calculations: CVA = Exposure × PD × LGD. However, there's a cancellation effect when deriving PD from credit spreads using the same LGD, making the precise LGD choice less critical than credit spread accuracy. The bigger issue is timing - CDS settle quickly (settled recovery) while derivatives take years to work out (actual recovery), creating potential value differences.
common_traps: Using different LGD values to derive PD versus calculate CVA (creates inconsistency)
Assuming all senior unsecured claims have identical recovery (seniority nuances exist)
Ignoring that derivative recoveries may take years longer than bond recoveries
questions.real_world_example: After Lehman Brothers defaulted, CDS auctions determined a settled recovery of 8.6% for senior debt within weeks. However, derivatives counterparties experienced actual recoveries of 30-40% over subsequent years as the estate was wound down. A bank using 9% recovery in CVA calculations but ultimately receiving 35% significantly overestimated its credit loss.

questions.question: Why have banks largely converged on using risk-neutral default probabilities for CVA despite the challenges with illiquid credits?
questions.answer_short: Regulatory requirements (Basel III) and accounting standards (IFRS 13) mandate market-observable inputs and specifically reference CDS spreads. Auditors and regulators reject real-world probabilities even for illiquid credits, requiring proxy mapping instead.
questions.answer_long: The convergence to risk-neutral PDs stems from three forces: (1) Basel III CVA capital rules explicitly require CDS spreads where available and proxy spreads otherwise, (2) IFRS 13 fair value accounting mandates exit prices using market-observable inputs, making historical default rates inconsistent with the standard, and (3) the development of CVA hedging practices means CVA should reflect hedge costs. While this creates challenges for illiquid credits (no direct market data, harder to hedge, increased volatility), regulators view consistent risk-neutral treatment as preferable to mixing methodologies. By 2015, the vast majority of large banks use risk-neutral PDs across their entire counterparty population.
questions.why_it_matters: The shift to risk-neutral PDs typically increases CVA by 2-5x compared to real-world calculations, directly impacting P&L, pricing of new trades, and capital requirements. More importantly, it changes CVA's nature from a statistical reserve to a market price. This means CVA becomes much more volatile and responsive to market conditions, requiring active management, hedging, and sophisticated proxy mapping for thousands of illiquid counterparties.
common_traps: Using blended approaches (mix of real-world and risk-neutral) which auditors typically reject
Arguing that lack of hedgeability justifies historical PDs (regulators don't accept this)
Not recognizing that proxy mapping subjectivity is unavoidable but must be systematic
questions.real_world_example: A European bank has 2,000 SME counterparties with derivatives exposure totaling €5bn. Only 50 have external ratings and none have CDS. Using real-world PDs, CVA was €50m. After regulatory pressure, they implemented a proxy mapping to CDS indices by rating/sector, and CVA jumped to €180m, forcing wider bid-offer spreads and repricing of client relationships.

questions.question: What are the key differences between using direct observables, single-name proxies, and generic proxies for credit curve mapping?
questions.answer_short: Direct observables (counterparty's own CDS/bond) offer best hedging but poor liquidity; single-name proxies (similar credit) provide medium liquidity and spread hedging but no capital relief; generic proxies (indices) are most liquid with partial capital relief but least counterparty-specific.
questions.answer_long: Direct observables use the counterparty's actual traded instruments (their CDS or bonds), providing perfect spread and default hedging plus full capital relief, but these exist for very few counterparties and often only at 5-year tenor. Single-name proxies use a similar entity (parent, peer, or sovereign), offering reasonable spread correlation and hedging but no default protection and currently no Basel III capital relief, though this may change. Generic proxies map to indices by rating/region/sector, providing excellent liquidity and hedging with partial capital relief (via the standardized CVA charge) but much weaker correlation to specific counterparty credit movements. The choice involves trading off precision against practicality.
questions.why_it_matters: Most banks have direct observables for <5% of counterparties, forcing systematic proxy mapping for the remaining 95%+. The mapping choice affects CVA accuracy, hedging effectiveness, P&L volatility, and capital efficiency. Using overly generic proxies (e.g., one index for all corporates) reduces CVA volatility but creates basis risk and potential mispricing. Overly granular mapping (seeking perfect proxies) introduces idiosyncratic noise and operational complexity.
common_traps: Over-relying on single-name proxies that provide good spread hedges but trigger no capital relief
Using generic indices too broadly, mapping unrelated credits to the same curve
Not adjusting single-name proxies with basis when the credit quality clearly differs
questions.real_world_example: A bank trades with an unrated Asian manufacturing subsidiary of a European parent (for which a 5Y CDS exists at 150 bps). Options: (1) Use parent CDS directly (single-name proxy, spread hedge, no capital relief), (2) Add 50 bps to parent CDS to reflect weaker subsidiary credit (adjusted proxy, no capital relief), or (3) Map to iTraxx Asia Industrials at 180 bps (generic proxy, partial capital relief). The choice affects CVA, hedging strategy, and capital costs.

questions.question: What are the main credit indices used in European credit markets and what types of credits do they reference?
questions.answer_short: iTraxx Europe Main (125 investment-grade credits), iTraxx Non-financials (100 IG corporates), iTraxx Crossover (40 sub-IG credits), iTraxx Financials (senior and subordinated), and iTraxx SovX (sovereign credits across regions).
questions.answer_long: The European CDS index family provides standardized exposure to different credit segments. iTraxx Europe Main covers the 125 most liquid investment-grade entities across all sectors. It's subdivided into iTraxx Non-financials (100 BBB and better corporates), which itself has sector sub-indices (industrials, energy, TMT, consumers, autos). iTraxx Crossover targets 40 BBB-rated and below names for sub-investment grade exposure. iTraxx Financials splits into senior and subordinated tranches. iTraxx SovX covers sovereign credits segmented by region (Western Europe, CEEMEA, Asia Pacific, Latin America, G7, BRIC). Typical liquid tenors are 3Y, 5Y, 7Y, and 10Y for main indices, while sub-indices often only have 5Y and 10Y liquidity.
questions.why_it_matters: CDS indices are the primary generic proxies for mapping illiquid counterparties. Understanding the index structure is essential for systematic credit curve mapping. Using the wrong index (e.g., mapping an Asian bank to iTraxx Europe Financials) creates geographic and structural mismatches. Index liquidity also determines hedging feasibility and capital relief availability under Basel III advanced CVA rules.
common_traps: Using overly broad indices (e.g., iTraxx Main) when more specific sector indices exist
Not recognizing liquidity differences between main indices and sub-indices
Assuming all regional index families (iTraxx, CDX, Asia) have identical structures
questions.real_world_example: A German utility company without CDS would typically map to iTraxx Europe Non-financials (if investment grade) or potentially a more specific industrials sub-index. A Chinese bank might map to iTraxx Asia Financials rather than iTraxx Europe Financials to capture regional credit dynamics. The index choice directly determines the proxy credit spread used in CVA calculations.

questions.question: What is the fundamental trade-off between granularity and data availability when constructing generic credit curves, and how should a bank balance this?
questions.answer_short: More granular curves (e.g., A-rated US utilities) better differentiate counterparties but have fewer data points per curve, risking idiosyncratic volatility. Broader curves (e.g., all A-rated corporates) have more data but worse differentiation. Balance by using granularity only when sufficient liquid CDS exist.
questions.answer_long: Generic curve construction faces a classic bias-variance trade-off. Highly granular mapping (rating + region + sector, e.g., 'BBB Western Europe Financials') creates 7 ratings × 7 regions × 3 sectors = 147 possible curves, but many buckets will have zero or very few liquid CDS quotes. This forces extrapolation/interpolation and makes the curve vulnerable to idiosyncratic moves in the few constituent credits. Broader mapping (e.g., only rating-based) provides more data points per curve but fails to capture important credit differences between, say, European banks and Asian corporates. Best practice uses granularity where data supports it (e.g., separate financials in Europe/US/Asia) and consolidates where data is sparse (e.g., combining emerging market sectors). Curves should have minimum thresholds (e.g., 5+ liquid single-names) before treating as separate.
questions.why_it_matters: Poor curve construction cascades through CVA for thousands of counterparties. Overly granular curves create spurious MTM volatility when one credit in a small basket widens idiosyncratically. Overly broad curves misprice credit risk, potentially undercharging risky clients and overcharging safer ones. The construction methodology must balance accuracy, stability, and operational feasibility while satisfying auditors and regulators who expect rating/region/sector differentiation.
common_traps: Creating 147 theoretical curves without checking if many have zero or one data point
Using single-credit movements as curve levels (essentially creating noisy single-name proxies)
Not having a systematic hierarchy (e.g., if sector has insufficient data, fall back to regional curve)
questions.real_world_example: A bank initially created separate generic curves for 'A-rated Latin American Industrials' based on 2 CDS. One credit widened 150 bps due to company-specific fraud, causing all 50 counterparties in that bucket to show large CVA increases unrelated to their actual credit quality. After review, they consolidated to 'A-rated Latin America' (15+ CDS), accepting less granularity for more stability.

questions.question: Why might actual recovery on a defaulted derivative differ significantly from the settled recovery determined in a CDS auction?
questions.answer_short: CDS auctions settle quickly (days/weeks) by trading defaulted bonds, while derivative recoveries require lengthy bankruptcy processes (months/years) to determine net claims after netting and collateral, often yielding different recovery values.
questions.answer_long: Settled recovery occurs immediately after default via CDS auctions where bondholders can sell defaulted bonds, providing quick price discovery. This reflects market expectations of ultimate recovery. Actual recovery on derivatives takes much longer because: (1) netting across potentially hundreds of trades must be calculated and agreed with administrators, (2) collateral positions must be resolved, (3) set-off rights against other claims may apply, and (4) derivatives cannot be traded individually like bonds. The bankruptcy process for derivatives can take years. Empirically, Lehman's CDS auction settled at 8.6% but derivative counterparties ultimately received 30-40%, a 3-4x difference.
questions.why_it_matters: Banks typically use settled recovery (CDS-implied) for CVA calculations because it's market-observable and used for PD derivation. However, the P&L realized in actual default may differ materially. This creates timing risk (when will recovery occur?) and amount uncertainty. For CVA hedging using CDS, the hedge pays out based on settled recovery while the actual loss reflects actual recovery years later, creating basis risk that's hard to quantify prospectively.
common_traps: Assuming CDS auction recovery is the actual amount the bank will receive
Not reserving for the timing difference (receiving recovery years later has NPV impact)
Overlooking that set-off rights and collateral may improve derivative recovery vs. bonds
questions.real_world_example: A bank had $100m exposure to Lehman when it defaulted. They hedged with CDS, which paid out 91.4% (100% - 8.6% recovery) quickly, providing $91.4m. Their actual derivative claim was agreed at $95m after netting, but they ultimately received $35m (37% recovery) over 5 years. The $91.4m CDS payout minus $35m actual recovery left $56.4m profit, but the timing mismatch created multi-year uncertainty and funding costs.

questions.question: What are the main technical mismatches between using CDS as hedges for counterparty credit risk on derivatives?
questions.answer_short: CDS credit events (failure to pay, bankruptcy, restructuring) may not include derivative payment failures; CDS delivers bonds/loans not derivatives; and CDS LGD may differ from actual derivative recovery, creating basis risk.
questions.answer_long: Several structural issues complicate CDS hedging of counterparty risk: (1) Credit event definitions under ISDA CDS contracts specify failure to pay on bonds/loans, bankruptcy, or restructuring. A counterparty failing to post derivative margin might not trigger the CDS. Cross-default provisions help but aren't universal. (2) Physical settlement requires delivering bonds or loans to receive par, but derivative receivables aren't deliverable obligations, creating a basis if derivative recovery differs from bond recovery. (3) As discussed previously, CDS settle based on bond prices (settled recovery) while derivatives may ultimately recover different amounts. These mismatches mean a CDS hedge provides correlation but not perfect protection.
questions.why_it_matters: Banks relying on CDS hedges for CVA assume the hedge will pay out when needed. However, in edge cases (e.g., technical default on derivatives without broader failure to pay, or recovery differences), the hedge may not perform as expected. This is particularly relevant for determining capital relief under Basel III, which requires genuine hedging effectiveness. Understanding these gaps helps set risk limits and reserve policies.
common_traps: Assuming a CDS is a perfect hedge for derivative counterparty risk (it's correlation, not replication)
Not verifying whether derivative failure to pay would trigger the specific CDS contract
Ignoring that LGD assumptions in CVA calculations may not match actual CDS payouts
questions.real_world_example: A European bank hedged counterparty risk on a sovereign using that sovereign's CDS. When the sovereign's bonds were restructured, the CDS was triggered and paid out. However, the derivative transactions were not restructured and continued to perform normally. The bank received the CDS payout (profit) but still held the performing derivative (over-hedged position), demonstrating the basis between CDS credit events and derivative default.

questions.question: What are the advantages and disadvantages of using third-party generic credit curves (like Markit sector curves) versus building internal curves?
questions.answer_short: Third-party curves offer independence (audit benefit), lower cost, and consistency but lack flexibility in classification and create MTM volatility outside the bank's control. Internal curves allow customization and control but require resources and may face audit scrutiny.
questions.answer_long: Third-party providers like Markit construct generic curves using systematic methodologies across ratings and sectors, averaging liquid single-name CDS at 1Y, 5Y, and 10Y tenors with interpolation between. Advantages: (1) independence supports audit requirements, (2) lower cost than building full infrastructure, (3) consistent methodology. Disadvantages: (1) rigid classification may not match bank's exposure profile, (2) methodology changes by provider create unexplained P&L, (3) limited control over which credits are included or excluded. Internal curves allow flexibility (e.g., regional bank can over-weight local credits) and stability (changes are deliberate) but require significant resources, robust governance, and must satisfy auditors that the methodology is unbiased.
questions.why_it_matters: For smaller banks or those with limited CVA infrastructure, third-party curves provide a quick, auditable solution. However, larger banks with active CVA desks typically need internal curves to align with their hedging strategies and risk management. The choice affects not just CVA calculations but also hedge accounting treatment, capital efficiency, and operational flexibility. Poor alignment between curves and actual hedges creates unexplained basis that's difficult to justify to regulators.
common_traps: Using third-party curves but hedging with different indices (creates intentional basis)
Not understanding the methodology behind vendor curves (what's included, how weighted)
Switching between internal and external curves opportunistically (raises audit flags)
questions.real_world_example: A mid-sized European bank uses Markit financials curves for CVA but hedges with iTraxx Financials index. When Markit changed their curve methodology (removing certain banks from the basket), CVA moved 50 bps but hedges didn't, creating €15m unexplained P&L. They now document the expected basis and reserve against it.

questions.question: What is a hazard rate and how does it relate to the instantaneous probability of default and the credit spread?
questions.answer_short: The hazard rate (λ) is the instantaneous default intensity. For a flat credit spread s and constant LGD, the hazard rate is approximately λ ≈ s/LGD. The survival probability is Q(t) = exp(-λt).
questions.answer_long: The hazard rate λ(t) represents the conditional default probability per unit time at instant t, given survival to t. It's related to credit spreads through λ(t) ≈ s(t)/LGD under continuous time assumptions. The survival probability (not defaulting by time t) is Q(t) = exp(-∫₀ᵗ λ(u)du). For a flat hazard rate λ, this simplifies to Q(t) = exp(-λt). The default probability over a period [t₁,t₂] is Q(t₁) - Q(t₂). More sophisticated models use piecewise constant or deterministic functions of time λ(t) to match market credit spreads at all tenors, essentially bootstrapping the hazard rate curve from the credit curve.
questions.why_it_matters: Hazard rates provide the rigorous mathematical framework for converting credit spreads to default probabilities. While the simple formula (PD = s×Δt/LGD) works for quick estimates, CVA systems typically bootstrap hazard rate curves to precisely match market credit spreads at all observable tenors. This ensures consistency: the CVA calculation will exactly reproduce market CDS prices if the exposure is a constant notional. Understanding hazard rates is essential for implementing CVA models correctly and for debugging pricing discrepancies.
common_traps: Confusing hazard rate (intensity) with default probability (they have different units)
Using survival probability Q(t) directly instead of the period default probability
Not bootstrapping hazard rates properly, leading to arbitrage opportunities between tenors
questions.real_world_example: A CVA system uses the simple formula approximation and prices 5Y CVA using a 5Y CDS spread. Separately, it prices 3Y CVA using a 3Y spread. These are inconsistent - the implied hazard rates don't match, creating arbitrage. Proper implementation bootstraps a hazard rate curve λ(t) such that the present value of default probabilities exactly matches all CDS tenors (1Y, 3Y, 5Y, 7Y, 10Y) simultaneously.

questions.question: Why are funding costs difficult to define objectively for FVA purposes?
