Their top 100 counterparties represent €400M of €550M total CVA, yet get the same crude mapping as tiny exposures. After a methodology review, they implement a 3-tier system: Tier 1 (80 names, €380M CVA) gets single-name or detailed proxies; Tier 2 (400 names, €140M CVA) gets granular sector/rating curves; Tier 3 (2,020 names, €30M CVA) stays with broad indices. This increases accuracy from 75% to 95% on mark-to-market while only doubling operational costs (focusing resources on what matters), and improves capital efficiency by €15M through better hedge recognition on Tier 1.

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between a real-world default probability and a risk-neutral default probability?
questions.answer_short: Real-world PD is estimated from historical default data, while risk-neutral PD is derived from market prices (bonds/CDS) and includes a risk premium that investors demand.
questions.answer_long: Real-world default probabilities come from analyzing historical default rates by rating category. Risk-neutral default probabilities are extracted from market instruments like bonds or credit default swaps. The risk-neutral measure is systematically higher because it includes a risk premium - investors demand extra compensation beyond expected losses for bearing credit risk. Empirically, risk-neutral PDs can be 2-17 times higher than real-world PDs depending on credit quality.
questions.why_it_matters: This distinction is critical for CVA pricing. Using real-world PDs significantly underprices counterparty risk compared to market exit prices. Modern accounting standards (IFRS 13) and Basel III regulations require risk-neutral measures, making this fundamental to proper valuation.
common_traps: Thinking real-world PDs give 'correct' expected losses - they miss the market price of risk
Using real-world PDs for illiquid credits 'because there's no CDS' - regulators require market-consistent approaches
Ignoring that the PD choice fundamentally changes CVA from actuarial reserve to market price
questions.real_world_example: A single-A rated corporate might have a 0.13% one-year historical default rate but a 1.28% risk-neutral PD from CDS markets - nearly 10x higher. A bank using real-world PD would charge 1/10th the CVA compared to a competitor using risk-neutral, creating competitive distortions and mispricing.

questions.subtopic: Loss given default and recovery rates
questions.question: What is Loss Given Default (LGD) and how does it relate to recovery rate?
questions.answer_short: LGD is the percentage lost when a counterparty defaults. It equals one minus the recovery rate (e.g., 60% LGD means 40% recovery).
questions.answer_long: Loss Given Default represents the proportion of exposure that is not recovered following a counterparty default. It is simply one minus the recovery rate. For OTC derivatives, the claim typically ranks pari passu with senior unsecured debt, which standard CDS contracts assume at 60% LGD (40% recovery) for investment grade corporates. The actual LGD can vary dramatically by seniority, sector, and economic conditions - ranging from near 0% to 100% as seen in the 2008 examples where Fannie Mae senior recovered 91.5% while Glitnir subordinated recovered only 0.1%.
questions.why_it_matters: LGD is required to convert credit spreads into default probabilities. However, in CVA calculations there is a cancellation effect (CVA = LGD × PD × Exposure, but PD is derived assuming an LGD), so the exact LGD assumption matters less than the credit spread. What matters more is whether the derivative seniority truly matches the reference instrument.
common_traps: Overthinking LGD precision - credit spread calibration matters far more for CVA
Assuming standard 60% LGD always applies - structured products or subordinated trades differ
Confusing settled recovery (CDS auction ~9% for Lehman) with actual recovery (30-40% received years later)
questions.real_world_example: In the Lehman Brothers bankruptcy, the CDS auction settled at ~9% recovery (91% LGD) within weeks. However, actual recoveries on derivatives received over subsequent years were 30-40%, creating a 20-30% benefit not reflected in initial CVA calculations. This timing mismatch is a real operational consideration for managing defaulted exposures.

questions.question: Given a credit spread and LGD, what is the approximate formula for calculating the default probability between two dates, and what is its key limitation?
questions.answer_short: The approximation is PD(t[i-1], t[i]) ≈ s[t] × (t[i] - t[i-1]) / LGD. It fails to account for the credit curve shape before t[i-1], worsening as the curve slope increases.
questions.answer_long: The simple formula PD(t[i-1], t[i]) ≈ s[t] × Δt / LGD provides an unconditional default probability for the period, where s[t] is the credit spread at time t and Δt is the time increment. This is only an approximation because it ignores the term structure of spreads prior to the period. When spreads are steeply upward or inverted, this creates material errors. A proper bootstrap from CDS spreads accounts for survival probabilities from all prior periods and produces more accurate results, especially for longer-dated exposures.
questions.why_it_matters: This formula is widely used for quick CVA estimates and risk calculations. Understanding its limitations prevents mispricing on steep credit curves or when precise term structure matters. For regulatory capital or accounting CVA, more accurate bootstrapping is typically required.
common_traps: Using this on inverted or steep curves without checking accuracy - errors compound over time
Forgetting these are unconditional probabilities, not conditional on survival
Not recognizing that interpolated spreads between liquid points magnify approximation errors
questions.real_world_example: For a flat 300bps curve with 60% LGD, the 1Y PD is approximately 300bps × 1 / 60% = 5.0%, close to the exact 4.88%. But on a steep upward curve starting at 100bps and reaching 500bps at 5Y, this approximation at year 1 would significantly overestimate PD if using the 5Y spread instead of bootstrapping from the 1Y point.

questions.question: Why can two credit curves with identical 5-year spreads produce dramatically different annual default probabilities across the term structure?
questions.answer_short: Because the shape matters, not just the level. An upward-sloping curve implies lower near-term and higher long-term default risk than a flat curve, while an inverted curve shows the opposite pattern.
questions.answer_long: Three curves - flat, upward-sloping, and inverted - can all have 300bps at the 5-year point but distribute default probability very differently across time. The upward-sloping curve has lower spreads initially, producing lower default probability in years 1-3 but much higher in years 6-10. The inverted curve front-loads default risk. This happens because cumulative default probability at 5Y must match (given the same 5Y spread), but the path to get there reflects the entire curve shape. The mathematical bootstrapping process ensures consistency across the full term structure.
questions.why_it_matters: CVA calculations are extremely sensitive to when defaults are expected to occur, not just the total probability. A corporate with deteriorating credit (inverted curve) will have much higher near-term CVA contribution than one with improving prospects (upward curve), even if 5Y spreads match. This affects hedging strategies and capital allocation.
common_traps: Using only a single maturity point (like 5Y) and assuming flat PDs - misses term structure completely
Extrapolating beyond 10Y linearly when curve shape may change dramatically
Not updating curve shapes as credit conditions change, leading to stale PD profiles
questions.real_world_example: During the European sovereign crisis, peripheral sovereign curves were heavily inverted (short spreads far wider than long), reflecting immediate default concerns. Greece's 1Y spread exceeded 5Y by thousands of basis points. Using only the 5Y spread would massively underestimate near-term default risk and misprice short-dated CVA by orders of magnitude.

questions.subtopic: Move to risk-neutral PDs in practice
questions.question: Why have accounting standards (IFRS 13) and Basel III capital rules forced banks to use risk-neutral default probabilities even for illiquid counterparties where no CDS exists?
questions.answer_short: IFRS 13 requires market-observable inputs and exit price notions. Basel III explicitly references CDS spreads in CVA capital formulas. Both frameworks prioritize market consistency over actuarial approaches.
questions.answer_long: The regulatory and accounting convergence to risk-neutral PDs stems from the market-based valuation philosophy. IFRS 13 mandates that fair value reflects an exit price - what you could trade the position for, not expected loss. Basel III CVA capital rules explicitly use credit spreads in the standardized approach and require CDS-based calibration. This creates a consistent framework across pricing, capital, and accounting. Even for illiquid credits, regulators require banks to use proxy spreads based on rating, region, and sector rather than historical default rates, ensuring that CVA includes the market price of risk, not just actuarial expectations.
questions.why_it_matters: This shift increased CVA charges by 2-17x for many institutions, fundamentally changing counterparty risk economics. It makes CVA more volatile but also more aligned with hedging instruments (CDS market). Banks must build sophisticated mapping frameworks for thousands of illiquid names, creating operational challenges but also more consistent risk measurement across the industry.
common_traps: Arguing to auditors that illiquid credits should use real-world PDs 'because there's no market' - regulators reject this
Using blended approaches (mixing real-world and risk-neutral) without clear justification - creates inconsistency
Not recognizing this creates a hedge-ability problem - CVA is priced at market levels but hedges may not exist
questions.real_world_example: A regional bank with 2000 SME counterparties has CDS on perhaps 5 of them. They must map the other 1995 to generic curves or proxies based on their internal ratings and sectors. An ECB asset quality review would challenge any use of historical PDs and require demonstration that CDS-based market proxies are used consistently, even though the bank cannot actually hedge these exposures in the CDS market.

questions.question: What are the main types of CDS instruments available for credit curve mapping, and which provides the most direct credit spread information?
questions.answer_short: Single-name CDS, CDS indices (like iTraxx, CDX), asset swap spreads, and bond-implied spreads. Single-name CDS provides the cleanest, most direct credit spread quote.
questions.answer_long: The CDS market offers several reference points: single-name CDS on individual entities (most direct), CDS indices that average 20-125 credits by category (more liquid), asset swap spreads from bond markets (requires benchmark assumptions), and credit spreads derived from bond prices. Single-name CDS is preferred because the premium directly equals the credit spread without needing to separate components. Indices include iTraxx Europe (investment grade corporates), CDX North America (US credits), regional sovereign indices (iTraxx SovX), and sector-specific variants (financials, high yield, emerging markets), each trading at 3Y, 5Y, 7Y and 10Y tenors.
questions.why_it_matters: Understanding the CDS market structure is fundamental to credit curve mapping. For ~80% of counterparties, single-name CDS won't exist, forcing mapping to indices or proxies. Knowing which indices cover which credit types enables systematic mapping frameworks that satisfy regulators while providing hedge-able reference points.
common_traps: Assuming CDS market is liquid for most credits - it covers only hundreds of names vs thousands of potential counterparties
Not recognizing technical differences - CDS may not trigger on derivative payment failures
Ignoring that CDS references bonds/loans for delivery, not derivatives, creating basis risk
questions.real_world_example: A European bank trading with a BBB-rated French utility company might find no single-name CDS. They could map to iTraxx Europe (125 investment grade names) or the more specific iTraxx Non-financials index. While less precise than a single-name, the index provides a hedge-able market reference that satisfies the 'rating, region, sector' regulatory requirement and offers capital relief under Basel III.

questions.question: What standard LGD assumptions are embedded in major CDS indices, and when might a practitioner adjust these?
questions.answer_short: Standard CDS contracts assume 60% LGD (40% recovery) for corporates. Adjustments are made for structural seniority (secured/subordinated trades), securitization SPVs, or documented recovery experience above market standards.
questions.answer_long: iTraxx Europe and CDX North America indices trade with an assumed 60% LGD convention for standard senior unsecured reference obligations. Individual CDS contracts may use different assumptions for subordinated debt or secured obligations. Practitioners might adjust LGD downward (assume better recovery) for derivatives with securitization vehicles that have structural seniority, for transactions with credit enhancements beyond standard collateral, or when strong historical work-out experience can be documented. However, auditors and regulators require solid evidence for departures from market conventions, especially after cases like Lehman where initial settled recovery (~9%) differed materially from eventual actual recovery (30-40%).
questions.why_it_matters: While LGD has a cancellation effect in CVA (it's in both the PD calculation from spreads and the loss calculation), structural differences matter significantly. A derivative ranking senior to bonds could have 20-30% better recovery. With CVA potentially in millions, a 20% LGD difference on a €10M exposure at default is €2M - material enough to justify careful analysis.
common_traps: Always using 60% because 'it's standard' - ignoring actual seniority of the derivative claim
Over-optimizing LGD assumptions to reduce CVA without solid documentation - auditors will challenge
Not recognizing that recovery timing matters - settled vs actual recovery can differ by years
questions.real_world_example: A bank trading derivatives with a CLO special purpose vehicle may document that their swaps rank senior to all note holders and are fully collateralized by the CLO assets, potentially justifying a 30-40% LGD instead of 60%. However, they must document this structural seniority clearly in legal opinions and demonstrate it would survive bankruptcy. Without this, auditors would require standard 60% LGD assumptions.

questions.question: Compare the three main credit spread mapping approaches (direct observables, single-name proxies, generic proxies) in terms of liquidity, hedging ability, and capital relief.
questions.answer_short: Direct observables offer poor liquidity but full hedging and capital relief. Single-name proxies have medium liquidity, provide spread hedging only, and no capital relief. Generic proxies are most liquid, provide spread hedging, and partial capital relief.
questions.answer_long: Direct observables (actual counterparty CDS/bonds) give the most accurate spread but are often illiquid single points, making hedging expensive but providing full capital relief when hedged. Single-name proxies (parent companies, similar credits) offer better liquidity and good spread correlation but don't provide default protection (different legal entity), so Basel III historically gave no capital relief, though BCBS 2015 proposes changes. Generic proxies (CDS indices by rating/sector/region) are most liquid and hedge-able but less specific, providing only partial capital relief via index hedges. The choice involves trading off precision, hedge-ability, and capital efficiency.
questions.why_it_matters: This mapping decision directly impacts CVA P&L volatility, hedging costs, and capital requirements. A bank mapping 1000 illiquid corporates to generic indices will have more stable, hedge-able CVA but less precise pricing. One using single-name proxies has better accuracy but no capital relief. The strategy must balance operational efficiency, accounting accuracy, and regulatory capital costs.
common_traps: Choosing the most liquid reference without considering hedge basis risk
Using single-name proxies extensively and being surprised by lack of capital relief
Not documenting the mapping methodology - regulators and auditors require clear, consistent frameworks
questions.real_world_example: A bank with exposure to a BBB-rated subsidiary of a publicly traded A-rated parent faces a choice: map to the parent's CDS (single-name proxy - tighter spread, no capital relief), or map to iTraxx Crossover index (generic - wider spread, partial capital relief). If the subsidiary spread is ~250bps but parent is 150bps, using the parent creates a 100bps mismatch and no capital relief. Using Crossover at 300bps may be more conservative and provides capital relief on index hedges, but introduces basis risk if the subsidiary defaults while the index performs well.

questions.question: What is the fundamental trade-off in choosing the granularity of generic credit curve classifications (e.g., broad 'A-rated' vs. specific 'A-rated US utility')?
questions.answer_short: Granular classifications better distinguish different counterparty risks but have fewer data points per curve, increasing idiosyncratic noise. Broad classifications have more data for stability but less differentiation between credits.
questions.answer_long: Generic curve construction faces a key tension: more granular bucketing (rating × region × sector) provides better fundamental distinction between a European financial and an Asian industrial at the same rating, but drastically reduces the number of CDS quotes available to construct each curve. With 7 ratings × 7 regions × 3 sectors = 147 combinations, many buckets will have sparse or no data, forcing interpolation or extrapolation. Broader buckets (just rating, or rating plus region) have more data points for robust curve fitting but treat dissimilar credits identically, reducing pricing accuracy. The optimal balance depends on data availability and exposure concentration.
questions.why_it_matters: This granularity choice affects thousands of counterparty CVA calculations and total CVA P&L volatility. Too granular and curves become unstable, driven by one or two idiosyncratic credits - your CVA moves for reasons unrelated to your actual counterparties. Too broad and you misprice materially, treating a distressed sector the same as a stable one simply because they share a rating.
common_traps: Blindly following regulatory guidance ('rating, region, sector') when data doesn't support it
Not monitoring how many liquid CDS points feed each generic curve - some may have zero
Creating granular curves that move based on one credit's idiosyncratic news, creating false CVA volatility
questions.real_world_example: A European bank might map all BBB European non-financials to one curve constructed from 40 CDS quotes. If they tried to separate this by sector (utilities, industrials, TMT, energy, etc.), each curve might have only 5-8 quotes, and a single credit event or rating downgrade would swing the entire curve dramatically. The bank chooses the broader bucket for stability, accepting that a BBB utility and BBB auto manufacturer get the same spread, despite sector differences.

questions.question: What are the main advantages and disadvantages of using third-party provider generic curves (like Markit sector curves) versus building curves in-house?
questions.answer_short: Third-party curves are independent, auditable, and cheaper to implement but lack customization and create volatility outside your control. In-house curves are tailored and controllable but require infrastructure and may face auditor independence challenges.
questions.answer_long: Third-party curves offer immediate implementation, clear audit trail, and independence that satisfies auditors and regulators without building internal infrastructure. They typically cover standard classifications (rating, sector, region) using established methodologies. However, they're rigid - you cannot adjust classifications for your specific exposure profile, and methodological changes by the provider create mark-to-market volatility you cannot control. In-house curves require significant infrastructure (data, models, governance) but allow customization to your portfolio and control over curve behavior. The choice often depends on bank size, CVA desk sophistication, and whether customization value exceeds the build cost.
questions.why_it_matters: This decision affects CVA infrastructure costs, P&L volatility, and audit relationships. A small regional bank with 500 counterparties may find third-party curves optimal - the customization benefit is small relative to build costs. A global bank with 10,000 counterparties and an active CVA hedging desk needs custom curves to optimize hedging and capital, justifying the infrastructure investment.
common_traps: Underestimating the infrastructure cost of in-house curves - requires data feeds, model build, daily operations, controls
Using third-party curves without understanding their methodology - you own the CVA but not the curve behavior
Not testing whether third-party classifications match your exposure profile - you may pay for granularity you don't need
questions.real_world_example: A bank uses Markit sector curves but discovers their large exposure to Nordic corporates is being mapped to a pan-European curve, missing the fact that Nordic credits trade 50-100bps tighter due to stronger credit fundamentals. The third-party curve doesn't offer a Nordic subdivision. They either accept the mismatch or build a custom Nordic curve, but then face auditor questions about cherry-picking external data versus internal models. This example shows the control trade-off inherent in the decision.

questions.question: Why might a CDS hedge fail to provide complete protection for a derivative exposure, even if the credit events appear aligned?
questions.answer_short: CDS triggers on failure to pay, bankruptcy, or restructuring, but derivative payment failures may not qualify. The deliverable obligation is bonds/loans, not derivatives, creating LGD basis risk. Timing differences between CDS settlement and derivative work-out create additional gaps.
questions.answer_long: Several technical mismatches create basis risk between CDS hedges and derivative exposures: (1) Credit event definitions may not cover derivative payment failures specifically, though cross-default provisions can help. (2) CDS settles by delivering bonds/loans, while derivatives rank pari passu but may have different recovery characteristics. (3) CDS settles quickly via auction (days to weeks), while derivative claims take months to determine and years to recover. (4) CDS uses standard reference obligations that may have different seniority than the actual derivative contract. These create situations where CDS pays out differently than the derivative loss, either in timing, amount, or trigger conditions. This means apparent hedges provide partial, not complete, protection.
questions.why_it_matters: CVA desks often hedge with CDS assuming 1:1 protection, but these technical issues create residual risk. In the Lehman bankruptcy, CDS settled at ~9% while derivative recoveries eventually reached 30-40% but took years. A perfectly hedged position on paper still experienced timing losses, funding costs from the delay, and uncertainty. Understanding these gaps is essential for risk management and explaining CVA hedge performance.
common_traps: Assuming CDS is a perfect hedge because 'credit event = credit event' - missing technical mismatches
Not negotiating cross-default provisions in CSA/ISDA to ensure derivative failures trigger CDS
Ignoring LGD basis between CDS reference obligations (bonds) and actual derivative seniority
questions.real_world_example: A bank hedges €50M CVA exposure to a corporate with CDS protection. The corporate misses a derivative payment (their treasury error) but continues paying bonds, so the CDS doesn't trigger. Later they restructure bonds (triggering CDS), but the derivative claim is unimpaired in the restructuring. The CDS pays out on the bond restructuring (low recovery), but the bank's derivative survives with full value. The 'hedge' created a loss instead of offsetting one, due to credit event definition mismatch.

questions.question: For a long-dated (20-year) derivative exposure, you have CDS quotes at 5Y and 10Y but need spreads to 20Y. What approaches could you use for extrapolation, and what risks does each carry?
questions.answer_short: Options include flat extrapolation from 10Y, linear extrapolation of spreads, or fitting to longer-dated bonds if available. Flat extrapolation underprices long-term risk; linear may create unrealistic spreads; bonds may have liquidity premiums. All introduce significant model risk.
questions.answer_long: Extrapolating beyond liquid CDS tenors (typically 10Y) is highly subjective with several approaches: (1) Flat extrapolation: assume 10Y spread continues - simple but ignores that longer-dated risk typically commands higher spreads. (2) Linear extrapolation: extend the 5Y-10Y slope - can produce unrealistically high or even negative spreads if the curve inverts. (3) Bond-based anchoring: use 15Y or 20Y bond spreads if available, adjusted for liquidity premiums - but long-dated bonds are often very illiquid with wide bid-offer. (4) Fundamental modeling: use equity volatility or structural models to estimate long-term default probability - model-dependent and hard to validate. Each method creates material uncertainty in PD estimates for the 10-20Y period, which can drive significant CVA differences for long-dated portfolios like power derivatives or long-term currency swaps.
questions.why_it_matters: Long-dated exposures are increasingly common (energy derivatives, infrastructure swaps, pension hedges), but credit curves are usually only liquid to 10Y. The extrapolation choice can change CVA by 30-50% for these trades. Since there's no 'right' answer, banks must document methodology clearly, apply consistently, and perform sensitivity analysis to show auditors and risk committees the impact of different assumptions.
common_traps: Flat extrapolation 'because it's conservative' - actually underprices long-term risk in most cases
Using illiquid 15Y or 20Y bond quotes without adjusting for massive liquidity premiums
Not stress-testing the extrapolation method - CVA can be hypersensitive to this assumption for long-dated books
questions.real_world_example: A utility enters a 20-year cross-currency swap with a bank. The bank has 5Y CDS at 150bps and 10Y at 200bps on the utility. Flat extrapolation gives 200bps for years 10-20. Linear extrapolation (adding 50bps per 5Y) gives 300bps at 15Y and 400bps at 20Y. The CVA differs by ~€3M on a €100M notional swap - the extrapolation method alone drives a material P&L difference. The bank chooses linear but documents it as a model risk item and shows sensitivity to +/-50bps at 20Y to satisfy risk committee and auditors.

questions.question: A bank maps an illiquid counterparty to a single-name proxy CDS (similar company) which provides excellent spread correlation. Why might they still prefer mapping to a less accurate but liquid CDS index from a capital efficiency perspective?
questions.answer_short: Under Basel III CVA capital rules, index hedges receive capital relief but single-name proxy hedges historically receive none (though BCBS 2015 proposes changes). The capital saving from index mapping can exceed the CVA accuracy benefit of the single-name proxy.
questions.answer_long: The Basel III standardized CVA capital charge allows capital relief only for hedges on the exact counterparty name or approved indices. A single-name proxy - even if economically a very similar credit providing excellent spread hedge - receives no capital relief under current rules because it's not the legal entity of the counterparty. An index hedge (e.g., iTraxx) receives partial relief proportional to the index weight and sensitivity. For a €10M CVA position, mapping to single-name proxy might save €1M in CVA accuracy but generates €2M higher capital charge vs. index mapping, creating a net €1M penalty. BCBS 2015 proposals recognize this and suggest allowing proxy single-name relief, but until implemented, the capital economics favor index mapping despite lower fundamental accuracy. Banks must balance accounting accuracy, hedge effectiveness, and capital efficiency.
questions.why_it_matters: Capital charges on CVA can exceed the CVA itself, making capital efficiency the dominant decision factor over pricing accuracy. A CVA desk might have the 'right' proxy from a credit perspective but choose a less accurate index map purely for capital relief. This creates tension between front office (wants best hedge), CVA quants (want best model), and capital managers (want capital relief), requiring senior management to set policy.
common_traps: Optimizing for hedge quality without checking capital rules - economically best hedge may have worst capital outcome
Assuming regulators will give capital relief for 'obviously good' proxies - rules are mechanical, not judgment-based
Not quantifying the capital cost difference - it often dominates the CVA pricing benefit by 2-3x
questions.real_world_example: A European bank trades with the German subsidiary of a US parent company. The US parent has a liquid 5Y CDS at 120bps, providing an excellent economic hedge for the subsidiary exposure (internal analysis shows 0.95 correlation). The German subsidiary would map generically to iTraxx Europe at 80bps. Using the parent CDS is fundamentally more accurate and provides better CVA hedge, but under Basel III it attracts full capital charge with no hedge relief. Mapping to iTraxx at 80bps provides 50% capital relief on index hedges. The capital saving is €800K vs €200K better CVA pricing from using parent, so they choose iTraxx mapping and accept the basis risk, documenting the capital-driven trade-off.

questions.question: Why is the distinction between 'settled recovery' (from CDS auction) and 'actual recovery' (from bankruptcy work-out) important for managing defaulted derivative exposures, and how can this create P&L surprises?
questions.answer_short: Settled recovery occurs weeks after default, allowing quick position closing at CDS auction prices (~9% for Lehman). Actual recovery occurs years later, often materially higher (30-40% for Lehman). The timing and magnitude differences create funding costs and unexpected gains/losses.
questions.answer_long: When a counterparty defaults, there are two recovery processes with different timing and economics: (1) Settled recovery through the CDS auction happens within 30-60 days of the credit event, establishing a market clearing price for defaulted obligations. This allows immediate monetization if you sell the claim. (2) Actual recovery through bankruptcy administration takes months to years as assets are liquidated, claims validated, and distributions made. For derivatives, the claim amount itself may take months to agree due to netting complexity and collateral disputes. The Lehman case showed 9% settled vs 30-40% actual recovery over 5+ years. This creates several issues: funding costs during the wait, uncertainty in reserving, tax treatment differences, and potential P&L volatility if the actual recovery materially exceeds initial marks based on settled levels. Banks must decide whether to sell claims early at settled recovery or work through bankruptcy for potentially higher but delayed actual recovery.
questions.why_it_matters: For a large default (like Lehman with ~$40bn in derivatives claims), the difference between 9% and 35% recovery is ~$10bn across the industry. Individual banks with €500M claims faced €130M vs €175M recovery - the €45M difference is material P&L but took years to realize. Managing defaulted books requires weighing certain but lower settled recovery against uncertain but potentially higher actual recovery, with funding costs for the delay. This is a CFO-level decision involving treasury, legal, and CVA teams.
common_traps: Assuming CDS auction price equals final recovery - it's typically the floor, not the ceiling
Not calculating funding costs of waiting years for actual recovery - can erode the benefit
Marking positions at settled recovery and being surprised by actual recovery years later creating 'mystery' P&L
questions.real_world_example: After Lehman's bankruptcy, Bank A sold their €200M derivative claim at the CDS auction for ~9% recovery (€18M), receiving cash within weeks. Bank B held their €200M claim through bankruptcy, dealing with administrator negotiations for 18 months to agree the claim amount, then waiting another 3-4 years for distributions that eventually totaled ~35% (€70M). Bank B gained €52M more, but faced funding costs of ~3% annually on €200M for 5 years (€30M), netting €22M benefit. They also had balance sheet uncertainty for years. Both choices were defensible, but Bank B's decision required clear governance and ongoing explanation to management about when the 'extra' recovery would arrive.

questions.subtopic: Credit curve mapping challenges and decision-making
questions.question: A bank must choose between three mapping approaches for an illiquid BBB-rated Asian industrial: (1) an illiquid single-name CDS on a similar regional company, (2) iTraxx Asia index, or (3) a bond price from the secondary market. How should they weigh the trade-offs of accuracy, liquidity, hedge-ability, and capital relief?
questions.answer_short: The single-name gives best fundamental accuracy but may be too illiquid to hedge with no capital relief. The index is liquid and hedge-able with partial capital relief but less accurate. The bond requires basis adjustments and cannot be shorted easily. Optimal choice depends on whether hedging/capital or accuracy dominates.
questions.answer_long: This mapping decision requires balancing multiple competing objectives: (1) Single-name proxy: Best credit fundamentals, similar company provides good spread reference, but if illiquid (~€10M daily volume) then hedging is expensive with high bid-offer (~20-30bps). Currently no capital relief under Basel III for proxy names. (2) iTraxx Asia: Very liquid (€500M+ daily), easy to hedge, provides 30-40% capital relief on CVA capital charge, but includes 50 diverse Asian credits so basis risk is significant if the specific industrial sector moves differently. (3) Bond-based: Good fundamental reference if it's the actual counterparty's bond, but requires benchmark curve assumption for spread calculation, likely illiquid so prices are stale, and cannot be shorted for hedging. The decision framework should prioritize liquidity and capital relief for large exposures being actively hedged, but accuracy for smaller buy-and-hold positions. Most banks would choose the iTraxx index for an actively managed CVA desk, accepting basis risk for hedge-ability and capital efficiency, while documenting the approach clearly for auditors and performing regular basis analysis.
questions.why_it_matters: This three-way trade-off applies to thousands of counterparty mapping decisions for any large bank. Getting the framework right affects total CVA levels, P&L volatility, hedging costs, and capital charges. A systematic policy (e.g., 'use indices for exposures >€50M, single-name proxies for €10-50M, generic curves for <€10M') creates consistency while allowing optimization. Senior management must understand that the 'most accurate' credit reference is not always the right operational choice.
common_traps: Choosing purely on fundamental credit accuracy without considering operational and capital implications
Using illiquid single-name proxies and being unable to hedge when needed, or facing massive bid-offer
Not stress-testing basis risk between index hedges and specific counterparty spreads - can be 100-200bps in stress
questions.real_world_example: During the Asian infrastructure boom, a European bank had growing exposure to 20 BBB-rated Asian construction companies, none with CDS. They initially mapped each to the most similar regional single-name CDS (other construction companies), creating 20 different references. When Asian credit deteriorated, they wanted to hedge but found single-name CDS were ~50bps wide on bid-offer and couldn't execute €10M+ sizes. They switched to mapping all 20 to iTraxx Asia index, losing granularity but gaining ability to hedge €200M aggregate exposure efficiently in the liquid index market. CVA capital relief improved by 35%, justifying the less precise mapping. This shows how operational reality often trumps theoretical accuracy.

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between real-world and risk-neutral default probabilities?
questions.answer_short: Real-world probabilities come from historical default data, while risk-neutral probabilities are derived from market prices and include a risk premium that investors demand for taking credit risk.
questions.answer_long: Real-world default probabilities are estimated from historical default rates tied to credit ratings. Risk-neutral default probabilities are extracted from market instruments like bonds or CDS. Risk-neutral probabilities are systematically higher because they embed a risk premium that compensates investors for bearing default risk. Empirical research shows risk-neutral probabilities can be 2-17 times higher than real-world probabilities, especially for higher-rated credits.
questions.why_it_matters: This distinction is crucial for CVA calculation. Using real-world probabilities significantly underestimates CVA compared to market-consistent risk-neutral approaches. Regulatory requirements (Basel III) and accounting standards (IFRS 13) mandate risk-neutral probabilities for fair value measurement.
common_traps: Thinking the difference is just a mathematical technicality rather than a fundamental valuation principle
Using real-world probabilities for CVA because they seem more 'realistic'
Not recognizing that the risk premium component can be larger than the actual default component for investment grade credits
questions.real_world_example: For a single-A rated counterparty, the one-year real-world default probability might be 0.13%, but the risk-neutral probability derived from CDS spreads could be 1.28% - nearly 10 times higher. This dramatically affects CVA calculations and hedging decisions.

questions.subtopic: Credit Spread to Default Probability Conversion
questions.question: How do you approximate the default probability between two dates from a credit spread?
questions.answer_short: Use the formula: PD(t_i-1, t_i) ≈ s_t × Δt / LGD, where s_t is the credit spread, Δt is the time interval, and LGD is loss given default.
questions.answer_long: The simple approximation converts credit spreads to unconditional default probabilities by dividing the spread times the time period by the assumed LGD. For example, with a 300 bps spread, one year period, and 60% LGD, the annual default probability is (0.03 × 1) / 0.60 = 5%. This approximation works reasonably well for flat curves but becomes less accurate with steeply sloped curves, where a full bootstrapping approach is needed.
questions.why_it_matters: This conversion is the foundation for translating observable market credit spreads into the default probabilities required for CVA calculation. Understanding both the simple formula and its limitations helps practitioners know when more sophisticated bootstrapping is necessary.
common_traps: Forgetting that the resulting probability is unconditional, not conditional on survival
Using this formula for very steep credit curves where the approximation breaks down
Not adjusting the LGD assumption when dealing with different seniorities
questions.real_world_example: A CVA desk receives a 5-year 400 bps credit spread for a BBB corporate. Using 60% LGD and the simple formula, they estimate approximately 7.1% annual default probability in year 5. However, if the curve is strongly upward-sloping, a full bootstrap might show 9% or more for that period.

questions.question: Why does the shape of a credit curve matter when two curves have the same 5-year spread?
questions.answer_short: The curve shape determines how default probability is distributed over time. An upward-sloping curve implies lower near-term and higher long-term default risk, while an inverted curve suggests higher near-term default risk.
questions.answer_long: Three curves with identical 5-year spreads of 300 bps can have dramatically different annual default probabilities. A flat curve distributes risk evenly. An upward-sloping curve might show 2% annual PD in year 1 but 8% in year 5, reflecting deteriorating credit outlook. An inverted curve reverses this pattern. For CVA calculation, this matters because exposure may be concentrated at specific maturities where the actual default probability differs significantly from what a flat curve would suggest.
questions.why_it_matters: CVA practitioners must capture the full term structure, not just spot spreads. A swap portfolio concentrated in the 3-5 year tenor needs accurate default probabilities for those specific periods. Misestimating the curve shape can lead to material CVA pricing errors, especially for portfolios with non-uniform maturity profiles.
common_traps: Assuming all maturities have proportional default risk when using a single spread quote
Extrapolating long-dated default probabilities from short-dated spreads without considering curve shape
Not recognizing that inverted curves signal near-term stress and higher immediate default risk
questions.real_world_example: During the 2011 European sovereign crisis, some bank credit curves became inverted with 1-year CDS at 500 bps but 5-year at 350 bps. A CVA calculation using flat interpolation would severely underestimate the near-term default risk for short-dated derivatives.

questions.question: Why do regulators and auditors insist on risk-neutral default probabilities even for illiquid credits without CDS markets?
questions.answer_short: IFRS 13 requires market-observable inputs for fair value (exit price), and Basel III CVA capital rules explicitly reference credit spreads to ensure consistency with hedging markets and risk-based capital treatment.
questions.answer_long: Regulators push risk-neutral PDs because fair value accounting demands exit prices based on market participant assumptions. Even for illiquid credits, banks must estimate what market price would be if the position were transferred. Basel III CVA capital charges are designed to capture mark-to-market volatility of CVA, which only makes sense with market-implied (risk-neutral) probabilities. Additionally, this approach promotes consistency across banks and prevents understating CVA by using historically low real-world default rates.
questions.why_it_matters: This regulatory stance forces banks to develop sophisticated credit curve mapping methodologies for thousands of counterparties. It also increases CVA levels and volatility compared to historical approaches, driving hedging activity and creating the need for CVA desks. Banks must explain mapping choices to auditors and regulators.
common_traps: Trying to use blended real-world/risk-neutral approaches to reduce CVA charges
Not documenting the mapping methodology rigorously enough for audit scrutiny
Assuming that illiquidity justifies deviating from risk-neutral framework
questions.real_world_example: A regional bank with 800 SME counterparties argued that since none have CDS markets, historical default rates were more appropriate. Their auditor rejected this after the ECB's CVA challenger model showed their CVA was 40% below the risk-neutral benchmark, forcing a P&L hit.

questions.subtopic: Loss Given Default and Recovery Rates
questions.question: What is the difference between settled recovery and actual recovery for OTC derivatives?
questions.answer_short: Settled recovery is the market price shortly after default (e.g., from CDS auction), while actual recovery is what is ultimately received through the bankruptcy process, which may take years and can differ materially.
questions.answer_long: When a credit event occurs, CDS settle quickly via auction establishing a settled recovery rate. Bondholders can sell at this price immediately. However, OTC derivatives cannot be traded individually due to netting and their bespoke nature. The actual recovery on derivatives comes through bankruptcy proceedings that can take years. For Lehman Brothers, the settled recovery was around 9%, but actual recoveries on derivatives eventually reached 30-40% due to the workout process and offsetting of claims.
questions.why_it_matters: CVA calculations typically use market-standard recovery assumptions (e.g., 40% for senior unsecured), but the actual economics of a default may be quite different. Banks with strong workout capabilities may achieve higher recoveries, though auditors often require substantial evidence before allowing more favorable LGD assumptions. This timing difference also affects liquidity and funding strategies.
common_traps: Assuming the CDS auction recovery applies directly to derivative claims
Not accounting for the time value of money during multi-year bankruptcy processes
Ignoring potential benefits from set-off rights or other structural enhancements
questions.real_world_example: A bank with $100M exposure to Lehman derivatives could have marked the claim at $9M immediately post-default based on CDS auction. However, over subsequent years they received actual recoveries totaling $35M, though the present value was lower due to the delay. This windfall was not reflected in their CVA model.

questions.question: What are the three main sources of credit spread information for mapping a counterparty, and when would you use each?
questions.answer_short: Direct observables (liquid CDS/bonds on the actual counterparty), single-name proxies (similar entity like parent company), and generic proxies (index-based mapping by rating/region/sector). Use the most specific available source.
questions.answer_long: Direct observables provide the best mapping when the counterparty itself has liquid CDS or bonds, allowing both spread and default hedging plus full capital relief. Single-name proxies use a related entity (parent, similar company, or sovereign) and provide spread hedging but not default protection or capital relief under current rules. Generic proxies map via indices based on rating/region/sector when no direct reference exists, providing spread hedging and partial capital relief but less precision. The choice involves trade-offs between accuracy, liquidity, hedging capability, and capital treatment.
questions.why_it_matters: Most banks have thousands of counterparties but only hundreds of liquid CDS names. The mapping methodology determines CVA levels, P&L volatility, hedging effectiveness, and regulatory capital requirements. A well-designed hierarchy balances these competing objectives while satisfying auditor and regulator expectations.
common_traps: Using illiquid single-name proxies instead of more liquid generic indices
Choosing mapping based solely on capital relief rather than economic appropriateness
Not documenting why a particular proxy was selected over alternatives
questions.real_world_example: A bank trades with a mid-sized German automotive supplier (no CDS). They could use: (1) the parent company CDS (single-name proxy), (2) the iTraxx Autos index (generic proxy), or (3) a single-A German industrial CDS (single-name proxy). They chose the iTraxx Autos for better liquidity and partial capital relief despite less specificity.

questions.question: What is the difference between single-name CDS and CDS indices, and why does it matter for CVA?
questions.answer_short: Single-name CDS reference one specific entity and provide both spread and default protection. CDS indices reference a basket of names and only provide spread hedging (no single-name default protection).
questions.answer_long: A single-name CDS is a contract on one reference entity. If that entity defaults, the protection buyer receives a payout. This makes it ideal for hedging a specific counterparty's CVA, providing both spread risk and jump-to-default protection. CDS indices (like iTraxx or CDX) reference 50-125 names. They hedge spread movements across the sector but don't protect against any single name defaulting. For CVA, this means indices provide only partial hedging but are typically much more liquid than single-name CDS.
questions.why_it_matters: CVA desks must choose between precise but illiquid single-name hedges versus liquid but imprecise index hedges. This choice affects hedge effectiveness, transaction costs, and regulatory capital relief. Under Basel III, only certain hedges qualify for capital relief, making this not just an economic but also a regulatory capital decision.
common_traps: Assuming index hedges protect against counterparty default when they only hedge spread risk
Not recognizing the basis risk between single-name spreads and index spreads
Underestimating the liquidity advantage of indices for large hedging programs
questions.real_world_example: A CVA desk has exposure to 30 A-rated European corporates with no liquid single-name CDS. Rather than buying illiquid single-name protection, they hedge the aggregate spread risk with iTraxx Europe. When one counterparty defaults, the index hedge provides no payout, leaving them with the full CVA loss on that name.

questions.question: What is the trade-off between granularity and data availability when constructing generic credit curves?
questions.answer_short: More granular curves (e.g., A-rated US utilities) better distinguish counterparties but have fewer data points for calibration. Broader curves (e.g., all A-rated) have more data but less differentiation.
questions.answer_long: A highly granular classification by rating, region, and sector (e.g., 7×7×3 = 147 combinations) provides better differentiation between counterparties. However, many buckets will have few or no liquid CDS quotes, requiring interpolation or extrapolation. This creates idiosyncratic volatility from individual names. Broader classifications aggregate more data points for stable curves but fail to capture important differences between sectors or regions. The optimal approach balances these factors based on the bank's exposure profile and available market data.
questions.why_it_matters: This trade-off directly affects CVA accuracy and stability. Over-granular curves with sparse data create artificial P&L volatility as individual names jump between buckets or dominate thin categories. Under-granular curves mispriced exposures by failing to distinguish materially different credit profiles. Banks must defend their choice to regulators and auditors.
common_traps: Creating too many buckets that end up with single-name or zero-name populations
Not having a fallback methodology when a specific bucket has no data
Letting a single illiquid credit dominate a bucket and create unrepresentative volatility
questions.real_world_example: A bank created separate curves for 'BBB-rated Asian technology companies' (very granular). Only two CDS names fit this category, and when one widened 100 bps due to company-specific news, their entire Asian tech counterparty CVA jumped 40%. They simplified to 'BBB-rated Asian corporates' for more stability.

questions.question: Why might CDS protection not pay out even when a derivatives counterparty defaults?
questions.answer_short: CDS credit events (failure to pay, bankruptcy, restructuring) may not be triggered by a failure to make derivative payments. Also, CDS deliver into bonds/loans, not derivative receivables, creating basis risk in recovery values.
questions.answer_long: Standard ISDA CDS contracts define specific credit events: failure to pay on bonds or loans, bankruptcy, or restructuring. A counterparty failing to post collateral or make a derivative payment may not constitute a CDS credit event unless there's explicit cross-default language. Additionally, CDS settle by delivering bonds or loans at the recovery value. The actual recovery on derivative claims may differ from bond recovery due to the bankruptcy process, netting, collateral, and negotiation with administrators. This creates basis risk between the CDS hedge payout and the actual derivative loss.
questions.why_it_matters: CVA hedging is imperfect even with well-matched CDS protection. Practitioners must understand the technical mismatches between CDS mechanics and derivative credit risk. This affects hedge effectiveness, accounting treatment (hedge accounting qualification), and capital requirements. Some banks purchase enhanced CDS with cross-default triggers but at higher cost.
common_traps: Assuming CDS provides perfect CVA hedging without considering credit event definitions
Not accounting for the difference between bond recovery and derivative recovery
Failing to document basis risk when claiming hedge accounting treatment
questions.real_world_example: During the Greek sovereign crisis, some derivatives counterparties stopped posting collateral and were in technical default on their CSA obligations. However, this did not trigger the CDS credit event definitions, leaving protection buyers unhedged despite clear counterparty distress. The CDS only triggered later when Greece restructured its bonds.

questions.question: Why is defining funding costs for FVA more subjective than defining default probabilities for CVA?
questions.answer_short: Funding costs depend on a bank's overall funding strategy, funding tenor, collateral remuneration terms, and are not directly observable in markets for most situations. Unlike credit spreads, there is no liquid market instrument that directly prices funding.
questions.answer_long: While credit spreads can be extracted from CDS or bonds, funding costs are institution-specific and depend on multiple factors: the bank's own credit quality, its access to various funding markets (unsecured, secured, repo), the maturity structure of funding needs, regulatory liquidity requirements, and the specific terms of collateral agreements (remuneration rates). There is no single 'funding curve' observable in markets. Banks must construct internal funding curves based on their actual borrowing costs, often differentiated by tenor and collateral type.
questions.why_it_matters: FVA calculations require subjective inputs that can vary significantly between banks and even between desks within a bank. This creates challenges for fair value accounting (exit price concept), trade pricing disputes, and P&L reconciliation. The lack of consensus on funding costs has made FVA more controversial than CVA in the industry.
common_traps: Using a single funding spread for all situations regardless of tenor or collateral
Not distinguishing between secured and unsecured funding costs
Assuming funding costs equal the bank's own CDS spread without adjustments
questions.real_world_example: One bank calculates FVA using their unsecured senior debt issuance curve (3M LIBOR + 80 bps). Another uses their secured funding rate (OIS + 20 bps) arguing derivatives are collateralized. The same trade could have FVA differing by 60 bps × notional × duration between these banks, creating pricing disputes.

questions.question: What components determine the cost of capital used in KVA calculations?
questions.answer_short: The required return on equity that shareholders demand, adjusted for tax benefits of debt financing. This reflects the risk-free rate plus an equity risk premium and depends on the bank's capital structure.
questions.answer_long: KVA requires assessing the cost of holding regulatory capital against exposures. The cost of equity capital is typically estimated using CAPM (risk-free rate plus beta times market risk premium) or by observing the bank's actual return on equity targets. This must be adjusted for tax effects since debt financing creates tax shields. Banks typically use a hurdle rate of 10-15% post-tax. The cost reflects what shareholders require to compensate them for tying up capital in the derivatives business rather than returning it or investing elsewhere.
questions.why_it_matters: The assumed cost of capital directly determines KVA magnitude and therefore trade pricing. A 10% cost versus 15% cost creates a 50% difference in KVA. This affects competitiveness, profitability assessment, and capital allocation decisions. Senior management often debates the appropriate hurdle rate, making KVA even more subjective than FVA.
common_traps: Using pre-tax cost of capital without adjusting for tax shields
Not aligning the KVA hurdle rate with the bank's actual ROE targets and strategic planning
Assuming the cost of capital is constant across all businesses and risk types
questions.real_world_example: A bank's derivatives business targets 12% post-tax ROE. Using this in KVA makes long-dated, capital-intensive trades unprofitable. A competitor uses 8% (arguing diversification benefits), prices more aggressively, and wins the business. The first bank must decide: lower their hurdle rate or exit these products?

questions.question: When might you use an LGD lower than the standard 60% assumption for derivatives CVA?
questions.answer_short: When structural seniority enhances recovery (e.g., derivative priority in securitization SPVs), when credit enhancements exist beyond modeled collateral, or when documented work-out experience justifies it.
questions.answer_long: Standard LGD is 60% (40% recovery) for senior unsecured claims, matching CDS conventions. Lower LGDs (better recovery) may apply when: (1) Derivatives have structural seniority over other claims, common in securitization structures; (2) Additional credit support exists that isn't captured in exposure modeling; (3) Historical experience with similar counterparties shows consistently better recoveries, though this requires substantial documentation for auditors. The choice must align with the seniority of the actual derivative claim and be defensible under audit scrutiny.
questions.why_it_matters: LGD directly scales CVA values. Using 40% LGD instead of 60% reduces CVA by one-third. While practitioners might be tempted to use favorable assumptions to reduce CVA charges, auditors and regulators scrutinize LGD choices carefully. Unjustified assumptions can lead to audit adjustments and restatements. The trade-off is accuracy versus conservatism.
common_traps: Using better recovery rates without proper documentation or structural justification
Applying Lehman's eventual 35-40% recovery prospectively without recognizing it was exceptionally high
Not considering that recovery rates are highly variable and scenario-dependent
questions.real_world_example: A bank regularly trades with SPVs in securitization structures where derivatives are senior to note holders. They document this structural seniority and use 30% LGD (70% recovery). When a vehicle defaults, they recover 85% through the waterfall, validating their assumption. Their auditor accepts this for similar SPV trades.

questions.question: Why might a bank choose a less accurate generic proxy over a better single-name proxy for credit curve mapping?
questions.answer_short: Because Basel III CVA capital rules (currently) give no capital relief for single-name proxy hedges but provide partial relief for index hedges, even if the proxy is more accurate economically.
questions.answer_long: Under Basel III standardized CVA capital charge, only certain hedges reduce capital: single-name CDS on the actual counterparty or index CDS. Single-name proxies (e.g., parent company CDS) provide no capital relief even if they're excellent economic hedges. Generic index proxies provide 50% capital relief despite being less precise. This creates a perverse incentive: a bank might map to an index (getting capital relief) rather than a more accurate but non-qualifying single-name proxy. BCBS 2015 proposes allowing proxy single-name relief, but until implemented, this tension remains.
questions.why_it_matters: Capital optimization can drive mapping choices as much as economic accuracy. CVA desks must balance accurate valuation, effective hedging, and capital efficiency. This affects which instruments they trade, P&L volatility, and overall competitiveness. Understanding regulatory capital rules is essential for practical CVA management, not just pricing accuracy.
common_traps: Optimizing purely for capital relief while creating significant economic basis risk
Not recognizing that regulatory rules may change and strand hedging strategies
Failing to document the economic rationale when mapping deviates from capital-optimal choices
questions.real_world_example: A bank has exposure to a German Landesbank subsidiary (no liquid CDS). The parent Landesbank has liquid CDS and is an excellent proxy. However, hedging with parent CDS gives zero capital relief. They instead map to iTraxx Financials (less accurate) because the hedge provides 50% capital relief, reducing RWA by €200M despite worse economic hedging.

questions.question: Why is the simple formula PD ≈ s×Δt/LGD insufficient for steep credit curves, and what is the alternative?
questions.answer_short: The simple formula ignores survival probability and curve shape before the period in question. The proper approach is bootstrapping hazard rates that account for cumulative survival probabilities.
questions.answer_long: The approximation PD ≈ s×Δt/LGD treats each period independently and works for flat curves. For steep curves, it fails because the spread at time t reflects not just default risk in period t but also the probability of surviving to t. The correct method is to extract piecewise constant hazard rates (instantaneous default intensities) by bootstrapping: starting from the shortest maturity, calculate the hazard rate that makes the CDS spread match market, then move to the next maturity using the previously calculated survival probability. This ensures no-arbitrage pricing across the curve.
questions.why_it_matters: For portfolios concentrated at specific maturities or with strongly sloped counterparty credit curves, the approximation can be off by 20-50%. Proper bootstrapping is essential for accurate CVA, especially when pricing must align with CDS hedge instruments. Most production systems use full bootstrapping, and auditors expect this rigor for material exposures.
common_traps: Using the simple formula for convenience when the curve is clearly non-flat
Not recognizing that bootstrapping requires assumptions about interpolation between points
Failing to handle negative forward hazard rates that can arise with inverted curves
questions.real_world_example: A stressed European bank's credit curve shows 1Y at 600 bps, 3Y at 500 bps, 5Y at 450 bps (inverted). Using the simple formula suggests similar ~8-9% annual PD across all periods. Proper bootstrapping reveals year 1 has 15% PD, while years 4-5 have only 5% PD. CVA on a 2-year forward starting 3-year swap is materially mispriced with the approximation.

questions.question: What are the trade-offs between building internal generic credit curves versus using third-party provider curves like Markit sector curves?
questions.answer_short: Third-party curves are cheaper and independent (good for audits) but rigid in classification and produce volatility beyond your control. Internal curves are tailored and controllable but require more resources and may face auditor independence questions.
questions.answer_long: Third-party curves (like Markit sector curves by rating, region, sector) offer cost efficiency, no development burden, and independent validation that auditors appreciate. However, they use fixed methodologies that may not align with a bank's exposure profile, can create P&L volatility from their specific choices (averaging, interpolation), and cannot be customized for specific needs. Internal curves can be tailored to the bank's counterparty mix, hedging strategy, and capital optimization, but require significant infrastructure, expertise, and ongoing maintenance. They may also face auditor skepticism about independence and subjectivity.
questions.why_it_matters: This choice affects the entire CVA infrastructure, P&L behavior, and operational costs. Smaller banks often use third-party curves due to resource constraints, while larger banks build internal systems for competitive advantage. The decision should consider not just current needs but also future regulatory changes and business strategy (e.g., moving to advanced CVA capital approaches).
common_traps: Underestimating the ongoing cost of maintaining internal curves
Choosing third-party curves for convenience without checking if their classification fits your exposures
Not having fallback procedures when third-party curves become unavailable or show anomalous behavior
questions.real_world_example: A mid-sized bank used Markit sector curves, which classify by broad sector. When a major counterparty (automotive) defaulted, the Markit curve incorporated this name, widening all similarly-mapped counterparties by 50 bps overnight. The bank's CVA P&L swung wildly on unrelated names. They built custom curves with more granular controls to avoid such idiosyncratic impacts.

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between a real-world default probability and a risk-neutral default probability?
questions.answer_short: Real-world default probability is estimated from historical default data, while risk-neutral default probability is derived from market prices and includes a risk premium that investors demand.
questions.answer_long: Real-world default probabilities come from historical default statistics typically linked to credit ratings. Risk-neutral default probabilities are extracted from market instruments like CDS or bonds and include not just the expected default loss but also a risk premium that risk-averse investors require for holding credit risk. Empirically, risk-neutral probabilities are consistently higher than real-world probabilities, especially for better-rated credits.
questions.why_it_matters: Using the wrong type of default probability fundamentally changes CVA from an actuarial reserve to a market price. This distinction affects hedging strategies, P&L volatility, regulatory capital requirements, and accounting treatment under IFRS 13.
common_traps: Thinking the difference is small or negligible—it can be 5-15 times larger for investment grade credits
Using historical default rates for CVA when market practice and regulation require risk-neutral measures
Not understanding that risk-neutral PDs imply the existence of hedging instruments that may not actually be liquid
questions.real_world_example: A single-A rated corporate might have a 1-year real-world default probability of 0.13% based on historical data, but the CDS market implies a risk-neutral probability of 1.28%—nearly 10 times higher. A bank using real-world PDs would drastically understate CVA and fail regulatory and audit requirements.

questions.question: Why have banks and regulators increasingly required the use of risk-neutral default probabilities for CVA calculation, even for illiquid counterparties where CDS prices are not observable?
questions.answer_short: IFRS 13 requires market-observable inputs and exit pricing, while Basel III explicitly references credit spreads. Risk-neutral PDs align CVA with market pricing and hedging practices.
questions.answer_long: The shift stems from accounting standards (IFRS 13) requiring exit prices using market-observable data wherever possible, and Basel III CVA capital rules explicitly requiring CDS spreads or proxies. Risk-neutral PDs treat CVA as a market price rather than an actuarial reserve, aligning with the development of CDS markets and CVA hedging. Despite challenges with illiquid credits, regulators view this as necessary for consistency with how banks mark other credit risks like trading book bonds and loans.
questions.why_it_matters: This industry shift means CVA becomes much larger and more volatile than under historical methods, but without liquid hedges for most counterparties. It forces banks to develop sophisticated proxy and mapping methodologies, and creates significant operational and model risk challenges.
common_traps: Using blended historical and risk-neutral approaches—regulators and auditors generally reject this
Applying risk-neutral only to 'liquid credits' and historical to others—inconsistent and not accepted
Not recognizing that mapped risk-neutral PDs for illiquid names create basis risk since hedges don't exist
questions.real_world_example: A regional bank with 500 corporate counterparties might have direct CDS quotes for only 10-15 names. They must still map all 500 to risk-neutral curves using proxies, creating CVA volatility driven by index movements that may not reflect their actual counterparty credit quality—yet this is the regulatory and accounting requirement.

questions.question: What is the simple approximation formula for converting a credit spread into an unconditional default probability for a time period, and what are its key limitations?
questions.answer_short: PD(t₁, t₂) ≈ s × Δt / LGD, where s is the credit spread, Δt is the time interval, and LGD is loss given default. It doesn't account for the prior curve shape and gets worse with steeper curves.
questions.answer_long: The approximation PD(t₁, t₂) ≈ s × Δt / LGD provides a simple unconditional default probability between two dates. However, it ignores the shape of the credit curve before time t₁, making it increasingly inaccurate when the curve is steeply sloped. More accurate methods involve bootstrapping the hazard rate structure from the full credit curve, accounting for survival probabilities at each point.
questions.why_it_matters: This formula provides a quick estimate but can materially misstate default probabilities, especially for steep or inverted curves. For precise CVA calculations, proper bootstrapping is required. Understanding when the approximation is adequate versus when full bootstrapping is needed affects both accuracy and computational efficiency.
common_traps: Using this formula for steeply sloped curves where it significantly overstates or understates risk
Applying it to forward periods without adjusting for cumulative survival probability
Forgetting that it produces unconditional probabilities, not conditional ones
questions.real_world_example: For a flat 300 bps curve with 60% LGD, the 1-year PD is approximately 5%. But if the curve is strongly inverted (starting at 500 bps and dropping to 300 bps at 5 years), using the simple formula at each tenor without proper bootstrapping will overstate near-term default risk and understate longer-term risk.

questions.question: Why does the shape of the credit curve (flat, upward-sloping, or inverted) dramatically affect annual default probabilities even when the 5-year spread is identical across all three curves?
questions.answer_short: The curve shape determines how default probability is distributed across time. An upward-sloping curve implies lower near-term and higher long-term default risk, while inverted curves show the opposite.
questions.answer_long: Even with the same 5-year cumulative default probability, curve shape determines the timing distribution of defaults. An upward-sloping curve suggests improving credit quality in the short term but deterioration later, concentrating default probability in outer years. An inverted curve implies near-term stress with improvement expected later. The market's expectation of when default is most likely fundamentally changes the annual default probabilities, which is critical for CVA since exposure profiles vary through time.
questions.why_it_matters: For a derivative with high exposure in early years, an inverted credit curve produces much higher CVA than an upward-sloping one, even with identical 5-year spreads. Ignoring term structure can lead to material mispricing. This is especially important when extrapolating beyond observable tenors or when exposure profiles are uneven across time.
common_traps: Assuming a flat credit curve when market data shows clear term structure
Using only the 5-year spread to calculate CVA without considering when exposure peaks
Extrapolating beyond 10 years without considering what curve shape assumption is being made
questions.real_world_example: A 10-year interest rate swap with a corporate has peak exposure around year 5. If the counterparty has an inverted credit curve (near-term stress), CVA will be dominated by high near-term default probabilities. If the curve is upward-sloping, the high exposure period coincides with lower default probabilities, resulting in materially lower CVA despite the same 5-year spread.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'settled recovery' and 'actual recovery' for OTC derivatives, and why does this matter for CVA calculation?
questions.answer_short: Settled recovery is what could be realized quickly (e.g., via CDS auction), while actual recovery is what's received after a lengthy bankruptcy process. Actual recovery may be higher but takes years.
questions.answer_long: Settled recovery occurs shortly after default through mechanisms like CDS auctions or secondary market sales—typically within weeks. Actual recovery for derivatives is the amount ultimately received after the bankruptcy workout, which can take years and may be substantially different. For Lehman Brothers, settled recovery was around 9% but actual recoveries eventually reached 30-40%. The difference matters for CVA timing and funding implications, though accounting CVA typically uses market-implied recovery rates.
questions.why_it_matters: Using settled recovery rates (from CDS auctions) for CVA is market-consistent and hedgeable, but banks may actually experience higher recoveries. This creates a P&L opportunity but also timing and funding issues since the cash comes years later. For risk management, understanding both is important for stress testing and capital planning.
common_traps: Assuming CDS auction recovery is the final recovery—it's often a conservative estimate
Not recognizing that derivative recoveries can be enhanced through netting, set-off, or collateral
Using non-market recovery assumptions that auditors and regulators may reject without evidence
questions.real_world_example: After Lehman's bankruptcy, a bank with a $10 million unsecured derivative claim could have participated in the CDS auction and received roughly $900k (9% recovery) within weeks. However, by waiting through the bankruptcy process for several years, they might ultimately receive $3-4 million. The trade-off is immediate liquidity at lower recovery versus delayed higher recovery.

questions.question: What are the key trade-offs between using an illiquid single-name proxy versus a liquid CDS index when mapping credit curves for illiquid counterparties?
questions.answer_short: Single-name proxies are more fundamentally relevant but may not provide hedging or capital relief. Indices are liquid and hedgeable with partial capital relief but less specific to the counterparty.
questions.answer_long: Single-name proxies (e.g., parent company or similar credit) better represent the actual credit risk but often don't provide default protection in a hedge and currently give no Basel III capital relief. They may also have limited liquidity. CDS indices are highly liquid, enable spread hedging, and provide partial regulatory capital relief, but are less specific to the individual counterparty and represent a basket of credits. The choice involves balancing fundamental accuracy against practical hedging and capital efficiency.
questions.why_it_matters: This trade-off affects CVA accuracy, hedging effectiveness, P&L volatility, and regulatory capital consumption. A bank mapping many credits to indices achieves operational efficiency and capital relief but accepts basis risk. Using single-name proxies provides better credit representation but with higher capital charges and potentially unhedgeable risk.
common_traps: Choosing based solely on liquidity without considering how well it represents the actual credit
Not recognizing that index hedges provide spread protection but not single-name default protection
Ignoring the capital implications—indices give relief while single-name proxies currently don't under Basel III
questions.real_world_example: A European bank trading with a mid-sized German automotive supplier might map to either (1) the parent company's CDS if it exists—better credit representation but no capital relief, or (2) the iTraxx Autos index—liquid, hedgeable, partial capital relief, but represents a basket of 10-15 names and may not track the supplier's credit well during idiosyncratic events.

questions.question: What are the main CDS indices used for credit curve mapping in Europe, and how do they differ in terms of credit quality and composition?
questions.answer_short: iTraxx Europe Main (125 investment grade), iTraxx Non-financials (100 names BBB and better), iTraxx Crossover (40 sub-investment grade), iTraxx Financials (senior and subordinated), and iTraxx SovX (sovereigns).
questions.answer_long: The iTraxx family provides the main European credit indices: Main covers 125 most liquid investment grade names, Non-financials focuses on 100 corporate credits rated BBB and above, Crossover targets 40 sub-investment grade credits, High Volatility includes the 30 widest spreads from Main, and Financials covers banks and insurance companies in both senior and subordinated tranches. SovX covers various sovereign regions. These indices trade at 3Y, 5Y, 7Y, and 10Y maturities, with 5Y being most liquid.
questions.why_it_matters: Understanding the index structure is fundamental for mapping illiquid credits to appropriate proxies. The choice of index affects CVA levels, hedging costs, and P&L volatility. Using the wrong index (e.g., Main for a BB-rated credit) misrepresents risk and creates basis issues. Index knowledge is essential for both CVA calculation and communication with front office about hedging strategies.
common_traps: Mapping investment grade corporates to Crossover or vice versa—massive spread differences
Using Main index for financials when Financials index exists and is more appropriate
Not recognizing that index composition changes every six months (rolls), affecting continuity
questions.real_world_example: A CVA desk mapping a BBB-rated European utility company would typically use iTraxx Europe Non-financials (or Main) as the base proxy. If they mistakenly used Crossover (sub-investment grade), the spread might be 3-5 times wider, drastically overstating CVA and creating P&L issues when the mapping is corrected. Index selection must match the fundamental credit quality.
