(2) Tier 2 (Single-name proxy): Parent company CDS, sovereign +spread, or close comparable; apply documented spread adjustment (±50-200 bps); review monthly; accepts no capital relief but better hedge. (3) Tier 3 (Generic): Rating (7 levels) × Region (5 areas) × Sector (3 types) = ~100 buckets; use indices where possible for liquidity; interpolate/extrapolate for missing buckets; update daily for liquid indices, weekly for constructed curves. (4) Governance: Document all mappings in database; quarterly review for appropriateness; challenge large movements; align with hedge portfolio construction; ensure capital model consistency. (5) Exceptions: Flag counterparties where mapping materially affects P&L (>$1M CVA); senior approval for non-standard mappings; back-test mappings post-default.
questions.why_it_matters: A systematic, well-documented mapping framework is essential for managing CVA across thousands of names. It must satisfy regulatory requirements (risk-neutral, market-observable), be operationally sustainable (can't manually review 2,000 names daily), support hedging strategies, and align with capital models. This is the backbone of a professional CVA operation.
common_traps: Creating an overly complex decision tree that cannot be operationalized consistently
Not aligning the mapping with actual hedge portfolio and capital model requirements
Failing to review and update mappings regularly as market conditions change
questions.real_world_example: A global bank implements this framework for 3,500 counterparties: 180 Tier 1 (direct CDS), 520 Tier 2 (proxies), 2,800 Tier 3 (generic). The Tier 1 names represent 65% of CVA exposure despite being only 5% by count. Quarterly review identifies 30 counterparties that moved from investment grade to high yield, requiring remapping from iTraxx Main to Crossover, creating a €5M CVA increase. The documented framework allows clean explanation to audit and regulators of the methodology and review process.

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between real-world and risk-neutral default probabilities?
questions.answer_short: Real-world default probabilities are estimated from historical default data, while risk-neutral default probabilities are derived from market prices (like CDS spreads) and include a risk premium investors demand for bearing credit risk.
questions.answer_long: Real-world default probabilities represent actual historical default frequencies observed in credit rating cohorts. Risk-neutral default probabilities are extracted from market instruments like bonds or CDS and are systematically higher because they embed a risk premium that compensates investors for bearing default risk. Studies show risk-neutral probabilities can be 2-17 times higher than real-world equivalents, especially for higher-quality credits. The difference reflects market participants' risk aversion and required compensation beyond expected losses.
questions.why_it_matters: Using the wrong type of default probability fundamentally changes CVA calculation. Real-world PDs give actuarial reserves; risk-neutral PDs give exit prices for fair value accounting and hedging. Modern accounting standards (IFRS 13) and Basel III capital rules require risk-neutral PDs, making this distinction critical for regulatory compliance and accurate CVA valuation.
common_traps: Assuming real-world and risk-neutral PDs are interchangeable in CVA calculations
Using historical default rates without recognizing they underestimate market-implied credit risk
Ignoring that the risk premium component is largest for high-quality credits (can be 10-15x difference for AA/AAA)
questions.real_world_example: A AA-rated corporate has a 0.06% one-year historical default rate but a 0.78% risk-neutral default probability from its CDS spread—a 13x difference. A CVA desk using real-world PDs would massively undervalue CVA and fail audits under IFRS 13.

questions.question: Why have banks and regulators converged on using risk-neutral default probabilities for CVA despite the challenges with illiquid credits?
questions.answer_short: Accounting standards (IFRS 13) require market-observable inputs and exit pricing, Basel III CVA capital explicitly references credit spreads, and risk-neutral PDs align with CVA hedging practices using CDS instruments.
questions.answer_long: The convergence to risk-neutral PDs is driven by three forces: First, IFRS 13 mandates fair value measurements using market-observable inputs wherever possible, treating CVA as an exit price rather than an actuarial reserve. Second, Basel III CVA capital rules explicitly require CDS spreads for liquid credits and appropriate proxies for illiquid ones. Third, as CVA hedging with CDS became standard practice, pricing CVA consistently with hedge instruments became operationally necessary. Despite creating challenges for illiquid credits (requiring proxy spreads) and potentially increasing volatility, regulators view risk-neutral PDs as more forward-looking and market-consistent than backward-looking historical rates.
questions.why_it_matters: This shift fundamentally changed CVA magnitude and volatility. Risk-neutral CVA can be 2-10x larger than historical-based CVA, affecting P&L significantly. Understanding this regulatory and accounting requirement prevents costly non-compliance and ensures CVA systems are built correctly from the start.
common_traps: Attempting to use blended historical-risk-neutral approaches to reduce volatility (regulators reject this)
Believing illiquidity justifies using historical PDs (auditors will challenge this)
Underestimating the operational complexity of mapping thousands of illiquid credits to risk-neutral proxies
questions.real_world_example: In the 2012 Ernst & Young survey, 13 of 19 banks used risk-neutral PDs. By 2015, EBA reported near-complete convergence across European banks. Small regional banks attempting to use historical PDs faced audit qualifications and regulatory pressure to adopt market-implied approaches.

questions.subtopic: Extracting Risk-neutral PDs from Credit Spreads
questions.question: Using the simple approximation formula PD(t_i-1, t_i) ≈ s_t × Δt / LGD, calculate the one-year default probability for a counterparty with a 300 bps credit spread and 60% LGD. What is the key assumption this formula makes?
questions.answer_short: PD ≈ 0.03 × 1 / 0.60 = 5.0%. The formula assumes a flat credit spread curve and doesn't account for the shape of the curve prior to time t_i-1.
questions.answer_long: The calculation gives PD ≈ 300 bps × 1 year / 60% = 5.0% annual default probability. This approximation assumes the credit spread has been constant over the period and doesn't properly account for survival probabilities or the term structure shape. The approximation degrades as the credit curve becomes more steeply sloped. For accurate CVA calculations, bootstrapping methods that properly account for cumulative survival probabilities should be used (see Appendix 12A in Gregory). The simple formula is useful for quick estimates but can introduce material errors in CVA calculations for non-flat curves.
questions.why_it_matters: This formula is widely used for quick CVA estimates and initial pricing, but professionals must understand its limitations. Using it blindly on steep or inverted curves can create 10-20% errors in calculated CVA, leading to mispricing and hedge ineffectiveness.
common_traps: Applying this formula to long tenors with steep curve shapes (error compounds)
Forgetting that PD is unconditional (not conditional on survival to t_i-1)
Using inconsistent LGD assumptions between PD extraction and CVA calculation
questions.real_world_example: A junior CVA analyst used this formula across a 5-year upward-sloping credit curve (100 bps at 1Y, 500 bps at 5Y). By ignoring the curve shape, he overestimated near-term PDs by 30% and underestimated far-term PDs by 25%, producing a CVA error of 15% on a long-dated swap portfolio.

questions.question: Compare how an upward-sloping credit curve versus an inverted credit curve (both with the same 5-year spread of 300 bps) affects the distribution of default probabilities over time. Which curve creates higher near-term CVA?
questions.answer_short: An inverted curve front-loads default probability into early years, creating higher near-term PDs and higher CVA for short-dated exposures. An upward-sloping curve defers default probability to later years.
questions.answer_long: For identical 5-year cumulative default probabilities (both curves at 300 bps and 60% LGD give 22.12% cumulative PD), the timing distribution differs dramatically. An inverted curve (e.g., 500 bps at 1Y declining to 200 bps at 5Y) produces high 1-year PDs around 8% but declining annual PDs thereafter. An upward-sloping curve (e.g., 100 bps at 1Y rising to 500 bps at 10Y) produces low near-term PDs around 2% but higher far-term PDs. Since CVA is exposure-weighted and discounted, the inverted curve typically produces higher CVA for portfolios with near-term exposure peaks (like FX forwards). The upward-sloping curve produces higher CVA for long-dated swaps with deferred exposure.
questions.why_it_matters: CVA for the same counterparty can vary by 30-50% purely based on credit curve shape assumptions. Trading desks must understand whether counterparty curves are inverted (often seen in stressed credits) or upward-sloping (typical for stable credits) to price and hedge CVA correctly.
common_traps: Using only the 5-year spread without considering full term structure
Assuming curve shape doesn't matter if cumulative PDs match at one tenor
Extrapolating linearly beyond observable tenors (creates artificial curve shapes)
questions.real_world_example: During the European sovereign crisis, peripheral sovereign curves inverted sharply (2Y > 5Y spreads). CVA on short-dated government derivatives with these sovereigns spiked because near-term default risk dominated. Meanwhile, upward-sloping curves for stable corporates kept near-term CVA moderate.

questions.subtopic: Loss Given Default and Recovery Rates
questions.question: What is Loss Given Default (LGD) and how does it differ from recovery rate? What standard LGD is typically used for senior unsecured derivatives?
questions.answer_short: LGD is the percentage lost upon default; recovery rate is the percentage recovered. They sum to 100% (LGD = 1 - Recovery). Standard LGD for senior unsecured derivatives is 60% (40% recovery), matching CDS market convention.
questions.answer_long: Loss Given Default quantifies the economic loss as a percentage of exposure when a counterparty defaults, accounting for the eventual recovery through bankruptcy proceedings. Recovery rate is simply the complement (Recovery = 1 - LGD). For OTC derivatives ranking pari passu with senior unsecured debt, market convention uses 60% LGD (40% recovery), matching iTraxx Europe and CDX indices. However, actual recoveries vary widely by sector, seniority, and economic conditions—the Fannie/Freddie senior recoveries were over 90%, Lehman senior bonds recovered around 9% (later 30-40% for derivatives), and subordinated debt can recover almost nothing.
questions.why_it_matters: LGD directly scales CVA magnitude—using 60% versus 40% LGD changes CVA by 50%. While LGD matters less than credit spreads due to partial cancellation effects in CVA calculations, using inconsistent LGD between PD extraction and CVA calculation creates systematic errors.
common_traps: Confusing LGD with probability of default (they are independent parameters)
Using overly optimistic recovery assumptions without documentation (auditors reject this)
Ignoring seniority differences (secured vs senior vs subordinated) when available
questions.real_world_example: A structured product desk assumed 40% LGD (60% recovery) for derivatives with an SPV based on structural seniority, while the CVA desk used standard 60% LGD. This 20% LGD difference translated to 33% CVA discrepancy, causing pricing disputes and hedge misalignment.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'settled recovery' and 'actual recovery' for derivatives, and why does this create a practical challenge in CVA risk management?
questions.answer_short: Settled recovery is the immediate market-implied recovery (e.g., from CDS auction) occurring days after default. Actual recovery is what's eventually received from bankruptcy process, which can take years and may differ materially from settled recovery.
questions.answer_long: Settled recovery represents the market-clearing price established quickly post-default (typically through CDS auctions within days), allowing bondholders to monetize positions. For derivatives, actual recovery is realized much later through bankruptcy proceedings because derivative portfolios must be netted, collateral resolved, and close-out valuations agreed—a process taking months or years. This creates practical challenges: CVA models implicitly assume settled recovery for pricing and hedging, but firms actually experience the delayed actual recovery. The Lehman case illustrates this: CDS settled around 8.6% for senior debt, but many derivative counterparties eventually recovered 30-40% after lengthy bankruptcy proceedings. This gap creates funding and P&L timing mismatches.
questions.why_it_matters: This timing gap affects DVA realization, capital planning, and hedging effectiveness. A bank that suffers a counterparty default may need to carry unrealized losses for years before actual recovery, creating capital strain. CVA hedges settle quickly while actual recoveries drag out, producing basis risk.
common_traps: Assuming derivative recovery timing matches bond recovery (it doesn't—derivatives are slower)
Not planning for the liquidity gap between CVA hedge settlement and actual recovery
Ignoring potential recovery improvements from netting, collateral offset, or set-off rights
questions.real_world_example: After Lehman's default, banks holding long CDS protection received quick payouts based on 8.6% recovery. But banks with derivatives receivables waited years for bankruptcy resolution, eventually recovering 30-40%. This 3-4x recovery difference versus hedge payout created multi-year P&L distortions.

questions.question: Why is credit curve mapping particularly challenging for banks compared to end-users, and what are the key trade-offs between liquidity, accuracy, and capital relief?
questions.answer_short: Banks have thousands of illiquid counterparties (corporates, SMEs) without traded CDS/bonds, requiring proxy mapping. Key trade-offs: liquid proxies (indices) allow hedging and capital relief but less accuracy; illiquid single-name proxies are more accurate but provide no capital relief.
questions.answer_long: Banks face thousands of counterparties—many small corporates, SMEs, regionals without liquid CDS or bonds—compared to end-users trading with ~10-20 bank counterparties (all liquid). This creates a mapping challenge where choices involve trade-offs: (1) Liquid instruments like CDS indices allow hedging and partial capital relief but are generic and less representative; (2) Single-name proxies (parent companies, similar credits) better represent idiosyncratic risk but provide no capital relief under current Basel III rules and limited hedging; (3) Direct illiquid observables (secondary bonds) are most accurate but can't be shorted for hedging. Additionally, most liquid data exists at 5Y tenor only, while derivative portfolios extend beyond 10Y, requiring extrapolation. Regional banks in Asia/LatAm face even worse data availability.
questions.why_it_matters: Poor mapping choices create a vicious cycle: inaccurate CVA leads to mispricing and P&L volatility, while overly conservative mapping inflates CVA charges and drives business away. Capital relief considerations may force suboptimal hedging strategies. Large banks may have 70-80% of counterparties mapped to generic proxies, representing 30-40% of total exposure.
common_traps: Choosing single-name proxies purely for accuracy while ignoring zero capital relief implications
Over-granular mapping with insufficient data points (creates idiosyncratic noise)
Failing to document proxy rationale (auditors and regulators require justification)
questions.real_world_example: A European bank mapped a US corporate subsidiary to its parent's CDS (single-name proxy). The parent's idiosyncratic spread widening due to unrelated M&A caused 40% CVA MTM loss on the subsidiary exposure. No capital relief was available despite the hedge, and the CVA desk absorbed the volatility.

questions.question: What are the main CDS index families used in Europe for credit curve mapping, and how are they classified by entity type and credit quality?
questions.answer_short: iTraxx Europe indices: Main/Non-financials (investment grade corporates), Financials (banks/insurers), Crossover (sub-investment grade), High Volatility (widest spreads), and SovX (sovereigns). Each typically trades at 3Y, 5Y, 7Y, and 10Y maturities.
questions.answer_long: European CDS indices provide standardized credit exposure across entity types and quality. iTraxx Main/Non-financials covers 100 investment-grade corporate credits (BBB and better), with sub-indices by sector (TMT, industrials, energy, consumers, autos). iTraxx Crossover includes 40 sub-investment grade corporates. iTraxx Financials covers banks and insurers, split into senior and subordinated tranches. iTraxx SovX references sovereign credits across regions (Western Europe, CEEMEA, Asia Pacific, LatAm). Indices roll every six months, with 5Y being most liquid, followed by 3Y, 7Y, 10Y. These provide liquid hedging and mapping benchmarks, though indices trade wider than fair single-name averages due to standardization and liquidity premiums.
questions.why_it_matters: Understanding index structure is fundamental for CVA mapping and hedging. Indices provide the baseline for generic proxy curves and are the primary hedging instruments for non-single-name CVA risk. They also determine capital relief under Basel III standardized CVA approach.
common_traps: Treating index spreads as simple averages of constituents (they include liquidity premiums)
Assuming all tenors are equally liquid (5Y dominates, others may be stale)
Mapping financials to corporate indices or vice versa (structural risk profiles differ significantly)
questions.real_world_example: A CVA desk mapped mid-tier European banks to iTraxx Main instead of iTraxx Financials during the 2011 sovereign crisis. When bank-specific risks drove Financials index 200 bps wider while Main stayed stable, their CVA was understated by 35%, causing a hedging disaster.

questions.question: What are the key technical mismatches between using CDS as a credit hedge for derivative CVA exposure, and how can these create basis risk in a default scenario?
questions.answer_short: CDS credit events (failure to pay, bankruptcy, restructuring) may not trigger on derivative payment failures. CDS delivers bonds/loans, not derivatives, creating LGD basis risk. Derivative close-out and recovery timing differs from CDS settlement, creating cash flow mismatches.
questions.answer_long: Several technical disconnects create CDS-CVA basis risk: (1) Credit event mismatch: Standard CDS triggers are failure to pay on bonds/loans, bankruptcy, or restructuring. A counterparty could fail to pay on a derivative without triggering CDS unless documentation includes cross-default provisions. (2) Deliverable mismatch: CDS pays out based on bond recovery (established in auctions), but derivatives rank pari passu and may have different actual recoveries due to netting, collateral, and lengthy close-out processes. This creates LGD basis—Lehman CDS settled at 8.6% while derivative counterparties recovered 30-40%. (3) Timing mismatch: CDS settles within days via auction; derivative recovery takes months to years. This creates funding gaps. (4) Reference obligation differences: CDS typically references senior unsecured debt, which should match derivative seniority but doesn't account for derivatives-specific netting and collateral benefits.
questions.why_it_matters: These mismatches mean CDS provides spread hedging but imperfect default hedging for CVA. In a default, the CDS payout may be 50-75% of actual CVA loss. Practitioners must size hedges accounting for expected basis and maintain capital buffers for this residual risk. Jump-to-default CVA models should incorporate expected basis.
common_traps: Assuming CDS provides perfect default hedge (it doesn't—expect 20-40% basis in default)
Not documenting cross-default provisions in CDS confirmations when critical for trigger alignment
Ignoring timing basis: CDS payout is immediate, derivative recovery is delayed by years
questions.real_world_example: When a European corporate defaulted, the bank's CVA desk held CDS protection expecting 60% LGD (40% recovery). The CDS auction settled at 35% recovery, paying out 65% loss. Meanwhile, the derivative close-out with netting and collateral ultimately yielded 50% recovery, creating a 15% basis loss on the hedged position.

questions.question: When is it appropriate to use an LGD different from the standard 60% for OTC derivatives, and what evidence would auditors require to support a more favorable assumption?
questions.answer_short: Lower LGD (higher recovery) may be justified for: (1) structurally senior positions (e.g., SPV derivatives), (2) positions with credit enhancements beyond modeled collateral, (3) demonstrated favorable workout experience. Auditors require documentation, legal opinions, and historical evidence.
questions.answer_long: Standard 60% LGD matches market convention for senior unsecured claims, but exceptions exist. Acceptable deviations: (1) Structural seniority: Derivatives with securitization SPVs or structured entities often rank super-senior and may justify 30-40% LGD based on legal waterfall analysis. (2) Credit enhancements: Explicit guarantees, over-collateralization beyond what's modeled in exposure, or set-off rights against other claims can improve recovery. (3) Empirical evidence: Demonstrated recovery experience on similar exposures, though single data points (like Lehman) are insufficient without broader statistical support. Auditors demand: legal opinions confirming seniority, documentation of enhancement mechanisms, and conservative assumptions when using historical data. Many banks have observed better-than-60% LGD recoveries but cannot use them without meeting evidence standards. Recovery assumptions also cannot be used to justify overly aggressive CVA reductions without observable market support.
questions.why_it_matters: LGD assumptions directly scale CVA magnitude. Using 40% vs 60% LGD reduces CVA by 33%, materially affecting pricing, capital, and competitiveness. But unsupported assumptions create audit findings and regulatory pushback. Practitioners must balance economic reality with documentation standards.
common_traps: Extrapolating from Lehman's favorable derivative recovery (single data point, not statistically valid)
Using structural seniority arguments without legal opinions confirming waterfall priority
Double-counting: using both favorable LGD and modeling collateral (collateral should flow through exposure calculation)
questions.real_world_example: A structured products desk argued for 25% LGD on derivatives with a CLO based on senior position in the waterfall. Legal confirmed super-senior status, and auditors accepted 35% LGD (conservative vs 25% claimed). This 40% CVA reduction made the economics viable versus competitors using standard 60%.

questions.question: You need to map credit spreads for a mid-sized unlisted Japanese manufacturing company with no traded CDS or bonds. Walk through the decision tree to determine the appropriate credit spread source, considering liquidity, hedging, and capital relief.
questions.answer_short: No direct CDS/bond available. Check for single-name proxy (parent, peer, Japan sovereign + spread). If none suitable, map to generic proxy: iTraxx Asia index or Japan sector curve at appropriate rating. Generic proxy allows partial hedging and capital relief.
questions.answer_long: Following the decision tree: (1) Check liquid CDS—none exists for unlisted mid-cap. (2) Check alternative benchmark (bonds)—unlisted company has no public bonds. (3) Evaluate single-name proxy: Is there a listed parent or peer with liquid CDS? Is Japan sovereign CDS + spread (say 50-100 bps) reasonable? If yes, use single-name proxy with spread adjustment, but note: provides spread hedge only, no capital relief. (4) If no good single-name proxy, use generic proxy: Map by rating (say A-rated), region (Japan/Asia), sector (industrials). Use iTraxx Japan (if rated constituents match) or iTraxx Asia industrials sub-index. Alternatively, construct generic curve from Japan A-rated corporates with traded bonds. Generic proxy provides: reasonable spread hedge via index CDS, partial capital relief under Basel III, but introduces idiosyncratic noise. Document rationale: rating assessment, sector classification, regional economic linkage. This case likely leads to iTraxx Asia or Japan sector curve usage.
questions.why_it_matters: This scenario is extremely common—most bank counterparties lack liquid quotes. The mapping decision affects CVA magnitude (potentially 50-100 bps spread difference between choices), hedge effectiveness, and capital treatment. Wrong choices create unhedgeable risk or excessive capital charges.
common_traps: Defaulting to Japan sovereign CDS without sector/rating adjustment (understates idiosyncratic risk)
Using single-name proxy of unrelated company just because it's Japanese (introduces wrong idiosyncratic risk)
Failing to document decision rationale (regulatory and audit requirement)
questions.real_world_example: A European bank mapped a mid-cap Japanese auto supplier to Japan sovereign + 75 bps. When the supplier's sector hit distress (unrelated to sovereign), spreads widened 300 bps while their mapped spread moved only 50 bps. CVA was understated by 60%, causing a hedging failure and a €3M P&L hit.

questions.question: What are the key trade-offs between broad versus granular classification when constructing generic credit curves (e.g., single 'A-rated' curve vs 'A-rated US utilities' curve)?
questions.answer_short: Broad classification (e.g., single A-rated) provides many data points for stable curves but less differentiation between counterparties. Granular classification (A-rated US utilities) better distinguishes risk but with fewer data points, creating potential idiosyncratic volatility from individual credits.
questions.answer_long: Generic curve construction balances granularity against data sufficiency. Broad approach (rating only: AAA, AA, A, BBB, etc.): Uses many credits per bucket (e.g., 50-100 A-rated names), producing stable, well-averaged curves that smooth idiosyncratic noise. However, treats an A-rated US utility identically to an A-rated European telecom, ignoring sector and regional risks. Granular approach (rating + region + sector: e.g., 7 ratings × 7 regions × 3 sectors = 147 buckets): Better represents actual credit risk differences, allowing a US utility to differ from European telecom. But many buckets have few or zero liquid quotes, requiring interpolation/extrapolation or collapsing granularity. When only 2-3 credits per bucket, idiosyncratic movements dominate, creating artificial volatility. Regulatory guidance suggests rating + region + sector, but acknowledges data may not support full granularity. Practical implementations use hybrid approaches: more granularity where data allows (US/Europe investment grade), broader buckets where sparse (Asia high yield).
questions.why_it_matters: Curve construction methodology directly impacts CVA for 70-80% of a bank's counterparties. Overly broad curves understimate idiosyncratic risk; overly granular curves create unwarranted volatility from sparse data. Finding the right balance is critical for stable, defensible CVA that satisfies regulators and auditors.
common_traps: Forcing full rating × region × sector granularity despite insufficient data (creates noisy curves)
Using single broad curve globally (ignores clear regional and sector risk differences)
Not reviewing and adjusting bucket definitions as market liquidity evolves
questions.real_world_example: A bank used highly granular classification (147 buckets). For 'BB-rated LatAm utilities', only one liquid CDS existed. That single credit's idiosyncratic M&A spread tightening reduced CVA by 30% for a dozen mapped counterparties, creating arbitrary P&L. Collapsing to 'BB-rated LatAm' with 10 credits smoothed the volatility.

questions.question: What are the key advantages and disadvantages of using third-party generic credit curves (like Markit sector curves) versus building proprietary internal curves?
questions.answer_short: Third-party curves offer independence (appealing to auditors), lower cost, and standardization but lack flexibility, may produce uncontrolled MTM volatility, and use rigid classifications that may not match a bank's specific risk view or exposure profile.
questions.answer_long: Third-party curves (e.g., Markit sector curves): Advantages include: (1) Independence—auditors prefer external, unbiased sources; (2) Lower cost—no build/maintenance; (3) Standardization—consistent methodology, documented approach; (4) Market acceptance—widely used benchmark. Disadvantages include: (1) Rigid classification—fixed rating/sector buckets may not align with specific exposures or regional concentrations; (2) Uncontrolled volatility—methodology changes or idiosyncratic constituents create MTM moves outside bank's control; (3) Limited customization—can't adjust for specific knowledge (e.g., regional expertise, counterparty-specific insights); (4) Availability gaps—may not cover all regions/sectors needed. Proprietary curves offer full control, customization to exposure profile, and ability to incorporate internal credit views, but require significant infrastructure, ongoing maintenance, and face greater auditor scrutiny (independence concerns). Many banks use hybrid: third-party for standard cases, proprietary for concentrated exposures or regions with unique expertise.
questions.why_it_matters: The build-vs-buy decision affects operational costs, audit results, and MTM volatility. Third-party curves save costs but can produce unwanted P&L swings. Proprietary curves offer control but require skilled teams and strong model governance. The choice must align with bank size, resources, and exposure characteristics.
common_traps: Adopting third-party curves without validating methodology aligns with portfolio (classification mismatches)
Building proprietary curves without adequate governance/validation resources (audit failures)
Using third-party curves in regions where provider has limited data (quality issues)
questions.real_world_example: A regional US bank adopted Markit sector curves to save costs. A methodology change in Markit's curve construction caused a 20% CVA MTM swing in one month, shocking CFO and causing questions from the board. The bank later built proprietary curves for top 50 exposures while keeping Markit for long-tail.

questions.question: Compare direct observables, single-name proxies, and generic proxies for credit mapping in terms of liquidity, hedging effectiveness, and Basel III capital relief. Which approach would you use for a €100M exposure to an unlisted A-rated UK corporate?
questions.answer_short: Direct observable: best for all but unavailable (unlisted). Single-name proxy (UK parent/peer CDS): good spread hedge, no capital relief. Generic proxy (iTraxx Europe): liquid hedge, partial capital relief. For €100M exposure, prioritize single-name proxy if excellent match; otherwise generic proxy for capital efficiency.
questions.answer_long: Comparison: (1) Direct observables (own CDS/bond): Provide best accuracy, full hedging (spread + default), full capital relief but almost never available for unlisted/illiquid credits. (2) Single-name proxies (parent, peer, or sovereign + spread): Moderate liquidity, provide spread hedge but no default hedge (idiosyncratic differences), zero capital relief under current Basel III (though BCBS 2015 proposes changes). Best when proxy is very close match (e.g., guaranteed subsidiary, near-identical peer). (3) Generic proxies (indices): High liquidity, spread hedge only (diversified away idiosyncratic), partial capital relief (50% risk weight reduction for index hedge). Best for large tail of exposures. For €100M unlisted UK corporate: If a close single-name proxy exists (e.g., listed parent or near-peer), use it for accuracy despite no capital relief. If no excellent proxy, use iTraxx Europe (A-rated corporates) for partial capital relief and liquid hedging, accepting some basis risk. €100M is material enough to warrant single-name proxy search; smaller exposures default to generic. Document decision with proxy selection rationale.
questions.why_it_matters: This decision impacts CVA accuracy, hedge effectiveness, and capital charges—potentially 8-10% RWA difference between full and no capital relief. With large exposures, poor mapping creates material capital inefficiency or unhedgeable risk. Understanding the three-way trade-off is essential for CVA optimization.
common_traps: Always choosing single-name proxy for accuracy while ignoring capital relief loss (economically suboptimal)
Always choosing generic proxy for capital relief while ignoring poor fit (measurement and hedge basis risk)
Not updating mapping as market liquidity changes (single-name CDS may emerge or disappear)
questions.real_world_example: A bank mapped a €150M exposure to unlisted UK corporate to the listed parent's CDS (single-name proxy). Accurate CVA but zero capital relief cost €12M in extra capital annually. Switching to iTraxx Europe with documented rationale gave 50% capital relief (€6M saving) with only 15% CVA basis risk, a clear win.

questions.question: You are constructing an A-rated European corporate generic curve. You have 25 observable CDS at 5Y tenor but only 8 observable at 10Y. How would you approach combining points at each tenor and extending the curve to 15Y for long-dated swap CVA?
questions.answer_short: At each tenor: Combine observables using liquidity-weighted average, excluding outliers. Interpolate between 5Y-10Y (enough data). Extrapolate to 15Y using either: constant spread (conservative), constant hazard rate (common), or fit to longer-tenor bonds if available. Document approach and test sensitivity.
questions.answer_long: Step-by-step methodology: (1) 5Y tenor (25 quotes): Calculate liquidity-weighted average—weight by bid-ask spread or recent trading volume to emphasize more liquid credits. Exclude statistical outliers (>2.5 std dev) from specific situations (M&A, distress). This produces robust 5Y anchor point. (2) 10Y tenor (8 quotes): Fewer data points, so outlier exclusion more critical. Use median or trimmed mean to avoid single-credit dominance. If quotes are stale, adjust for basis to 5Y. (3) Interpolation 5Y-10Y: Use standard methods (linear in hazard rate space preferred, or Nelson-Siegel). Sufficient data makes this stable. (4) Extrapolation 10Y-15Y: Three approaches—(a) Flat spread: Assumes 10Y spread continues to 15Y (conservative, overstates long risk), (b) Constant hazard rate: Assumes constant annual default intensity (market standard, reasonable), (c) Bond curve fitting: If longer-dated corporate bonds exist, fit spread curve to them. Use (b) as baseline unless specific information suggests otherwise. (5) Validation: Test CVA sensitivity to extrapolation choice (typically 10-20% variation). Document rationale. Update quarterly as data evolves.
questions.why_it_matters: Curve construction details materially affect CVA for long-dated portfolios (15-30Y swaps). Extrapolation to 15Y is often guesswork—constant spread vs hazard rate can produce 20-30% CVA differences. Sound methodology with documented assumptions protects against audit and regulatory challenges.
common_traps: Linear interpolation in spread space (wrong—should use hazard rate or log-survival space)
Extrapolating linearly beyond 10Y (creates unrealistic PD acceleration)
Not testing CVA sensitivity to extrapolation method (hides model risk)
Including stale or outlier quotes without adjustment (distorts curve)
questions.real_world_example: A bank used flat spread extrapolation beyond 10Y for A-rated curve. This overstated 15Y CVA by 25% versus constant hazard rate approach, making long-dated swaps uncompetitive. Competitors using standard hazard rate extrapolation consistently won trades. Switching methods recovered business and reduced CVA by €5M.

questions.question: How does the concept of a funding curve differ from a credit curve in xVA calculations, and why must they be kept separate despite both being derived from similar market instruments?
questions.answer_short: Credit curves (for CVA) reflect counterparty default risk from CDS/bonds and use risk-neutral PDs. Funding curves (for FVA) reflect an institution's own funding costs from issuance spreads and repo rates, representing liquidity and capital costs beyond pure default risk. They measure different economics and must not be conflated.
questions.answer_long: Credit curves quantify the market-implied default risk of a counterparty, extracted from CDS spreads or bond yields, representing the risk-neutral probability-weighted expected loss from counterparty default. These are used in CVA/DVA calculations. Funding curves, by contrast, quantify an institution's own cost to raise secured or unsecured funding for financing derivative exposures or posting initial margin, extracted from issuance spreads, repo rates, or internal transfer pricing. Funding curves reflect: (1) Own default risk (part of DVA), (2) Liquidity premiums (term funding liquidity risk), (3) Regulatory capital costs (balance sheet usage), (4) Market segmentation. While both may use similar instruments as inputs (e.g., own CDS for DVA and funding), they serve different purposes: credit curves are market exit prices for counterparty risk; funding curves are internal transfer prices for funding and capital. FVA/MVA require funding curves; CVA requires credit curves. Conflating them leads to double-counting (e.g., including funding spread in both DVA and FVA). Proper xVA frameworks maintain distinct curves with clear governance over their construction and application.
questions.why_it_matters: Confusing credit and funding curves creates systematic xVA errors and double-counting. A bank using its own CDS spread for both DVA and FVA double-counts its own default risk, inflating values. Conversely, using counterparty credit curves for FVA underestimates funding costs. Clear separation ensures xVA components are correctly measured and decisions (pricing, hedging) are economically sound.
common_traps: Using own CDS spread interchangeably for DVA and FVA (double-counts own default risk)
Applying counterparty credit curves to estimate FVA funding costs (ignores liquidity premium)
Not documenting which curve is used for which xVA component (creates audit confusion)
Assuming funding curve = risk-free rate + own CDS spread (oversimplifies, ignores liquidity and capital)
questions.real_world_example: A mid-sized bank used its own 5Y CDS spread (200 bps) for both DVA and FVA on uncollateralized swaps. This double-counted 200 bps of own-default risk, making derivative values appear 15% higher than economically justified. After auditor challenge, they separated curves: DVA used CDS; FVA used blended issuance curve (250 bps including liquidity premium), correcting the overstatement.

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between real-world and risk-neutral default probabilities?
questions.answer_short: Real-world default probabilities are estimated from historical default data, while risk-neutral default probabilities are derived from market prices (bonds, CDS) and include a risk premium demanded by investors.
questions.answer_long: Real-world default probabilities represent actual historical default frequencies, typically derived from rating agency data. Risk-neutral default probabilities are extracted from market instruments like CDS or bonds and are systematically higher because they incorporate a risk premium that risk-averse investors demand for bearing default risk. The risk-neutral probability equals the real-world probability plus this market risk premium.
questions.why_it_matters: Understanding this distinction is critical because CVA calculations use risk-neutral probabilities (per accounting and regulatory requirements), which produce significantly higher values than real-world approaches. This affects pricing, hedging, and capital requirements.
common_traps: Assuming the two probabilities are interchangeable or similar in magnitude
Believing that credit spreads only reflect expected default losses
Using historical default rates when market-implied values are required by regulation
questions.real_world_example: A single-A rated corporate might have a 0.13% real-world one-year default probability but a 1.28% risk-neutral probability derived from its CDS spread - almost 10 times higher. Using the wrong one dramatically changes CVA calculations.

questions.question: Why have banks and regulators converged on using risk-neutral rather than real-world default probabilities for CVA, despite the challenges for illiquid credits?
questions.answer_short: Regulators and accounting standards (IFRS 13, Basel III) require market-observable inputs and exit prices. Risk-neutral PDs align with CDS market prices, enabling CVA hedging and fair value measurement.
questions.answer_long: The shift to risk-neutral default probabilities was driven by IFRS 13's requirement to use market-observable inputs for fair value, Basel III's explicit use of credit spreads in CVA capital formulas, and the development of CDS markets that allow CVA hedging. While this creates challenges for illiquid counterparties requiring proxy spreads, regulators view risk-neutral PDs as necessary for consistent, hedgeable, and forward-looking risk measurement rather than backward-looking actuarial reserves.
questions.why_it_matters: This fundamental shift changed CVA from an internal reserve to a market price, increased CVA volatility, created challenges for illiquid credits, and made CVA hedging central to managing counterparty risk. It affects thousands of counterparties at major banks.
common_traps: Using blended approaches mixing real-world and risk-neutral PDs without regulatory approval
Assuming all counterparties have liquid CDS that can be used directly
Underestimating the CVA volatility that results from using market-implied spreads
questions.real_world_example: A regional bank with 500 corporate counterparties may have liquid CDS for only 20 of them. They must map the other 480 to proxy spreads, creating model risk and potentially higher CVA volatility than if using stable historical default rates.

questions.subtopic: Calculating Risk-neutral PD from Credit Spreads
questions.question: Using the simple approximation formula, what is the approximate annual default probability for a counterparty with a 300 bps credit spread and 60% LGD?
questions.answer_long: The simple formula PD(t, t+Δt) ≈ (s_t × Δt) / LGD gives: 300 bps = 0.03, time period = 1 year, LGD = 0.60, so PD = 0.03 / 0.60 = 0.05 or 5%. This approximation works well for flat or mildly sloped credit curves but becomes less accurate when curves are steeply sloped, as it doesn't account for the forward credit curve shape.
questions.why_it_matters: This simple calculation allows practitioners to quickly estimate default probabilities from observable credit spreads for CVA and capital calculations. Understanding when the approximation breaks down is crucial for accurate risk measurement.
common_traps: Forgetting to divide by LGD (not Recovery Rate)
Applying the formula to steeply sloped curves where it's inaccurate
Confusing unconditional and conditional default probabilities
questions.real_world_example: A CVA desk needs to quickly estimate the one-year PD for a new counterparty trading at 450 bps. With 60% LGD, they calculate 450/10000 / 0.60 = 7.5% PD. This rough estimate helps them assess whether detailed curve bootstrapping is needed.

questions.question: Why do three different credit curves (flat, upward-sloping, inverted) with identical five-year spreads of 300 bps produce very different default probability distributions over time?
questions.answer_short: The curve shape determines how default risk is distributed over time. Upward-sloping curves imply higher near-term survival but more tail risk, while inverted curves imply higher near-term default risk.
questions.answer_long: Even though all three curves have the same five-year cumulative default probability, the shape dictates the timing distribution. An upward-sloping curve has lower spreads initially, implying lower near-term default probabilities but accelerating risk later. An inverted curve has high near-term spreads, implying elevated default risk in early years that decreases over time. The flat curve distributes default risk evenly. This critically affects CVA calculations where exposure profiles interact with these time-varying default probabilities.
questions.why_it_matters: CVA is highly sensitive to when defaults are likely to occur relative to when exposure peaks. Wrong assumptions about curve shape can materially misprices CVA, especially for long-dated or path-dependent exposures. Extrapolation beyond liquid tenors amplifies this sensitivity.
common_traps: Assuming a flat credit curve when only one tenor is observable
Ignoring term structure when exposure is concentrated at specific maturities
Extrapolating long-dated spreads without considering market conventions
questions.real_world_example: A bank has a 10-year swap with exposure peaking at year 7. Using a flat 300 bps curve gives a 7-year PD of 30%, but the actual upward-sloping curve implies 35% at that tenor, understating CVA by 15%.

questions.subtopic: Loss Given Default and Recovery Rates
questions.question: What is the difference between Loss Given Default (LGD) and recovery rate, and what is the standard LGD assumption for senior unsecured derivatives?
questions.answer_short: LGD = 1 - Recovery Rate. Standard LGD for senior unsecured derivatives is 60% (40% recovery), matching the convention used in most CDS contracts.
questions.answer_long: Loss Given Default is the percentage lost in a default event, while recovery rate is the percentage recovered. They are complementary: LGD + Recovery = 100%. For derivatives ranking pari passu with senior unsecured debt, market convention uses 60% LGD (40% recovery), which aligns with CDS market standards for indices like iTraxx Europe and CDX NA. This assumption is used to convert credit spreads into default probabilities.
questions.why_it_matters: LGD is needed to extract default probabilities from credit spreads and to calculate CVA. While LGD has a cancellation effect in CVA formulas (reducing its sensitivity), choosing the wrong seniority assumption can significantly misstate risk for structured or subordinated positions.
common_traps: Confusing LGD with recovery rate in calculations
Assuming all derivatives have the same recovery regardless of seniority
Using CDS auction recovery without considering delayed OTC derivative settlement
questions.real_world_example: In the Lehman bankruptcy, CDS settled at 8.6% recovery (91.4% LGD), but actual OTC derivative recoveries took years and ended up around 30-40% - a massive difference affecting realized CVA losses.

questions.question: When should a CVA desk use settled recovery (from CDS auction) versus actual recovery from a derivative bankruptcy workout, and what are the practical implications?
questions.answer_short: Use settled recovery for mark-to-market CVA pricing (exit price concept). Actual recovery matters for realized P&L and may be higher but takes years to materialize.
questions.answer_long: CVA should be marked using settled recovery because IFRS 13 requires exit prices - what you could receive by immediately selling the claim (participating in the CDS auction or selling defaulted bonds). However, banks that hold derivative claims through bankruptcy may receive higher actual recoveries after months or years, especially if they can offset other claims or access set-off rights. The timing difference is critical: settled recovery provides immediate liquidity, actual recovery may be 2-5% higher annually but is illiquid and uncertain.
questions.why_it_matters: This distinction affects liquidity management, capital planning, and whether to sell or hold derivative claims post-default. It also explains why some banks argue for higher recovery assumptions based on experience, though regulators prefer market-implied (settled) values for CVA.
common_traps: Marking CVA with optimistic actual recovery expectations instead of market-implied settled recovery
Ignoring the time value of money when comparing settled vs actual recovery
Assuming all derivatives will achieve the same favorable actual recovery as past cases
questions.real_world_example: Post-Lehman, a bank's CVA used 8.6% settled recovery for marking. They eventually received 35% actual recovery after 4 years. While this improved realized P&L, using 35% for CVA marking would have been incorrect and unhedgeable.

questions.question: What are the three main challenges that make credit curve mapping for illiquid counterparties more than just a technical exercise?
questions.answer_short: The three challenges are: (1) lack of observable market data for most counterparties, (2) tension between mapping accuracy and hedge availability, and (3) balancing capital relief with CVA accuracy.
questions.answer_long: Credit curve mapping faces fundamental challenges: First, most counterparties lack liquid CDS or bonds, requiring subjective proxy selection. Second, the best fundamental mapping (e.g., similar company) may not be tradeable for hedging, while liquid hedges (e.g., indices) may be poor credit matches. Third, regulatory capital relief rules favor index hedges over single-name proxies, even when proxies better represent credit risk. Banks must balance these competing objectives while meeting auditor and regulator expectations for risk-neutral, market-based curves.
questions.why_it_matters: These tensions force practical compromises that affect CVA accuracy, hedging effectiveness, and capital efficiency. Poor mapping decisions can result in unhedgeable CVA volatility, regulatory challenge, or excessive capital charges. This is especially acute for regional banks or those with many SME counterparties.
common_traps: Choosing mapping methodology purely for capital relief rather than risk accuracy
Mapping to liquid instruments without considering fundamental credit similarity
Failing to document the rationale for subjective mapping decisions
questions.real_world_example: A European bank has 200 mid-sized corporate counterparties with no CDS. Mapping all to iTraxx Crossover provides hedging and capital relief but introduces basis risk. Mapping to parent company CDS where available is more accurate but provides no capital relief under current rules.

questions.question: What are the main CDS indices used for credit curve mapping in Europe and how do they differ by credit quality?
questions.answer_short: Main European indices: iTraxx Europe (125 investment grade names), iTraxx Non-financials (BBB and better), iTraxx Crossover (40 sub-investment grade), iTraxx Financials, and iTraxx SovX for sovereigns.
questions.answer_long: The iTraxx family provides tiered credit exposure: iTraxx Europe Main (125 most liquid investment grade credits) serves as the benchmark. iTraxx Non-financials captures 100 corporate credits rated BBB or better. iTraxx Crossover focuses on 40 sub-investment grade corporates (the widest spreads from the main index). iTraxx Financials covers bank and financial credits. iTraxx SovX references sovereign credits across regions. These indices trade at standard tenors (3, 5, 7, 10 years) with good liquidity, making them practical mapping targets.
questions.why_it_matters: These indices are the liquid instruments available for hedging CVA and obtaining capital relief. Understanding their composition and credit quality helps determine appropriate mapping for counterparties without direct market quotes. They form the foundation of generic proxy curves.
common_traps: Mapping investment grade corporates to iTraxx Crossover because exposure is large
Using main index when crossover better reflects actual counterparty credit quality
Assuming all index names have equal weight (they don't in some versions)
questions.real_world_example: A CVA desk maps a BB-rated Italian manufacturer to iTraxx Crossover rather than iTraxx Europe Main because the credit quality and spread levels match better, even though the company isn't in the index. This provides a better hedge than using the tighter main index.

questions.question: A derivatives portfolio with a securitization SPV has structural seniority making it effectively super-senior. Should you use the standard 60% LGD, and what would be the impact of using 40% LGD instead?
questions.answer_short: No, use a lower LGD (e.g., 40% or 30%) to reflect super-senior status. Using 60% LGD overstates default probability and CVA, potentially by 30-50%.
questions.answer_long: Standard 60% LGD applies to senior unsecured claims. Structural seniority (common in securitizations where derivatives receive priority) justifies lower LGD, potentially 30-40%. Since PD ≈ spread/LGD, using 40% instead of 60% increases the extracted default probability by 50% (60/40 = 1.5x). However, in CVA calculations, there's a partial cancellation because both PD extraction and loss calculation use LGD. The net effect is still material: CVA could decrease by 20-30%, making proper LGD assessment important for these structures.
questions.why_it_matters: Structural seniority features are common in securitizations, covered bonds, and some corporate structures. Using incorrect LGD overstates CVA, making the bank uncompetitive on pricing. However, claiming favorable LGD requires strong documentation and may face auditor scrutiny.
common_traps: Applying standard 60% LGD to all derivatives regardless of seniority
Using overly optimistic LGD without legal documentation of seniority
Forgetting that LGD affects both PD extraction and CVA calculation (partial cancellation)
questions.real_world_example: A bank structures a derivative with a AAA-rated ABS SPV where the swap is super-senior to the notes. Using 40% LGD instead of 60% reduces CVA by 25%, allowing competitive pricing. Auditors require legal opinions confirming the seniority structure.

questions.question: Compare the three credit curve mapping approaches (direct observable, single-name proxy, generic proxy) in terms of capital relief availability and hedge effectiveness.
questions.answer_short: Direct observables: full capital relief, best hedging. Single-name proxies: no capital relief (currently), spread hedge only. Generic proxies: partial capital relief, spread hedge but no default protection.
questions.answer_long: Direct observables (the counterparty's own CDS) provide perfect hedging and full capital relief under Basel III. Single-name proxies (e.g., parent company CDS) hedge spread risk but not default risk if entities are separate, and currently attract no capital relief, though BCBS 2015 proposes changing this. Generic proxies (indices) are most liquid but provide only spread hedging with no default protection; they give partial capital relief via the standardized CVA charge. The hierarchy forces tradeoffs: liquidity vs specificity, hedge effectiveness vs capital efficiency.
questions.why_it_matters: This three-way tradeoff drives practical mapping decisions at every bank. Large global banks may prioritize capital relief and use more generic mapping. Regional banks with concentrated exposures may prefer specific proxies despite capital costs. The choice affects P&L volatility, capital consumption, and hedge portfolio composition.
common_traps: Using single-name proxies assuming they provide capital relief like direct observables
Relying on generic proxies for names where reasonable single-name proxies exist
Failing to monitor basis risk between generic hedges and actual counterparty credit
questions.real_world_example: A bank has exposure to a mid-sized US utility with no CDS. Its parent company CDS trades at 120 bps. Mapping to the parent hedges spread risk but provides no capital relief. Mapping to iTraxx Europe seems wrong (US entity). Mapping to CDX IG gives 150 bps spread and partial capital relief but worse hedge.

questions.question: A bank needs to construct a generic A-rated European corporate curve. They have 8 single-name CDS quotes at 5Y ranging from 90 to 140 bps. What are the key methodological decisions they must make?
questions.answer_short: Key decisions: (1) which names to include (liquidity filter), (2) how to weight/average the 8 quotes, (3) how to interpolate to other tenors (1Y, 3Y, 7Y, 10Y), and (4) how to handle outliers.
questions.answer_long: Constructing the generic curve requires several choices: First, filter the 8 names for liquidity (wide bid-offer may indicate stale prices). Second, decide on averaging methodology - equal weight, volume-weighted, or median to reduce outlier impact. Third, determine term structure by observing these names at other tenors or using a credit curve shape model. Fourth, handle outliers that may represent idiosyncratic rather than systematic A-rated European corporate risk. Finally, establish governance for updating the curve (daily, weekly) and documented decision rules for adding/removing constituents.
questions.why_it_matters: Generic curves determine CVA for potentially hundreds of counterparties, so construction choices have large aggregate impact. Poor methodology introduces noise (reducing hedge effectiveness) or bias (systematic CVA misstatement). Regulators expect documented, consistent approaches that can be defended in audits.
common_traps: Including illiquid names that introduce idiosyncratic volatility
Equal-weighting without considering that some names may be distorted
Failing to document and consistently apply the curve construction methodology
questions.real_world_example: A bank constructs an A-rated European industrial curve using 12 names. One name suddenly widens to 200 bps due to idiosyncratic news. Without an outlier filter, the generic curve jumps 15%, affecting CVA on 80 counterparties who have no connection to the distressed name.

questions.question: Why does the regulatory guidance to map by rating, region, and sector create practical challenges, and how do banks balance granularity against data availability?
questions.answer_short: The 7 ratings × 7 regions × 3 sectors = 147 combinations vastly exceed available liquid CDS. Banks must aggregate categories (e.g., fewer regions) or accept sparse data in some buckets, creating extrapolation risk.
questions.answer_long: Regulatory guidance for rating-region-sector mapping assumes more market liquidity than exists. With perhaps 500-1000 liquid single-name CDS globally and the need for 147+ combinations, many buckets have zero or few observable quotes. Banks respond by: (1) reducing granularity (e.g., combining regions into Western Europe vs. Other), (2) using CDS indices as building blocks even when not perfectly matched, (3) applying spread adjustments to parent categories, or (4) accepting that some buckets must be extrapolated or proxied. Each approach has drawbacks: less granularity means poorer differentiation, more extrapolation increases model risk.
questions.why_it_matters: This tension between regulatory expectations and market reality forces banks to make subjective choices that materially affect CVA for large portions of their counterparty populations. Different banks may reach different conclusions on the same counterparty, creating inconsistency. Model validation and audit become challenging.
common_traps: Creating overly granular mappings with insufficient data, increasing noise
Mechanically applying rating-region-sector without considering data quality
Failing to validate that mapped curves actually trade in the market ranges observed
questions.real_world_example: A global bank needs a BBB Eastern European sovereign curve. No liquid CDS exist in this category. They use: (1) sovereign index for curve shape, (2) regional BBB corporate spread for level, and (3) expert judgment. Three different methodologies give spreads ranging from 250-350 bps - massive ambiguity.

questions.question: What are the advantages and disadvantages of using third-party generic curves (e.g., Markit sector curves) versus building internal curves?
questions.answer_short: Third-party curves offer independence and lower cost but lack flexibility in classification and may produce undesirable volatility. Internal curves allow customization but require more resources and may face auditor skepticism.
questions.answer_long: Third-party curves (like Markit sector curves) provide: standardized methodology, auditor comfort with independence, lower maintenance costs, and consistency with peers. Disadvantages include: rigid classification that may not match the bank's portfolio, inability to adjust for specific information, potential volatility from methodology changes outside the bank's control, and cost of subscriptions. Internal curves offer: tailored classification for the bank's specific exposures, control over methodology and updates, ability to incorporate bank-specific views, and integration with internal risk systems. However, they require significant development and maintenance resources and face greater auditor scrutiny.
questions.why_it_matters: This build-versus-buy decision affects hundreds of counterparties and involves tradeoffs between cost, control, and credibility. Many banks use a hybrid: third-party curves as benchmarks or fallbacks with internal curves for material exposures. The choice impacts P&L volatility and audit outcomes.
common_traps: Assuming third-party curves are always 'safer' with auditors without understanding their methodology
Building internal curves without sufficient resources for ongoing maintenance
Using third-party curves without understanding their classification and potential mismatch with your portfolio
questions.real_world_example: A mid-sized bank uses Markit sector curves for 80% of counterparties. When Markit changes their averaging methodology, the bank experiences unexpected 10% CVA volatility. They had no control and insufficient understanding of the methodology to predict or explain the impact to management.

questions.question: A corporate bond trades at 350 bps spread while its CDS trades at 300 bps. The derivative claim ranks pari passu with senior unsecured. Which spread should be used for CVA and why might they differ?
questions.answer_short: Use the 300 bps CDS spread. The 50 bps difference (negative basis) likely reflects bond-specific factors like liquidity premium or repo specialness, which don't apply to derivatives.
questions.answer_long: The CDS spread is the cleaner measure of pure credit risk for derivatives because: (1) CDS isolates credit risk without bond-specific liquidity or repo effects, (2) CDS markets are typically more liquid for trading credit risk, (3) CVA hedging uses CDS not bonds, so consistency is important. The CDS-bond basis (here -50 bps, meaning bond is wider) can reflect: bond liquidity premium, repo market effects, funding costs embedded in bonds, technical supply/demand, or convertibility features. Since derivatives rank with senior unsecured and CDS references the same seniority, 300 bps is appropriate. Using 350 bps would overstate CVA and create basis risk with hedging instruments.
questions.why_it_matters: Many counterparties have bonds but no CDS (or vice versa). Understanding basis drivers prevents systematic CVA misstatement. It's especially important when creating proxies: a bond spread needs adjustment before being used as a CDS equivalent. This basis can be 20-100 bps, materially affecting CVA.
common_traps: Using bond spreads directly without basis adjustment when CDS is the hedging instrument
Assuming CDS and bond spreads should be identical for the same credit
Failing to check which instrument is more liquid before choosing mapping source
questions.real_world_example: During the 2011 Eurozone crisis, Italian bank bonds traded 100-200 bps wider than CDS due to forced selling by constrained investors. Using bond spreads would have overstated CVA and created massive hedge basis for banks using CDS to hedge.

questions.question: Why does the simple approximation PD ≈ s × Δt / LGD break down for steeply sloped credit curves, and what is the more accurate approach?
questions.answer_short: The approximation assumes constant hazard rate between time points, which fails when the curve is steeply sloped. The accurate method bootstraps hazard rates from CDS spreads sequentially from short to long maturities.
questions.answer_long: The simple formula treats each period independently, but CDS spreads are cumulative - a 5Y CDS protects against default anytime in the next 5 years. When the curve is steeply sloped (e.g., inverted with high short-term spreads declining to lower long-term spreads), the forward default probability depends on both the current tenor spread and all previous tenors. The bootstrapping approach works sequentially: extract the hazard rate for 1Y from the 1Y CDS, then use that to extract the incremental hazard rate for 1Y-2Y from the 2Y CDS spread, and so on. This properly accounts for the probability of surviving to each period. The difference can be 20-50% for highly sloped curves.
questions.why_it_matters: Proper bootstrapping is essential for accurate CVA when exposures have specific maturity concentrations or for long-dated trades. Using the simple approximation for steep curves can materially misstate CVA and result in poor hedging decisions. It's especially important for emerging market credits with inverted curves.
common_traps: Using the simple approximation without checking credit curve slope
Bootstrapping in the wrong direction (long to short instead of short to long)
Forgetting that bootstrapped hazard rates must be converted to forward default probabilities
questions.real_world_example: A distressed corporate has an inverted curve: 1Y = 800 bps, 2Y = 700 bps, 5Y = 500 bps. Simple approximation gives Year 2 PD = 11.7%. Bootstrapping gives Year 2 forward PD = 7.2% (much lower because many defaults happen in Year 1). CVA differs by 30%.

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between a real-world default probability and a risk-neutral default probability?
questions.answer_short: Real-world default probabilities are estimated from historical default data, while risk-neutral default probabilities are derived from market prices (bonds, CDS) and include a risk premium that investors demand.
questions.answer_long: Real-world default probabilities represent actual historical default frequencies, typically estimated from rating agency data. Risk-neutral default probabilities are implied from market instruments like bonds or CDS and are systematically higher because they include a risk premium that investors require for bearing credit risk. This premium compensates investors beyond expected losses and reflects risk aversion in the market.
questions.why_it_matters: Using the correct type of default probability is critical for CVA: real-world PDs underestimate market costs, while risk-neutral PDs align with exit pricing and hedging requirements under IFRS 13 and Basel III.
common_traps: Thinking real-world PDs are more 'accurate' because they're based on actual defaults
Not understanding that risk-neutral PDs contain a premium beyond expected loss
Using real-world PDs for CVA when regulations require risk-neutral measures
questions.real_world_example: A BBB-rated corporate has a 5-year historical default rate of 2%, but its 5-year CDS trades at 238 bps (implying ~7% risk-neutral probability with 60% LGD). A desk using 2% would drastically undercharge CVA.

questions.question: Why are risk-neutral default probabilities typically much higher than real-world default probabilities, and how does this gap vary by credit quality?
questions.answer_short: Risk-neutral PDs include a risk premium that investors demand for bearing credit risk. This gap is largest for high-quality credits (10-15x for AAA/AA) and smallest for distressed credits (1.2-2x for B/CCC).
questions.answer_long: The gap between risk-neutral and real-world default probabilities reflects investor risk aversion and market liquidity premiums. Studies show this ratio can be 16x for Aaa credits but only 1.2x for B-rated credits. Higher quality credits have smaller absolute default risks, so the risk premium dominates. For distressed credits, actual default risk is so high that the additional premium is relatively smaller. This has major implications for CVA calculations across different counterparty qualities.
questions.why_it_matters: Understanding this relationship prevents massive overcharging of CVA for high-quality counterparties if you mistakenly treat risk-neutral PDs as 'true' default likelihoods, and helps calibrate models correctly across rating categories.
common_traps: Assuming the risk premium is constant across all rating grades
Not adjusting for this effect when comparing CVA to actual loss experience
Treating the full credit spread as purely default-driven
questions.real_world_example: An Aaa-rated sovereign has a 1-year real-world PD of 0.04% but a risk-neutral PD of 0.67% (67 bps CDS with 60% LGD). A trader incorrectly interpreting the 0.67% as 'true' default risk would be shocked that defaults are much rarer than CVA suggests.

questions.question: Why have regulators and accounting standards pushed banks toward using risk-neutral default probabilities for CVA, even for illiquid counterparties?
questions.answer_short: IFRS 13 requires market-observable inputs and exit pricing, while Basel III CVA capital rules explicitly reference CDS spreads. Risk-neutral PDs align with hedging instruments and reflect how the market would price the risk.
questions.answer_long: The shift reflects three drivers: (1) IFRS 13's fair value requirements demand exit prices using market data where possible, (2) Basel III CVA capital rules explicitly use CDS spreads in formulas, and (3) the development of CDS markets created observable hedging instruments. Even for illiquid credits, regulators argue that using proxy spreads based on rating/sector/region provides a more forward-looking, market-consistent approach than backward-looking historical data. This creates challenges but aligns CVA with trading book valuation principles.
questions.why_it_matters: This requirement fundamentally changed CVA from an actuarial reserve to a market-based valuation, affecting pricing, hedging strategy, P&L volatility, and capital requirements for all derivatives desks.
common_traps: Thinking you can use real-world PDs for small illiquid counterparties to avoid volatility
Not understanding that auditors will challenge any deviation from risk-neutral
Assuming this requirement only applies to liquid credits with CDS
questions.real_world_example: A regional bank with 500 SME counterparties (none with CDS) tried using historical PDs for CVA. Auditors rejected the approach, forcing a complete rebuild using proxy mapping to CDS indices, increasing CVA by 3-4x.

questions.question: What is the simple formula to convert a credit spread to an approximate default probability for a period, and what does each term represent?
questions.answer_short: PD(t,T) ≈ s(T) × (T-t) / LGD, where s(T) is the credit spread to maturity T, (T-t) is the time period, and LGD is the loss given default.
questions.answer_long: The approximation PD(t,T) ≈ s × Δt / LGD converts an observed credit spread into an unconditional default probability for a time period. The credit spread compensates for expected loss (PD × LGD), so dividing the spread by LGD and multiplying by the time interval gives the default probability. For example, a 300 bps spread with 60% LGD over 1 year gives approximately 5% default probability. This assumes constant spread and LGD but is widely used for practical calculations.
questions.why_it_matters: This is the fundamental building block for all CVA calculations - converting observable market spreads into the default probabilities needed for expected loss computations. Every CVA system implements this conversion thousands of times per calculation.
common_traps: Forgetting to divide by LGD, giving probabilities that are far too low
Using this for long periods when the credit curve is steeply sloped (accuracy degrades)
Not understanding these are unconditional probabilities, not survival-conditional
questions.real_world_example: A 5-year swap counterparty with a 450 bps CDS and 60% LGD has annual PDs of approximately 7.5% per year. A junior analyst who forgot to divide by LGD calculated 4.5% and undercharged CVA by 40%.

questions.question: How does the shape of a credit spread curve (flat, upward-sloping, inverted) impact the distribution of default probability over time, even when the 5-year spread is identical?
questions.answer_short: An upward-sloping curve front-loads default probability in early years, while an inverted curve back-loads it. For the same 5-year spread, annual default probabilities can differ by 2-3x depending on curve shape.
questions.answer_long: Credit curve shape dramatically affects the timing of default risk. With a 300 bps 5-year spread but flat curve, you get roughly equal annual default probabilities. An upward-sloping curve (say 100 bps at 1Y, 300 bps at 5Y) implies lower near-term risk but higher long-term risk. An inverted curve (500 bps at 1Y, 300 bps at 5Y) implies immediate distress with improving outlook. The 5-year cumulative default probability is the same in all cases, but CVA will differ substantially because exposure timing matters. This makes curve interpolation and extrapolation critical.
questions.why_it_matters: CVA is highly sensitive to the timing of default probability due to exposure profiles. Using an incorrect curve shape can lead to errors of 30-50% in CVA even when the benchmark tenor is correct.
common_traps: Assuming a flat credit spread when only one tenor is available
Not considering that curve shape contains information about credit trajectory
Extrapolating linearly beyond available tenors without considering credit fundamentals
questions.real_world_example: A distressed counterparty with an inverted curve (800 bps at 1Y, 400 bps at 5Y) has 10% default probability in year 1 but only 3% in year 5. A desk that flat-extrapolated the 5-year spread badly mispriced short-dated CVA.

questions.subtopic: Loss Given Default and Recovery Rates
questions.question: What is Loss Given Default (LGD), how does it relate to recovery rate, and what is the standard assumption for senior unsecured debt?
questions.answer_short: LGD is the percentage lost in default, equal to (1 - recovery rate). Standard market assumption for senior unsecured debt is 60% LGD (40% recovery), which is the convention used in most CDS contracts.
questions.answer_long: Loss Given Default measures the severity of loss when a counterparty defaults, expressed as a percentage of exposure. It equals one minus the recovery rate. For senior unsecured claims (where derivatives typically rank), the market convention is 60% LGD or 40% recovery. This is standardized in CDS contracts for corporates (iTraxx, CDX). Actual recoveries vary widely by sector, seniority, and economic conditions - as seen with Lehman (9% CDS auction, but 30-40% actual workout). Derivatives recovery may differ from bond recovery due to netting, collateral, and lengthy bankruptcy processes.
questions.why_it_matters: LGD directly scales CVA calculations - using 40% instead of 60% would reduce CVA by one-third. Understanding the difference between market-implied, settled, and actual recovery is critical for risk management and explaining CVA P&L.
common_traps: Thinking LGD is precisely known or constant across credit events
Not distinguishing between CDS-implied (settled) recovery and actual derivative workout recovery
Assuming subordinated derivatives rank the same as senior debt
questions.real_world_example: After Lehman bankruptcy, CDS settled at 8.6% recovery (91.4% LGD), but derivative claims eventually recovered 30-40% after years of workout. Banks using the 9% assumption booked large initial losses but recovered more over time.

questions.question: When should you use 'settled recovery' versus 'actual recovery' for CVA calculations, and how do timing differences affect this choice?
questions.answer_short: Settled recovery (from CDS auctions, quickly available) should be used for market-consistent CVA and hedging. Actual recovery (from bankruptcy workout, taking years) may be higher but is uncertain and not usable for exit pricing.
questions.answer_long: Settled recovery is realized immediately after default through CDS auctions or secondary bond markets - typically within weeks. This is the market-implied recovery and what your CDS hedges pay. Actual recovery on derivatives comes after the bankruptcy process completes, which can take years and involves agreeing on the claim value. While actual recovery may be higher (Lehman: 30-40% actual vs 9% settled), you cannot use this for fair value CVA because: (1) it's not observable at transaction time, (2) there's significant uncertainty, and (3) IFRS 13 requires exit price not workout value. Actual recovery matters for economic capital and provisioning, but not mark-to-market CVA.
questions.why_it_matters: Using 'expected actual recovery' in CVA would violate fair value accounting, make hedging ineffective, and fail audit. However, understanding the difference helps explain why realized CVA losses may be lower than initial charges.
common_traps: Arguing for higher LGD assumptions based on better historical workout experience
Not modeling the time value of money for delayed actual recovery
Confusing CVA (mark-to-market) with credit loss provisioning (expected outcome)
questions.real_world_example: A bank's derivative claim on Lehman was marked down 91% at default (based on CDS auction), but over 5 years recovered 35%. The bank couldn't use 35% prospectively for CVA on similar credits, despite the precedent.

questions.question: A regional Asian bank has 800 corporate counterparties, only 5 of which have liquid CDS quotes. What are the three main approaches to mapping credit curves for the other 795, and what are the trade-offs?
questions.answer_short: The three approaches are: (1) single-name proxies (similar credits or parent companies), (2) generic proxies (indices by rating/sector/region), or (3) bond-derived spreads. Trade-offs involve liquidity vs relevance, hedgeability vs accuracy, and capital relief vs granularity.
questions.answer_long: For illiquid counterparties: (1) Single-name proxies use a traded similar credit or parent company - provides good spread hedge but no default protection and no capital relief under current Basel rules, though relevance is high.
