(2) Generic proxies use CDS indices based on rating/sector/region - highly liquid and hedgeable with partial capital relief, but may not match individual credit risk well. (3) Bond-derived spreads from secondary markets or asset swaps - counterparty-specific but illiquid, requires basis adjustments to CDS-equivalent, and may not be hedgeable. Most banks end up with a hybrid approach using all three methods depending on counterparty characteristics.
questions.why_it_matters: Credit curve mapping is the largest source of subjectivity and model risk in CVA calculations. Poor mapping creates incorrect pricing, ineffective hedging, and audit challenges. For banks with thousands of counterparties, this is a systematic problem requiring robust frameworks.
common_traps: Over-relying on single methodology when hybrid approaches are more appropriate
Not considering hedgeability and capital relief when choosing mapping approach
Creating overly granular classifications without sufficient data points
questions.real_world_example: A European bank mapped 300 mid-sized corporate clients to single-name parent company CDS (better credit spreads). When parents defaulted during COVID stress, the mapping created false correlation and CVA jumped 200%, though actual client stress was lower.

questions.question: What are the main CDS instruments available for credit curve mapping, and how do single-name CDS differ from CDS indices in terms of liquidity and use?
questions.answer_short: Single-name CDS reference individual entities (corporates, banks, sovereigns) and provide precise spread and default protection but are less liquid. CDS indices (iTraxx, CDX) reference baskets of credits, are more liquid, and provide generic spread hedging but not individual default protection.
questions.answer_long: Single-name CDS trade on hundreds of large corporates, financial institutions, and sovereigns, providing exact credit spread curves and both spread and default hedging for the specific entity. However, liquidity has declined post-crisis, with often only 5-year tenor actively trading. CDS indices like iTraxx Europe (125 credits), CDX North America (125 credits), and various sectoral/regional sub-indices are much more liquid and trade at 3Y, 5Y, 7Y, and 10Y tenors. Indices provide generic spread hedging for portfolios and attract better capital relief but don't protect against individual defaults. The choice depends on whether you need precision or liquidity.
questions.why_it_matters: Understanding the CDS market structure guides your entire credit curve mapping and hedging strategy. Using liquid indices for mapping illiquid credits creates basis risk but enables risk management, while single-name focus may be more accurate but unhedgeable.
common_traps: Assuming all credits with single-name CDS have liquid markets (often only 5Y trades)
Using indices for specific credit hedging and being surprised by basis risk
Not checking whether CDS reference the correct seniority (senior vs subordinated)
questions.real_world_example: A desk mapped 200 European BBB industrials to iTraxx Main index for CVA. When an individual counterparty was downgraded to BB, its CVA should have spiked, but the iTraxx Main mapping (which excludes BB) didn't capture this until the mapping was refreshed months later.

questions.question: Why is LGD typically set at standard values (40% recovery, 60% LGD) rather than being implied from market prices, and when might you deviate from this assumption?
questions.answer_short: Recovery swaps rarely trade, so market-implied LGD is not available. Standard 60% LGD aligns with CDS conventions. Deviations are justified for structural seniority (SPV derivatives), credit enhancements, or strong historical workout experience, but require auditor acceptance.
questions.answer_long: Unlike default probabilities, LGD cannot be directly observed from liquid instruments - recovery locks/swaps only trade for distressed credits. Therefore, market convention uses standardized LGD (60% for iTraxx/CDX) which is embedded in CDS pricing. This creates consistency across credit spread curves. You might deviate to lower LGD (higher recovery) when: (1) derivatives are structurally senior (e.g., SPV trades), (2) credit enhancements exist beyond collateral already modeled, or (3) strong historical evidence shows better recovery. However, regulators and auditors scrutinize any deviation from standards heavily, requiring empirical support. The practical impact is limited since LGD largely cancels out between PD calculation and CVA application.
questions.why_it_matters: While LGD assumptions matter less than credit spread due to cancellation effects, unjustified deviations create audit risk and inconsistencies with hedging instruments. Understanding when adjustments are appropriate prevents both under-reserving and over-conservatism.
common_traps: Changing LGD to manipulate CVA without proper justification
Not adjusting LGD consistently between PD calibration and CVA calculation (breaks the math)
Assuming your bank's better workout experience justifies lower LGD without strong evidence
questions.real_world_example: A bank used 30% LGD for derivatives with a well-capitalized sovereign-owned utility (assuming implicit guarantee). Auditors accepted this after seeing legal analysis and strong parent support history, reducing CVA by one-third relative to standard assumptions.

questions.question: When building a generic credit curve for 'A-rated European non-financial corporates,' how do you balance granularity (more specific classification) against data availability?
questions.answer_short: More granular classification (adding sector, sub-region) better distinguishes individual credits but requires more data points. Too granular creates volatile, unreliable curves from sparse data; too broad loses credit differentiation. Typically aim for 10+ liquid credits per bucket.
questions.answer_long: Generic curve construction faces a fundamental trade-off: granular classifications (e.g., 'A-rated German automotive') provide better credit discrimination but may have only 2-3 observable CDS, making curves noisy and unstable. Broad classifications (e.g., 'A-rated European corporate') aggregate 50+ credits for stable curves but don't differentiate between sectors with very different risk profiles (e.g., tech vs utilities). Best practice uses a decision tree: start with rating/region/sector, but collapse categories when fewer than ~10 liquid credits are available. This requires testing curve stability and avoiding idiosyncratic volatility from single credits dominating small buckets. Regulators suggest rating/region/sector but accept broader groupings when data is limited.
questions.why_it_matters: Poor granularity choices create either unstable CVA (too specific) or mis-pricing (too broad). This affects thousands of counterparties and creates unexplainable P&L volatility or persistent mis-hedging.
common_traps: Creating 100+ curve classifications that most have <5 data points each
Using overly broad curves that don't distinguish between very different credit risks
Not monitoring when classifications become too sparse and need consolidation
questions.real_world_example: A bank created separate curves for each European country × rating × sector combination (7 countries × 7 ratings × 3 sectors = 147 curves). Over 60% had fewer than 3 CDS, creating wild daily CVA swings. Consolidating to regional curves (Western/Eastern Europe) by rating/sector reduced buckets to 42 and stabilized P&L.

questions.question: Walk through the decision process for mapping the credit spread of a mid-sized unlisted Asian pharmaceutical company with no CDS, no traded bonds, but a BBB internal rating. What are the key considerations at each step?
questions.answer_short: No direct CDS → check for liquid bonds (unlikely) → check for single-name proxy (parent, sovereign + spread) → map to generic proxy (iTraxx Asia BBB or sector curve). Consider hedgeability, capital relief, and regional specificity at each step.
questions.answer_long: Step 1: Check for liquid single-name CDS - none exists for unlisted mid-cap. Step 2: Check for liquid bonds - Asian corporate bond market is thin, unlikely. Step 3: Evaluate single-name proxies - if there's a listed parent, use parent CDS + spread adjustment for subsidiary risk; or use sovereign CDS (say Singapore) + spread for corporate risk. This gives precise but unhedgeable mapping with no capital relief. Step 4: If no good proxy, map to generic - BBB-rated healthcare/pharmaceutical curve based on iTraxx Asia BBB index plus sector adjustment. Considerations: Asian CDS market is less liquid than Europe/US, so may need to reference regional broader indices; pharmaceutical sector may warrant different spread than industrials; internal BBB rating needs to be validated against external rating equivalence; and hedge strategy determines whether proxy or generic is preferable (generic allows index hedging with capital relief).
questions.why_it_matters: This multi-step decision process is repeated for thousands of counterparties and must be systematic, documented, and defensible to auditors. The choices directly impact CVA levels, P&L volatility, hedge effectiveness, and capital requirements.
common_traps: Stopping at first available data point without considering hedgeability
Using sovereign proxy with insufficient spread adjustment (underpricing risk)
Not documenting the decision process, making audits difficult
Failing to update mappings when market conditions or counterparty fundamentals change
questions.real_world_example: A bank mapped an unlisted BBB Japanese pharma company to the Japanese sovereign curve + 100 bps. When COVID hit, pharmaceutical credits actually tightened while Japanese sovereign spreads widened, creating a wrong-way mapping that overstated CVA deterioration by 150 bps.

questions.question: What are the advantages and disadvantages of using third-party generic credit curves (like Markit sector curves) versus building curves in-house?
questions.answer_short: Third-party curves are independent (audit-friendly), cheaper, and standardized, but inflexible in classification, create uncontrollable volatility, and may not align with your hedging strategy. In-house curves are customizable and hedge-aligned but require resources and audit justification.
questions.answer_long: Third-party providers like Markit offer pre-built generic curves across ratings, sectors, and regions based on liquid CDS. Advantages: (1) independence satisfies auditors, (2) lower development cost, (3) standardized methodology, (4) covers global universe. Disadvantages: (1) rigid classification may not match your counterparty base, (2) methodology changes are beyond your control and can create P&L volatility, (3) may not align with your hedging instruments or strategy, (4) limited transparency into underlying data selection and adjustments, (5) may not provide necessary granularity or may be too granular. In-house curves allow customization to your portfolio, alignment with hedge program, and control over methodology, but require significant quant resources, data licensing, and must be thoroughly documented for audit. Most large banks use hybrid approaches.
questions.why_it_matters: The choice affects CVA P&L volatility, hedge effectiveness, operational costs, and audit burden. Banks must weigh control versus convenience, particularly when dealing with thousands of mapped counterparties.
common_traps: Assuming third-party curves are automatically 'correct' or audit-proof without understanding methodology
Building in-house without sufficient resources, leading to stale or unstable curves
Not testing whether third-party curves align with your hedging instruments
Switching providers and creating discontinuous P&L jumps without proper communication
questions.real_world_example: A bank switched from in-house to Markit sector curves to reduce operational burden. Three months later, Markit changed their averaging methodology, creating a one-time 15% CVA jump across 400 counterparties that was extremely difficult to explain to senior management and had no underlying credit reason.

questions.question: Why might a single-name proxy CDS (e.g., using parent company CDS for subsidiary counterparty) provide an excellent credit spread hedge but receive no capital relief under Basel III, and how does this create a conflict in mapping strategy?
questions.answer_short: Basel III CVA capital rules give relief only for index hedges or direct single-name CDS on the exact counterparty, not proxies. This creates tension: proxy may be best credit hedge (spread correlation), but using generic indices provides capital relief despite worse hedging.
questions.answer_long: Under Basel III standardized CVA rules, capital relief is only granted for: (1) single-name CDS on the exact counterparty being hedged, or (2) index CDS with partial recognition based on overlap. A single-name proxy - even if it's the parent company with 90%+ spread correlation - receives zero capital relief because it doesn't meet the 'same counterparty' requirement (BCBS 2015 proposes to change this, but not yet implemented). This creates a strategic conflict: from a pure risk management view, mapping a subsidiary to its parent's CDS and hedging there may be the best credit hedge available. However, from a capital perspective, mapping to a generic index (even with lower correlation) attracts 50% capital relief, reducing RWA substantially. Banks must balance P&L hedge effectiveness against capital efficiency, often choosing sub-optimal hedges purely for capital treatment.
questions.why_it_matters: This regulatory friction means your mapping strategy cannot optimize purely for credit accuracy or hedge effectiveness - capital considerations dominate. Understanding this drives decisions affecting billions in RWA and millions in capital costs.
common_traps: Optimizing mapping purely for credit accuracy without considering capital implications
Not quantifying the capital cost difference between proxy and index approaches
Assuming regulatory changes (like proxy recognition) are implemented when they're only proposed
Failing to document the trade-off analysis between hedge quality and capital relief
questions.real_world_example: A bank had $50bn exposure to subsidiaries of 20 large multinationals with liquid parent CDS. Using parent proxies would give 80% hedge effectiveness but zero capital relief. Using sectoral indices gave 40% hedge effectiveness but 50% capital relief, saving $200mm in capital charges annually - they chose indices despite worse hedging.

questions.question: When you observe only 1Y, 5Y, and 10Y CDS spreads for a counterparty, what are the main methods to construct a complete default probability curve, and what are the risks of each approach?
questions.answer_short: Main methods: (1) flat interpolation of spreads, (2) linear interpolation of spreads, (3) bootstrapping hazard rates and interpolating those. Risks include creating unrealistic forward default probabilities, missing short-term or long-term risk spikes, and extrapolation errors beyond 10Y.
questions.answer_long: Three approaches: (1) Flat spread interpolation - simple but creates unrealistic 'kinked' default probability curves and can produce negative forward hazard rates between observed points. (2) Linear spread interpolation - smooth spread curve but may still create non-monotonic cumulative default probabilities if curve is inverted. (3) Bootstrap hazard rates - solve for the constant hazard rate in each period that reprices the CDS spreads, then interpolate hazard rates (often using piecewise constant or exponential). This is most theoretically correct and ensures monotonic default probabilities. However, all methods struggle with: extrapolation beyond last liquid tenor (10Y), short-end behavior with only 1Y data point, and sensitivity to outliers in illiquid markets. For CVA with long-dated derivatives, extrapolation assumptions dominate results.
questions.why_it_matters: Poor interpolation creates artificial P&L volatility when market data updates, mispricing of maturity-specific risk, and potential arbitrage opportunities. The method must be consistent with your pricing and hedging instruments.
common_traps: Using simple linear spread interpolation without checking for negative forward hazard rates
Flat-extrapolating beyond 10Y without considering mean reversion or rating drift
Not testing interpolation methods for stability and consistency with hedge instruments
Changing interpolation methods without understanding P&L impact
questions.real_world_example: A desk linearly interpolated between 5Y (300 bps) and 10Y (250 bps) spreads, creating a declining curve. The implied 7Y forward default probability was negative. When auditors caught this, switching to hazard rate bootstrapping changed 7-10Y CVA by 40% for all affected counterparties.

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between a real-world default probability and a risk-neutral default probability?
questions.answer_short: Real-world PD is based on historical default data, while risk-neutral PD is derived from market prices (like CDS spreads) and includes a risk premium that investors demand for taking credit risk.
questions.answer_long: Real-world default probabilities are estimated from historical default data via credit ratings. Risk-neutral default probabilities are derived from market instruments like bonds or CDS. Risk-neutral PDs are typically higher because they include a risk premium - investors are risk-averse and demand compensation beyond the expected default rate. For example, studies show credit spreads are about twice as large as realized default losses, with the difference particularly pronounced for higher quality credits.
questions.why_it_matters: XVA practitioners must use risk-neutral PDs for CVA calculations to align with accounting standards (IFRS 13) and regulatory requirements (Basel III). Using real-world PDs would significantly underestimate CVA and create inconsistency with market pricing and hedging.
common_traps: Thinking real-world and risk-neutral PDs are interchangeable - they differ by 2-17x depending on credit quality
Using real-world PDs because they seem more 'actuarial' - this is inconsistent with fair value accounting
Ignoring that risk-neutral PDs imply the existence of hedges that may not exist for illiquid credits
questions.real_world_example: A AA-rated counterparty has a 1-year real-world PD of 6 bps (from Moody's historical data) but a risk-neutral PD of 78 bps (from CDS market). Using real-world PD would understate CVA by 13x, creating misalignment with hedging costs and regulatory capital requirements.

questions.question: Why have banks increasingly adopted risk-neutral default probabilities for CVA calculations despite challenges with illiquid credits?
questions.answer_short: Regulatory requirements (Basel III requires CDS spreads) and accounting standards (IFRS 13 requires market-observable inputs) mandate risk-neutral PDs. This aligns CVA with market pricing even though many counterparties lack liquid CDS quotes.
questions.answer_long: The move to risk-neutral PDs is driven by: (1) IFRS 13 requiring market-observable inputs for fair value, (2) Basel III CVA capital rules explicitly referencing credit spreads, and (3) the need for consistency with CVA hedging practices. By 2012, 13 of 19 major banks used market data for PD estimation. While this creates challenges for illiquid credits (requiring proxy mapping), regulators and auditors do not accept deviations. The approach interprets CVA as a market price rather than an actuarial reserve, which better reflects the economics of hedging.
questions.why_it_matters: This shift fundamentally changed CVA from a reserve to a fair value adjustment. Practitioners must understand proxy mapping techniques and accept higher CVA volatility for illiquid names, even without perfect hedges. It affects P&L volatility, capital requirements, and pricing decisions.
common_traps: Attempting to use blended real-world/risk-neutral approaches - regulators generally reject this
Assuming historical PDs are acceptable for illiquid credits - auditors increasingly challenge this
Not recognizing that risk-neutral PDs imply hedging obligations even when hedges don't exist
questions.real_world_example: A European bank with 2,000 counterparties has liquid CDS for only 200. For the remaining 1,800, they must map to index proxies or sector curves. The ECB's CVA challenger model explicitly requires CDS-based benchmarks, forcing banks to use proxies like 'Single-A European Corporate' curves even for unique SME clients.

questions.question: Given a credit spread of 400 bps and an LGD of 60%, what is the approximate annual default probability using the standard approximation formula?
questions.answer_short: Using PD ≈ s/(1-LGD) = 0.04/(1-0.60) = 0.04/0.40 = 10%, the annual default probability is approximately 10% (unconditional).
questions.answer_long: The standard approximation is PD(t-1,t) ≈ st × Δt / (1-LGD), where st is the credit spread, Δt is the time period, and LGD is loss given default. For a 400 bps spread with 60% LGD: PD = 0.04/(1-0.60) = 0.10 or 10% per year. This is unconditional (not conditional on survival to t-1). This approximation works reasonably well for flat or mildly sloped credit curves but becomes less accurate for steep curves because it doesn't account for the full curve shape prior to time t.
questions.why_it_matters: This calculation is the foundation for CVA pricing and risk management. Practitioners use this daily to convert CDS spreads into default probabilities for exposure calculations. Understanding its limitations (curve shape sensitivity, LGD assumptions) prevents material pricing errors.
common_traps: Confusing conditional and unconditional PDs - this formula gives unconditional probability
Using this approximation on steeply sloped curves without correction - can be significantly wrong
Forgetting to adjust LGD for different seniorities (senior vs subordinated debt)
questions.real_world_example: A trader prices a 5Y CVA on a BBB corporate with 350 bps CDS spread. Using 60% LGD gives 8.75% annual PD. If the curve is actually inverted (common for stressed credits), the approximation overstates near-term default risk. The trader should bootstrap the full curve to avoid mispricing, especially for wrong-way risk situations.

questions.question: Why does the shape of a credit curve (flat, upward-sloping, inverted) matter significantly even when all curves have the same 5-year credit spread?
questions.answer_short: Curve shape determines when defaults are more likely - upward curves imply lower near-term risk, inverted curves imply higher near-term risk. This dramatically affects annual default probabilities and CVA for exposures with different maturity profiles.
questions.answer_long: Even with identical 5Y spreads of 300 bps, three curve shapes produce very different default probability distributions. An upward-sloping curve gives lower 1Y PD (maybe 2%) but higher 10Y PD (8%), while an inverted curve reverses this (8% at 1Y, declining later). For CVA calculation, this matters because: (1) near-term exposure may be higher for some trades (e.g., after cashflow payments), (2) discount factors weight near-term defaults more, and (3) wrong-way risk may concentrate in specific tenors. The same 5Y cumulative PD of 22% hides these critical differences.
questions.why_it_matters: CVA calculations are highly sensitive to the timing of expected defaults. A practitioner who incorrectly assumes a flat curve when the true curve is inverted will materially misprice near-term risk. This is especially critical for portfolios with strong wrong-way risk or collateral that expires.
common_traps: Using only 5Y CDS spreads and assuming flat curves - misses crucial term structure effects
Interpolating credit curves linearly between sparse points - can create unrealistic shapes
Extrapolating beyond liquid tenors without considering credit fundamentals
questions.real_world_example: A bank calculates CVA on a 10Y interest rate swap with quarterly cashflows. Using an upward-sloping curve (common for stable credits) gives lower CVA than assuming flat, because near-term exposures from cashflows are weighted by lower PDs. If the counterparty deteriorates and the curve inverts, CVA can jump 50%+ even with the same 5Y spread, purely from term structure change.

questions.subtopic: Loss Given Default and Recovery Rates
questions.question: What is the difference between 'settled recovery' and 'actual recovery' for OTC derivatives, and why does this distinction matter?
questions.answer_short: Settled recovery is the value achievable shortly after default (e.g., via CDS auction, typically days/weeks). Actual recovery is what's received from the bankruptcy process for derivatives (often months/years later) and may differ materially due to netting, set-off, and bankruptcy delays.
questions.answer_long: Settled recovery is realized quickly post-default by selling claims or participating in CDS auctions (e.g., Lehman's 9% bond recovery). Actual recovery on derivatives takes much longer because: (1) bilateral OTC trades are bespoke and can't be quickly traded, (2) netting across many trades creates a single complex claim, and (3) bankruptcy processes take years to resolve. In Lehman's case, actual derivative recoveries were 30-40%, much higher than the 9% settled recovery. This distinction matters for timing cash flows, funding costs, and whether to sell claims early or wait for final bankruptcy resolution.
questions.why_it_matters: CVA practitioners must decide whether to value CVA using settled (market-consistent, hedgeable) or actual recovery (potentially higher but uncertain and delayed). This affects pricing, hedging strategy, and capital allocation. Banks may improve recoveries through set-off rights not priced in CVA but available in workout.
common_traps: Assuming CDS auction recoveries apply directly to derivatives - derivatives may recover more due to structural benefits
Ignoring the time value of money between settled and actual recovery - years of delay matter
Not accounting for netting and collateral benefits that improve derivative recovery over bonds
questions.real_world_example: After Lehman defaulted, bonds traded at 8-9 cents on the dollar. Banks with derivative claims initially valued at this recovery but later received 30-40 cents through bankruptcy proceedings due to favorable netting and collateral positions. A bank that sold its Lehman claim at 10 cents missed a 3-4x improvement, while one that held it faced years of funding costs and uncertainty.

questions.subtopic: CDS Market for Credit Curve Mapping
questions.question: What are the three main types of CDS instruments used for credit curve mapping, and when is each appropriate?
questions.answer_short: Single-name CDS (for the exact counterparty or close proxy), single-name proxy CDS (for similar entities like parent companies), and CDS indices (for generic mapping by rating/sector/region when no single-name exists).
questions.answer_long: Credit curve mapping uses three instrument types hierarchically: (1) Single-name CDS on the actual counterparty provides the best match and allows full hedging and capital relief, but is only available for ~hundreds of liquid names globally. (2) Single-name proxy CDS uses a similar entity (parent, sovereign, peer) and provides spread hedging but not default hedging, with no capital relief under current rules. (3) CDS indices (iTraxx, CDX) are most liquid and allow spread hedging with partial capital relief, used for generic mapping when no suitable single-name exists. Most counterparties (especially SMEs, smaller corporates) require index-based generic mapping.
questions.why_it_matters: Choosing the right instrument type involves trade-offs between accuracy, liquidity, hedging effectiveness, and capital relief. Practitioners must balance getting the 'right' credit spread against the ability to manage CVA risk and achieve regulatory capital benefits. Poor choices lead to unhedgeable P&L volatility.
common_traps: Prioritizing direct observability over hedgeability - an illiquid bond price may be less useful than a liquid index
Not considering capital relief implications - proxy single-names currently give no Basel III relief
Assuming all single-name CDS are liquid - many trade very infrequently and have wide bid-offers
questions.real_world_example: A bank has exposure to a mid-sized French utility company. Options: (1) use the company's own 5Y CDS (trades once a month, wide spread), (2) use EDF (state-owned utility) as proxy (liquid but imperfect match), or (3) use iTraxx Europe Main (very liquid, allows hedging/capital relief but generic). They choose (3) with a +50bp adjustment for idiosyncratic risk, accepting basis risk for liquidity.

questions.question: A bank is calculating CVA for derivatives with a securitization SPV where derivatives rank senior to all other debt. Should they use the standard 60% LGD assumption, and if not, how should they adjust it?
questions.answer_short: No - they should use a lower LGD (higher recovery) because structural seniority means derivatives will recover more in default. They might use 30-40% LGD based on securitization waterfalls and structural analysis.
questions.answer_long: Standard CDS contracts assume 60% LGD (40% recovery) for senior unsecured debt. But derivatives with SPVs often have structural seniority - they're paid before other creditors in the waterfall. This dramatically improves recovery, so using 60% LGD would overstate CVA. The bank should: (1) analyze the SPV waterfall structure, (2) model scenarios for underlying collateral performance, (3) estimate derivative recovery could be 60-70% (30-40% LGD) or even higher. However, auditors require strong documentation, and conservative banks may use intermediate values like 50% LGD unless they have clear evidence of structural benefits.
questions.why_it_matters: LGD directly scales CVA - using 60% instead of 40% LGD increases CVA by 50%. For portfolios with structural seniority (common in structured products, securitizations, some corporate structures), using standard assumptions significantly overstates counterparty risk and makes pricing uncompetitive.
common_traps: Using standard 60% LGD for all derivatives regardless of seniority - misses structural benefits
Assuming favorable LGD without documentation - auditors will challenge this
Not considering that LGD may vary by jurisdiction and bankruptcy regime
questions.real_world_example: A dealer calculates CVA for derivatives with a CLO SPV. The derivatives are 'super-senior' in the waterfall, only subordinate to senior AAA notes with massive overcollateralization. Historical CLO data shows senior tranche recoveries near 90%. Using 60% LGD would give CVA of 200 bps; using 20% LGD (justified by structure) gives 67 bps, completely changing trade economics.

questions.question: When should a practitioner choose a liquid CDS index over a less liquid single-name proxy for credit curve mapping?
questions.answer_short: Choose the index when: liquidity/hedgeability is critical, you need capital relief, the proxy fit is poor (requiring large spread adjustments), or idiosyncratic proxy volatility would distort CVA. Choose the proxy when credit fundamentals match closely and spread hedge without default hedge is acceptable.
questions.answer_long: The choice involves multiple trade-offs: (1) Liquidity - indices are much more liquid and tradeable, critical for active CVA desks. (2) Capital relief - indices provide partial Basel III relief, proxy single-names currently provide none (though this may change). (3) Credit fit - if a proxy requires >100bp adjustment, it's probably too different and an index is better. (4) Volatility - proxy idiosyncratic moves (earnings, M&A rumors) create undesired CVA volatility. (5) Default correlation - if the counterparty would likely default with the proxy, it's a better fit. In practice, most banks use a decision tree: direct CDS first, then evaluate proxy quality vs index liquidity, typically preferring indices for >70% of names.
questions.why_it_matters: This decision affects CVA P&L volatility, hedging costs, and capital requirements. A bad choice means either: (1) unhedgeable volatility from illiquid instruments, (2) large basis risk from poor proxies, or (3) over-generic mapping that doesn't reflect counterparty-specific risk. Getting this right is fundamental to CVA desk profitability.
common_traps: Always preferring 'more specific' proxies even when they're illiquid and create problems
Not considering that proxy idiosyncratic risk increases CVA volatility incorrectly
Ignoring capital relief implications - can be material to overall profitability
questions.real_world_example: A bank has exposure to Toyota Manufacturing UK. Proxies: (1) Toyota Motor Corp CDS (trades daily, parent company, but Japanese HQ may have different credit dynamics), (2) iTraxx Europe Main +50bp (very liquid, generic industrials). They choose (2) because Toyota single-name trades in CDX (USD-denominated, illiquid in EUR), and parent-subsidiary basis is uncertain. The index gives better hedging and capital treatment despite being less specific.

questions.question: What is the fundamental trade-off between granularity and data availability when constructing generic credit curves, and how should practitioners resolve it?
questions.answer_short: More granular classifications (e.g., 'A-rated US utilities') better distinguish counterparties but have fewer data points per curve, risking idiosyncratic volatility. Broader classifications (e.g., 'A-rated corporates') smooth volatility but lose important distinctions. Optimize by using the most granular categorization that still has sufficient liquid data points (typically 5-10+) per tenor.
questions.answer_long: Generic curve construction requires classifying counterparties by rating, region, and sector. Fine granularity ('AA North American Technology') creates many curves but may have only 1-2 CDS per curve, making the curve unstable and reflecting idiosyncratic risk incorrectly. Coarse granularity ('A Global Corporate') has many data points but treats very different credits identically (oil companies vs retailers). Best practice: (1) start with regulatory minimum (rating/region/sector), (2) combine categories where data is sparse (e.g., merge AA/AAA), (3) ensure each curve has 5-10+ reference entities for stability, (4) use index levels as floor/ceiling checks. Typical result: ~50-70 distinct curves rather than theoretical 147 (7 ratings × 7 regions × 3 sectors).
questions.why_it_matters: Poor granularity choices create either: (1) excessive CVA volatility from thin data, or (2) material mispricing by treating different credits the same. This directly affects pricing competitiveness and P&L stability. A systematic approach prevents both gaming (using the most favorable curve) and excessive conservatism.
common_traps: Creating too many curves with insufficient data - generates noise rather than signal
Treating all corporates identically regardless of sector - misses systematic sector risk differences
Not revisiting curve structure as CDS market liquidity evolves
questions.real_world_example: A European bank initially created 147 curves per the regulatory framework. They found 89 curves had <3 reference CDS, creating wild volatility. They collapsed to 58 curves by: (1) combining AA/AAA (few entities), (2) merging Eastern Europe + Middle East (sparse data), (3) combining telecoms + technology (similar credit profiles). This reduced unexplained CVA P&L volatility by 40% while maintaining meaningful credit differentiation.

questions.question: When should a CVA desk build proprietary generic credit curves versus using third-party curves like Markit sector curves?
questions.answer_short: Build proprietary curves when: you need custom classifications matching your portfolio, you want control over MTM volatility, you have sufficient expertise/resources, or third-party methodologies don't align with hedging. Use third-party when: you need independence for auditors, lack resources, or have non-material CVA requiring simple solutions.
questions.answer_long: Proprietary curves offer: (1) custom granularity matching actual exposures, (2) control over interpolation/extrapolation and smoothing, (3) alignment with actual hedge portfolio (indices used), (4) ability to incorporate internal credit views, (5) transparency into methodology. Third-party curves offer: (1) independence valued by auditors, (2) lower resource requirements, (3) standard methodology, (4) but are rigid, create uncontrollable volatility, and may not match hedge instruments. Large banks with material CVA (>$500M) typically build proprietary curves to control volatility and align with hedging, while smaller banks or those with immaterial CVA prefer third-party solutions. Hybrid approaches use third-party as validation/floor.
questions.why_it_matters: This choice affects CVA P&L volatility, operational costs, audit complexity, and hedging effectiveness. A large CVA desk losing control over curve methodology can experience unexplained P&L swings from third-party provider changes. Conversely, a small desk building curves without expertise creates operational risk and audit challenges.
common_traps: Small desks building complex proprietary systems without resources to maintain them
Large desks using third-party curves that don't match their hedge portfolio instruments
Not having governance over third-party methodology changes that impact P&L
Building proprietary curves without robust control framework and audit trail
questions.real_world_example: A mid-sized bank with $200M CVA used Markit sector curves initially (simple, auditor-friendly). After experiencing 15% unexplained CVA volatility from Markit methodology changes (sector reclassifications), they built proprietary curves aligned to their actual hedges (iTraxx Main/Xover/FinSen). This reduced unexplained volatility to <5% but required hiring two quants and building robust controls. A cost-benefit analysis showed the investment paid back in 18 months through tighter hedging and lower capital volatility.

questions.question: Given CDS quotes of 250 bps (3Y), 300 bps (5Y), and 350 bps (7Y) with 60% LGD, explain the bootstrapping process to derive individual period default probabilities. Why can't you just use the simple formula for each tenor?
questions.answer_short: Bootstrapping sequentially derives default probabilities ensuring consistency across tenors. Simple formulas don't account for survival probability from earlier periods. Bootstrap: derive 0-3Y PD from 3Y spread, then derive 3-5Y PD from 5Y spread conditional on surviving to 3Y, etc.
questions.answer_long: The simple formula PD ≈ s/(1-LGD) gives unconditional PDs but doesn't ensure consistency - the 5Y spread must reflect both 0-3Y and 3-5Y defaults. Bootstrapping works iteratively: (1) From 3Y spread (250 bps), derive survival probability S(3Y) = exp(-∫₀³ h(t)dt) where h is hazard rate, typically assuming h is constant over 0-3Y. (2) The 5Y spread (300 bps) implies survival S(5Y) that must satisfy: 300 bps = [expected loss 0-5Y]/[expected exposure 0-5Y]. Given S(3Y) from step 1, solve for S(5Y), then derive the 3-5Y period hazard rate. (3) Repeat for 7Y. This ensures the credit curve is arbitrage-free and properly reflects the term structure. The simple formula ignores that longer spreads include shorter-period defaults already priced in.
questions.why_it_matters: Proper bootstrapping is essential for accurate CVA calculation, especially for portfolios with maturity-dependent exposures. Using simple formulas for each tenor independently creates arbitrage opportunities and misprices time-dependent risk. This is particularly critical for callable structures or trades with backend maturity risk.
common_traps: Applying the simple formula independently at each tenor - creates inconsistent probabilities
Not handling the conditional vs unconditional probability correctly
Assuming constant hazard rates between observed tenors without interpolation scheme
Ignoring that market quotes are mid-market and may not be simultaneously tradeable
questions.real_world_example: A CVA quant calculates risk on a 7Y swap with large notional exchange at maturity. Using simple formulas: 3Y PD=6.25%, 5Y PD=7.5%, 7Y PD=8.75%. But this implies 3-5Y PD of only 1.25% and 5-7Y PD of 1.25%, much lower than 0-3Y's 6.25% - inconsistent with an upward-sloping curve. Proper bootstrapping gives: 0-3Y hazard=4.5%, 3-5Y hazard=5.5%, 5-7Y hazard=6.2%, consistent with rising credit risk. This changes CVA by 12% because backend exposure is now properly weighted.

questions.question: A bank has exposure to a small unrated regional airline in Southeast Asia with no CDS, illiquid bonds, and the sovereign CDS is 200 bps but the airline is clearly riskier. Walk through the mapping challenges and suggest a pragmatic solution with its limitations.
questions.answer_short: Challenges: no direct data, sovereign proxy too tight, sector CDS (if any) are US/EU based with different dynamics. Solution: use Asian High Yield index as base, add spread adjustment (+300-500 bps) based on internal rating mapped to external equivalents, cross-check with any available bond data. Limitations: high basis risk, idiosyncratic risk not captured, may not correlate with available hedges.
questions.answer_long: This represents a common real-world challenge. Process: (1) Internal rating: credit analysts assign internal rating (e.g., 'B+') based on financials. (2) Base curve selection: iTraxx Asia HY (if airline is HY-rated) or use sovereign +spread if investment grade. Sovereign at 200 bps is too low given airline sector risk (cyclical, capital intensive). (3) Spread adjustment: benchmark regional airline CDS if available (e.g., Air Asia, Philippine Airlines) even if different country - apply differential. Alternatively, use US airline CDS (Delta, American) and adjust for regional/sovereign basis. Typical adjustment: +300-500 bps over sovereign. (4) Validation: compare with any secondary market bond prices (adjusted for bond-CDS basis). (5) Documentation: clearly document methodology, comparables, and rationale. Limitations: final curve is highly judgmental, basis risk to any hedges, won't respond to company-specific credit events quickly, probably too smooth (doesn't capture idiosyncratic volatility).
questions.why_it_matters: Illiquid credit mapping is unavoidable for banks with diverse counterparty bases, especially in emerging markets. Poor methodology creates either: (1) excessive conservatism making you uncompetitive, or (2) underpricing creating unexpected losses. Understanding the judgment calls and documenting them defensibly is essential for surviving audits and regulatory reviews.
common_traps: Just using sovereign +fixed spread without sector/credit analysis - too simplistic
Using US/European sector comparables without adjusting for regional differences
Not documenting the methodology clearly - auditors will reject undocumented judgment
Assuming the mapped curve will correlate with available hedges - it probably won't
questions.real_world_example: A Singapore bank priced derivatives with Garuda Indonesia (Indonesian flag carrier). No Garuda CDS exists. Indonesia sovereign trades at 150 bps. They mapped using: (1) iTraxx Asia ex-Japan (investment grade) at 110 bps as regional base, (2) added airline sector premium of +150 bps based on Thai Airways and Korean Air CDS, (3) added Indonesia sovereign basis of +40 bps over Asia index, (4) added company-specific adjustment of +50 bps based on leverage vs peers. Final curve: ~350 bps vs 150 bps sovereign. This avoided massive underpricing but required quarterly review and clear documentation for audit.
